title: Kratom wars come to K Street
body_text:
CRAZY OVER KRATOM: The Trump administration has moved to clamp down on 7-hydroxymitragynine , a derivative of the increasingly popular herbal supplement kratom, and industry groups representing kratom producers are building out their lobbying operation in response.

— One of the industry’s main lobbying groups, the American Kratom Association , retained Michael Best Strategies at the beginning of August, according to a new disclosure. Michael Best, which is led by former White House chief of staff Reince Priebus , briefly lobbied for the association in 2023.

— Priebus is not a registered lobbyist, but two of his former West Wing colleagues, Alexander Angelson and Ninio Fetalvo , are registered to work on the account, along with Democratic lobbyist Brett Ewer .

— Also last month, another industry group, the Global Kratom Coalition , tapped BGR Group health and life sciences practice head Remy Brim , as well as former Hill staffers John Stone and Brent Del Monte , to “provide strategic counsel and advocate on issues related to FDA enforcement and DEA scheduling,” per a disclosure.

— The hires came days after top Trump administration health officials announced at a news conference that they were taking the first steps toward scheduling 7-hydroxymitragynine, also known as 7-OH, as a controlled substance subject to restrictions on production, distribution and possession.

— Kratom, which is made from leaves of a plant native to Southeast Asia, has been around for thousands of years. Now it’s available in pill, powder and gummy form, and in teas and drinks as both an energy booster and pain reliever.

— Proponents say it could be an answer to the opioid addiction crisis. Though Trump officials did not target the natural leaf variant, public health officials argue that kratom has its own potential for abuse, and the DEA lists the supplement as a “drug and chemical of concern.” More concerning to those officials are kratom products made with more potent synthetic derivatives like 7-OH have flooded gas stations and smoke shops, earning them the moniker “gas station heroin.”

— That’s fueled a push from producers of natural leaf kratom for federal regulators to bless their products while getting synthetic products off shelves. 7-OH manufacturers, however, deny their products are any less safe and argue that leaf kratom companies are just threatened because they are losing market share.

— The administration’s 7-OH announcement had been a major priority for the natural kratom producers. Mac Haddow , a senior public policy fellow with the American Kratom Association, told PI that the group was “pleasantly surprised” by the scheduling announcement and the fanfare that it received. A joint press conference featured HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. , Deputy Secretary Jim O’Neill and FDA Commissioner Marty Makary .

— Holistic Alternative Recovery Trust , which represents 7-OH manufacturers, retained its first federal lobbyists at the beginning of 2025, disclosures show. But kratom producers on the other side of the fight continue to have the upper hand in terms of lobbying muscle. AKA spent $550,000 lobbying Washington last year, and the group is on pace to surpass that in 2025. They also have Upstream Consulting , First Amendment Partners , David Carlucci Consulting , Kountoupes Denham Carr & Reid and Mickenberg on retainer.

— In addition to BGR, GKC has Troutman Pepper Strategies on retainer. The coalition is also funding a new advocacy group, Stop Gas Station Heroin , that retained Checkmate Government Relations back in July.

— There’s been a wave of kratom legislation moving through state legislatures , including some bills that would implement a blanket ban on all kratom products, which groups like AKA and GKC oppose. Other bills would place age restrictions on sales, ban marketing geared toward kids and teens and institute standards for manufacturing practices and labeling — regulations with broad support across the competing kratom factions.

— AKA is also working with lawmakers in both the House and Senate to craft an updated version of a 2023 bill that would’ve asked FDA to study kratom and blocked the agency from regulating the substance in a manner more restrictive than existing regulations for food and dietary supplements.

TRAVEL INDUSTRY’S SHUTDOWN PLEA: The U.S. Travel Association warned congressional leadership today that letting federal funding lapse next week would cost the U.S. travel economy more than $1 billion per week.

— A shutdown would be “a wholly preventable blow” that would affect “millions of travelers and businesses while placing unnecessary strain on an already overextended federal travel workforce,” U.S. Travel President and CEO Geoff Freeman argued in a letter to the Hill today.

— With less than a week until funding runs out, congressional leaders remain at an impasse , even after POLITICO ’s Sophia Cai reported last night that the White House is planning mass federal layoffs in the event of a shutdown.

— A U.S. Travel spokesperson did not immediately respond to an inquiry about how such layoffs would change the trade group’s calculations. But as it stands, a shutdown would exacerbate existing staffing shortages at TSA, which would immediately be felt by air travelers. It would also disrupt the onboarding of new, sorely needed air traffic controllers as well as the air traffic control modernization efforts that Republicans just approved $12.5 billion for, according to Freeman.

COMING ATTRACTIONS: “A senior Justice Department official has instructed more than a half dozen U.S. attorneys’ offices to draft plans to investigate a group funded by George Soros , the billionaire Democratic donor who President Trump has demanded be thrown in jail,” The New York Times’ Devlin Barrett reports.

— “The official’s directive, a copy of which was viewed by The New York Times, goes as far as to list possible charges prosecutors could file, ranging from arson to material support of terrorism. The memo suggests department leaders are following orders from the president that specific people or groups be subject to criminal investigation — a major break from decades of past practice meant to insulate the Justice Department from political interference.”

ANOTHER FEC COMMISSIONER DOWN: “The vice chair of the Federal Election Commission, the federal agency charged with enforcing campaign finance laws, will resign from his post after five years with the agency,” POLITICO ’s Faith Wardwell reports, “leaving just two commissioners behind as the agency nears five months without quorum,”

— GOP Commissioner Trey Trainor told the Washington Examiner that he plans to step down next month as he “seriously” weighs a bid for the House seat that will open up with the retirement of Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas).

— President Donald Trump “tapped Trainor — a Republican lawyer who represented Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign — for the FEC in 2017, and his nomination stalled in the Senate until 2020. … Trainor’s confirmation allowed the FEC to reach quorum in 2020 — the last time the agency went undermanned.”

— The president ousted Democratic Commissioner Ellen Weintraub in February, in a move she maintained was illegal, leaving Trainor as “the last Republican commissioner serving; Sean Cooksey left the commission and took a role in the vice president’s office in January, while Allen Dickerson stepped down from his seat in April, ending the quorum on the commission.”

— “Trainor’s retirement now leaves four of the FEC’s six seats vacant, with just two Democrats remaining. Neither party by law can have more than three commissioners presiding over the agency, and the agency needs four commissioners to conduct business.”

MORE ANNALS OF CAMPAIGN FINANCE: “Two Republican super PACs paid nearly $1 million this month to quietly settle an inquiry into whether they illicitly coordinated with the campaign of Lee Zeldin , a member of President Trump’s Cabinet, during his 2022 run for governor of New York,” per the Times’ Nicholas Fandos and Shane Goldmacher .

— “The state’s top elections watchdog spent years investigating the matter, using subpoenas to try to show that there was illegal overlap between the Zeldin campaign and two groups that spent $20 million supporting it, Save Our State Inc. and Safe Together New York .”

— “An agreement to settle the case, reached in recent days, ultimately does not include an admission of wrongdoing by the super PACs, a copy of the document obtained through a Freedom of Information request shows. Mr. Zeldin, who is now the head of the Environmental Protection Agency, was not a party to the agreement.”

— “But the $900,000 fine is the largest ever paid in a super PAC coordination case in New York, where the free-spending groups seeking to sway elections have grown in size and number over the last decade.”

PBMS’ PITCH: “Pharmacy middlemen are working on a proposal to voluntarily change some of their business practices in an effort to avoid new regulation from the Trump administration,” according to Bloomberg ’s John Tozzi and Rachel Cohrs Zhang .

— The Pharmaceutical Care Management Association , which represents the industry in Washington, “has drafted proposals to bring to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, according to a document viewed by Bloomberg News.”

— “Among the proposals under discussion are ensuring patients don’t pay more than a pharmacy would charge to someone without insurance, increasing the use of lower-cost versions of expensive biologic drugs and boosting payments to rural and independent pharmacies.”

— “Part of the industry’s pitch to the agency is that a splashy announcement of the initiative will generate favorable news coverage, according to the document viewed by Bloomberg” — a strategy similar to “one deployed by health insurers earlier this year, when they pledged to cut red tape for approvals.”

— The hires came days after top Trump administration health officials announced at a news conference that they were taking the first steps toward scheduling 7-hydroxymitragynine, also known as 7-OH, as a controlled substance subject to restrictions on production, distribution and possession.

— Kratom, which is made from leaves of a plant native to Southeast Asia, has been around for thousands of years. Now it’s available in pill, powder and gummy form, and in teas and drinks as both an energy booster and pain reliever.

— Proponents say it could be an answer to the opioid addiction crisis. Though Trump officials did not target the natural leaf variant, public health officials argue that kratom has its own potential for abuse, and the DEA lists the supplement as a “drug and chemical of concern.” More concerning to those officials are kratom products made with more potent synthetic derivatives like 7-OH have flooded gas stations and smoke shops, earning them the moniker “gas station heroin.”

— That’s fueled a push from producers of natural leaf kratom for federal regulators to bless their products while getting synthetic products off shelves. 7-OH manufacturers, however, deny their products are any less safe and argue that leaf kratom companies are just threatened because they are losing market share.

— The administration’s 7-OH announcement had been a major priority for the natural kratom producers. Mac Haddow, a senior public policy fellow with the American Kratom Association, told PI that the group was “pleasantly surprised” by the scheduling announcement and the fanfare that it received. A joint press conference featured HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., Deputy Secretary Jim O’Neill and FDA Commissioner Marty Makary.

— Holistic Alternative Recovery Trust, which represents 7-OH manufacturers, retained its first federal lobbyists at the beginning of 2025, disclosures show. But kratom producers on the other side of the fight continue to have the upper hand in terms of lobbying muscle. AKA spent $550,000 lobbying Washington last year, and the group is on pace to surpass that in 2025. They also have Upstream Consulting, First Amendment Partners, David Carlucci Consulting, Kountoupes Denham Carr & Reid and Mickenberg on retainer.

— In addition to BGR, GKC has Troutman Pepper Strategies on retainer. The coalition is also funding a new advocacy group, Stop Gas Station Heroin, that retained Checkmate Government Relations back in July.

— There’s been a wave of kratom legislation moving through state legislatures, including some bills that would implement a blanket ban on all kratom products, which groups like AKA and GKC oppose. Other bills would place age restrictions on sales, ban marketing geared toward kids and teens and institute standards for manufacturing practices and labeling — regulations with broad support across the competing kratom factions.

— AKA is also working with lawmakers in both the House and Senate to craft an updated version of a 2023 bill that would’ve asked FDA to study kratom and blocked the agency from regulating the substance in a manner more restrictive than existing regulations for food and dietary supplements.

BGR SCOOPS UP SMITH TAX AIDE: Kathryn Reed , a top GOP tax aide who helped craft congressional Republicans’ sweeping tax cuts earlier this year, has decamped from the Hill after nearly a decade to join BGR Group as a vice president in the tax, commerce and financial services practices.

— Reed has spent the past four years as a tax adviser to Rep. Jason Smith (R-Mo.), who became chair of the Ways and Means Committee in 2023. Before that, she worked for former Rep. Kevin Brady (R-Texas), Smith’s predecessor on the powerful tax writing panel.

— In a statement provided by the firm, Smith called Reed “integral” to the drafting of the GOP megabill’s tax provisions, which permanently extended a slew of tax cuts prized by the business community while overhauling key safety net programs and winding down clean energy tax incentives.

— Reed worked particularly closely on the bill’s new initiative to set up investment accounts for children as well as its expansion of the Opportunity Zones program and Child Tax Credit, she said in an interview.

— The child investment plan has set off a scramble by lobbyists seeking to shape the new program. Reed noted that other new tax programs in the law, such as no tax on tips, will also require new guidance from regulators — in contrast to tax breaks with existing regulatory guidance that were extended by the law.

— Beyond that, Reed told PI that her position provided insight into the issues and priorities that animate a broad swath of members on the Hill. Having that kind of “insider scoop on where Congress is on policy,” especially when it comes to tax, will be “super helpful and beneficial to BGR,” she predicted.

— Reed is just the latest staffer who worked on the reconciliation bill to head downtown since it became law in July. Brett Horton , who served for the past decade as chief of staff to House Majority Leader Steve Scalise , will start next month as the top lobbyist at the American Hotel & Lodging Association . Andrew Siracuse , a longtime aide and tax adviser for Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas), joined Holland & Knight in August.

— Molly Fromm , who served as Ways and Means’ general counsel and parliamentarian under both Smith and Brady, joined the health policy-heavy firm Nickles Group in May, around the same time the GOP megabill cleared the House.

— Vivek Chandrasekhar , who provided guidance on the GOP’s One Big Beautiful Bill and Democrats’ Inflation Reduction Act while working in Treasury’s Office of Tax Policy, joined the law and lobbying firm Perkins Coie in September as a partner in the tax and environment, energy and resources practices.

— Autor went on to serve as a consultant in the private sector, holding public policy roles with drugmakers like AstraZeneca and Mylan .

— She joined the board of Hims & Hers last year, and takes over as head of its global influence operation as the company comes under scrutiny for its advertising practices and readjusts is business model regarding popular weight-loss drugs. Regulators are moving to crack down on sales of cheaper, compounded versions of name brand drugs.

— Hims & Hers has ramped up its influence machine over the last two years, going from $310,000 in federal lobbying expenditures in 2024 to $860,000 through the first three quarters of 2025. The company also launched a PAC last summer, and donated $1 million to President Donald Trump ’s inauguration earlier this year.

GET THE PICTURE?: “For select House of Representatives committee chairs, a decidedly artistic perk for their legislative service is a custom-made portrait, created by an artist of their choosing in coordination with the U.S. Capitol Historical Society . These paintings adorn the walls of congressional hearing rooms and are destined to hang for perpetuity inside the Capitol” — and they’re “also a magnet for lobbyists and special interest money ,” NOTUS ’ Dave Levinthal writes.

— “This decade, corporations, unions, trade associations and individual lobbyists with significant business before Congress have poured more than $600,000 into portrait funds for several current and former federal lawmakers.” The congressional portrait funds are governed by few rules, and the only entities required to disclose their donations are registered lobbyists or the entities that employ them.

— Brady, the former Ways and Means chair, “is among the most popular beneficiaries of lobbyist money directed toward his portrait, painted by the artist Stephen Craighead and unveiled in 2022.” Some $132,500 from companies, trade groups, PACs and individual lobbyists were donated ahead of its unveiling.

— The portrait fund for his Democratic successor, Massachusetts Rep. Richie Neal , has received $128,000 in contributions since 2023 from organizations including MetLife , MGM Resorts , HCA Healthcare , Altria and FedEx — though a spokesperson told NOTUS that Neal “has no idea who donated” to his portrait fund.

INSURANCE POLICY: “Insurers and drug companies facing dire threats to their bottom lines this year from President Donald Trump and Republicans in Congress had to make a choice: Stand and fight, or go to ground and cut some deals. Insurers fought in a bid to kill the threat; drugmakers cut deals to mitigate the damage. The early results are revealing,” per POLITICO ’s Amanda Chu .

— “Trump this month called out the ‘money sucking Insurance Companies’ on Truth Social and pledged to redirect their Obamacare funding to patients. Two days before, he stood with drug companies that’d agreed to cut prices, called the CEOs ‘great talented people’ and friends and said he didn’t begrudge them their profits: ‘They’re entitled to the money because the companies are doing very well.’”

— “Insurers’ prospects of getting what they want – an extension of expiring Obamacare subsidies Democrats supersized during the pandemic – look bleak. Meanwhile, the 100 percent tariffs Trump threatened pharma with are still on hold, pending more deals.”

— “Trump’s diverging take on two of Washington’s most powerful industry rivals was a case study for lobbyists trying to figure out how to handle the mercurial president and his populist approach to politics: Currying favor helps, fighting is risky business.”

HERITAGE TURMOIL AIN’T OVER: Heritage Foundation President Kevin Roberts ’ video defending Tucker Carlson for his interview with Holocaust denier Nick Fuentes has continued to roil the venerated think tank. Longtime board member Robert P. George is just the latest to announce his resignation over the incident.

— In a Facebook post today, George “said he can no longer remain part of the foundation without a ‘full retraction’ of the video released last month ” by Roberts, POLITICO ’s Cheyanne M. Daniels reports.

— “Although Kevin publicly apologized for some of what he said in the video, he could not offer a full retraction of its content. So, we reached an impasse,” George wrote, one day after Trump defended Carlson to reporters.

— Roberts tried to contain the backlash over his video by downplaying his knowledge of Fuentes and pinning blame on his chief of staff, who has since resigned. At least five members of the think tank’s antisemitism task force have quit in protest of the post , CBS News reported, along with prominent conservative economist Stephen Moore .

CHAMBER OF PROGRESS EYES STATEHOUSES: Liberal-leaning tech lobbying group Chamber of Progress is launching a new influence initiative to shape how Democratic statehouses approach AI regulation.

— The group’s new State AI Leadership Project, or SAIL, is in large part a response to the recent flood of state legislation related to AI — itself a function of the deepening tech-policy paralysis in Washington. “We, just like many other organizations, are supportive of a federal framework, but it’s very clear states are not waiting,” said Koustubh “K.J.” Bagchi , head of U.S. policy and government relations at Chamber of Progress and leader of the new initiative.

— Bagchi said SAIL will push back against AI “doomerism” and “pessimism” by promoting tech-friendly bills in blue states; encouraging AI adoption by state governments; and advancing policies that promote the increased energy production needed to power new data centers.

— Chamber of Progress is funded by AI industry heavyweights like Google , Andreessen Horowitz and Nvidia — companies that have all worked to limit the political influence of individuals and organizations worried about AI risks. The group’s new SAIL initiative aims to extend that work into blue states, where legislators have recently advanced bills that would impose new safety frameworks and other restrictions on the technology.

— Autor went on to serve as a consultant in the private sector, holding public policy roles with drugmakers like AstraZeneca and Mylan.

— She joined the board of Hims & Hers last year, and takes over as head of its global influence operation as the company comes under scrutiny for its advertising practices and readjusts is business model regarding popular weight-loss drugs. — Hims & Hers has ramped up its influence machine over the last two years, going from $310,000 in federal lobbying expenditures in 2024 to $860,000 through the first three quarters of 2025. — “This decade, corporations, unions, trade associations and individual lobbyists with significant business before Congress have poured more than $600,000 into portrait funds for several current and former federal lawmakers.” The congressional portrait funds are governed by few rules, and the only entities required to disclose their donations are registered lobbyists or the entities that employ them.

FIRST IN PI — CHECKMATE TEAMS UP WITH AGS: Checkmate Government Relations has struck up a strategic partnership with American Global Strategies , the geopolitical advisory firm started by former Trump national security adviser Robert O’Brien and National Security Council chief of staff Alex Gray . The firm was also previously home to John Ratcliffe , who President Donald Trump nominated to lead the CIA for his second term.

— Checkmate founder Ches McDowell told PI that the partnership came about because the two firms share “a lot of work right now,” especially with Checkmate’s new Tokyo outpost , and that it “just made sense to formalize it.”

— In a statement, Gray hailed McDowell as the “leader of the new generation of public affairs professionals who understand the current Administration and its political movement to their core,” going on to praise the rest of the Checkmate team as “extremely effective operators who bring significant insight and expertise to get clients results.”

— AGS is the latest strategic partnership for Checkmate since the lobbying firm launched in D.C. in the aftermath of Trump’s election. In February, Checkmate rolled out a partnership with the lobbying firm run by GOP fundraiser Jeff Miller . And in June, the North Carolina-based firm announced it was teaming up with Florida and D.C. lobbying giant Ballard Partners to expand both firms’ state lobbying operations across the southeast.

— Checkmate isn’t the first lobbying shop to team up with AGS. The consultancy has had a partnership since 2023 with Skyline Capitol , the firm founded by former Rep. Chris Stewart (R-Utah).

AFP GOES ON THE AIR IN ACA SUBSIDIES FIGHT: As Washington barrels toward a government shutdown amid a fight over the fate of enhanced Obamacare subsidies with potentially massive political implications for next year’s midterms, Koch-backed Americans for Prosperity is rolling out a six-figure ad blitz urging Republicans to let the subsidies expire at the end of the year.

— The campaign is focused solely within the Beltway, and derides the Covid-era enhanced subsidies as a “Washington handout” that’s being pocketed by insurance companies and encouraging fraud. “Congress must end these inflated subsidies and focus on real reforms that lower costs and put families first,” the narrator of one 30-second spot says.

— Lawmakers’ clash over the Affordable Care Act subsidies has taken center stage in government funding talks. A stopgap spending bill passed by the House but rejected by Senate Democrats does not include an extension of the boosted tax credits. Letting the subsidies expire is projected to send health insurance premiums surging, which could lead to millions losing or dropping their coverage.

— The issue has pitted centrist and battleground Republicans — who have signed on to a bipartisan bill to extend the credits — against fiscal hardliners — whose opposition echoes AFP’s line of argument. Complicating matters further is the recent interjection by anti-abortion groups into the standoff .

MFA TAPS A NEW TOP LOBBYIST: John Van Etten is joining the Managed Funds Association as the hedge fund lobby’s new managing director and head of U.S. government affairs. Van Etten spent the past eight years at JPMorgan Chase , most recently as director of strategy and operations for regulatory affairs. He’ll report to Jillien Flores , who was named chief advocacy officer for the trade group earlier this year.

— Before that, he did stints as an in-house lobbyist for HSBC , New York Life Insurance Co. and Clearing House (now known as the Bank Policy Institute ), and worked as legislative director to former Rep. Nan Hayworth (R-N.Y.).

FRIENDS IN HIGH PLACES: “In 2018, Paul Atkins was paid $1,450 an hour to be an expert witness by Devon Archer ’s lawyers as they tried to undermine accusations that their client defrauded a Native American tribal entity and others out of $60 million,” The New York Times’ Ken Vogel reports.

— “While Mr. Archer was convicted anyway, he was pardoned by President Trump in March. And last week, with Mr. Atkins serving as the Trump-appointed chairman of the Securities and Exchange Commission, his agency moved to dismiss a civil case against Mr. Archer related to the same fraud.”

— Archer became well-known on the right for his revelations about Hunter Biden, his former business partner, “but the Bidens were not implicated in the fraud that was the subject of the S.E.C. enforcement action.”

— “An S.E.C. spokesman said Mr. Atkins recused himself from the decision to drop the case. But the episode highlighted critics’ concerns about the deregulatory instincts and Wall Street connections of Mr. Atkins, who built a lucrative career advising some of the very financial interests he is now meant to oversee.”

WOULDN’T WANNA B YA: The abrupt rollout of the Trump administration’s new plan to levy a $100,000 price tag on applicants to the H-1B visa program for high-skill workers “could upend the tech industry, which is scrambling to figure out just how forcefully to respond,” POLITICO ’s Nick Niedzwiadek and Brendan Bordelon report.

— The announcement “blindsided Big Tech’s powerful trade associations — groups that exist in large part to keep their Silicon Valley clients from being surprised by Washington. The move leaves hundreds of thousands of jobs in the balance, from cutting-edge AI researchers to workaday coders and other specialty occupations.”

— “Tech industry representatives are weighing whether to sue over the new fee and warning that it could force top firms to forgo innovation driven by foreign-born workers or potentially shift more jobs abroad.”

— “Several are opting to lay low publicly and holding out hope of winning exemptions from the costly requirement, as the proclamation Trump signed allows Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem to grant carveouts to individuals, companies or even entire sectors.”

SIGN OF THE TIMES?: As Washington is gripped yet again by concerns about escalating political violence, Democratic FEC Commissioner Dara Lindenbaum called on Congress today to eliminate a requirement that individual donors’ addresses be published in public campaign finance disclosures, warning that the disclosures may pose a safety risk for donors who may not even be aware that their address has been exposed.

— “An ordinary person making a political contribution probably doesn’t think about whether their address might be used against them,” Lindenbaum wrote in an op-ed in The Washington Post , adding later that “Americans shouldn’t have to risk their personal safety to participate in democracy.”

— She ran through a number of “easily imaginable scenarios,” including the use of FEC disclosures to track down law enforcement or national security officials with sensitive jobs as well as poll workers, local election officials, domestic violence survivors, or even just vengeful students or former dates.

— Lindenbaum’s proposal to Congress received the unanimous backing of her fellow commissioners last year, but lawmakers have yet to take any action on such a change.

MEET THE NEW BOSS: “ Drew Maloney , the Edison Electric Institute ’s new president, has a lengthy record in lobbying , Congress and presidential politics. He’ll need to draw on that experience as he seeks to steady a group that has been beset by leadership turmoil and staffing losses,” E&E News’ Tim Cama writes in a profile of the new leader of the utilities lobby.

— “Maloney, who worked at Treasury during Donald Trump’s first term, as an adviser on Mitt Romney ‘s 2012 presidential campaign and an aide to former Rep. Tom DeLay (R-Texas), said he couldn’t speak to what happened before he got to EEI but laid out a vision for the future under his leadership.”

FIRST IN PI — HILLEAST ENDS LAWSUIT AGAINST PIENAAR’S C5: Government relations firm HillEast Group has ended its lawsuit for alleged non-payment of lobbying bills it had filed against tech investment firm C5 Capital , likely indicating a settlement has been reached, Daniel L. reports.

— HillEast, which counts former Rep. John Katko (R-N.Y.) among its ranks as a senior adviser, in June sued C5 Capital , run by André Pienaar . In the original suit, HillEast said the two parties had entered into a written agreement in May in which C5 agreed to pay HillEast $32,000 on a four-month payment plan. The public affairs firm said it hadn’t started to receive the promised payments.

— HillEast, founded by former Katko chief of staff Brad Gentile , C5 Capital and its lawyers didn’t respond to requests for comment.

— An Associated Press investigation found last year that C5 or other Pienaar-controlled entities have been sued numerous times for allegedly not returning money in an investment or not paying back wages or rent. One suit was settled and the other suits were dismissed quickly after getting filed, meaning the parties likely reached settlements.

FIRST IN PI : North Carolina Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley has praised the Trump administration for its ouster of Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro , calling it “a very important step.” He said he was “so proud” of how Delta Force handled his capture, Daniel L. reports.

— What Whatley didn’t mention is that he and his family have up to a million plus dollars invested in three major oil companies that saw spikes in their shares after President Donald Trump said he would increase oil production in Venezuela, according to his personal financial disclosure filed in late November.

— Whatley, a former energy lobbyist , and his immediate family own between $321,000 and $890,000 in stock in Chevron , which is the only American oil major operating in Venezuela. The company is their largest individual holding, according to a PI analysis of the disclosure. They also own between $83,000 and $245,000 in stock in Exxon Mobil and between $3,000 and $45,000 in shares of ConocoPhillips .

— After the Venezuela operation, those companies’ share prices jumped after Trump pledged to revive the nation’s energy sector. Between Jan. 2 and when the market opened on the Monday morning after the raid, Chevron stock increased 6.3 percent, Exxon Mobil went up 2.1 percent and ConocoPhillips rose 4.6 percent. The increase in the shares would have boosted the value of the Whatley family’s investment in those companies between $22,000 and $63,000, according to PI calculations. All three companies’ share prices have continued to go up significantly since.

— Whatley spokesperson Jonathan Felts said Whatley had held these and other stocks for many years “as part of a diversified, balanced portfolio.”

— “The idea that Michael would support Maduro’s arrest to boost his stocks is completely false and absurd — the sort of genius-level scheme dreamed up by liberal media,” he said in a statement. He also added: “Michael Whatley has spent decades supporting energy policies that ensure affordable, reliable energy for all Americans.”

— Whatley, a onetime staffer for the Energy Department and for then-Sen. Elizabeth Dole (R-N.C.), is a former longtime oil lobbyist who helped launch and lead the Consumer Energy Alliance , an oil-backed advocacy group. Chevron, Exxon Mobil and ConocoPhillips have been affiliated with the group for more than 15 years.

BGR SNAGS COOKSEY: Sean Cooksey , the former FEC chair who’s most recently been serving as a chief legal and policy adviser to Vice President JD Vance , is joining BGR Group as a managing director in the firm’s commerce and infrastructure practice.

— Cooksey plans on registering to lobby, and aims to act as an interpreter of sorts for companies struggling to figure out how to engage Trump and Vance’s office, especially on issues at the nexus of law and policy.

— “President Trump and Vice President Vance were elected by working-class Americans to make the country more prosperous and secure,” Cooksey told PI in a text. “There are tremendous opportunities for businesses and individuals to contribute to that mission, but they need help navigating this new kind of Republican administration.”

— Cooksey steered the federal campaign finance regulator during the 2024 election and stepped down from the commission a year ago to join Vance’s staff. Before joining the FEC, Cooksey worked as a top adviser to Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Ted Cruz (R-Texas) — lawmakers who, with their former Senate colleague Vance, represent the tip of the spear for the increasingly influential populist right.

— In Vance’s office, Cooksey shepherded last month’s deal to place TikTok ’s U.S. assets into the care of a consortium of American investors and helped stand up a new DOJ initiative to crack down on fraud.

THE HIRING SPREE CONTINUES: Netflix has added yet another antitrust lobbyist to its cadre of hired guns. The streaming giant last month enlisted Democratic antitrust veteran Seth Bloom of Bloom Strategic Counsel for help pushing through its proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery , according to a disclosure filing.

— This isn’t Bloom’s first time working to help sell a major corporate tie-up. The former longtime counsel for Senate Judiciary’s antitrust subcommittee has previously worked for JetBlue on its proposed merger with Spirit Airlines ; for Sprint on its merger with T-Mobile ; for Amazon on its acquisition of Whole Foods and for Aetna on its proposed merger with Humana , to name a few. Bloom also represented Comcast in connection with its 2014 proposed takeover of Time Warner Cable — a spin-off of one of WBD’s corporate predecessors.

— The streamer still has an uphill battle ahead of it, if Tuesday’s congressional hearing on the deal — during which Netflix and Warner Bros. Discovery executives worked to parry deep skepticism from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle — is any indication. As PI reported earlier this week , Netflix has retained three other new outside firms since the WBD deal was announced in December, including Republican antitrust guru Joseph Gibson of the Gibson Group ; S-3 Group and Avoq .

KARP OUT : “ Brad Karp , the leader of Paul Weiss , one of the country’s biggest law firms, resigned as chair in the wake of new revelations about his association with Jeffrey Epstein ,” The Wall Street Journal ’s Erin Mulvaney reports.

— “Karp is an influential lawyer in corporate circles, who advised boards of directors and business leaders, including the Apollo Global Management co-founder Leon Black . Karp faced criticism in legal circles last year after he brokered a deal with President Trump to resolve an executive order that cracked down on law firms. The 1,200-lawyer firm said it appointed Scott Barshay , one of the firm’s most prominent rainmakers, as its new chair.”

— Documents newly released by DOJ last week revealed discussions between Karp and Epstein about Black, as well as a request for Epstein’s help finding a role for Karp’s son in a Woody Allen film. “Leading Paul Weiss for the past 18 years has been the honor of my professional life. Recent reporting has created a distraction and has placed a focus on me that is not in the best interests of the firm,” Karp told the Journal in a statement.

TAKE IT TO DEBANK : “Some of the largest banks in the nation for years have eschewed the business of private prison giants like GEO Group and CoreCivic , the two firms that operate more than half the private carceral facilities in the country, including many U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention centers,” The Intercept ’s Biplob Kumar Das reports, moves that have “cost the prison companies billions in potential financing.”

— “Now, the private prison firms are fighting back, spending millions on lobbying Congress to pass a law to require that the banks can’t deny their business. The two prison giants spent millions lobbying for legislation known as the Fair Access to Banking Act, a pending bill that seeks to prevent banks from denying access to institutions or people including those involved in ‘politically unpopular businesses but that are lawful under Federal law.’”

RELATED READ : “Big US banks boost Washington lobbying muscle as policy fights heat up,” by Reuters’ Douglas Gillison .

ANNALS OF DARK MONEY: “Super PACs powered by unknown funders are roiling Democratic politics in Illinois , diving into a trio of open House primaries six weeks before voters effectively pick their new members of Congress in these deep blue-district primary elections,” per NBC News’ Ben Kamisar .

— “Two groups, Elect Chicago Women and Affordable Chicago Now , just blinked into existence in recent days and quickly started six-figure television buys backing three candidates in key Chicago-area races over Democratic primary opponents, including progressives who have been critical of Israel.”

— “There’s no hard evidence on who is funding the groups. But some candidates in these races have pointed their fingers at AIPAC , the pro-Israel advocacy group whose aligned super PAC has spent tens of millions of dollars in Democratic congressional primaries in recent years.”

— Tuyet Duong is now chief strategy officer, Katelyn Israelski is now chief program officer and Maria Javier is director of digital strategy and infrastructure at the National Asian Pacific American Women’s Forum .

— Teresa Kosmidis is now a partner for McDermott Will & Schulte ’s transactions practice group. She previously worked at the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

title: Bagchi heads back to Chamber of Progress
body_text:
FIRST IN PI — RESHUFFLING AT CHAMBER OF PROGRESS: KJ Bagchi is rejoining the Chamber of Progress to serve in the newly created role of vice president of U.S. policy and government relations. Bagchi was most recently the inaugural vice president for the Center for Civil Rights and Technology based out of the Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights , and before that, he served as vice president of tech policy for the Chamber.

— Bagchi’s new role will bring the Chamber’s tech policy vertical, which covers issues like content moderation, under the same umbrella as civic innovation policy, which covers issues like autonomous vehicles and the gig and sharing economy; as well as economic policy, which includes things like crypto and fintech. He’ll oversee the Chamber’s work on all of those issues along with coalition building and the group’s state and local government relations operations.

— The move will bring “more cohesion and depth to the work that we’ve already been doing,” Bagchi told PI, creating a more unified structure as the Chamber expands its footprint in places like Europe and Canada.

— The reorg also comes as the Chamber, whose funders include Apple , Amazon , Uber , Google and Intuit , is diving more into what Bagchi describes as “thought leadership” work. That includes the group’s cost of living agenda released last year and its newly launched effort to mend the tech industry’s ties with Democrats.

FIRST IN PI II — RETAIL LEADERS ADD TRADE PRO : The Retail Industry Leaders Association has tapped Sung Chang to be its new top trade lobbyist as the industry grapples with the fallout of President Donald Trump ’s tariffs. Chang left USTR in January after more than seven years with the trade office, most recently serving as senior adviser for policy and executive communications. He has also worked as an attorney adviser at the Commerce Department.

— In a statement, RILA senior vice president for government affairs Evan Armstrong noted that Chang’s arrival couldn’t come at a better time, arguing that his “unique insight into the inner workings of policymaking … will allow him to advocate on behalf of retailers who seek certainty and clarity amid a rapidly evolving trade landscape.”

— Chang will succeed RILA’s former vice president of international trade, Blake Harden , who decamped last month for EY .

— The New York Times first reported last month that McDowell — a hunting buddy of Donald Trump Jr. ’s — had been working with BakerHostetler , the law firm steering Zhao’s pardon lobbying campaign. McDowell declined to comment on whether his work for Binance involved pardon lobbying.

— Last week, Bloomberg reported that Binance was close to a deal with the Justice Department to drop a requirement for an outside compliance monitor. The requirement was imposed as part of Binance’s settlement of charges it didn’t do enough to prevent money laundering.

DEMS OPEN HOMAN PROBES: “House and Senate Democrats have opened separate investigations into the Trump administration’s decision to close a criminal F.B.I. inquiry into Tom Homan , Mr. Trump’s border czar, that began after he was recorded last year accepting a bag with $50,000 in cash,” per The New York Times’ Michael Gold .

— In a 2024 encounter recorded by undercover FBI agents posing as businesspeople, Homan agreed to help the agents secure federal border security-related contracts . The meeting triggered an investigation for potential bribery or corruption charges before the probe was dropped by the Trump administration earlier this year, per the Times.

— “ In a letter on Monday, Democrats on the House Judiciary Committee demanded that Attorney General Pam Bondi and Kash Patel , the F.B.I. director, provide ‘all recordings from Mr. Homan’s meeting,’ all of their investigative material and any communications between the White House and their agencies over the case.”

— A group of Democrats on the Senate Judiciary Committee followed up today with their own letters to Patel , Bondi and deputy AG Todd Blanche demanding that they turn over “recordings of Mr. Homan receiving cash from undercover F.B.I. agents.”

MORE PENTA MOVES: Penta Group has acquired the Democratic public affairs firm FIO360 . Adam Weiss , who co-founded FIO360 in 2019, will become a partner at Penta as a result of the merger. The acquisition comes almost two months after private equity firm Shamrock Capital acquired Penta from majority stakeholder Falfurrias Capital Partners .

— “One set of activists is urging the environmental movement to join a broader anti-billionaire campaign led by Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), which accuses the Trump administration of attacking democracy to benefit the very wealthiest Americans.”

— “Others want to double down on the Biden administration’s portrayal of climate action as a pocketbook issue — contending that Republican attacks on investments in electric vehicles, wind farms and other clean energy technologies will wipe out jobs and burden consumers with higher costs.”

— “Whichever path they choose, green groups big and small are grappling with political and financial threats unlike any they’ve confronted in decades. … They also face still-unknown potential dangers from the Trump administration’s vows to crack down on liberal-leaning nonprofits that it accuses of fomenting violence, a campaign that Democrats warn could be a pretext for a broad suppression of dissent.”

That’s more clients than Ballard lobbied DOJ for during the first Trump administration and the entire Biden administration combined.

— What changed between then and now? One of the firm’s own, Pam Bondi , is now in charge of the Justice Department. Among the clients for whom Ballard reported lobbying DOJ this year, all but one signed with the firm since Trump’s election and his nomination of Bondi for attorney general.

— A similar phenomenon is occurring across K Street at lobbying firms that have former employees in top roles with the Trump administration, your host reported over the weekend. At BGR Group , where now-Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy was previously a lobbyist and member of the firm’s advisory board, lobbyists have reported outreach to DOT on behalf of 19 clients who have paid the firm more than $1.8 million so far this year.

— That’s up from 14 clients during the Biden administration, which included passage of the first major infrastructure bill in years. BGR contacted DOT on behalf of six different clients during Trump’s first term, according to an analysis of lobbying disclosures.

— Bondi and Duffy signed ethics agreements prior to being confirmed. For one year, they vowed not to participate “personally and substantially in any particular matter involving specific parties” involving their former firms and clients of their former firms, as well as their own former clients, unless they receive an ethics waiver.

— But the lobbying by Ballard and BGR Group illustrates how, just six months into Trump’s second term, the firms have been able to cash in on their unique ties to the administration.

— A Ballard spokesperson told your host that the firm has fully complied with all lobbying requirements and has not had any lobbying contact with Bondi. A spokesperson for the attorney general said that the AG “adheres to the highest applicable ethical obligations in all matters and her prior work before taking office has no nexus with her work as Attorney General.”

— A spokesperson for Duffy similarly said that the secretary “has and will continue to abide by his signed ethics agreement” and maintained that “no single individual or company is given preferential treatment.”

DURBIN-MARSHALL CREDIT CARD MANDATES WILL HARM MILITARY FAMILIES The Defense Credit Union Council is sounding the alarm on the Durbin–Marshall credit card mandates. This proposal would increase fraud risk, restrict access to credit, eliminate rewards, and hand a massive windfall to corporate mega-retailers at the expense of consumers, small businesses, and community financial institutions. DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED —OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

NAB SPEAKS: The media industry is at an “unprecedented” moment in its history, National Association of Broadcasters head Curtis LeGeyt warned this weekend. It was the trade group’s first public comments on the firestorm over ABC ’s decision to pull late night host Jimmy Kimmel off the air over comments about the murder of conservative activist Charlie Kirk .

— “Let me first state affirmatively that broadcasters must be able to make decisions about the content on our airwaves free from government influence,” LeGeyt wrote in a blog post on Sunday, stressing that the “mere perception that broadcasters acted because of undue pressure is a problem for our credibility and the trust we have built with our audiences.”

— At the same time, political pressure on the media has been a feature of Democratic and Republican administrations alike, LeGeyt argued, pointing to several incidents during the Obama and Biden administrations.

— ABC parent company Disney announced today that Kimmel’s show will return to the air Tuesday night. But the network’s move last week touched off intense backlash because it followed FCC Chair Brendan Carr ’s suggestion hours earlier that his agency might suspend broadcast licenses.

— Two NAB members, Nexstar and Sinclair , were quick to announce their own preemption of Kimmel’s show, setting off concerns that the announcements amounted to corporate capitulation aimed at winning regulatory approval from the administration.

— NAB publicly remained quiet about the incident in the following days, though LeGeyt suggested that the association had been mounting any of its pushback in private. LeGeyt also warned that potential political interference risks distracting the industry from its fight for survival in a media ecosystem disrupted by tech innovation.

CONTINENTAL ADDS TRADE LAWYER: President Donald Trump ’s tariffs continue to represent a gold mine for the lobbying industry, and Continental Strategy has added an administration alum to beef up the firm’s trade expertise.

— George Bogden is joining Continental to serve as a senior counselor for trade and tariff matters. Bogden previously led Customs and Border Protection’s Office of Trade Relations, where he helped the trade industry navigate Trump’s rapidly shifting tariff policies.

— Bogden left DHS this spring amid a turf war over Trump’s tariffs. The Washington Post also reported in April that Bogden was ousted after photos circulated of him attending the 2019 wedding of former Trump DHS official Miles Taylor , the author of an anonymous New York Times op-ed published in 2018 and titled, “I Am Part of the Resistance Inside the Trump Administration.”

FIRST IN PI — DOORDASH ADDS COMMS VETS: DoorDash has added a pair of Democratic communications staffers to bolster the gig company’s policy comms shop. Elana Ross is joining DoorDash as policy communications manager covering the West, while Samantha Ramirez will be policy communications manager covering the East.

— Ross was most recently deputy communications director for California Gov. Gavin Newsom . Ramirez was most recently communications director for Rep. Maxwell Frost (D-Fla.) and is a Charlie Crist alum.

SBA PUSHES RESTRICTIONS IN OBAMACARE EXTENSION: Anti-abortion advocates are pressing Republicans to prevent any extension of soon-to-expire Obamacare subsidies from covering procedures that end pregnancies, Benjamin reports.

— House GOP staffers were confronted with the issue Friday, when Susan B. Anthony Pro-Life America senior policy adviser Autumn Christensen and federal affairs director Jamie Dangers briefed aides to members of the conservative Republican Study Committee .

— Christensen and Dangers distributed a memo stating that lawmakers must not extend the subsidies without ensuring that “Obamacare tax credits no longer fund health plans that include abortion.”

— The demand could create a major dilemma for GOP lawmakers who want to work with Democrats to avoid letting the subsidies expire at year’s end — but also not alienate their base and influential anti-abortion advocates. Senate Finance ranking member Ron Wyden said in a statement that no progress will be made on an extension compromise “if you start handing out right-wing trophies.”

COMING DOWN THE PIPELINE: “Last year, as Democrats were dealt big setbacks in federal races nationwide, a small crop of well-funded candidates in Florida picked up 15 school board seats that had been targeted by conservative groups in competitive counties. Now, the obscure organization that backed those Florida candidates is planning a substantial expansion to cover more than half the country,” The New York Times’ Nick Corasaniti writes.

— “ Pipeline Fund , a left-leaning group that helped funnel more than $1 million, plus support and training, into the Florida races, is vying to establish itself as a liberal counter to the sprawling down-ballot infrastructure on the right that has helped Republicans notch wins on school boards, in county offices and in local judicial races.”

— “A spinoff from the Sixteen Thirty Fund , a network of liberal organizations funded by George Soros , the Pipeline Fund started on its own last year with a focus on down-ballot elections. The group is part benefactor and part matchmaker, identifying candidates for these races and connecting them with state and national organizations for funding and support.”

— Vivek Chandrasekhar has joined Perkins Coie as a partner in the tax and environment, energy and resources practices. He was most recently acting deputy tax legislative counsel at the Treasury Department.

PANAMA, BRAZIL LOBBY UP: Amid heartburn across South and Latin America over the Trump administration’s trade and foreign policy, a pair of the president’s top targets have brought on additional lobbying muscle in Washington.

— The Panamanian government inked a three-month contract with Checkmate Government Relations for “strategic counsel and outreach” to government officials, NGOs and more.

— Panama will pay Checkmate a monthly retainer of $80,000, according to a copy of the contract filed with DOJ this week. The new lobbying help comes as the Trump administration amasses military assets in the Caribbean following a series of U.S. strikes on multiple alleged drug boats in international waters this month.

— Meanwhile, the administration’s pressure on the Panamanian government to root out Chinese influence in the country — building on President Donald Trump ’s months-long campaign to return control of the Panama Canal to the U.S. — has begun to prompt backlash against Panama’s leadership.

— The Panamanian government already brought on two new lobbying firms — BGR Group and VantageKnight — in January amid Trump’s Panama Canal threats. In May, Checkmate registered to represent Panama’s Maritime Authority, the entity that oversees Panama’s shipping registry and ports.

— Farther south, the Brazilian government, which has been bracing for retribution from the White House after a Brazilian court sentenced former President (and Trump ally) Jair Bolsonaro to 27 years in prison last week, has tapped Arnold & Porter Kaye Scholer to provide lobbying advice in addition to the firm’s previous legal work.

— “On August 22, 2025, the Foreign Principal engaged the Registrant via a signed agreement letter to represent it in proceedings related to administrative sanctions and similar measures applied by the government of the United States, including litigation matters,” the firm said in DOJ filings.

— Brazil has signaled it will fight U.S. sanctions and visa restrictions on Brazilian officials, including the Supreme Court justice who tried Bolsonaro’s case. Brazil also faces steep 50 percent tariffs on exports to the U.S., which the government has said it may also challenge in court.

— Last week, Arnold & Porter and Brazil agreed to expand the scope of its work for the next four years to include advice on relations with the federal government, according to the filings. The total value of the contract will be capped at $3.5 million, the firm said, which includes both non-registrable legal services and any possible lobbying activity.

WESTEXEC ADDS GOP HEFT: WestExec Advisors , the consulting firm started by a slew of Democratic foreign policy heavyweights such as former Secretary of State Antony Blinken , has hired former GOP Rep. Mike Garcia as a principal.

— The Navy veteran served two terms in the House before losing reelection in November, and he now serves as head of the California chapter of the pro-Trump think tank America First Policy Institute .

— Garcia is the latest in a string of GOP hires for WestExec and comes at a time when the consultancy has lost several big-name clients who were in search of closer ties to the Trump administration, as Daniel L. reported in the spring.

— In March, WestExec brought on Johnnie Kaberle , a longtime former aide to former Rep. Kay Granger (R-Texas), as a senior vice president. The same month, the firm added Rob Blair , a former White House and Commerce Department staffer in the first Trump administration, as a principal.

— WestExec has continued to strengthen its Democratic credentials as well. Wally Adeyemo , who served as deputy Treasury secretary during the Biden administration, joined the firm in March as well, also as a principal.

DEPT. OF ODD BEDFELLOWS: A coalition of half a dozen industry groups typically at odds in disputes over rail policy is imploring the Surface Transportation Board to clarify federal authority over railroads amid “encroachment” by state and local governments across the country.

— “The STB and most courts have recognized ICCTA’s preemption provision to be one of the broadest and most comprehensive preemption statutes ever adopted,” trade groups representing railroads and rail customers said in a letter to STB members today, referring to the federal statute that gives the STB exclusive jurisdiction over rail transport.

— “Notwithstanding this, the national uniformity Congress intended is being eroded across the country every day when local authorities misunderstand or misapply ICCTA in various scenarios,” which leads to project delays, uncertainty and litigation for the rail sector and industries that use it, the groups continued.

— Preemption disputes have arisen in recent years over state efforts to require trains to follow certain emissions standards , for example.

— Today’s letter, which was signed by the American Chemistry Council , American Short Line and Regional Railroad Association , Association of American Railroads , Intermodal Association of North America , National Grain and Feed Association and National Industrial Transportation League , asks STB to “provide essential and authoritative guidance to industry, to state and local authorities” as well as other stakeholders. They want STB to clarify the scope of ICCTA preemption, which the industry groups argue will “facilitate the uniformity originally intended by Congress, while curtailing state or local encroachment into an inherently federal jurisdiction.”

BALLING OUT: “Contribute money to the new White House ballroom President Trump is constructing and, in exchange, donors may be able to choose a Trumpian option : their names etched inside the White House forever. At least that’s one option that has been discussed,” per CBS News ’ Arden Farhi and Jennifer Jacobs .

— “Multiple companies have pledged to donate $5 million or more for what was projected to be a $200 million addition to the executive mansion, according to sources familiar with the matter,” with Trump reportedly making overtures to some executives personally.

— Among those who have contributed already are Google , R.J. Reynolds , Booz Allen Hamilton , Lockheed Martin , Palantir and NextEra Energy , along with several tech, manufacturing, banking and health companies, per CBS.

ON MUTE: “ ABC ’s decision to ‘indefinitely’ suspend comedian Jimmy Kimmel has alarmed free speech advocates — but apparently not the self-described ‘chief advocate of broadcasters in our nation’s capital,’ the National Association of Broadcasters . At least not publicly,” per NOTUS ’ Taylor Giorno .

PANAMA, BRAZIL LOBBY UP: Amid heartburn across South and Latin America over the Trump administration’s trade and foreign policy, a pair of the president’s top targets have brought on additional lobbying muscle in Washington.

— The Panamanian government inked a three-month contract with Checkmate Government Relations for “strategic counsel and outreach” to government officials, NGOs and more.

— Panama will pay Checkmate a monthly retainer of $80,000, according to a copy of the contract filed with DOJ this week. The new lobbying help comes as the Trump administration amasses military assets in the Caribbean following a series of U.S. strikes on multiple alleged drug boats in international waters this month.

— Meanwhile, the administration’s pressure on the Panamanian government to root out Chinese influence in the country — building on President Donald Trump’s months-long campaign to return control of the Panama Canal to the U.S. — has begun to prompt backlash against Panama’s leadership.

— The Panamanian government already brought on two new lobbying firms — BGR Group and VantageKnight — in January amid Trump’s Panama Canal threats. In May, Checkmate registered to represent Panama’s Maritime Authority, the entity that oversees Panama’s shipping registry and ports.

— Farther south, the Brazilian government, which has been bracing for retribution from the White House after a Brazilian court sentenced former President (and Trump ally) Jair Bolsonaro to 27 years in prison last week, has tapped Arnold & Porter Kaye Scholer to provide lobbying advice in addition to the firm’s previous legal work.

— “On August 22, 2025, the Foreign Principal engaged the Registrant via a signed agreement letter to represent it in proceedings related to administrative sanctions and similar measures applied by the government of the United States, including litigation matters,” the firm said in DOJ filings.

— Brazil has signaled it will fight U.S. sanctions and visa restrictions on Brazilian officials, including the Supreme Court justice who tried Bolsonaro’s case. Brazil also faces steep 50 percent tariffs on exports to the U.S., which the government has said it may also challenge in court.

— Last week, Arnold & Porter and Brazil agreed to expand the scope of its work for the next four years to include advice on relations with the federal government, according to the filings. The total value of the contract will be capped at $3.5 million, the firm said, which includes both non-registrable legal services and any possible lobbying activity.

title: Thomas-Greenfield lands at APCO
body_text:
BIG HIRE FOR APCO: Linda Thomas-Greenfield , who served as ambassador to the United Nations under former President Joe Biden , has joined the lobbying and communications firm APCO Worldwide as a senior adviser and a member of the firm’s International Advisory Council. The veteran diplomat served as assistant secretary of State for African affairs during the Obama administration following postings in Liberia, Pakistan, Kenya, Nigeria, and Jamaica.

— Between her stints in government, Thomas-Greenfield was a senior vice president at Albright Stonebridge Group , the consulting firm founded by former Secretary of State Madeleine Albright that has since been absorbed by DGA Group . Her clients there included Hilton , Endeavor Energy Holdings , Amazon , Microsoft and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation , according to her 2021 financial disclosures.

— Thomas-Greenfield, who also sits on the board of the Council on Foreign Relations , is expected to support APCO’s efforts to make inroads across Africa, where the firm’s clients include the governments of Côte d’Ivoire, Mauritania and Congo. “As APCO’s work continues to expand across the African continent, Linda’s insights will strengthen our ability to support clients and seize new opportunities in this dynamic and rapidly evolving region,” firm founder and executive chair Margery Kraus said in a statement.

DAVENPORT ALREADY PICKING UP CLIENTS: Doug Davenport has hit the ground running after rejoining DCI Group to lead the firm’s lobbying affairs practice. Davenport, who worked for all three of Donald Trump’s presidential campaigns, has already signed four new clients, according to disclosure filings, including Meta and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology .

— Davenport also registered to lobby on “no tax on tips” and labor issues for gig company DoorDash , and on trade issues for Swiss aircraft manufacturer Pilatus Aircraft . (The latter work is being carried out as a subcontractor to Nelson Mullins Riley & Scarborough .)

— “Now those in Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again Movement plan events in nearly a dozen cities, from Florida to California, on Sept. 27 to thank him for sticking up for kids’ health, they said during a call with supporters.”

— “The advocates said they want to show lawmakers that MAHA represents a powerful political force and that those who oppose Kennedy do it at their own political risk. President Donald Trump has long believed his alliance with Kennedy is a boon to the GOP, but some Republicans began to waver after Kennedy fired the director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention last month.”

— “‘One way you can really back Secretary Kennedy is to send a message to your senator, to your congressman, that you believe that Bobby Kennedy is trying hard to restore public trust in our health agencies, you support him, you want them to and you’re not going to vote for them if they don’t do it,’ said Tony Lyons , the president of MAHA Action , an advocacy group leading the movement, during the call Wednesday.”

— Kennedy’s allies did not go so far as to push for political consequences against the HHS secretary’s Republican detractors in Congress, but instead “called on fellow Kennedy supporters to show members of Congress how important the health secretary and his policies are to them.”

RAGE ROOM: “Corporate leaders regularly praise the Trump administration and its policies in public. Behind closed doors, their mood is darker ,” The Wall Street Journal ’s Chip Cutter writes.

— “At a meeting of CEOs and other executives on Wednesday convened by the Yale School of Management , dozens of America’s business leaders sounded off on their concerns about tariffs, immigration, foreign policy matters and what many described as an increasingly chaotic, hard-to-navigate business environment.”

— “‘They’re being extorted and bullied individually, but in private discourse, they’re really upset,’ said Jeffrey Sonnenfeld , a Yale management professor who organized the event, referring to recent deals that give the U.S. government a cut of certain Nvidia chip sales and a ‘golden share’ in U.S. Steel .”

— “Many who shared their concerns Wednesday in the confines of a private conference room didn’t want to speak publicly for fear that their companies could be targeted by the administration or that they could attract criticism from Trump.” But “in a series of poll questions, the executives in the room made their frustrations known.”

— Still, “not all CEOs in the room criticized the administration, according to attendees.” Executives also overwhelmingly expressed more confidence in America’s capitalist economy when pitted against China’s socialist one.

IF YOU MISSED IT WEDNESDAY: “House Oversight Chair James Comer has invited the heads of four tech platforms to testify about how their users are being radicalized,” POLITICO ’s Anthony Adragna reports.

— “Comer invited the heads of Discord , Steam , Twitch and Reddit to appear on Oct. 8 to testify about the ‘radicalization of online forum users, including incidents of open incitement to commit violent politically motivated acts’ in the aftermath of the killing of Charlie Kirk . The man charged with aggravated murder in Kirk’s death was reportedly active on Discord .”

— “‘Congress has a duty to oversee the online platforms that radicals have used to advance political violence,’ Comer said in a statement, adding the platform CEOs ‘must appear before the Oversight Committee and explain what actions they will take to ensure their platforms are not exploited for nefarious purposes.’”

FLYING IN: Construction groups are kicking off a new lobbying push ahead of next year’s expiration of surface transportation authorizations. More than 300 members of the National Stone, Sand and Gravel Association , National Asphalt Pavement Association and National Ready Mixed Concrete Association headed to the Hill today for a joint fly-in to discuss the industry’s priorities for a new surface transportation bill, including sustained funding levels and investment in safety improvements.

— The trade groups were slated to meet with Senate Majority Leader John Thune , Sens. Kevin Cramer (R-N.D.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.); House Transportation Chair Sam Graves (R-Mo.) and Reps. Rick Larsen (D-Wash.), David Rouzer (R-N.C.), Salud Carbajal (D-Calif.), Greg Stanton (D-Ariz.) among others.

— More than 300 auto care industry professionals hit the Hill today for the Auto Care Association ’s Legislative Summit. Auto parts manufacturers, retailers and installers are advocating for advancement of the federal REPAIR Act. Advocates had over 150 meetings slated with members of House Energy and Commerce, House Transportation and Senate Commerce.

— The National Association of Community Health Centers was also on the Hill today for its second fly-in of the year. More than 100 community health center leaders will urge lawmakers to approve long-term reauthorization of federal grant funding for health centers. The current short-term funding extension is set to expire at the end of the month.

Thomas-Greenfield lands at APCO

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO 

09/18/2025 06:47 PM EDT

Presented by

With Daniel Lippman

BIG HIRE FOR APCO: Linda Thomas-Greenfield, who served as ambassador to the United Nations under former President Joe Biden, has joined the lobbying and communications firm APCO Worldwide as a senior adviser and a member of the firm’s International Advisory Council. The veteran diplomat served as assistant secretary of State for African affairs during the Obama administration following postings in Liberia, Pakistan, Kenya, Nigeria, and Jamaica.

— Between her stints in government, Thomas-Greenfield was a senior vice president at Albright Stonebridge Group, the consulting firm founded by former Secretary of State Madeleine Albright that has since been absorbed by DGA Group. Her clients there included Hilton, Endeavor Energy Holdings, Amazon, Microsoft and the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, according to her 2021 financial disclosures.

— Thomas-Greenfield, who also sits on the board of the Council on Foreign Relations, is expected to support APCO’s efforts to make inroads across Africa, where the firm’s clients include the governments of Côte d’Ivoire, Mauritania and Congo. “As APCO’s work continues to expand across the African continent, Linda’s insights will strengthen our ability to support clients and seize new opportunities in this dynamic and rapidly evolving region,” firm founder and executive chair Margery Kraus said in a statement.

DAVENPORT ALREADY PICKING UP CLIENTS: Doug Davenport has hit the ground running after rejoining DCI Group to lead the firm’s lobbying affairs practice. Davenport, who worked for all three of Donald Trump’s presidential campaigns, has already signed four new clients, according to disclosure filings, including Meta and the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

— Davenport also registered to lobby on “no tax on tips” and labor issues for gig company DoorDash, and on trade issues for Swiss aircraft manufacturer Pilatus Aircraft. (The latter work is being carried out as a subcontractor to Nelson Mullins Riley & Scarborough.)

RFK JR. GETS BACKUP: “The MAHA movement is rallying behind its leader, Robert F. Kennedy Jr., after senators berated the health secretary in back-to-back hearings this month for firing the CDC’s director and moving to revise vaccine guidance,” per POLITICO’s Carmen Paun.

— “Now those in Kennedy’s Make America Healthy Again Movement plan events in nearly a dozen cities, from Florida to California, on Sept. 27 to thank him for sticking up for kids’ health, they said during a call with supporters.”

— “The advocates said they want to show lawmakers that MAHA represents a powerful political force and that those who oppose Kennedy do it at their own political risk. President Donald Trump has long believed his alliance with Kennedy is a boon to the GOP, but some Republicans began to waver after Kennedy fired the director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention last month.”

— “‘One way you can really back Secretary Kennedy is to send a message to your senator, to your congressman, that you believe that Bobby Kennedy is trying hard to restore public trust in our health agencies, you support him, you want them to and you’re not going to vote for them if they don’t do it,’ said Tony Lyons, the president of MAHA Action, an advocacy group leading the movement, during the call Wednesday.”

— Kennedy’s allies did not go so far as to push for political consequences against the HHS secretary’s Republican detractors in Congress, but instead “called on fellow Kennedy supporters to show members of Congress how important the health secretary and his policies are to them.”

RAGE ROOM: “Corporate leaders regularly praise the Trump administration and its policies in public. Behind closed doors, their mood is darker,” The Wall Street Journal’s Chip Cutter writes.

— “At a meeting of CEOs and other executives on Wednesday convened by the Yale School of Management, dozens of America’s business leaders sounded off on their concerns about tariffs, immigration, foreign policy matters and what many described as an increasingly chaotic, hard-to-navigate business environment.”

— “‘They’re being extorted and bullied individually, but in private discourse, they’re really upset,’ said Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a Yale management professor who organized the event, referring to recent deals that give the U.S. government a cut of certain Nvidia chip sales and a ‘golden share’ in U.S. Steel.”

— “Many who shared their concerns Wednesday in the confines of a private conference room didn’t want to speak publicly for fear that their companies could be targeted by the administration or that they could attract criticism from Trump.” But “in a series of poll questions, the executives in the room made their frustrations known.”

— Still, “not all CEOs in the room criticized the administration, according to attendees.” Executives also overwhelmingly expressed more confidence in America’s capitalist economy when pitted against China’s socialist one.

IF YOU MISSED IT WEDNESDAY: “House Oversight Chair James Comer has invited the heads of four tech platforms to testify about how their users are being radicalized,” POLITICO’s Anthony Adragna reports.

— “Comer invited the heads of Discord, Steam, Twitch and Reddit to appear on Oct. 8 to testify about the ‘radicalization of online forum users, including incidents of open incitement to commit violent politically motivated acts’ in the aftermath of the killing of Charlie Kirk. The man charged with aggravated murder in Kirk’s death was reportedly active on Discord.”

— “‘Congress has a duty to oversee the online platforms that radicals have used to advance political violence,’ Comer said in a statement, adding the platform CEOs ‘must appear before the Oversight Committee and explain what actions they will take to ensure their platforms are not exploited for nefarious purposes.’”

title: How Trump’s Monaco broadsides are playing on K Street
body_text:
IS THAT A CHILL IN THE AIR OR IS IT JUST US: Donald Trump ’s attempt to jawbone Microsoft into firing former Biden DOJ official Lisa Monaco as a top D.C. operative has put K Street on high alert about who they hire, Caitlin reports with Brendan Bordelon and Yasmin Khorram .

— Much of the private sector is paralyzed by Trump’s broader efforts to leverage the might of the government to bend companies to his whims. But that pressure is magnified in government affairs shops across Washington, where corporations are desperate to curry Trump’s favor and avoid his wrath.

— “Anything that comes across my desk now is like, ‘What Republican can we hire? And is the Republican MAGA?’” said Jeff Forbes , a founding partner at Forbes Tate Partners . The job market is so precarious in the Trump era, he added, that it’s been tough for even moderate Republicans to get land a top job in Washington, let alone Democrats.

— In a town where political connections to whomever is in power amount to currency, it’s not unusual for corporate lobbyists to cycle out of prominent roles when their party loses power. But “to have a target on your back because of past political affiliation in what has traditionally been a very nonpartisan area is a totally new dynamic,” said one veteran Democratic consultant.

— The Monaco episode is the latest manifestation of a threat that’s been hanging over corporate America since Trump’s first term in office, but has only escalated during his second presidency.

— Corporate America is still searching for the best way to stay on Trump’s good side, which has largely amounted to a combination of trying to stay under the radar while being vocal about wins that could reflect well on Trump. That caution has trickled down into lobbying hires as well.

— “A lot of companies are being extremely careful and selective about who they hire, who they put forward” for jobs in their D.C. offices, according to the Democratic consultant.

— It’s more important than ever for companies to weigh how regularly a prospective hire might be interfacing with the Trump administration or external stakeholders, the consultant noted. “It’s really had a very, very chilling effect.”
