BRAZILIAN INDUSTRY HIRES BALLARD FOR TARIFF FIGHT: The largest industry group in Brazil, the Brazilian National Confederation of Industry , has hired Ballard Partners to represent it in the ongoing battle over President Donald Trump’s severe tariffs on imports from the South American country, according to a newly filed disclosure report.

— Earlier this week, PI brought you the news that CNI has been shopping around for a Washington lobbyist that can help Brazilian industry get in the door with the Trump administration after the country was hit with a 50 percent tariff rate last month. Hiring Ballard, which has become the most sought-after firm in Trump’s Washington, is a strong start.

— Brian Ballard and former White House senior adviser for policy and strategy Hunter Morgen will handle the account, according to the filing. Morgen primarily worked on trade and immigration issues while serving in the first Trump administration and, most importantly, was a deputy to trade adviser Peter Navarro .

— Ballard and the industry leaders will likely face stiff resistance on any efforts to lower the tariffs. Complicating matters in Washington is Eduardo Bolsonaro , son of disgraced former Brazilian President Jair Bolsonaro . The younger Bolsonaro has been living in the U.S. since February and lobbying the Trump administration to take a harsh position toward the Brazilian government in apparent retaliation for Brazil’s prosecution of his father on charges of conspiring to overturn the country’s 2022 presidential election.

— Bolsonaro’s lobbying may have succeeded in escalating Trump’s rhetoric and economic vindictiveness toward Brazil, but today it also earned him a formal accusation of obstruction of justice by the Brazilian federal police.

— News of Ballard’s hiring comes one day after CNN Brasil reported that Brazilian business leaders are set to fly out to Washington next month to press their case in person. The report indicated leaders plan to meet with U.S. officials, but didn’t provide specifics. One official who’s unlikely to open his door? Peter Navarro — who posted “Free Jair Bolsonaro!” on X in response to PI’s earlier reporting.

Happy Thursday and welcome to PI. Hope you enjoyed today’s brief sweater weather. FIRST COMES LOVE: Donald Trump’s other son-in-law Michael Boulos and his family have financially benefited from their ties to the Trump clan ever since Boulos proposed to younger Trump daughter Tiffany in 2021, Justin Scheck , Tariq Panja , Jo Becker and Bradley Hope report for The New York Times .

— The Times report details two transactions involving Boulos and his cousin that included either investment from a Trump family member or attempts to sell the appearance of closeness to the first family. Boulos personally received $400,000 from the two deals and denies any wrongdoing.

— In the first deal, Boulos and his cousin’s yacht brokerage firm convinced the more famous Trump son-in-law Jared Kushner to invest in a yacht flipping enterprise to the tune of approximately $15 million. Text messages obtained by the Times show the firm overcharged Kushner by $2.5 million, though it’s unclear if Boulos was aware.

— The second deal involved the same Boulos cousin and a Saudi businessman seeking the appearance of closeness to the Trump family as part of an effort to regain real estate holdings that had been seized by the Saudi government as part of a corruption crackdown in 2017. The businessman would eventually pay $100,000 in an ultimately unsuccessful effort to secure an invite to the Boulos-Trump wedding.

QUID PRO BONO: Two of the major law firms that struck deals with the Trump administration earlier this year have been quietly doing free work for the Commerce Department, Michael Schmidt , Matthew Goldstein and Maggie Haberman report for The New York Times .

— Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison and Kirkland & Ellis have been working with Commerce on a “range of matters” that potentially includes trade deals with other countries. The Times had previously reported that a third deal-making firm, Skadden Arps , had been connected to Commerce by Trump lawyer Boris Epshteyn , though it’s not clear if Skadden has performed any work for the department.

— “The Commerce Department is not only taking an active role in trade and tariff negotiations but also discussing taking equity stakes in some U.S. companies like the chip maker Intel. In a statement, the department said it and its secretary, Howard Lutnick, ‘are working with some of America’s top law firms and legal minds to cement the truly historic trade deals that President Trump negotiated for the American people.’”

— SUBSTACK SPAM: Former DNC Chair Jaime Harrison had some folks grumbling last week when they learned they had been subscribed to his new Substack against their will. “Harrison appears to have run afoul of Substack’s terms of service by mass-subscribing his former campaign email list and other personal contacts,” Daniel L. scoops .

— “Last week, Harrison’s Substack showed that he had a million subscribers, but most of Harrison’s posts have less than a dozen likes. After POLITICO started asking questions, the number of subscribers became private. A Harrison spokesperson declined to comment on why the subscription number is no longer public.”

HOLLAND & KNIGHT HIRES TRUMP 1.0 OFFICIAL: Demand for high-ranking Trump 1.0 officials remains high, even as Trump 2.0 officials start their moves to K Street. Today, Holland & Knight announced its hiring of former State Department official Ambassador Nathan Sales , who served as acting undersecretary for civilian security, democracy and human rights and ambassador-at-large and coordinator for counterterrorism.

— “Nathan’s extensive capabilities and connections to the current Trump administration will be integral to a wide variety of the firm’s lobbying and government contract clients,” leader of the firm’s public policy & regulation group Rich Gold said in a statement. “His wide-ranging contacts in foreign governments will be especially helpful with the firm’s trade and tariff policy engagements and U.S. consular matters around the world.”

Jobs report

— David Meale is now China practice head of the Eurasia Group . He most recently was a senior foreign service officer at the State Department, where he spent more than three decades, with his last overseas assignment as the deputy chief of mission at the U.S. Embassy in Beijing.

— Former Biden deputy national security adviser for cyber and emerging technology Anne Neuberger has joined Andreessen Horowitz as a senior adviser. She previously spent more than 11 years at the National Security Agency before heading to the White House.

— The Edison Electric Institute has added three new members to its C-suite. Rachael Marsh joins the association as chief legal officer, coming from Calpine Corporation , where she served as vice president of government affairs and managing counsel. Emily Schillinger has been tapped to serve as EEI’s new chief communications officer, moving on from the American Investment Council , where she was executive vice president of public affairs. Finally, Kiel Weaver joins as chief advocacy officer. He was most recently director of environmental policy for NextEra Energy .

— Kendra Wharton , most recently associate deputy attorney general at the Justice Department and a former member of Trump’s personal defense team, has left government to return to Wharton Law .

— Best Best & Krieger LLP has added two new Interior Department alums to its environment and natural resources practice group. Michael Brain , who will also lead the firm’s government affairs team, joins as partner, and Gary Gold joins as of counsel.

title: India hires Mercury
body_text:
— India, which is currently subject to a 25 percent reciprocal tariff, has until Wednesday to try to convince the Trump administration not to impose an additional 25 percent punitive tariff for continuing to buy Russian oil during the invasion of Ukraine. Speaking to reporters yesterday, White House trade adviser Peter Navarro said he anticipates the additional tariff will go into effect as scheduled.

— “I see that taking place,” Navarro said during a gaggle. “India doesn’t appear to want to recognize its role in the bloodshed. It simply doesn’t.”

— The contract between the embassy and Mercury runs from mid-August to mid-November and will net the firm $75,000 a month for a total of $225,000. That’s a paltry sum compared to the $1.8 million India already committed to pay former Trump adviser Jason Miller’s SHW Partners LLC .

— India isn’t the first foreign country to hire Mercury since Trump re-entered the White House. The president’s chief of staff, Susie Wiles , ran the firm’s Florida and Washington offices until she left for Trump’s 2024 campaign, and the embassies of Denmark , Ecuador , Armenia and South Korea likely took that relationship into consideration when deciding to hire the lobby shop.

NVIDIA CONTINUES HIRING SPREE: Last Friday , PI reported that chipmaker Nvidia had hired Brownstein amid a notable increase in its lobbying spending since last year. This week, the hiring spree continued, with disclosures showing the August hiring of The Vogel Group and BGR .

— The hirings bring the total number of Washington firms on Nvidia’s payroll to five, up from just two as recently as last year. In the first half of 2025 (before these latest hires) the company had already more than doubled its total lobbying spending from last year.

— The BGR hire in particular positions Nvidia closer to the Trump administration, which recently allowed the company to sell a modified version of its semiconductor chips to China in exchange for a 15 percent cut of the profit. On the BGR account are Trump White House alums Dan Greenwood and Joseph Lai .

— “Blake’s deep understanding of international trade dynamics and her proven track record of success will be an invaluable asset to our clients in the current political and policy landscape,” WCEY head Ray Beeman said in a statement. Harden’s first day is Monday.

SELLING THE OBBB: The National Federation of Independent Business (NFIB) has launched a new ad campaign thanking lawmakers for making the 20 percent small business tax deduction permanent as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill.

— Lawmakers getting praise in the ads include House Speaker Mike Johnson and Ways and Means Chair Jason Smith , key players in getting Trump’s tax agenda through Congress. The ads will play on radio and be displayed digitally as well as on billboards in states across the country.

— Making the deduction permanent was a major goal for the small business lobby that ran television ads earlier this year urging Congress to prioritize its inclusion in the OBBB. First introduced as part of Trump’s 2017 package of tax cuts, the deduction was set to expire at the end of this year.

BACK IN THE SADDLE: Joe Francescon has been tapped to be the next deputy director of the National Security Agency, POLITICO’S John Sakellariadis and Maggie Miller scooped yesterday .

— The move means Francescon, a former NSA intelligence analyst and Trump National Security Council director for counterterrorism, will leave his current post at defense contractor DZYNE Technologies , where he has served as chief external affairs officer for the past two years.

TROUBLE AT TARGETSMART: Major Democratic data firm TargetSmart has lost roughly a quarter of its staff this year, Daniel L. and Holly Otterbein scooped in Morning Score .

— “The exodus, which includes at least 12 people out of 50-plus employees, has left some Democrats worried that a key piece of their party’s data infrastructure is being hollowed out. Employees who have departed TargetSmart include its former CEO and chief technology officer. Last month, two top leaders also left data firm Statara Solutions , which is owned by the same parent company as TargetSmart.”

— “TargetSmart enhances Democratic state parties’ voter files, a precious resource in the party ecosystem that is used by campaigns and liberal groups to reach and better understand the electorate. Some former employees said they quit because they were concerned the company has recently been too focused instead on creating a new digital ad-buying platform. Others were laid off.”

— The States Forum has appointed Lise Clavel as its first executive director. She was most recently a senior fellow at the Center for American Progress and is a Biden White House alum.

— Brownstein has added two new senior policy advisers to its government relations department. Annick Miller is a veteran of the House Natural Resources Committee, where she most recently served as the Republican staff director for the Water, Wildlife and Fisheries subcommittee. Aaron Thiele previously served as a senior adviser in the Department of the Interior and was Sen. Lisa Murkowski ’s adviser while she chaired the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee.

title: Trade boss shuffle
body_text:
MOVERS AND SHAKERS: A trio of powerful downtown trade groups are heading into the end-of-year sprint in Washington with new leaders. NCTA – The Internet & Television Association has tapped former Sen. Cory Gardner to be its next president and CEO, beginning later this month.

— Gardner will step down as chair of the Senate Leadership Fund for the new role. He will remain on the board of the Senate GOP’s super PAC after overseeing the transfer of power from allies of outgoing GOP leader Mitch McConnell to those of new GOP leader John Thune .

— Gardner’s post with NCTA, whose members include Charter Communications , Comcast and Cox Communications , isn’t his first gig downtown. The Colorado Republican has worked with a number of trade groups since leaving office in 2021, including serving as the chief political strategist for the Crypto Council for Innovation .

— He was also an adviser to the National Cannabis Roundtable (which merged with another advocacy group earlier this year to become the U.S. Cannabis Roundtable ) and has been a member of the board of Michael Best Strategies .

— Meanwhile the Independent Petroleum Association of America , which represents smaller oil and gas producers, announced this morning that Edith Naegele will join the trade group later this month, amid a feverish lobbying campaign by the energy industry for Congress to pass a permitting overhaul by the end of the year.

— Naegele is currently vice president for membership and strategic development at the American Gas Association , and before that she spent 18 years with the U.S. Chamber of Commerce .

— And over at the Financial Services Forum — whose members include JPMorgan Chase , Bank of America , Wells Fargo , Citigroup , Goldman Sachs , Morgan Stanley , BNY Mellon and State Street — Amanda Eversole has taken over for Kevin Fromer as president and chief executive of the Wall Street group. Eversole was previously chief advocacy officer at the American Petroleum Institute .

POLITICO Forecast

In a fragmented global landscape, understanding how policy and politics intersect across borders is critical. Forecast synthesizes POLITICO’s global reporting to connect key developments and global convenings, giving readers a clearer view of what’s ahead. Subscribe Now .

Happy Tuesday and welcome back to PI , where we’re grateful that Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce decided to drop the news of their engagement on one of our days off. What’s going on out there? Add Caitlin on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 and email her at [email protected] , and you can add Daniel on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email Daniel at [email protected] . And follow us on X : @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns .

FIRST IN PI: As D.C. turns to the implementation phase of Republicans’ new tax and spending law, Avoq has brought on veteran tax lobbyist Jeff Levey as a senior adviser. Levey spent the past 16 years shaping tax policy and advising clients at Washington Council Ernst & Young , where he was a managing director. Before that, he spent more than a dozen years as head of tax policy for Citi .

SPEAKING OF PERMITTING REFORM: API has launched a seven-figure ad campaign to press lawmakers on updating permitting rules — an issue nearing “Infrastructure Week” status in terms of having broad bipartisan support but little concrete action.

— The ad blitz, which will include digital, cable and podcast spots in addition to billboards around D.C., nods to Washington’s lip service on the issue by featuring clips of every American president dating back to Jimmy Carter calling for U.S. energy independence and urging Congress to “pass permitting reform now.”

— Meanwhile more than 500 local and national trade associations (including API, IPAA and the AGA) have signed on to a Chamber letter calling on lawmakers “to enact durable legislation this fall that reflects the urgency and opportunity” for a bipartisan, comprehensive permitting overhaul.

— Koch-backed Americans for Prosperity is joining the push by pouring seven figures into its own permitting campaign. It kicked off today with a supportive video message from House Majority Leader Steve Scalise .

— AFP will criss-cross the country to hold events and rallies at sites where local energy projects “have been hit with delays as a result of red tape” and will run ads highlighting the need for reforms — without which America risks falling behind, AFP says in its first spot .

WHAT ELSE IS ON THE AGENDA: Did we say sprint? Washington’s to-do list for the next three months might feel more like a marathon, starting with the government funding deadline at the end of September. Precision Strategies ’ Mike Spahn , Matt Williams and Henry Connelly have a helpful guide for navigating the congressional calendar that runs down some of the top unanswered questions heading into the spending fight.

— Their guide also previews a handful of other issues that will be simmering in the background — from the potential for bipartisan action on permitting, tech accountability and the must-pass NDAA to a possible second reconciliation bill; trade action; and as-yet-to-be-determined fallout from redistricting, economic volatility and the wrangling over the Epstein files.

— Among their advice? “Keeping your priorities moving forward — or keeping them off the menu — requires proactive engagement to maintain pressure on lawmakers and Congressional Leadership,” the memo notes.

FLYING IN: “Evangelical Christians who made an alliance with President Donald Trump to end abortion rights are now seeing how much it’s cost one of their other priorities ,” POLITICO ’s Carmen Paun reports: caring for the poor.

— “Trump’s decision to pull back hundreds of millions in foreign aid and shutter the agency that dispensed it have proven costly to evangelicals who run some of the many nonprofits that have long partnered with the U.S. government to provide help to countries that don’t have enough food.”

— “Eager to see assistance flowing again, the National Association of Evangelicals will take its concerns to Capitol Hill after lawmakers return this week from their summer break. The lobbying campaign by the association’s 40 Christian denominations marks a rare policy split with Trump. Its success or failure will show whether evangelicals have enough clout to convince GOP lawmakers loyal to Trump to cross him.”

MAHA’S NEXT FIGHT: “A White House call to curtail the marketing of unhealthy food to children would be vulnerable to industry lobbying that killed previous government efforts,” nutrition and public health experts tell Reuters’ Waylon Cunningham and Samantha Marshak .

— According to drafts of an upcoming report from the Make America Healthy Again Commission led by HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. , the Trump administration will criticize “the food industry for annually spending ‘billions’ on ‘targeted marketing of unhealthy foods to children via television and social media,’” and is expected to direct federal agencies to look into “potential industry guidelines” that would limit such advertising.

— Top food conglomerates have already “beefed up [their] lobbying since Trump took office in January. Companies have sought to push the White House and other officials on policies such as children’s nutrition programs, packaging label rules and the upcoming commission report, according to lobbying disclosures.”

WHAT WE WERE READING OVER THE BREAK

— “ For targets of Trump’s retribution, this is the lawyer on speed dial ,” by Daniel Barnes.

— “ Trump Family Amasses $5 Billion Fortune After Crypto Launch ,” by The Wall Street Journal ’s Angus Berwick .

— “ Trump’s Lobbying Probe May Chill Critics, Ethics Watchdogs Warn ,” by Bloomberg ’s Kate Ackley .

— “ Health care giants are pushing hard for Congress to extend ACA insurance subsidies ,” by Stat News ’ Daniel Payne .

— “ Taxes, Psychedelics, Crypto: Kyrsten Sinema Sees Opportunity Under Trump ,” by WSJ’s Eliza Collins and Richard Rubin .

— “ DOJ drops charges against another client of AG Pam Bondi’s brother Brad ,” by ABC News ’ Olivia Rubin , Alexander Mallin and Lucien Bruggeman .

— “ A Dark Money Group Is Secretly Funding High-Profile Democratic Influencers ,” by Wired ’s Taylor Lorenz .

— “ Super PAC aims to drown out AI critics in midterms, with $100M and counting ,” by The Washington Post ’s Nitasha Tiku , Will Oremus and Elizabeth Dwoskin .

Jobs report

— Alex Keeton is joining the Association for Accessible Medicines as executive director of the Biosimilars Council and senior vice president of policy for AAM. Keeton was most recently vice president of pharmacy care services at UnitedHealth Group and is a Biotechnology Innovation Organization and America’s Health Insurance Plans alum.

— The Association for Consumer Debt Relief has tapped Michael Lukso as head of government affairs. He was previously director for the Americas on Kraken ’s policy and government relations team and is an American Investment Council alum.

— Lawren Geer is joining Servier as associate director of policy and public affairs. She previously was senior director of federal policy at the McManus Group .

— Stuart Holliday will be senior vice president and chief public affairs officer at Lockheed Martin . He currently is CEO of Meridian International Center .

— Courtney Cox has been named a partner and managing director of public affairs at the Moore Agency .

— Advantage Inc. has hired Dee Stewart as a partner. Stewart previously directed the political operation of former Rep. Patrick McHenry (R-N.C.) and is the owner of The Stewart Group and co-owner of Strategic Partners Solutions .

— Evan Williams is joining the Investment Company Institute as senior government affairs officer. He comes to ICI from the Chamber’s Center for Capital Markets Competitiveness , where he was a vice president.

— Helen Dwight is joining The Picard Group as senior director of health policy. She was previously at AstraZeneca and Otsuka .

Trade boss shuffle

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO and DANIEL BARNES 

09/02/2025 06:24 PM EDT

Presented by

With Daniel Lippman

MOVERS AND SHAKERS: A trio of powerful downtown trade groups are heading into the end-of-year sprint in Washington with new leaders. NCTA – The Internet & Television Association has tapped former Sen. Cory Gardner to be its next president and CEO, beginning later this month.

— Gardner will step down as chair of the Senate Leadership Fund for the new role. He will remain on the board of the Senate GOP’s super PAC after overseeing the transfer of power from allies of outgoing GOP leader Mitch McConnell to those of new GOP leader John Thune.

— Gardner’s post with NCTA, whose members include Charter Communications, Comcast and Cox Communications, isn’t his first gig downtown. The Colorado Republican has worked with a number of trade groups since leaving office in 2021, including serving as the chief political strategist for the Crypto Council for Innovation.

— He was also an adviser to the National Cannabis Roundtable (which merged with another advocacy group earlier this year to become the U.S. Cannabis Roundtable) and has been a member of the board of Michael Best Strategies.

— Meanwhile the Independent Petroleum Association of America, which represents smaller oil and gas producers, announced this morning that Edith Naegele will join the trade group later this month, amid a feverish lobbying campaign by the energy industry for Congress to pass a permitting overhaul by the end of the year.

— Naegele is currently vice president for membership and strategic development at the American Gas Association, and before that she spent 18 years with the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

— And over at the Financial Services Forum — whose members include JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Citigroup, Goldman Sachs, Morgan Stanley, BNY Mellon and State Street — Amanda Eversole has taken over for Kevin Fromer as president and chief executive of the Wall Street group. Eversole was previously chief advocacy officer at the American Petroleum Institute.

FIRST IN PI: As D.C. turns to the implementation phase of Republicans’ new tax and spending law, Avoq has brought on veteran tax lobbyist Jeff Levey as a senior adviser. Levey spent the past 16 years shaping tax policy and advising clients at Washington Council Ernst & Young, where he was a managing director. Before that, he spent more than a dozen years as head of tax policy for Citi.

SPEAKING OF PERMITTING REFORM: API has launched a seven-figure ad campaign to press lawmakers on updating permitting rules — an issue nearing “Infrastructure Week” status in terms of having broad bipartisan support but little concrete action.

— The ad blitz, which will include digital, cable and podcast spots in addition to billboards around D.C., nods to Washington’s lip service on the issue by featuring clips of every American president dating back to Jimmy Carter calling for U.S. energy independence and urging Congress to “pass permitting reform now.”

— Meanwhile more than 500 local and national trade associations (including API, IPAA and the AGA) have signed on to a Chamber letter calling on lawmakers “to enact durable legislation this fall that reflects the urgency and opportunity” for a bipartisan, comprehensive permitting overhaul.

— Koch-backed Americans for Prosperity is joining the push by pouring seven figures into its own permitting campaign. It kicked off today with a supportive video message from House Majority Leader Steve Scalise.

— AFP will criss-cross the country to hold events and rallies at sites where local energy projects “have been hit with delays as a result of red tape” and will run ads highlighting the need for reforms — without which America risks falling behind, AFP says in its first spot.

WHAT ELSE IS ON THE AGENDA: Did we say sprint? Washington’s to-do list for the next three months might feel more like a marathon, starting with the government funding deadline at the end of September. Precision Strategies’ Mike Spahn, Matt Williams and Henry Connelly have a helpful guide for navigating the congressional calendar that runs down some of the top unanswered questions heading into the spending fight.

— Their guide also previews a handful of other issues that will be simmering in the background — from the potential for bipartisan action on permitting, tech accountability and the must-pass NDAA to a possible second reconciliation bill; trade action; and as-yet-to-be-determined fallout from redistricting, economic volatility and the wrangling over the Epstein files.

— Among their advice? “Keeping your priorities moving forward — or keeping them off the menu — requires proactive engagement to maintain pressure on lawmakers and Congressional Leadership,” the memo notes.

FLYING IN: “Evangelical Christians who made an alliance with President Donald Trump to end abortion rights are now seeing how much it’s cost one of their other priorities,” POLITICO’s Carmen Paun reports: caring for the poor.

— “Trump’s decision to pull back hundreds of millions in foreign aid and shutter the agency that dispensed it have proven costly to evangelicals who run some of the many nonprofits that have long partnered with the U.S. government to provide help to countries that don’t have enough food.”

— “Eager to see assistance flowing again, the National Association of Evangelicals will take its concerns to Capitol Hill after lawmakers return this week from their summer break. The lobbying campaign by the association’s 40 Christian denominations marks a rare policy split with Trump. Its success or failure will show whether evangelicals have enough clout to convince GOP lawmakers loyal to Trump to cross him.”

MAHA’S NEXT FIGHT: “A White House call to curtail the marketing of unhealthy food to children would be vulnerable to industry lobbying that killed previous government efforts,” nutrition and public health experts tell Reuters’ Waylon Cunningham and Samantha Marshak.

— According to drafts of an upcoming report from the Make America Healthy Again Commission led by HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., the Trump administration will criticize “the food industry for annually spending ‘billions’ on ‘targeted marketing of unhealthy foods to children via television and social media,’” and is expected to direct federal agencies to look into “potential industry guidelines” that would limit such advertising.

— Top food conglomerates have already “beefed up [their] lobbying since Trump took office in January. Companies have sought to push the White House and other officials on policies such as children’s nutrition programs, packaging label rules and the upcoming commission report, according to lobbying disclosures.”

title: Merck hires Ballard
body_text:
MERCK ADDS MORE LOBBYING FIREPOWER: Merck has retained Ballard Partners to lobby on issues related to drug pricing and tariffs — the drugmaker’s fourth new outside lobbying hire so far this year. Merck was one of more than a dozen pharmaceutical companies put on notice by the White House in July that they were not sufficiently complying with President Donald Trump ’s directive to tie their products’ prices to those in other countries.

— Ballard’s Brian Ballard , Hunter Morgen and Alison Anway began lobbying for Merck days before Trump’s warnings went out, according to a disclosure filing. Merck has brought on three other new firms already this year, including The Nickles Group and Harbinger Strategies .

— The drugmaker reported spending a quarterly record of nearly $5 million on lobbying from April through June, during which time congressional Republicans included a key delay from Medicare drug price negotiations for one of Merck’s drugs in their reconciliation package. But Trump also threatened in July to hit drug manufacturers with a 200 percent tariff on U.S. imports — a levy that has yet to come to fruition but which Trump ratcheted up to 250 percent last month .

— Merck’s surge in lobbying spending this year coincides with the arrival of Robert F. Kennedy Jr. to oversee the nation’s health care apparatus. The HHS secretary previously helped orchestrate litigation against Merck over alleged safety concerns stemming from Merck’s HPV vaccine. A trial over the allegations, which Merck has denied, was suspended following Kennedy’s confirmation .

FIRST IN PI: Kent Knutson is leaving his full-time role as chief government affairs officer at Shein , Daniel L. reports, marking another blow to the e-commerce giant’s lobbying footprint after the loss of a trade loophole key to its U.S. business model.

— Shein previously cut ties with all seven of its outside lobbying firms after Trump moved to shut down the de minimis exemption, which allowed the Asian fast fashion giant and rivals like Temu to import vast quantities of low-value goods duty-free.

— Shein spent $3.9 million on federal lobbying in 2024, and the company appeared likely to spend roughly the same amount this year, dropping $940,000 on lobbying in the first quarter of 2025. But those expenditures plunged to $510,000 in Q2, according to disclosure filings.

— Knutson, who joined Shein in 2024 to lead its growing D.C. office, will remain with the company as an adviser to executive chair Donald Tang .

GELLIE LANDS AT PILLSBURY: Jennifer Gellie , who steered the Justice Department’s FARA Unit during a pivotal moment in DOJ’s crackdown on illicit foreign influence campaigns, has joined the white shoe law and lobbying firm Pillsbury Winthrop Shaw Pittman as a partner in the international trade group.

— “Jennifer’s arrival comes at a time when being able to understand and adapt to evolving U.S. sanctions and export control policies is absolutely essential to U.S. and multinational companies as well as those based outside the U.S.,” Pillsbury Chair David Dekker said in a statement, touting Gellie as “uniquely qualified to guide clients through high-risk, high-profile national security issues.”

— Gellie left DOJ in July after nearly a decade at the department, during which she spent almost three years as head of the FARA Unit before being tapped to lead the Counterintelligence and Export Control Section. Under Gellie, DOJ continued the aggressive enforcement posture toward foreign lobbying violations that began under former special counsel Robert Mueller and Gellie’s predecessor Brandon Van Grack .

— The department pursued several high-profile foreign influence cases during her tenure atop the FARA Unit and CES (which houses the FARA Unit) — including securing convictions against former Sen. Bob Menendez (D-N.J.) and former Fugees rapper Pras Michel .

ON THE AIRWAVES: “ PhRMA is launching a seven-figure ad campaign pushing for Congress to change 340B, which allows some health care providers to get drugs at a steep discount from manufacturers participating in Medicaid — its biggest ad campaign on the program yet,” per NOTUS ’ Taylor Giorno .

— “Taxpayers don’t directly pay for the 340B program, which is the second-largest prescription drug program administered by the federal government. Drugmakers have long hated the program, arguing that hospitals don’t pass on the savings to patients. Hospitals say the program allows them to cover the most needy in their communities, and even keep their doors open.”

— “ The PhRMA ad , which is running in Washington through the end of the year, hits hospitals for marking up prices and ‘pocketing the difference.’ PhRMA has lobbied on 340B for nearly two decades , but sees fresh momentum following state and federal investigations into the program and Republicans’ willingness this summer to cut Medicaid .”

AUTO PARTS GROUP ACQUIRES OFF-ROADING LOBBY: The Specialty Equipment Market Association , which represents the automotive aftermarket sector, is merging with another industry group that represents a fast-growing part of the market. SEMA has acquired the Off-Road Business Association , which represents off-road and powersports industries such as motorcycles, ATVs and snowmobiles.

— ORBA’s members already make up the largest segment of the aftermarket auto parts market, according to SEMA. And the two groups’ advocacy work at the state and federal level has many overlaps, said SEMA spokesperson Matt Daigle , making the decision to join forces and bring the off-road lobby under the SEMA umbrella a no-brainer.

OH BABY: The Heritage Foundation “is set to propose sweeping revisions to U.S. economic policy meant to encourage married heterosexual couples to have more children ,” The Washington Post ’s Jacob Bogage reports.

— The conservative think tank “wants lawmakers to create new government-seeded savings accounts” for married couples only, part of an effort Heritage is framing as a “Manhattan Project” to nudge couples to have more children and “restore the nuclear family.”

— Heritage is hoping to “steer funding for child care away from programs like Head Start and toward individual families — specifically to encourage parents to stay home and rear children,” WaPo reports. “And the group wants Trump to issue executive orders requiring all proposed policies and regulations to ‘measure their positive or negative impacts on marriage and family’ — then overhaul or end programs that score poorly.”

— Hannah Matesic is now an assistant vice president for government affairs at the Association of American Railroads . She most recently was deputy assistant secretary for congressional affairs at DOT and is a Virginia Foxx and Bill Shuster alum.

— Chris Brown is joining the XR Association as vice president of public policy. He most recently was an adviser and interim executive director at the Association of Value Airlines and is a National Air Carrier Association and Airlines for America alum.

— Chris Burgoyne is now a consultant at Vox Public Affairs , advising clients on political strategy, PAC optimization and stakeholder engagement. He previously was senior vice president of government and political affairs at the American Hotel & Lodging Association and is a UnitedHealth Group , Scott Brown and Charlie Baker alum.

— Dave Dorey is now a partner at Fisher Phillips . He was previously a partner at Liff, Walsh & Simmons and is an alum of the first Trump administration.

— Patrick Velliky is joining HaloMD as chief external affairs officer and senior vice president for government affairs. He most recently served as senior vice president of government affairs at Envision Healthcare .

— Rachel Pollock is now vice president for government relations at the Society of Thoracic Surgeons . She previously was vice president for external affairs at Arnold Ventures and is an NIH and HHS alum.

— Pinpoint Policy Institute has named Eric Ventimiglia as its new executive director. Ventimiglia was most recently a research director with America Rising .

— Zac Rutherford is joining Crossroads Treatment Centers as vice president of government affairs. He was most recently chief of staff to Rep. Diana Harshbarger (R-Tenn.).

— Taylor Tougaw is now director of government affairs at the American Conservation Coalition Action . He previously was senior policy adviser at the Congressional Western Caucus .

— Katherine Bowles is now senior vice president and chief of staff at the Export-Import Bank. She previously was a professional staffer on the Senate Appropriations State-Foreign Operations Subcommittee, and is a Richard Shelby and Wilson Center alum.

— Ziad Ojakli has joined the board of trustees of Howard University . He was previously executive vice president of government operations at Boeing .

title: Big Law hiring spree
body_text:
ANNALS OF REVOLVING DOORS: A trio of former high-ranking government lawyers found new homes in Big Law today, the latest in a busy week of hiring for firms across Washington.

— Covington & Burling , Holland & Knight and Eversheds Sutherland announced new partners joining the firms from the Justice Department, Treasury Department and Commerce Department, respectively. And just yesterday, Wiley Rein and Perkins Coie announced new partners joining from the Department of Agriculture and Treasury’s Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

— Fresh off a nearly 30-year career at DOJ, Michael Granston will chair Covington’s false claims act investigations and litigation practice group. The move marks a homecoming for Granston, who was an associate at Covington in the 90s before entering government. After three decades climbing the ranks at Main Justice, Granston finished his government career as the assistant attorney general for the civil division’s commercial litigation branch.

— Over at Holland & Knight, sanctions expert Stephanie Connor has joined the firm’s international trade group from Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control. Connor will help clients navigate sanctions and regulations she helped develop while serving as that office’s assistant director of policy and assistant chief counsel.

— Wrapping up today’s Big Law announcements was the news that Blake Roberts has been appointed the new co-lead of the congressional investigations practice at Eversheds Sutherland. Roberts comes to the firm from Commerce, where he served as the principal deputy general counsel handling congressional oversight of the department.

— Today’s bundle of announcements brings the total number of former feds joining Big Law this week to at least five (that PI is aware of). Former acting general counsel of the USDA Mary Beth Schultz joined Wiley’s food and drug practice yesterday at the same time that Perkins announced its hiring of former acting senior deputy comptroller and chief counsel Ted Dowd .

title: FICO scores big-name Trump lobbyist
body_text:
FIRST IN PI — FICO VS. PULTE: Credit score generator Fair Isaac Corp. , or FICO, has hired Republican lobbyist Jeff Miller of Miller Strategies as the company continues to gear up for what promises to be sustained pressure from Federal Housing Finance Agency Director Bill Pulte . Trump-world political consultant Arthur Schwartz has also been hired to represent the interests of the company, two people who were granted anonymity because they were not authorized to discuss the hires told PI.

— Back in July , PI brought you the news that FICO had signed John McMickle of North South Government Relations to lobby on issues related to competition in credit scores and had significantly increased its own lobbying spending. That signing came as FICO stock, which is currently down 23 percent this year, had already plummeted in the wake of Pulte’s social media attacks.

— Miller and Schwartz both have close ties to the White House. Miller is a top Trump fundraiser who served as finance chair for both Trump inaugural committees. Schwartz is a top adviser to Donald Trump Jr. and a confidant of Vice President JD Vance .

— Pulte, who has garnered headlines for his referrals of New York Attorney General Letitia James , Sen. Adam Schiff and Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook for prosecution on mortgage fraud charges, has been going after FICO with equal vigor since May. He calls the company a “monopoly” and is using his position atop the U.S. mortgage market to implement policies that threaten the FICO’s dominance in the mortgage underwriting space.

— “We have been accused of raising our prices, and it’s true we have, but they’re still very very small relative to what we offer,” FICO CEO Will Lansing said on CNBC when asked about Pulte’s criticisms.

— Pulte has repeatedly accused FICO of using underhand tactics to influence his decision making, such as threatening regulators and using “ unregistered lobbyists .” The FHFA did not respond to questions about which individuals and what conduct Pulte was referring to in those posts.

— Schwartz was recently in the news for his involvement in an unorthodox lobbying campaign that succeeded in convincing Justice Department officials to settle an antitrust lawsuit against tech company Hewlett Packard Enterprise on the eve of trial. Schwartz, MAGA-judicial whisperer Mike Davis and former Justice Department chief of staff Will Levi were all involved in the effort to settle the case, which resulted in the firing of two top DOJ antitrust officials who disagreed with the decision.

— Despite Schwartz’s involvement and Pulte’s characterization of FICO as a monopoly, there’s no indication of an antitrust investigation into the company. FICO did not respond to a request for comment.

IF IT’S SEPTEMBER: College football is back and as the season gets underway, many political questions about the future of college athletics remain unanswered. The Big Ten Conference has hired Tommy Binion of OnMessage Public Strategies to lobby on issues related to college athletics and name, image and likeness rights, according to a newly filed disclosure report .

— Earlier this year, a federal court approved a settlement establishing a new system for schools to directly pay student-athletes a portion of sports revenue in addition to creating stricter guidelines around NIL deals involving third parties.

— But as POLITICO’s Gregory Svirnovskiy reported last week , questions remain about the labor rights of student athletes. President Donald Trump signed an executive order earlier this year that mandates additional scholarships for non-revenue generating sports and instructs the Labor Department to clarify the employment status of student-athletes. The House is currently considering a bill that would prevent student-athletes from being classified as employees.

PUT A CORK IN IT: Wine producers have something to toast to after securing an exemption for cork products to the 15 percent tariff on E.U. goods, Dee-Ann Durbin and Barry Hatton report for the Associated Press .

— “The cork carve-out was vital for Portugal. The European country is the world’s largest cork producer, accounting for about half of global production…Portuguese diplomats lobbied for the exemption on both sides of the Atlantic. Patrick Spencer , the executive director of the U.S.-based Natural Cork Council , raced from Salem, Oregon, to Washington, in June to explain cork’s origins to U.S. trade officials and to seek a tariff reprieve. The Wine Institute , which represents California vintners, said that it also pushed for the special dispensation.”

— “The U.S. is the second-largest market for Portuguese cork after France. In 2023, the U.S. imported $241 million worth of cork from Portugal; just over 70% of it came in the form of stoppers for wine, spirits, olive oil, honey and other liquids.”

TECH CEOS PRAISE TRUMP: Yesterday PI included a statement from the Tech Oversight Project raining on the parade of Big Tech CEOs headed to the White House to dine with the president on the newly remodeled Rose Garden patio. Turns out the weather took that literally, as the event had to be moved indoors due to storms.

— But the rain didn’t stop the CEOs of OpenAI, Apple, Meta, Alphabet and more from lavishing praise on Trump for his pro-business policies and focus on American tech innovation, according to Katherine Bunt , Meridith McGraw and Meghan Bobrowsky of The Wall Street Journal .

Jobs report

Kathleen Shannon , a veteran of the first Trump White House, is now a partner at Boies Schiller Flexner . She was most recently a partner at Blank Rome .

Michael Huneke is now a partner at Morgan Lewis . He joins the firm from Hughes Hubbard & Reed where he was co-chair of the sanctions, export controls and anti-money laundering practice group.

Monica Trauzzi has joined the Smart Electric Power Alliance as chief comms officer. She was most recently senior director of energy and climate public affairs and strategic comms at Invariant .

Former deputy undersecretary for food, nutrition and consumer services at USDA Cindy Long is now a national advisor at Manatt, Phelps & Phillips .

GrayRobinson has promoted Elizabeth Blair Hancock from government affairs consultant to senior government affairs adviser.

Alexander Ciccone has joined the National Taxpayers Union as policy and government affairs manager. He was previously a senior analyst at America Rising Corporation working on rapid-response comms for political campaigns.

Google has added Lauren Fine to its global communications and public affairs team working on policy comms. She is a veteran of House Majority Leader Steve Scalise ’s office, where she has served as communications director and other roles for nearly nine years.

TENCENT TAPS MCENTEE TO GET OFF PENTAGON BLACKLIST: Johnny McEntee , who served in multiple roles during the first Trump administration, including as head of the Office of Presidential Personnel as well as President Donald Trump ’s body man, has registered to lobby for the first time, according to a newly filed disclosure.

— The U.S. arm of Chinese tech giant Tencent , which owns the popular messaging app WeChat , hired the former White House aide in July for help addressing an “erroneous trade restriction designation,” the disclosure shows.

— In January, Tencent was one of several notable companies added to a Pentagon blacklist for companies linked to the Chinese military . Tencent has maintained that its inclusion was a “mistake.” The blacklisting was one of the final acts of the Biden administration, but Tencent didn’t have better luck during Trump’s first term, when Trump tried to ban WeChat.

— So the WeChat owner has been stocking up on GOP lobbyists. In April, Tencent hired former Trump adviser Bryan Lanza , former Sen. David Vitter and John Lonergan of Mercury Public Affairs . In June, they inked six-figure contracts with Republican lobbyist Marty Obst and former Trump aide Rob Goad of MO Strategies , as well as Republican Aaron Cutler of Hogan Lovells . Tencent also retains Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck , where GOP fundraiser Marc Lampkin is among the company’s lobbyists.

— Tencent’s blacklisting also made it a bit player in this year’s fight for FCC approval of the merger between Skydance Media and Paramount . In a complaint earlier this year, conservative media watchdog Center for American Rights flagged what it said were “serious questions” about “Skydance Media’s ties to the Chinese Communist Party” stemming from Tencent’s investment in the company years earlier.

— Skydance downplayed Tencent’s role with the new company and the prospect for “undue foreign influence” in a meeting with FCC Chair Brendan Carr days before the merger’s approval. Those reassurances seemed to resonate with the regulator, which said in its decision that while it treats the Pentagon blacklist “with utmost seriousness,” it did not “view Tencent’s ownership stake as raising sufficient national security concerns to alter our conclusions.”

DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED —OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

A LOOK AT THE QATARI LOBBY: In the years since Trump was first elected president — when he cheered the 2017 blockade of Qatar by powerful neighbors Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates — the Qatari government has built a Washington lobbying behemoth that has spent nearly $250 million on lobbying and PR firms, according to a new analysis from Ben Freeman and Nick Cleveland-Stout of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft .

— The blockade was eventually resolved diplomatically, but the experience was a “wake-up call” for Qatar of how important it is to invest heavily in Washington influence, Freeman and Cleveland-Stout write. body_text:
FIRST IN PI: Credit unions have been breathing a sigh of relief since GOP lawmakers spared the sector’s tax-exempt status from becoming a pay-for in their megabill this summer at the behest of rival lenders like community banks. But the incoming head of the industry’s main trade group, America’s Credit Unions , isn’t letting his guard down in Washington.

— “You said a ‘victory’ as though it’s concluded, and I don’t think it has,” Scott Simpson said in an interview on the sidelines of the group’s Congressional Caucus conference in Washington this week.

— Simpson will take over as ACU’s president and CEO in November from the group’s longtime leader, former Rep. Jim Nussle , who announced his retirement in April. Simpson is currently president and CEO of the California Credit Union League and Nevada’s Credit Unions in addition to serving as CEO of Utah’s Credit Union Association .

— “The No. 1 priority is to try to defend and enhance a business model that has had to struggle for its existence and survival from the very beginning,” Simpson told PI.

— Banks are readying for their latest showdown with the retail lobby and Sens. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) and Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) over swipe fee legislation. It’s those kinds of fast-moving efforts that can trip lobbying efforts up the most, Simpson argued.

— “Whenever tax policy may be considered germane to a topic, we’re going to have to pay attention to it. And it becomes germane when the voting threshold goes to” 51 in the Senate.

— The swipe fees bill falls under that category, he argued. But “there are any number of those that we have to be vigilant about.”

— ACU is also looking ahead to next year’s midterms. They’re preparing to financially back candidates who defended credit unions’ tax exemption, including vulnerable GOP incumbents like Reps. Young Kim of California and Celeste Maloy of Utah. “We’ve had a bunch of people that walked out on limbs for us in budget reconciliation, Simpson said, and “we’re going to make sure that they feel that we saw that.”

— Outside of Congress, credit unions are focused on chipping away at burdensome regulations and compliance regimes that Simpson said disproportionately impact his members. They leave lenders left with “one arm behind their back” as they try to compete against deep-pocketed — and increasingly influential — financial upstarts like cryptocurrency and “the wild frontier that is fintech.”

— ACU would also like to see a package of CFPB reforms , though Simpson conceded that’s a tall ask with Republicans looking to kill the agency.

— CFPB’s fate isn’t the only big regulatory question mark facing credit unions, after President Donald Trump fired two Democratic appointees to the independent National Credit Union Administration back in April. A federal district judge ruled in July that the removals were illegal, but an appeals court temporarily halted the appointees’ reinstatement days later. All of this, of course, has been unfolding against the backdrop of Trump’s saber rattling about the Fed .

— “The uncertainty is uncomfortable for us. There’s no question about that,” Simpson told PI. “[We] love an independent, fully constituted regulatory environment.”

— That carefully worded response is consistent with a sector that’s eager to stay above the fray. “I think credit unions are, by and large, ducking their heads and operating their credit unions, serving their members, and … welcoming relief whenever they can get it,” said Simpson.

WHY CAN’T WE BE FRIENDS?: The left-leaning tech lobby Chamber for Progress “is launching a new initiative to strengthen the frayed relationship between Democrats and Silicon Valley ahead of the 2026 midterm elections,” per Bloomberg ’s Emily Birnbaum .

Democrats in turn could benefit from Silicon Valley’s ample financial resources if relations improve, said Dave Vorland , who was hired to lead the effort and previously worked in the Defense Department during the Joe Biden and Barack Obama administrations.”

— It “will focus on ‘resetting’ the conversation about tech within the Democratic party” after four years of clashes with the Biden administration over antitrust and concerns about the threats posed by artificial intelligence drove Silicon Valley powerplayers to the right. “The project aims to produce proposals for a more tech-friendly Democratic policy agenda and advise the party’s policymakers about how to talk about the industry.”

It stops short of restrictions on pesticide use, focusing instead on changes like reforming FDA regulatory pathways, investigating food ingredients, modernizing American vaccines and improving the childhood vaccine schedule.”

— “In some areas, it advances long-held industry priorities that public health advocates say could increase the very health risks that have fueled the MAHA movement, such as accelerating reviews of new chemicals.”

— In all, the blueprint “represents a significant win for the farm industry,” which lobbied hard for the White House to rein in HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his “goal to crack down on common agriculture production practices.” Some of Kennedy’s allies in the MAHA movement saw the report that way as well, complaining that the report didn’t go far enough in cracking down on industry.

FLYING IN: The newly launched small business coalition DefendSBIR kicked off a two-day fly-in today. More than two dozen small technology firms are hitting the Hill to press lawmakers to reauthorize the expiring Small Business Innovation Research and Small Business Technology Transfer programs ahead of their expiration at the end of the month — while bucking proposed caps on funding for awardees with multiple grants.

— As the House Small Business Committee advanced a clean one-year extension of the program this afternoon, leaders of 28 small businesses from 10 different states are slated to hold more than 40 meetings with lawmakers and staff today and tomorrow — including the top Democrats on the House and Senate Small Business panels — to call for a clean, longer-term fix.

— Growth Energy , which represents the ethanol industry, is flying in this week as well to urge lawmakers to support year-round sales of E15 fuel, as well as the clean fuel production credit, the Renewable Fuel Standard and trade issues. Participants are set to have more than 200 meetings with lawmakers in both chambers across 36 states.

— Members of Stronger America Through Seafood are in town as well to promote the expansion of aquaculture in the U.S. Companies including Cargill , Cuna del Mar , Fortune Fish & Gourmet , Innovasea , Manna Fish Farms , Sysco and Zeigler — along with trade groups like the American Soybean Association , National Fisheries Institute and Soy Aquaculture Alliance — will work to rally support for the bipartisan Marine Aquaculture Research for America Act, which aims to cut red tape and boost the aquaculture industry.

IRS’LL BE YOUR SHELTER : “The Trump administration is quietly dismantling efforts by the Internal Revenue Service to shut down a slew of aggressive tax shelters used by America’s biggest multinational companies and wealthiest people,” The New York Times’ Jesse Drucker reports.

— “The administration, bowing to pressure from industry groups, right-wing activists and congressional Republicans, is quickly rolling back several I.R.S. law enforcement efforts, including one aimed at a lucrative tax shelter used by companies like Occidental Petroleum and AT&T .”

PERMIT ME: The American Petroleum Institute , the oil and gas industry’s leading lobby group, is urging Congress to pass comprehensive bipartisan legislation reform this year — even if it means renewable energy projects benefit too, Morning Energy reports.

— The Trump administration and Republicans have delivered major policy wins to the fossil fuel industry. But API argues that all will be for naught unless lawmakers make it easier to build energy projects of all types to satisfy the voracious appetite for electricity expected from AI data centers.

— “This isn’t just an oil and gas issue, it is an issue for every energy source and almost every industry,” API President and CEO Mike Sommers told Josh in an interview. “If we can’t build things again, there is no chance that this country is going to be able to beat China in the race for the AI future.”

— API has outlined its priorities for a permitting bill in a new policy roadmap , including expedited permitting reviews, restrictions on legal challenges under NEPA and changes to Clean Water Act reviews to make it harder for states to reject pipeline projects. The roadmap also calls out the need for reforms to ease the buildout of interstate transmission lines — the top priority of Democrats and clean energy advocates — in any deal.

EVERYTHING IS HAPPENING IN NEW YORK: Strategic comms firm Narrative Strategies is setting up shop in New York. Caleb Barnhart and Graham Newhall will join the firm as managing directors to lead the new Manhattan office, which CEO Ken Spain said will enable the firm to better serve the slew of clients headquartered there. This will be Narrative’s second office outside D.C. following an outpost in West Palm Beach that opened last year.

— Before joining Narrative, Barnhart served as a senior vice president at Sloane & Company . He’s also a Weber Shandwick and Hill + Knowlton Strategies alum. Newhall most recently served as a strategic communications and media adviser for a handful of crypto advocacy groups, including the DeFi Education Fund , Blockchain Association , and Apiary .

Kennedy Jr. and his “goal to crack down on common agriculture production practices.” Some of Kennedy’s allies in the MAHA movement saw the report that way as well, complaining that the report didn’t go far enough in cracking down on industry.

More than two dozen small technology firms are hitting the Hill to press lawmakers to reauthorize the expiring Small Business Innovation Research and Small Business Technology Transfer programs ahead of their expiration at the end of the month — while bucking proposed caps on funding for awardees with multiple grants.

title: The outside group influencing Trump’s AI policy
body_text:
By CAITLIN OPRYSKO , DANIEL LIPPMAN and DANIEL BARNES

09/10/2025 06:20 PM EDT

Presented by

FIRST IN PI — FAI’S FINGERPRINTS ON TRUMP’S AI POLICIES: As the Trump administration forges ahead with plans to implement AI in the federal government, one outside group with direct ties to the White House is proving to be a major force: the Foundation for American Innovation , Daniel L. reports.

— One sign of its influence came this spring when the Office of Management and Budget issued new memos concerning the government’s use of AI, as well as instructions on AI policy that Trump officials had given to the National Institute of Standards and Technology .

— Aspects of both directives had parallels with recommendations that FAI put out last year and with public statements from an FAI fellow-turned Trump White House staffer, Dean Ball . Ball said last year that AI safety guidance from the Biden administration pushed “a progressive cultural agenda on AI,” such as trying to mitigate racial and other biases and reduce inequality.

— The Trump administration eliminated the U.S. Artificial Intelligence Safety Institute’s focus on “AI safety” and instead ordered researchers to focus on enabling “human flourishing and economic competitiveness.”

— And in line with FAI’s recommendations, OMB now promotes the use of AI pilot projects across the government.

— OMB also removed Biden-era language that called for “minimum practices when using safety-impacting AI and rights-impacting AI” — something FAI had explicitly called for.

— Those are just a few of the examples. FAI’s imprint was also on some of DOGE’s early initiatives.

— There are a few key links between FAI and the administration. Michael Kratsios , who heads the Office of Science and Technology Policy, is a former board member of FAI. Also noteworthy: FAI was also a participant in the AI working group of the Heritage Foundation ’s Project 2025 , which has informed parts of Donald Trump ’s agenda so far.

— And Ball, a former fellow at FAI who later joined the White House, recently returned to FAI as a senior fellow. An OMB spokesperson didn’t respond to a request for comment.

— “We’re glad to see FAI’s work on improving government efficiency, procurement, and AI adoption find purchase in the Trump administration,” FAI executive director Zach Graves said in a statement to PI, adding that Ball is “a key talent working to accelerate American innovation.”

MORE PRIVATE EQUITY-FUELED CONSOLIDATION: Strategic comms and government affairs giant FGS Global is acquiring the health care lobbying shop Tarplin, Downs & Young , in the latest consolidation on K Street fueled by a rush of private equity money. The addition of TDY, which opened almost two decades ago, will grow the headcount of the combined firm’s health policy team to more than 50.

— “In the world of health care policy, their founders, partners and expertise are best in class. Full Stop,” Joel Johnson , who leads FGS’ D.C. office, told PI in a statement.

—  “Health care organizations face unprecedented, interconnected challenges, from regulatory shifts to reputational risks,” Kim James , the leader of FGS’ North America health practice, said in a statement. “Now more than ever, they need a single, integrated partner who can navigate the full spectrum of policy, communications and stakeholder dynamics.”

— A little over a year ago, FGS announced that private equity giant KKR was expanding its stake in the firm, buying out communications conglomerate WPP to become FGS’ majority shareholder.

— The firm’s union with TDY is the latest in a string of acquisitions announced by K Street businesses following an infusion of private equity cash. In 2023, lobbying firm Subject Matter acquired public affairs shop Kivvit after scoring a private equity investment. (The firms have since rebranded as Avoq .) Penta Group was formed via the merger of half a dozen other political firms in 2022 thanks to a private equity investment a year earlier.

— More recently, Monument Advocacy announced last month that it was acquiring another health lobbying shop, Horizon Government Affairs .

BALLARD ADVISING ‘BITCOIN JESUS’: Roger Ver , the wealthy crypto investor indicted on tax evasion charges last year, has enlisted some notable help for his upcoming legal fight after failing to win a presidential pardon from Trump. Ver, also known as “Bitcoin Jesus,” retained Ballard Partners this week to lobby “‘U.S. government crypto currency enforcement policy,” according to a disclosure filing.

— Founder Brian Ballard , along with Justin Sayfie , Syl Lukis and Leonard Curry, are working as subcontractors to Chris Kise & Associates , the law firm owned by former Trump defense attorney Chris Kise , who is representing Ver.

— A person familiar with the matter, granted anonymity to discuss the firm’s work, told PI that the firm isn’t lobbying for a pardon for Ver — or for anything at all. Rather, Ballard — which represents several crypto clients — is providing guidance and advising Kise on the current enforcement environment for cryptocurrency in order to help mount Ver’s defense. The firm is taking advantage of FARA’s exemption for LDA registrants given that Ver renounced his U.S. citizenship more than a decade ago, the person said.

— The hire comes on the heels of a very public pardon lobbying effort by Ver. The early Bitcoin booster was arrested last year on charges that include mail fraud and tax evasion, with prosecutors alleging that his actions had caused the IRS a $48 million loss. Ver is fighting extradition to the U.S. from Spain. Since Trump’s election last year, Ver had been dangling eight-figure paydays for lobbyists to help him secure a pardon, but the nature of this latest hire signals that Ver isn’t counting on relief any time soon.

GULF ACTION: A coalition of business leaders throughout the Gulf of Mexico is teaming up to convert the region’s economic muscle into political might in Washington. Founding members of the Gulf South Business Roundtable include energy company Entergy Corporation and its subsidiaries Alabama Power Company , Kinder Morgan and Mitsubishi Power Americas . Entergy’s John Hudson and Alabama Power’s Jeff Peoples will co-chair the Roundtable, while Ben Portis will serve as its executive director.

— “This region and these five states are an economic powerhouse, contributing massively to the national economy,” Hudson said in a statement. “It’s time the Gulf South gets the global recognition it deserves that will enhance the economic vitality of the area.”

ANNALS OF FUNDRAISING: “Seventeen Democratic members of Congress are demanding the president’s inaugural committee formally explain financial ‘inconsistencies’ and ‘discrepancies,’ ” NOTUS ’ Dave Levinthal reports.

— “The letter to the Trump Vance Inaugural Committee , dated Sept. 10, is signed by several of President Donald Trump’s leading antagonists including Reps. Jamie Raskin , a former Trump impeachment manager; Bennie Thompson , former chairman of the Select Committee to Investigate the January 6th Attack on the U.S. Capitol; Pramila Jayapal ; Jerrold Nadler ; and Mary Gay Scanlon .”

— “NOTUS in July reported that Amazon , General Motors and Microsoft told Congress they contributed significantly more money to Trump’s 2025 inaugural committee than the inaugural committee itself publicly reported to the Federal Election Commission.”

— “Similarly, insurer USAA correctly reported to Congress that it donated $100,000 to the Trump inaugural committee from its corporate treasury, while the Trump committee erroneously told FEC regulators that it received $100,000 from USAA’s political action committee.”

— “Following NOTUS’ report, the Trump inaugural committee, which raised nearly $250 million overall to more than double Trump’s 2017 inaugural record of $107 million, amended its financial disclosure to fix the errors.”

IT’S A NEW DAWN: “In recent months, Mr. Trump has announced a series of convention-bashing moves that have expanded the economic reach of the government into corporate America, setting companies on edge,” The New York Times’ Ana Swanson writes.

— In addition to Trump’s extraordinary pact to take a nearly 10 percent stake in computing giant Intel last month, “the administration has moved to take a stake in U.S. Steel and in a rare earths producer, MP Materials . Officials have suggested that the United States could take shares in other industries like defense and shipbuilding.”

— One of the key architects — and originators — of the proposals has been Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick , who “has an array of powerful economic levers to deploy. They include threatening to impose tariffs on goods like cars, chips and steel; halting manufacturing grants; and withholding licenses to export.”

FIRST IN PI: The Vogel Group is expanding its state-level and attorneys general practice with the additions of Brandon Smith , David Johnson and Mark Pinkert as principals. Smith, who is a former chief of staff to Tennessee AG Jonathan Skrmetti , will be based in the firm’s Nashville office.

— Johnson, who previously served as policy director and general counsel for the Republican Attorneys General Association , will open Vogel Group’s first Midwest office in Indianapolis, and Pinkert, who works for Vogel Group’s sister law firm Holtzman Vogel , will remain based in Miami.

—  “Health care organizations face unprecedented, interconnected challenges, from regulatory shifts to reputational risks,” Kim James, the leader of FGS’ North America health practice, said in a statement. “Now more than ever, they need a single, integrated partner who can navigate the full spectrum of policy, communications and stakeholder dynamics.”

— A little over a year ago, FGS announced that private equity giant KKR was expanding its stake in the firm, buying out communications conglomerate WPP to become FGS’ majority shareholder.

— The lobbying group may earn most of its publicity from its litigation efforts to overturn laws that tighten restrictions on the internet, but NetChoice spends its fair share of money in Washington as well. In the first half of this year, NetChoice spent $170,000 on outside lobbying firms to help advocate for its members on antitrust, Section 230 and privacy issues.

— A super PAC is a new move for the association that represents some of the largest (and richest) tech, social media and e-commerce companies in the world. Alibaba , Amazon , Google , Meta , Snap , X , Yahoo and YouTube are all NetChoice members. NetChoice did not respond to a request for comment on the creation of the PAC.

— A major goal of NetChoice has been protection of Section 230, a provision of the Communications Decency Act of 1996. That law immunizes websites from lawsuits stemming from content posted by users and allows website providers to moderate content without fear of civil liability.

— During a “Big-Tech censorship forum” hosted by the Justice Department’s antitrust division in April, administration officials from the FTC and FCC publicly stated their intention to pursue Section 230 reform to “smash the censorship cartel.”

— But Section 230 reform isn’t a partisan issue. Lawmakers from both parties have tried and failed to amend or repeal the law for years and both President Donald Trump and former President Joe Biden have both spoken out against the law or tried to limit its protections. The Supreme Court has so far upheld the law, but justices have indicated there are limits to its protections as technology continues to evolve.

FIRST IN PI — HIGH-TECH CONFLICT: Janet Egan , a tech and national security expert at the Center for a New American Security , last week wrote an op-ed that praised a significant technological shift by artificial intelligence company Anthropic . It was pretty standard fare except for one thing: She didn’t disclose several close connections her think tank has to the company, Daniel L. reports.

— Egan, a senior fellow and deputy director of the technology and national security program at CNAS, wrote an article Sept. 3 in Just Security applauding that Anthropic and Google had moved away from relying exclusively on Nvidia ’s chips. Now, Anthropic uses Amazon Web Services ’ hardware in addition to Google chips and some Nvidia chips.

— Unmentioned, however, was the fact that in June, CNAS CEO Richard Fontaine was named to Anthropic’s long-term benefit trust , an independent body to help Anthropic achieve its “public benefit mission.” And in August, Fontaine joined the company’s National Security and Public Sector Advisory Council , which helps the company work with governments. Anthropic’s head of global affairs, Michael Sellitto , is also an adjunct senior fellow at the think tank .

— Several major investors in the company have also donated to the think tank. Among other examples, Amazon , which has committed to invest $8 billion in Anthropic , contributed at least half a million dollars to CNAS between October 2023 and September 2024, and AWS gave between $100,000 to $250,000 to the think tank. Google, which has invested more than $3 billion in Anthropic and owns 14 percent of the company, gave between $250,000 and $500,000 to CNAS in that time period.

— Egan, a former staffer for the Australian government, did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for Anthropic declined to comment.

— “As a senior researcher at CNAS, Janet, like all our researchers, is driven by expertise, intellectual independence, and deep ongoing work that provides strong, pragmatic, and principled national security policies that serve the nation’s interest,” CNAS spokesperson David McKenzie said in a statement to PI.

— “As published on our website, CNAS funding is transparent and from a wide variety of sources,” he added. “As a research institution, CNAS maintains strict intellectual independence. Technology companies make their own investment choices into AI firms.”

— Egan is not the only foreign policy player in recent months to not disclose ties to AI companies in op-eds. PI reported last month that former Trump national security adviser Robert O’Brien wrote an op-ed criticizing the use of aggressive export controls on AI technology but didn’t disclose that his firm American Global Strategies works for Nvidia, which has pushed to export advanced chips to China.

ABA TASK FORCE FOR DEMOCRACY SPINS OFF: The American Bar Association Task Force for American Democracy issued its final report Wednesday, outlining a series of election-related reforms intended to address “the long-term systemic problems deeply rooted in our democracy” and pledging to continue its work independent of the ABA.

— Convened by the ABA in 2023, the task force initially focused on addressing low levels of trust in the democratic process ahead of the 2024 presidential election. Following Trump’s victory, the panel expanded its work to encourage adherence to the rule of law and attorney accountability. For the past two years, the task force has held listening tours across the country, featuring participation from state election officials, bar associations and law schools.

— Among the recommendations: a call to stop the partisan gerrymandering arms race via increased adoption of citizen redistricting commissions, proposed reforms to the process of hearing election-related lawsuits and a call for state bars to allow the commencement of disciplinary proceedings against current government officials.

— In an interview with PI, task force co-chair and former Secretary of Homeland Security Jeh Johnson acknowledged that reversing the trend of partisan gerrymandering would be “a steep mountain to climb” and that more work needs to be done by nonpartisan pro-democracy groups to engage younger Americans.

— To that end, the task force plans to continue its organizing work ahead of the midterm elections.

— “We concluded that there’s such interest across the country in maintaining and strengthening our democracy. … We decided we can’t just shut this down once the report is delivered,” Johnson said. “So we’re standing up a not-for-profit to continue the work, not issue another report, but to continue organizing, getting people involved, coordinating activities and so forth.”

— The Trump administration has taken a combative approach to the ABA since January, cutting off the group’s traditional access to judicial nominees and prohibiting Justice Department lawyers from attending ABA events. In June, the ABA sued the Trump administration over the president’s use of executive orders to punish law firms for past work representing his political opponents.

— “I’ve been very pleased with the responses of the ABA … in defending the judiciary and really stepping up during these challenging times,” Johnson said.

It was pretty standard fare except for one thing: She didn’t disclose several close connections her think tank has to the company, Daniel L. reports.

— Egan, a senior fellow and deputy director of the technology and national security program at CNAS, wrote an article Sept. 3 in Just Security applauding that Anthropic and Google had moved away from relying exclusively on Nvidia’s chips. Now, Anthropic uses Amazon Web Services’ hardware in addition to Google chips and some Nvidia chips.

— Unmentioned, however, was the fact that in June, CNAS CEO Richard Fontaine was named to Anthropic’s long-term benefit trust, an independent body to help Anthropic achieve its “public benefit mission.” And in August, Fontaine joined the company’s National Security and Public Sector Advisory Council, which helps the company work with governments. Anthropic’s head of global affairs, Michael Sellitto, is also an adjunct senior fellow at the think tank.

— Several major investors in the company have also donated to the think tank.
