FIRST IN PI — HOUSE JUDICIARY LAWYER REJOINS VOGEL: A top attorney for House Judiciary Chair Jim Jordan (R-Ohio) is headed back downtown to his old firm. Julian Yowell is rejoining the Vogel Group as a director after spending the last year and a half with the Judiciary panel, most recently as its counsel.

— Yowell’s portfolio on the committee included oversight of federal law enforcement agencies like DOJ and FBI and leading investigations touching on issues like national security, FARA, tech censorship and artificial intelligence. Yowell previously worked at the Vogel Group from 2021 to 2023. Yowell will also be an associate at Vogel Group’s sister law firm, Holtzman Vogel , focusing on investigations.

NEW BUSINESS: The Autonomous Vehicle Industry Association registered its first in-house lobbyist this week as Washington embarks on what may amount to the most concerted regulatory effort yet to get more driverless cars on the road.

— According to a disclosure filing, AVIA director of government affairs, Renée Gibson , registered to lobby for the trade group, whose members include Waymo , Lyft , Uber , Amazon , Zoox , FedEx , General Motors , Ford , Volvo and more. AVIA also retains Navigators Global and Venable .

— Meanwhile coconut water purveyor Vita Coco has hired Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld to help the company seek an exemption for coconut water from the Trump administration’s steep tariffs on imports from Brazil.

— The U.S. branches of a handful of foreign gun manufacturers and importers have also picked up new tariff lobbying help amid duties on both raw materials and finished products . The U.S. subsidiaries of Austria-based Glock , Brazil-based Taurus and U.S.-based importer Springfield Armory all retained Checkmate Government Relations last month to lobby on “issues related to trade and the rights guaranteed by the Second Amendment,” per disclosure filings.

ACTBLUE’S NEXT ACT: “ ActBlue is expanding beyond online fundraising by buying the Democratic digital organizing firm Impactive ,” POLITICO ’s Jessica Piper reports, in “the latest example of steps taken by ActBlue — the biggest donation processing tool for Democrats for two decades — to further expand its role in the campaign ecosystem .”

— “Impactive, formerly known as OutVote, has tools that support canvassing, phonebanking and other forms of voter outreach. … ActBlue characterized the acquisition as a step that would move the platform closer to a ‘one-stop solution’ for Democratic campaigns.”

ANOTHER W.H. PRESS AIDE CASHES IN: A second member of the White House press shop has decamped for K Street less than eight months into Trump’s second term. Alex Pfeiffer , a principal deputy communications director at the White House, left the role earlier this month to join the GOP public affairs firm Watchtower Strategy as a managing director, per Axios’ Mike Allen .

— Watchtower Strategy was started earlier this year by former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy , who serves as its chair, along with powerhouse GOP lobbyist Jeff Miller and Republican operatives Arthur Schwartz , Dan Conston , Cliff Sims and Brian O. Walsh .

— Pfeiffer has been in Trump’s orbit since 2022, working first with the president’s super PAC before joining his 2024 campaign and then the White House. He’s one of a handful of prominent West Wing aides to leave after short stints in the administration for lucrative gigs in the influence industry.

— The list includes Pfeiffer’s fellow White House comms colleague Harrison Fields , former deputy director of the Office of Presidential Personnel Trent Morse , former crypto adviser Bo Hines and former senior policy strategist May Davis Mailman .

FLYING IN: eBay CEO Jamie Iannone , along with several other eBay executives and sellers from across the country, fanned out across the Hill today for meetings with nearly three dozen lawmakers on both sides of the aisle. They included Senate Majority Leader John Thune , Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and House Energy and Commerce Chair Brett Guthrie (R-Ky.).

— The eBay delegation urged lawmakers to join the newly launched Recommerce Caucus , which promotes policies to support online sellers and technologies to strengthen trust in online marketplaces.

— The Transportation Intermediaries Association , which represents the third-party logistics industry, is flying in this week as well. TIA has more than 140 meetings on the books with offices all over the Hill to discuss ways to curb freight fraud and the upcoming surface transportation reauthorization process.

— Meanwhile the International Franchise Association wrapped up a three-day fly-in today that drew more than 400 of its members to Washington to lobby in support of a bipartisan bill to shield franchises from being considered a joint employer under the National Labor Relations Act.

— Members of the Direct Selling Association , the main trade group for multilevel marketing companies, were on the Hill today to lobby for a different labor bill that would explicitly classify direct sellers and real estate agents as independent contractors under federal labor law, amid an emerging patchwork of state laws.

— The group’s meetings included House Education and Workforce Chair Tim Walberg (R-Mich.) and staff for House Speaker Mike Johnson , and several executives also headed to the White House to meet with Trump administration officials.

ALSO IN TOWN THIS WEEK: AI startup Anthropic swept into D.C. on Monday and Tuesday for a string of events aimed at promoting the adoption of Anthropic’s products by the federal government.

— “With the scale of the company, it’s time to be a lot more public about our views in Washington,” Anthropic co-founder and policy chief Jack Clark told POLITICO ’s Gabby Miller of the unusually public lobbying blitz.

— “We found that — especially in D.C. — people had been ascribing views or actions to us that we weren’t doing or may have been slanted. We thought that we could respond by just being a lot louder and forthright and clear ourselves, including with the administration,” he said.

— Clark added: “Where we have points of disagreement, we’ve just been saying to the admin: ‘Hey, we have a different view to you here, just so you’re not surprised you should expect us to be saying this publicly.’ And similarly when we agree with them.” Read more from Clark’s chat with Gabby in today’s Morning Tech .

MEANS BUSINESS: “Dr. Casey Means , the nominee for surgeon general, promised in government filings that she would sell the stake in a company she co-founded and step away from work as an influencer promoting dietary supplements and wellness products,” the New York Times’ Christina Jewett and Benjamin Mueller report.

— Means’ confirmation hearing had been held up by her delay in filing required financial disclosures, which “detail holdings as varied as her advisory role at Levels , a company that provides glucose monitors, and family investments in tobacco and tech companies.”

— Means, a close ally of HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr ., shares Kennedy’s skepticism of the medical establishment, of which she is a former member. Means’ financial disclosures show how, “in a newsletter and in social media channels … she has monetized her worldview through payments from companies that sell supplements, home-delivered meals and other products.”

WELCOME TO THE RESISTANCE: “Over 100 largely liberal philanthropies, including those that are being targeted by the Trump administration as part of an expected crackdown after the killing of Charlie Kirk , are banding together to try and stave off attacks on the nonprofit sector,” the Times’ Teddy Schleifer reports.

— “The institutions, including the Ford Foundation and George Soros ’s Open Society Foundations , on Wednesday pushed out an open letter that forcefully defended the philanthropy sector, even as its list of signers doubled as a list of the types of left-leaning charities that President Trump may target. The statement condemned political violence and any possible retribution.”

— “Organizations should not be attacked for carrying out their missions or expressing their values in support of the communities they serve,” the groups wrote.

— “The nonprofit sector fears that Mr. Trump could pose an existential and financial threat to them by trying to revoke organizations’ tax-exempt status,” and the Times notes that many liberal philanthropies have spent much of this year concerned about possible retaliation by Trump. “Behind the scenes, these philanthropies have spent the last several days in close touch with one another as they try to prepare for a crackdown.”

DURBIN-MARSHALL CREDIT CARD MANDATES WILL HARM MILITARY FAMILIES The Defense Credit Union Council is sounding the alarm on the Durbin–Marshall credit card mandates. This proposal would increase fraud risk, restrict access to credit, eliminate rewards, and hand a massive windfall to corporate mega-retailers at the expense of consumers, small businesses, and community financial institutions. DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED —OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

Bob Menendez (D-N.J.). “It helps ground the allegations in sort of a very concrete and understandable way for a jury,” Rosenstein argued, while Sanderson noted that the fact pattern can help illustrate that “it wasn’t just a failure to file some forms.”

title: Airlines ask for a shutdown safety net
body_text:
TRUST US: With Congress poised to turn the page on the longest shutdown in history, the airline industry is mobilizing to prevent air travel from being used as a “political football” during future shutdowns. It wants to head off fiascos like the one that led to the cancellation of thousands of U.S. flights over the past five days due to FAA-mandated service cuts.

— “There are long term measures that can be taken to make sure that airlines, hotels, travel, the American public isn’t held hostage every time there’s a tough political debate in Washington,” Airlines for America chief Chris Sununu said during a briefing with reporters today. “This is affecting not just the airlines, but the entire American economy.”

— Sununu, who was joined by American Hotel & Lodging Association President and CEO Rosanna Maietta , said the travel industry will push lawmakers over the next one to two months to allow the FAA to tap its aviation trust fund to continue operations during future shutdowns. Congress, he said, needs to “absolutely get it done.”

— Airlines and passengers help finance the Airport and Airway Trust Fund through excise taxes on purchases of plane tickets or airline miles, air cargo and plane fuel. The funding is used to pay for capital improvements at airports along with other FAA operations, including air traffic control.

— “We’re paying into it as we speak. … Millions of dollars a day are going into this fund designed to pay for FAA costs that cannot or that are just simply not allowed during a shutdown,” Sununu said. By contrast, the Highway Trust Fund is authorized to serve as a stopgap during shutdowns, he noted.

“Why don’t we have this for the FAA? It’s so logical. The only reason you wouldn’t want to do this is if you wanted this to become some sort of political log jam, football every time.”

— Sununu didn’t try to hide his frustration with the current state of affairs in the Capitol. The U.S. aviation system is a private-public partnership, he said, and while airlines “are living up to their end of the bargain spectacularly … it’s the government side that is not.”

FWIW: Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) introduced legislation in March that would allow the FAA to lean on the aviation trust fund’s coffers during a shutdown. There aren’t any listed co-sponsors as of today, while dueling Democratic and GOP versions introduced in the House in September have 100 co-sponsors combined.

FIRST IN PI – BROWNSTEIN WROTE OFF PART OF C5 LOBBYING BILL: Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck wrote off $30,000 in lobbying fees for tech investment firm C5 Capital after it had to hire a collections agency to get C5 to pay its bills, Daniel L. reports. It was the second lobbying firm that has reported trouble getting C5 to pay invoices.

— Brownstein represented C5 Capital, run by André Pienaar , between 2021 and 2023, during which time it worked on cyber and space issues, among other things. Former Rep. Ed Royce (R-Calif.), the onetime chair of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, was among the lobbyists on the account.

— In recent weeks, Brownstein filed a formal amendment to its disclosures reflecting the fact that it received $30,000 from C5 in the second quarter of 2023, not $60,000 as it had originally reported.

— “Through the collections process, C5 paid the full amount,” a Brownstein spokesperson said in a statement to PI. “We had to write off a portion that was the collection agency’s fee.”

— Pienaar declined to comment on Brownstein’s write-off but earlier told PI that he doesn’t owe any money to the firm, and “there are no outstanding invoices.”

— In its lobbying reports, Brownstein reported charging C5 about a half-million dollars during the time it represented it. PI reported in September that HillEast Group recently ended its lawsuit for alleged non-payment of bills it had filed against C5.

— An Associated Press investigation found last year that C5 or other Pienaar-controlled entities have been sued numerous times for allegedly not returning money in an investment or not paying back wages or rent. One suit was ultimately settled, while the other suits were dismissed quickly after being filed, meaning the parties likely reached settlements.

WHO’S COMING TO DINNER: Trump will huddle with top Wall Street executives for a private dinner at the White House tonight, “as part of his effort to forge stronger ties with America’s business leaders and convince them to invest in U.S. manufacturing,” CBS News’ Jennifer Jacobs , Olivia Rinaldi , Richard Escobedo and Joe Walsh report.

— Expected attendees will include JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon , Nasdaq CEO Adena Friedman , Blackstone ’s Stephen Schwarzman , Morgan Stanley ‘s Ted Pick , BlackRock ‘s Larry Fink , Goldman Sachs’ David Solomon , Intercontinental Exchange ’s Jeffrey Sprecher , NYSE ’s Lynn Martin , Citadel ’s Ken Griffin , Kohlberg Kravis Roberts ’ Henry Kravis , Apollo Global Management ‘s Marc Rowan and SoftBank ‘s Masayoshi Son , along with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick , per CBS.

— Though bankers “have been pitching the administration on handling the IPO for Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac … Fannie and Freddie are not the focus of the dinner, sources said. TRUST US: With Congress poised to turn the page on the longest shutdown in history, the airline industry is mobilizing to prevent air travel from being used as a “political football” during future shutdowns. It wants to head off fiascos like the one that led to the cancellation of thousands of U.S. flights over the past five days due to FAA-mandated service cuts.

— “There are long term measures that can be taken to make sure that airlines, hotels, travel, the American public isn’t held hostage every time there’s a tough political debate in Washington,” Airlines for America chief Chris Sununu said during a briefing with reporters today. “This is affecting not just the airlines, but the entire American economy.”

— Sununu, who was joined by American Hotel & Lodging Association President and CEO Rosanna Maietta, said the travel industry will push lawmakers over the next one to two months to allow the FAA to tap its aviation trust fund to continue operations during future shutdowns. Congress, he said, needs to “absolutely get it done.”

— Airlines and passengers help finance the Airport and Airway Trust Fund through excise taxes on purchases of plane tickets or airline miles, air cargo and plane fuel. The funding is used to pay for capital improvements at airports along with other FAA operations, including air traffic control.

— “We’re paying into it as we speak. … Millions of dollars a day are going into this fund designed to pay for FAA costs that cannot or that are just simply not allowed during a shutdown,” Sununu said. By contrast, the Highway Trust Fund is authorized to serve as a stopgap during shutdowns, he noted.

“Why don’t we have this for the FAA? It’s so logical. The only reason you wouldn’t want to do this is if you wanted this to become some sort of political log jam, football every time.”

— Sununu didn’t try to hide his frustration with the current state of affairs in the Capitol. The U.S. aviation system is a private-public partnership, he said, and while airlines “are living up to their end of the bargain spectacularly … it’s the government side that is not.”

FWIW: Sen. Jerry Moran (R-Kan.) introduced legislation in March that would allow the FAA to lean on the aviation trust fund’s coffers during a shutdown. There aren’t any listed co-sponsors as of today, while dueling Democratic and GOP versions introduced in the House in September have 100 co-sponsors combined.

title: Scoop: How the left’s dark money behemoth spent its millions
body_text:
FIRST IN PI —SIXTEEN THIRTY FUND SPENDS BIG: The left’s preeminent dark money hub dished out nearly $311 million in 2024 backing progressive causes like abortion and voting rights, climate change and more.

— As detailed in a new tax filing shared with PI, the spending was more than double what the nonprofit Sixteen Thirty Fund steered to liberal groups and causes a year prior. But that was less than its total in 2020, when the group’s all-time high of $410 million in outlays helped sweep Democrats to unified control of Washington.

— Though Democrats suffered “devastating” losses of the White House and Senate in 2024, Sixteen Thirty Fund President Amy Kurtz pointed to last week’s Democratic victories in the off-year elections as affirmation of her group’s work a year earlier.

—This month’s election was a moment of “both validation and motivation,” Kurtz wrote , adding that “progress is built over years, not cycles, and that sustained advocacy, not just electoral wins, drives enduring change.”

— Sixteen Thirty Fund’s massive spending last year was made possible by a fundraising haul of more than $282 million, tax filings show — an increase of over $100 million compared with 2023.

— As a 501(c)4 group, Sixteen Thirty Fund is not required to disclose its donors, though past donors have included the nonprofit led by Swiss billionaire Hansjörg Wyss as well as the philanthropic network started by megadonor George Soros . Even though the group has said it supports reforms — backed by many on the left — that would require more transparency into nonprofits, Sixteen Thirty Fund’s fundraising and spending prowess signals that opaque and deep-pocketed left-leaning political funding hubs aren’t going anywhere.

— More than 60 percent of Sixteen Thirty Fund’s revenues in 2024 came from just five benefactors who cut eight-figure checks to the group, including one who gave $58.9 million and another who gave $51.4 million, according to the filings.

— The fund reported pouring almost $63 million into super PACs and other groups for political purposes, in addition to dropping more than $15 million on Sixteen Thirty Fund’s own direct political spending. That included $6.7 million to Your Community PAC , a super PAC that became a major last-minute spender in support of former Vice President Kamala Harris and Democratic House and Senate candidates in red states.

— Sixteen Thirty Fund also gave to the main super PACs supporting House and Senate Democrats and the Harris campaign. Roughly another $2 million went to Retire Career Politicians and Civic Truth Action each, super PACs that spent heavily to boost the independent challenger to Nebraska GOP Sen. Deb Fischer as well as third-party presidential candidates that could’ve eaten into President Donald Trump ’s votes.

— The group’s single biggest expenditure by far was a nearly $28 million grant for the liberal voter registration and turnout coalition America Votes . Sixteen Thirty Fund also doled out tens of millions of dollars backing state ballot initiatives, including $14 million for an unsuccessful campaign to expand abortion rights in Florida and $6 million for a failed anti-gerrymandering push in Ohio.

— Other spending by Sixteen Thirty Fund remains unknown, thanks to its model of fiscal sponsorship. It allows the nonprofit to operate as an incubator for new political advocacy groups like Protect Our Care Action , which has pushed back on conservative health care policies; Galvanize Action , which seeks to juice civic engagement among moderate women in the suburbs and rural areas; and Paid Leave for All .

Happy Friday and welcome to PI. Any fun weekend plans? Drop us a line at dbarnes@politico.com and coprysko@politico.com or on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and caitlinoprysko.17 . And don’t forget to follow us on X at @dnlbrns and @caitlinoprysko .

FIRST IN PI — HPE MERGER FIGHT CONTINUES: A bipartisan group of six former state attorneys general has weighed in on the continuing saga of the Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Juniper Networks merger. They sent a letter to Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser , urging him to abandon a multi-state legal effort that seeks to delay or potentially block court approval of the merger.

— “After reviewing the market share and national security facts surrounding the merger, we believe it is clear that the DOJ’s settlement represents a sound and balanced resolution — one that protects consumers and marketplace competition while strengthening the United States’ ability to compete globally,” the former attorneys general write in the letter .

— The letter is signed by three former Democratic AGs ( Andrew Ketterer of Maine, Michael Lilly of Hawaii and Oliver Koppell of New York) and three former Republican AGs ( Sean Reyes of Utah, Curtis Hill of Indiana and Dennis Vacco of New York).

— The Justice Department sued in January to block the $14 billion merger of the two tech companies, saying it would reduce competition in the commercial wireless network market. But in June, DOJ and HPE announced they had reached a settlement to allow the merger to proceed. Soon after, two antitrust division officials were fired and later spoke publicly against the settlement, accusing DOJ leaders of working with Trump-aligned lobbyists hired by HPE to negotiate a favorable settlement on the eve of trial.

— Amid the drama, attorneys general from 12 states plus D.C. submitted a motion to intervene in the case, asking a judge to carefully evaluate the proposed settlement and, if necessary, allow the states to oppose the merger in court. Weiser is leading the states’ effort.

— “Calling for further review of a benign case like this one could inadvertently create a precedent in which merger enforcement becomes politicized or increasingly subject to special-interest influence,” the former AGs caution Weiser in today’s letter. A hearing in the case is scheduled for Tuesday.

MORE MERGER MOVEMENT: Shareholders of Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern voted today to approve a proposed $85 billion merger between the two railroads, Josh Funk reports for the Associated Press .

— The proposed merger remains subject to approval by the U.S. Surface Transportation Board, which is not expected to oppose the deal after President Donald Trump fired the only board member who objected to a separate railroad merger two years ago.

— Union Pacific has heavily invested in the success of the merger. The railroad spent more than $1 million on Washington lobbying efforts in Q3 alone and has also donated to Trump’s White House ballroom project. Despite strong initial opposition, the nation’s largest railworkers union blessed the deal earlier this month after securing guarantees that no member would lose their job as a result of the merger.

FAMILY BUSINESS: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s financial services firm, Cantor Fitzgerald , has enjoyed a year of record profitability after its former CEO joined the Trump administration, Todd Gillespie reports for Bloomberg .

— Now controlled by Lutnick’s 27- and 29-year-old sons, Brandon and Kyle, the firm is on track to earn more than $2.5 billion in revenue in 2025. But don’t say it’s because of the firm’s Washington connections, firm leaders tell Gillespie.

— “Executives have pushed back on allegations of conflicts of interest, saying they now operate independently of Lutnick and were long positioned to profit in businesses inevitably set to heat up…’I promise you, we’re not getting anything handed to us,’ [co-CEO Sage Kelly ] said. ‘It’s easy for our competitors to say that because they’re not here living and breathing what we do every single day.’”

— But powerful Democrats in the Senate aren’t convinced. “‘When you’ve got the Commerce secretary’s son running the Commerce secretary’s old Wall Street firm, you’re going to face some tough questions about whether everything is on the level,’ Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) wrote in an email to Bloomberg in August.”

PAKISTAN’S LOBBYING SUCCESS: The government of Pakistan has invested heavily in Trump-aligned lobbyists since the start of the year and is now reaping the benefits, Pranav Baskar reports for The New York Times .

— In April, Pakistan signed a $1 million contract with Seiden Law , which subcontracted with Javelin Advisors , a lobbying firm founded by longtime Trump employees George Sorial and Keith Schiller . Sorial was an executive vice president at the Trump Organization , and Schiller is Trump’s former bodyguard who followed his boss to the White House in 2017.

— Additionally, Pakistan has hired Orchid Advisors , which has subcontracted with Squire Patton Boggs , the firm that employs Trump’s former economic adviser Everett Eissenstat and former Defense Secretary Mark Esper . In all, Pakistan has committed nearly $5 million to Washington lobbying efforts this year.

— Pakistan has obtained meetings between Trump and senior Pakistani officials, lower tariff rates than other Asian countries and higher tariff rates for regional archrival India.

WHAT’S NEXT FOR HEMP: The hemp industry’s lobbying efforts in Washington appear to be shifting their focus to the White House after failing to stop the Senate from including language in this week’s government funding bill that effectively bans THC consumables derived from legal hemp.

— Pro-hemp nonprofit Team Hemp has hired three new lobbying firms this month, two of which are helmed by Trump campaign vets. MO Strategies and Frontline Government Relations will lobby on issues related to the hemp industry, according to lobbying disclosures.

— On the account for MO Strategies are Martin Obst and Robert Goad . Obst served in multiple roles during the first two Trump campaigns, and Goad served as a special assistant to the president during the first Trump administration. John Pence , who served in multiple positions in the first Trump campaign, and Elliott Echols are on the account for Frontline.

11/14/2025 07:07 PM EST

Presented by

FIRST IN PI—SIXTEEN THIRTY FUND SPENDS BIG: The left’s preeminent dark money hub dished out nearly $311 million in 2024 backing progressive causes like abortion and voting rights, climate change and more.

— As detailed in a new tax filing shared with PI, the spending was more than double what the nonprofit Sixteen Thirty Fund steered to liberal groups and causes a year prior. But that was less than its total in 2020, when the group’s all-time high of $410 million in outlays helped sweep Democrats to unified control of Washington.

— Though Democrats suffered “devastating” losses of the White House and Senate in 2024, Sixteen Thirty Fund President Amy Kurtz pointed to last week’s Democratic victories in the off-year elections as affirmation of her group’s work a year earlier.

—This month’s election was a moment of “both validation and motivation,” Kurtz wrote, adding that “progress is built over years, not cycles, and that sustained advocacy, not just electoral wins, drives enduring change.”

— Sixteen Thirty Fund’s massive spending last year was made possible by a fundraising haul of more than $282 million, tax filings show — an increase of over $100 million compared with 2023.

— As a 501(c)4 group, Sixteen Thirty Fund is not required to disclose its donors, though past donors have included the nonprofit led by Swiss billionaire Hansjörg Wyss as well as the philanthropic network started by megadonor George Soros. Even though the group has said it supports reforms — backed by many on the left — that would require more transparency into nonprofits, Sixteen Thirty Fund’s fundraising and spending prowess signals that opaque and deep-pocketed left-leaning political funding hubs aren’t going anywhere.

— More than 60 percent of Sixteen Thirty Fund’s revenues in 2024 came from just five benefactors who cut eight-figure checks to the group, including one who gave $58.9 million and another who gave $51.4 million, according to the filings.

— The fund reported pouring almost $63 million into super PACs and other groups for political purposes, in addition to dropping more than $15 million on Sixteen Thirty Fund’s own direct political spending. That included $6.7 million to Your Community PAC, a super PAC that became a major last-minute spender in support of former Vice President Kamala Harris and Democratic House and Senate candidates in red states.

— Sixteen Thirty Fund also gave to the main super PACs supporting House and Senate Democrats and the Harris campaign. Roughly another $2 million went to Retire Career Politicians and Civic Truth Action each, super PACs that spent heavily to boost the independent challenger to Nebraska GOP Sen. Deb Fischer as well as third-party presidential candidates that could’ve eaten into President Donald Trump’s votes.

— The group’s single biggest expenditure by far was a nearly $28 million grant for the liberal voter registration and turnout coalition America Votes. Sixteen Thirty Fund also doled out tens of millions of dollars backing state ballot initiatives, including $14 million for an unsuccessful campaign to expand abortion rights in Florida and $6 million for a failed anti-gerrymandering push in Ohio.

— Other spending by Sixteen Thirty Fund remains unknown, thanks to its model of fiscal sponsorship. It allows the nonprofit to operate as an incubator for new political advocacy groups like Protect Our Care Action, which has pushed back on conservative health care policies; Galvanize Action, which seeks to juice civic engagement among moderate women in the suburbs and rural areas; and Paid Leave for All.

Happy Friday and welcome to PI. Any fun weekend plans? Drop us a line at dbarnes@politico.com and coprysko@politico.com or on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and caitlinoprysko.17. And don’t forget to follow us on X at @dnlbrns and @caitlinoprysko.

FIRST IN PI — HPE MERGER FIGHT CONTINUES: A bipartisan group of six former state attorneys general has weighed in on the continuing saga of the Hewlett Packard Enterprise and Juniper Networks merger. They sent a letter to Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser, urging him to abandon a multi-state legal effort that seeks to delay or potentially block court approval of the merger.

— “After reviewing the market share and national security facts surrounding the merger, we believe it is clear that the DOJ’s settlement represents a sound and balanced resolution — one that protects consumers and marketplace competition while strengthening the United States’ ability to compete globally,” the former attorneys general write in the letter.

— The letter is signed by three former Democratic AGs (Andrew Ketterer of Maine, Michael Lilly of Hawaii and Oliver Koppell of New York) and three former Republican AGs (Sean Reyes of Utah, Curtis Hill of Indiana and Dennis Vacco of New York).

— The Justice Department sued in January to block the $14 billion merger of the two tech companies, saying it would reduce competition in the commercial wireless network market. But in June, DOJ and HPE announced they had reached a settlement to allow the merger to proceed. Soon after, two antitrust division officials were fired and later spoke publicly against the settlement, accusing DOJ leaders of working with Trump-aligned lobbyists hired by HPE to negotiate a favorable settlement on the eve of trial.

— Amid the drama, attorneys general from 12 states plus D.C. submitted a motion to intervene in the case, asking a judge to carefully evaluate the proposed settlement and, if necessary, allow the states to oppose the merger in court. Weiser is leading the states’ effort.

— “Calling for further review of a benign case like this one could inadvertently create a precedent in which merger enforcement becomes politicized or increasingly subject to special-interest influence,” the former AGs caution Weiser in today’s letter. A hearing in the case is scheduled for Tuesday.

MORE MERGER MOVEMENT: Shareholders of Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern voted today to approve a proposed $85 billion merger between the two railroads, Josh Funk reports for the Associated Press.

— The proposed merger remains subject to approval by the U.S. Surface Transportation Board, which is not expected to oppose the deal after President Donald Trump fired the only board member who objected to a separate railroad merger two years ago.

— Union Pacific has heavily invested in the success of the merger. The railroad spent more than $1 million on Washington lobbying efforts in Q3 alone and has also donated to Trump’s White House ballroom project. Despite strong initial opposition, the nation’s largest railworkers union blessed the deal earlier this month after securing guarantees that no member would lose their job as a result of the merger.

FAMILY BUSINESS: Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick’s financial services firm, Cantor Fitzgerald, has enjoyed a year of record profitability after its former CEO joined the Trump administration, Todd Gillespie reports for Bloomberg.

— Now controlled by Lutnick’s 27- and 29-year-old sons, Brandon and Kyle, the firm is on track to earn more than $2.5 billion in revenue in 2025. But don’t say it’s because of the firm’s Washington connections, firm leaders tell Gillespie.

— “Executives have pushed back on allegations of conflicts of interest, saying they now operate independently of Lutnick and were long positioned to profit in businesses inevitably set to heat up…’I promise you, we’re not getting anything handed to us,’ [co-CEO Sage Kelly] said. ‘It’s easy for our competitors to say that because they’re not here living and breathing what we do every single day.’”

— But powerful Democrats in the Senate aren’t convinced. “‘When you’ve got the Commerce secretary’s son running the Commerce secretary’s old Wall Street firm, you’re going to face some tough questions about whether everything is on the level,’ Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Ore.) wrote in an email to Bloomberg in August.”

PAKISTAN’S LOBBYING SUCCESS: The government of Pakistan has invested heavily in Trump-aligned lobbyists since the start of the year and is now reaping the benefits, Pranav Baskar reports for The New York Times.

— In April, Pakistan signed a $1 million contract with Seiden Law, which subcontracted with Javelin Advisors, a lobbying firm founded by longtime Trump employees George Sorial and Keith Schiller. Sorial was an executive vice president at the Trump Organization, and Schiller is Trump’s former bodyguard who followed his boss to the White House in 2017.

— Additionally, Pakistan has hired Orchid Advisors, which has subcontracted with Squire Patton Boggs, the firm that employs Trump’s former economic adviser Everett Eissenstat and former Defense Secretary Mark Esper. In all, Pakistan has committed nearly $5 million to Washington lobbying efforts this year.

— Pakistan has obtained meetings between Trump and senior Pakistani officials, lower tariff rates than other Asian countries and higher tariff rates for regional archrival India.

WHAT’S NEXT FOR HEMP: The hemp industry’s lobbying efforts in Washington appear to be shifting their focus to the White House after failing to stop the Senate from including language in this week’s government funding bill that effectively bans THC consumables derived from legal hemp.

— Pro-hemp nonprofit Team Hemp has hired three new lobbying firms this month, two of which are helmed by Trump campaign vets. MO Strategies and Frontline Government Relations will lobby on issues related to the hemp industry, according to lobbying disclosures.

— On the account for MO Strategies are Martin Obst and Robert Goad. Obst served in multiple roles during the first two Trump campaigns, and Goad served as a special assistant to the president during the first Trump administration. John Pence, who served in multiple positions in the first Trump campaign, and Elliott Echols are on the account for Frontline.

title: Burr, Ferguson register to lobby
body_text:
RETIRED GOP LAWMAKERS REGISTER TO LOBBY: Former Sen. Richard Burr has registered to lobby for the first time now that the North Carolina Republican’s two-year ban on lobbying former colleagues has lapsed.

— Burr, who chaired both the Senate Intelligence and HELP committees during his nearly three decades in Congress, will lobby on a range of issues for the drug lobby PhRMA and on issues related to federal research funding and the endowment tax for his home state universities Duke and Wake Forest , according to disclosure filings.

— Burr joined DLA Piper in 2023 to lead a health policy strategic consulting practice at the firm. Since November’s election, Burr has been hosting a series of “office hours” webinars for the firm focused on issues from the election results and transition to government funding, trade, regulatory updates and what else is happening on the Hill.

— Burr will also lobby on existing accounts like the University of North Carolina , and drugmaker Eli Lilly , per Bloomberg ’s Kate Ackley , and for other AI, life sciences and aerospace clients.

— Burr’s not the only retired member of Congress who recently registered to lobby for the first time. Drew Ferguson , a former member of House GOP leadership, registered to represent the National Council for Mental Wellbeing and the credit reporting company Equifax , earlier this month, according to disclosure filings.

— Ferguson, who spent the past four years as GOP chief deputy whip, joined Alston & Bird shortly after leaving office in January. He’s subject to a yearlong “cooling off” period during which he’s barred from lobbying former colleagues on the Hill, but Ferguson is able to lobby the Trump administration right away.

NEW BUSINESS: A network of different firms with ties to President Donald Trump registered a slew of new clients over the weekend, the latest indicator that such relationships remain in high demand on K Street.

— Miller Strategies disclosed more than a dozen additions to its roster, including the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz , controversial stablecoin issuer Tether , Nasdaq , the futures exchange FMX , Zoom Communications and media conglomerates Nexstar and Tegna .

— Checkmate Government Relations registered to lobby for five new clients: Drugmakers Sanofi and GSK , manufacturer Vortex Optics , renal care company Vantive Health and the Raleigh-Durham Airport Authority .

— Continental Strategy , meanwhile, disclosed four new clients, including the gaming giant Bally’s and military moving company Total Military Management . Last week, Ballard Partners registered to lobby for Canadian oil company Irving Oil in addition to Vantive, Vanderbilt University , Mitsubishi , the advocacy group Care Action Now and Daimler Truck North America .

Happy Monday and welcome to PI . Send K Street tips and gossip: [email protected] And be sure to follow me on X : @caitlinoprysko .

NATHANSON+HAUCK POACHES 2 FROM INVARIANT: Health care-focused bipartisan government affairs firm Nathanson+Hauck is changing its name to Red+Blue Strategies as it expands its partnership. The firm has hired Katie Wise and Ben Klein away from Invariant to become partners and is adding Eden Tesfaye as chief strategy officer.

— Wise previously co-chaired Invariant’s health care practice and is a Federation of American Hospitals and Vern Buchanan alum, while Klein was a senior vice president and is a Palantir , Byron Dorgan and American Cancer Society alum. Tesfaye most recently served as senior adviser at CMS.

— “Health care increasingly touches so many other parts of policy,” Megan Hauck Marshall , one of the firm’s founding partners, told PI of the rebrand. “We really felt that Katie, Ben, and Eden have a team approach to this work that’s a perfect fit to what Melanie [ Nathanson ] and I do. So we wanted a new name reflecting the work of the whole team.”

MORE NEW BUSINESS FOR FORMER LAWMAKERS: Several other retired members of Congress have added new clients recently. They include former Rep. Tom Graves (R-Ga.), whose firm has signed on as a subcontractor to Bracewell to represent the FBI Agents Association , which has lobbied Congress to push back on potential job cuts within the bureau .

— The Canadian renewable energy company Boralex has retained a team at Greenberg Traurig that includes former House Financial Services Chair Rodney Frelinghuysen (R-N.J.) and former Rep. Charlie Bass (R-N.H.), while the developer of the Honduran “prosperity zone” Prospera retained former Rep. Filemon Vela (D-Texas).

— Meanwhile, Stanford University and Yale University have hired teams of lobbyists at Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld that include three former lawmakers. Former Sen. Joe Donnelly (D-Ind.), who just returned to the firm after serving as ambassador to the Vatican during the Biden administration, and former House Foreign Affairs Chair Ileana Ros-Lehtinen (R-Fla.) are working on the Stanford account, while former House Science Chair Lamar Smith (R-Tenn.) is lobbying for Yale.

IF YOU MISSED IT OVER THE WEEKEND: Top law firms are debating whether to make a public show of support for three major firms that have come under attack by the Trump administration, Daniel reports. But they’re racked by private worries they’d be targeted, too.

— In the past few weeks, Trump issued a now-temporarily blocked executive order that tried to bar Perkins Coie lawyers from interacting with federal agencies or even entering federal buildings. Trump also suspended active security clearances of numerous Covington and Burling lawyers, and on Friday did the same to lawyers for Paul Weiss , restricting firm access to federal buildings and terminating federal contracts with the firm so that tax dollars don’t “subsidize activities not aligned with American interests.”

— Since the start of Trump’s attack on Big Law, elite lawyers from many other firms have discussed issuing a statement supporting the firms and filing an amicus brief backing Perkins, according to two senior lawyers at large law firms and another person working with firms on the issue. A draft statement defending the rule of law and challenging attacks on it is expected to be circulated this weekend, they said.

— But it hasn’t been easy getting firms to sign on, according to one of the people. Many are afraid of going public and being perceived as anti-Trump. “The administration is viewed as very punitive and retributive,” with strong elements of McCarthyism, the person said.

FIRST IN PI: Crest Hill Advisors , the firm started by former top spectrum official Scott Blake Harris , has hired Victoria Flood as a partner focused on telecom, technology and energy policy. Flood was most recently a principal at Mehlman Consulting and before that she spent more than a decade working for Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), the new chair of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.

— “Victoria’s knowledge of telecommunications, technology, and energy policy is matched by her ability to turn ideas into results,” Moore Capito said in a statement provided by the firm. “I know she will be a great asset to clients navigating Congress and the White House and will be successful as a partner at Crest Hill Advisors.”

TIKTOK ON THE CLOCK: “The embattled app TikTok , in the face of a looming survival deadline, has launched an old-school campaign to sway Washington , blanketing Metro stations with ads to remind policymakers of its importance to the economy, and circulating new research that argues it’s not a security threat to the U.S.,” our Christine Mui reports.

— The campaign echoes a strategy tried by the app almost a year ago , when it sought unsuccessfully to fend off a congressional ban by mobilizing its users. But the ad blitz this time around comes as the White House mulls a pitch by Oracle to take over the app , which is technically illegal under the ban that Trump has vowed not to enforce.

WHO’S AFRAID OF THE MAHA MOMS: “A federal health roundtable last week ended with an unusual twist: a White House video featuring Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and others struggling to pronounce ingredients found in pantry items from Pop-Tarts to Little Debbie oatmeal creme pies,” The Wall Street Journal ’s Jesse Newman and Natalie Andrews write.

— The video “ capped off a week of meetings for Kennedy with food executives and mothers who have championed his Make America Healthy Again agenda — events where he pledged an overhaul of the ingredients found in American grocery products .” And it served as “an early sign of the pressure that food manufacturers face as the nation’s top health official and his supporters try to bend a major U.S. industry by swaying public opinion.”

FLYING IN: The American Biogas Council will kick off a two-day fly-in tomorrow, with more than 50 members slated to hit the Hill for meetings with about 40 offices from both sides of the aisle. The council will focus on a number of tax priorities, including tax incentives for renewable natural gas investments, clean fuel producers and tech neutral electricity, as well as the farm bill and recycling policy.

Ray previously was chief strategist for nonprofit and foundation clients at Social Capital . Kelemen previously was executive director at the Industry Council for Emergency Response Technologies .

She was previously a senior adviser in the Office of Global Affairs, Terrorist Financing and Financial Crimes at Treasury.

— Diem-Mi Lu has joined the National Venture Capital Association as its new vice president for government affairs. She was previously a counsel to former SEC Commissioner Jaime Lizárraga , and is an alum of Sen. Chris Van Hollen ’s (D-Md.) and Rep. Bill Foster ’s (D-Ill.) offices.

RETIRED GOP LAWMAKERS REGISTER TO LOBBY: Former Sen. Richard Burr has registered to lobby for the first time now that the North Carolina Republican’s two-year ban on lobbying former colleagues has lapsed.

— Burr, who chaired both the Senate Intelligence and HELP committees during his nearly three decades in Congress, will lobby on a range of issues for the drug lobby PhRMA and on issues related to federal research funding and the endowment tax for his home state universities Duke and Wake Forest, according to disclosure filings.

— Burr joined DLA Piper in 2023 to lead a health policy strategic consulting practice at the firm. Since November’s election, Burr has been hosting a series of “office hours” webinars for the firm focused on issues from the election results and transition to government funding, trade, regulatory updates and what else is happening on the Hill.

— Burr will also lobby on existing accounts like the University of North Carolina, and drugmaker Eli Lilly, per Bloomberg’s Kate Ackley, and for other AI, life sciences and aerospace clients.

— Burr’s not the only retired member of Congress who recently registered to lobby for the first time. Drew Ferguson, a former member of House GOP leadership, registered to represent the National Council for Mental Wellbeing and the credit reporting company Equifax, earlier this month, according to disclosure filings.

— Ferguson, who spent the past four years as GOP chief deputy whip, joined Alston & Bird shortly after leaving office in January. He’s subject to a yearlong “cooling off” period during which he’s barred from lobbying former colleagues on the Hill, but Ferguson is able to lobby the Trump administration right away.

NEW BUSINESS: A network of different firms with ties to President Donald Trump registered a slew of new clients over the weekend, the latest indicator that such relationships remain in high demand on K Street.

— Miller Strategies disclosed more than a dozen additions to its roster, including the venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz, controversial stablecoin issuer Tether, Nasdaq, the futures exchange FMX, Zoom Communications and media conglomerates Nexstar and Tegna.

— Checkmate Government Relations registered to lobby for five new clients: Drugmakers Sanofi and GSK, manufacturer Vortex Optics, renal care company Vantive Health and the Raleigh-Durham Airport Authority.

— Continental Strategy, meanwhile, disclosed four new clients, including the gaming giant Bally’s and military moving company Total Military Management. Last week, Ballard Partners registered to lobby for Canadian oil company Irving Oil in addition to Vantive, Vanderbilt University, Mitsubishi, the advocacy group Care Action Now and Daimler Truck North America.

NATHANSON+HAUCK POACHES 2 FROM INVARIANT: Health care-focused bipartisan government affairs firm Nathanson+Hauck is changing its name to Red+Blue Strategies as it expands its partnership. The firm has hired Katie Wise and Ben Klein away from Invariant to become partners and is adding Eden Tesfaye as chief strategy officer.

— Wise previously co-chaired Invariant’s health care practice and is a Federation of American Hospitals and Vern Buchanan alum, while Klein was a senior vice president and is a Palantir, Byron Dorgan and American Cancer Society alum. Tesfaye most recently served as senior adviser at CMS.

— “Health care increasingly touches so many other parts of policy,” Megan Hauck Marshall, one of the firm’s founding partners, told PI of the rebrand. “We really felt that Katie, Ben, and Eden have a team approach to this work that’s a perfect fit to what Melanie [Nathanson] and I do. So we wanted a new name reflecting the work of the whole team.”

MORE NEW BUSINESS FOR FORMER LAWMAKERS: Several other retired members of Congress have added new clients recently. They include former Rep. Tom Graves (R-Ga.), whose firm has signed on as a subcontractor to Bracewell to represent the FBI Agents Association, which has lobbied Congress to push back on potential job cuts within the bureau.

— The Canadian renewable energy company Boralex has retained a team at Greenberg Traurig that includes former House Financial Services Chair Rodney Frelinghuysen (R-N.J.) and former Rep. Charlie Bass (R-N.H.), while the developer of the Honduran “prosperity zone” Prospera retained former Rep. Filemon Vela (D-Texas).

— Meanwhile, Stanford University and Yale University have hired teams of lobbyists at Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld that include three former lawmakers. Former Sen. Joe Donnelly (D-Ind.), who just returned to the firm after serving as ambassador to the Vatican during the Biden administration, and former House Foreign Affairs Chair Ileana Ros-Lehtinen (R-Fla.) are working on the Stanford account, while former House Science Chair Lamar Smith (R-Tenn.) is lobbying for Yale.

IF YOU MISSED IT OVER THE WEEKEND: Top law firms are debating whether to make a public show of support for three major firms that have come under attack by the Trump administration, Daniel reports. But they’re racked by private worries they’d be targeted, too.

— In the past few weeks, Trump issued a now-temporarily blocked executive order that tried to bar Perkins Coie lawyers from interacting with federal agencies or even entering federal buildings. Trump also suspended active security clearances of numerous Covington and Burling lawyers, and on Friday did the same to lawyers for Paul Weiss, restricting firm access to federal buildings and terminating federal contracts with the firm so that tax dollars don’t “subsidize activities not aligned with American interests.”

— Since the start of Trump’s attack on Big Law, elite lawyers from many other firms have discussed issuing a statement supporting the firms and filing an amicus brief backing Perkins, according to two senior lawyers at large law firms and another person working with firms on the issue. A draft statement defending the rule of law and challenging attacks on it is expected to be circulated this weekend, they said.

— But it hasn’t been easy getting firms to sign on, according to one of the people. Many are afraid of going public and being perceived as anti-Trump. “The administration is viewed as very punitive and retributive,” with strong elements of McCarthyism, the person said.

FIRST IN PI: Crest Hill Advisors, the firm started by former top spectrum official Scott Blake Harris, has hired Victoria Flood as a partner focused on telecom, technology and energy policy. Flood was most recently a principal at Mehlman Consulting and before that she spent more than a decade working for Sen. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), the new chair of the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee.

— “Victoria’s knowledge of telecommunications, technology, and energy policy is matched by her ability to turn ideas into results,” Moore Capito said in a statement provided by the firm. “I know she will be a great asset to clients navigating Congress and the White House and will be successful as a partner at Crest Hill Advisors.”

— The campaign echoes a strategy tried by the app almost a year ago, when it sought unsuccessfully to fend off a congressional ban by mobilizing its users. But the ad blitz this time around comes as the White House mulls a pitch by Oracle to take over the app, which is technically illegal under the ban that Trump has vowed not to enforce.

Kennedy Jr. and others struggling to pronounce ingredients found in pantry items from Pop-Tarts to Little Debbie oatmeal creme pies,” The Wall Street Journal’s Jesse Newman and Natalie Andrews write.

— The video “capped off a week of meetings for Kennedy with food executives and mothers who have championed his Make America Healthy Again agenda — events where he pledged an overhaul of the ingredients found in American grocery products.” And it served as “an early sign of the pressure that food manufacturers face as the nation’s top health official and his supporters try to bend a major U.S. industry by swaying public opinion.”

title: Senate reconciliation experts strike out on their own
body_text:
SENATE GOP AIDES HANG A SHINGLE: A pair of former Senate Republican staffers who played key roles in the chamber’s recent reconciliation fights are setting up shop on K Street as the conference embarks on its massive push to advance President Donald Trump ’s tax, energy and immigration agendas via the arcane budget process.

A message from the Defense Credit Union Council:

DURBIN-MARSHALL CREDIT CARD MANDATES WILL HARM MILITARY FAMILIES The Defense Credit Union Council is sounding the alarm on the Durbin–Marshall credit card mandates. This proposal would increase fraud risk, restrict access to credit, eliminate rewards, and hand a massive windfall to corporate mega-retailers at the expense of consumers, small businesses, and community financial institutions. DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED —OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

— Scott Raab , a former top aide to Mitch McConnell , decamped for K Street after two and a half decades working for the longtime Senate GOP leader, most recently as his deputy chief of staff for policy. He’s launching Raab Government Strategies , a strategic consulting and government relations firm.

— Raab is “one of the very few people in Washington who, by their very involvement in an issue, signal that things are probably going to somehow work out,” McConnell said in farewell remarks from the Senate floor in December, adding that “in meetings anywhere in the Capitol, Scott speaks with my authority but a command of policy nuance and procedural nuance entirely his own.”

— Meanwhile, Matt Gallivan has left Leavitt Partners , where he’s served as a principal, to launch Genesis Health Strategies . The firm will work to help healthcare clients weather what Gallivan said is a “political reckoning” for the industry, in part by helping navigate the reconciliation process.

— Before leaving the Hill in 2018, Gallivan served as health policy director for now-Senate HELP Chair Bill Cassidy (R-La.) during the failed GOP effort to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act via reconciliation. He also worked as an aide to former Rep. Erik Paulsen (R-Minn.), handling his health and tax portfolio.

— Just like in 2021 when Democrats won unified control of Washington under President Joe Biden and began working to move pandemic relief and climate and infrastructure legislation with only a simple majority using the reconciliation process, expertise in the legislative maneuver is in high demand.

— That’s especially true as Republicans set out to persuade Senate parliamentarian Elizabeth MacDonough — who serves as the chief referee in deciding which provisions comply with the complex reconciliation rules and which must be struck from the bill — to allow them to use an atypical accounting method to permanently extend the 2017 tax cuts.

Happy Wednesday and welcome to PI . Send K Street tips and gossip: [email protected] And be sure to follow me on X : @caitlinoprysko .

KIES TO THE KINGDOM: “Tax super lobbyist Ken Kies is poised to become a top official at the Treasury Department — and it won’t be the first time he’ll have worked” for the president , POLITICO ’s Michael Stratford and Brian Faler report.

— In financial disclosures required as part of Kies’ nomination to oversee tax policy at the Treasury Department, the head of Federal Policy Group revealed that Trump paid him at least $5,000 for “tax technical advice” and “tax controversy advice.”

— “The form doesn’t provide the precise fee amount nor offer any additional details about why Trump retained Kies. Trump has battled the IRS for years over audits of his taxes.”

— Kies’ firm “has not registered to lobby the government on behalf of Trump. And it’s possible his work for Trump was for a one-off consultation or legal representation rather than an ongoing lobbying effort. Some of Kies’s major clients — such as Microsoft , Arch Capital , and Cruise Lines International Association — had already been made public through public lobbying disclosures.”

— “But his new disclosure paperwork offers new details about the companies who hired Kies for tax and legal advice. His clients included investment firms Glenview Capital Management , Elliott Management , General Atlantic , Millennium Management , as well as U.S. Mortgage Insurers , the Cigar Association of America , and Genie Energy .”

— “Kies wrote in a letter to Treasury’s top ethics official earlier this month that, if confirmed, he would ‘cease engaging in any business, including the representation of clients.’ The firm will ‘remain dormant’ and won’t advertise during his government service, Kies wrote.”

BRITT’S CHIEF HEADS DOWNTOWN: Clay Armentrout is leaving the Hill to join Allen Control Systems as its senior vice president of government relations. He most recently served as chief of staff for Sen. Katie Britt (R-Ala.) and before that he spent seven years with former Sen. Richard Shelby (R-Ala.), the former Senate Appropriations chair for whom Britt also worked.

— “I’ll forever be glad and grateful I was able to convince [Armentrout] to extend his exemplary service in the Senate another two years to help start our office to ensure we hit the ground running and had a successful 118th Congress,” Britt said in a statement, adding that Armentrout will be “a tremendous asset who elevates those around him, just as he has done both in my office and throughout his tenure on Capitol Hill.”

FLYING IN: Nearly three dozen members of the National Retail Federation ’s tax committee hit the Hill today to discuss extending the 2017 tax law. Retailers were slated to meet with senior staff from the offices of House Speaker Mike Johnson , House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries , House Majority Leader Steve Scalise , Senate Majority Leader John Thune , Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Steve Daines (R-Mont.) and the Senate Finance Committee.

BIG LAW’S TRUMPIAN QUAGMIRE: “Lawyers at some of the nation’s largest law firms are afraid of President Donald Trump. Not just afraid of what his policies might mean for their clients, but now for their own livelihoods, as his attacks on individual firms have left a shocked industry struggling to respond ,” per POLITICO ’s Daniel Barnes .

— “When Trump first took office in 2017, attorneys at Big Law firms lent thousands of pro-bono hours to legal efforts to stymie the administration’s most controversial policies. … After his efforts to overturn the results of the 2020 election and the Capitol riot on Jan. 6, 2021, Trump became even more anathema to major firms; several of his criminal defense lawyers had to leave their firms in order to take him on as a client.”

— “Now, as he returns triumphant from the political wilderness, Trump finds a Washington legal community facing a dilemma — keep their heads down and avoid cases that may pit them against the administration, or continue representing clients that might anger a president increasingly willing to use his power to seek vengeance.”

ANNALS OF RETRIBUTION: Trump “and his allies are aggressively attacking the players and machinery that power the left, taking a series of highly partisan official actions that, if successful, will threaten to hobble Democrats’ ability to compete in elections for years to come,” The New York Times’ Ken Vogel and Shane Goldmacher write of Trump’s efforts to go after law firms tied to Democrats, left-leaning fundraising platforms like ActBlue and liberal organizations like the consulting firm Arabella Advisors .

— “So far, the attacks have been diffuse and sometimes indiscriminate or inaccurate. But inside the administration, there are moves to coordinate and expand the assault. A small group of White House officials has been working to identify targets and vulnerabilities inside the Democratic ecosystem, taking stock of previous efforts to investigate them, according to two people familiar with the group’s work who requested anonymity to describe it.”

LCV TAPS NEW LEADER: “The League of Conservation Voters named Pete Maysmith as president , putting him atop the green movement’s most prominent political fundraiser and one of its most influential forces on Capitol Hill,” per POLITICO ’s Zack Colman . “Maysmith, who previously ran LCV’s campaigns operation, will also lead the group’s advocacy arm, the LCV Education Fund .”

— “He will begin his new role April 15, replacing Gene Karpinski who stepped down in September after 18 years atop the organization.” The leadership transition comes “as the environmental movement faces myriad institutional challenges , including downsizing at several brand name groups and fundraising headwinds.”

Senate reconciliation experts strike out on their own

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO 

03/19/2025 05:44 PM EDT

Presented by

With Daniel Lippman

SENATE GOP AIDES HANG A SHINGLE: A pair of former Senate Republican staffers who played key roles in the chamber’s recent reconciliation fights are setting up shop on K Street as the conference embarks on its massive push to advance President Donald Trump’s tax, energy and immigration agendas via the arcane budget process.

A message from the Defense Credit Union Council:

DURBIN-MARSHALL CREDIT CARD MANDATES WILL HARM MILITARY FAMILIES The Defense Credit Union Council is sounding the alarm on the Durbin–Marshall credit card mandates. This proposal would increase fraud risk, restrict access to credit, eliminate rewards, and hand a massive windfall to corporate mega-retailers at the expense of consumers, small businesses, and community financial institutions. DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED—OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

— Scott Raab, a former top aide to Mitch McConnell, decamped for K Street after two and a half decades working for the longtime Senate GOP leader, most recently as his deputy chief of staff for policy. He’s launching Raab Government Strategies, a strategic consulting and government relations firm.

— Raab is “one of the very few people in Washington who, by their very involvement in an issue, signal that things are probably going to somehow work out,” McConnell said in farewell remarks from the Senate floor in December, adding that “in meetings anywhere in the Capitol, Scott speaks with my authority but a command of policy nuance and procedural nuance entirely his own.”

— Meanwhile, Matt Gallivan has left Leavitt Partners, where he’s served as a principal, to launch Genesis Health Strategies. The firm will work to help healthcare clients weather what Gallivan said is a “political reckoning” for the industry, in part by helping navigate the reconciliation process.

— Before leaving the Hill in 2018, Gallivan served as health policy director for now-Senate HELP Chair Bill Cassidy (R-La.) during the failed GOP effort to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act via reconciliation. He also worked as an aide to former Rep. Erik Paulsen (R-Minn.), handling his health and tax portfolio.

— Just like in 2021 when Democrats won unified control of Washington under President Joe Biden and began working to move pandemic relief and climate and infrastructure legislation with only a simple majority using the reconciliation process, expertise in the legislative maneuver is in high demand.

— That’s especially true as Republicans set out to persuade Senate parliamentarian Elizabeth MacDonough — who serves as the chief referee in deciding which provisions comply with the complex reconciliation rules and which must be struck from the bill — to allow them to use an atypical accounting method to permanently extend the 2017 tax cuts.

Happy Wednesday and welcome to PI. Send K Street tips and gossip: [email protected] And be sure to follow me on X: @caitlinoprysko.

A message from the Defense Credit Union Council:

KIES TO THE KINGDOM: “Tax super lobbyist Ken Kies is poised to become a top official at the Treasury Department — and it won’t be the first time he’ll have worked” for the president, POLITICO’s Michael Stratford and Brian Faler report.

— In financial disclosures required as part of Kies’ nomination to oversee tax policy at the Treasury Department, the head of Federal Policy Group revealed that Trump paid him at least $5,000 for “tax technical advice” and “tax controversy advice.”

— “The form doesn’t provide the precise fee amount nor offer any additional details about why Trump retained Kies. Trump has battled the IRS for years over audits of his taxes.”

— Kies’ firm “has not registered to lobby the government on behalf of Trump. And it’s possible his work for Trump was for a one-off consultation or legal representation rather than an ongoing lobbying effort. Some of Kies’s major clients — such as Microsoft, Arch Capital, and Cruise Lines International Association — had already been made public through public lobbying disclosures.”

— “But his new disclosure paperwork offers new details about the companies who hired Kies for tax and legal advice. His clients included investment firms Glenview Capital Management, Elliott Management, General Atlantic, Millennium Management, as well as U.S. Mortgage Insurers, the Cigar Association of America, and Genie Energy.”

— “Kies wrote in a letter to Treasury’s top ethics official earlier this month that, if confirmed, he would ‘cease engaging in any business, including the representation of clients.’ The firm will ‘remain dormant’ and won’t advertise during his government service, Kies wrote.”

BRITT’S CHIEF HEADS DOWNTOWN: Clay Armentrout is leaving the Hill to join Allen Control Systems as its senior vice president of government relations. He most recently served as chief of staff for Sen. Katie Britt (R-Ala.) and before that he spent seven years with former Sen. Richard Shelby (R-Ala.), the former Senate Appropriations chair for whom Britt also worked.

— “I’ll forever be glad and grateful I was able to convince [Armentrout] to extend his exemplary service in the Senate another two years to help start our office to ensure we hit the ground running and had a successful 118th Congress,” Britt said in a statement, adding that Armentrout will be “a tremendous asset who elevates those around him, just as he has done both in my office and throughout his tenure on Capitol Hill.”

FLYING IN: Nearly three dozen members of the National Retail Federation’s tax committee hit the Hill today to discuss extending the 2017 tax law. Retailers were slated to meet with senior staff from the offices of House Speaker Mike Johnson, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, House Majority Leader Steve Scalise, Senate Majority Leader John Thune, Sens. John Cornyn (R-Texas) and Steve Daines (R-Mont.) and the Senate Finance Committee.

BIG LAW’S TRUMPIAN QUAGMIRE: “Lawyers at some of the nation’s largest law firms are afraid of President Donald Trump. Not just afraid of what his policies might mean for their clients, but now for their own livelihoods, as his attacks on individual firms have left a shocked industry struggling to respond,” per POLITICO’s Daniel Barnes.

— “When Trump first took office in 2017, attorneys at Big Law firms lent thousands of pro-bono hours to legal efforts to stymie the administration’s most controversial policies. … After his efforts to overturn the results of the 2020 election and the Capitol riot on Jan. 6, 2021, Trump became even more anathema to major firms; several of his criminal defense lawyers had to leave their firms in order to take him on as a client.”

— “Now, as he returns triumphant from the political wilderness, Trump finds a Washington legal community facing a dilemma — keep their heads down and avoid cases that may pit them against the administration, or continue representing clients that might anger a president increasingly willing to use his power to seek vengeance.”

ANNALS OF RETRIBUTION: Trump “and his allies are aggressively attacking the players and machinery that power the left, taking a series of highly partisan official actions that, if successful, will threaten to hobble Democrats’ ability to compete in elections for years to come,” The New York Times’ Ken Vogel and Shane Goldmacher write of Trump’s efforts to go after law firms tied to Democrats, left-leaning fundraising platforms like ActBlue and liberal organizations like the consulting firm Arabella Advisors.

— “So far, the attacks have been diffuse and sometimes indiscriminate or inaccurate. But inside the administration, there are moves to coordinate and expand the assault. A small group of White House officials has been working to identify targets and vulnerabilities inside the Democratic ecosystem, taking stock of previous efforts to investigate them, according to two people familiar with the group’s work who requested anonymity to describe it.”

LCV TAPS NEW LEADER: “The League of Conservation Voters named Pete Maysmith as president, putting him atop the green movement’s most prominent political fundraiser and one of its most influential forces on Capitol Hill,” per POLITICO’s Zack Colman. “Maysmith, who previously ran LCV’s campaigns operation, will also lead the group’s advocacy arm, the LCV Education Fund.”

— “He will begin his new role April 15, replacing Gene Karpinski who stepped down in September after 18 years atop the organization.” The leadership transition comes “as the environmental movement faces myriad institutional challenges, including downsizing at several brand name groups and fundraising headwinds.”

A message from the Defense Credit Union Council:

CONGRESS MUST REJECT DURBIN–MARSHALL

The Defense Credit Union Council is sounding the alarm on the Durbin–Marshall credit card mandates. This proposal would increase fraud risk, eliminate rewards programs, restrict access to credit, and hand a massive windfall to mega-retailers at the expense of consumers, small businesses, and community financial institutions. “This repeats the same mistakes consumers already paid for,” warns DCUC President & CEO Anthony Hernandez. A one-size-fits-all rewrite of the payments system would weaken fraud protections and hit servicemembers, veterans, and working families hardest. DCUC STRONGLY OPPOSES THIS BILL AND URGES ACTION TO SAFEGUARD THOSE WHO SERVE!
