title: Biden energy diplomat launching critical minerals practice at McLarty
body_text:
FIRST IN PI: Geoffrey Pyatt , the top U.S. diplomat for energy issues under former President Joe Biden, is joining global strategic advisory firm McLarty Associates to launch a new practice focused on helping companies navigate the increasingly fraught and complex geopolitical landscape for critical minerals and energy.

— Pyatt left the State Department earlier this year after more than three decades — during which he served as U.S. ambassador to Greece, Ukraine and, most recently, as assistant secretary for energy resources.

— “Few things will move markets or drive geopolitics more significantly in the next decade than energy and critical materials, and I’m looking forward to helping our clients succeed in this dynamic environment,” Pyatt said in a statement on the new practice, which he said will help clients with “market entry, energy resilience and advanced energy partnerships, and diversification of supply chains for key energy materials and technologies.”

— Even under President Donald Trump , who has railed against the electric vehicle industry for which the critical mineral supply chain is crucial, the sector has already played a massive role in the current administration’s diplomatic priorities. Trump signed an executive order just today aimed at boosting U.S. production of rare earth minerals, an arena currently dominated by China.

— Trump recently dispatched a congressional ally to the Democratic Republic of Congo , one of the world’s top producers of valuable minerals like copper, cobalt, diamonds and gold, to potentially discuss a minerals deal with the country’s leader. Greenland’s trove of rare earth minerals are also widely believed to play a role in Trump’s desire to take over the autonomous Danish territory.

— And last month’s Oval Office blow up between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was intended to be a precursor to the signing of a deal to grant U.S. access to Ukrainian rare earth minerals that are used in products like batteries and electronics. Trump told reporters this afternoon that the deal was back on track to be signed imminently.

— “Energy and critical minerals are remaking geopolitics and creating enormous economic competition and opportunity everywhere,” said Lee Feinstein , president of McLarty Associates, which was founded by former Bill Clinton chief of staff Mack McLarty and practices what it dubs “commercial diplomacy.”

Happy Thursday and welcome to PI , where your host is still rooting for the Dawgs to pull off an upset tonight. Send K Street tips and gossip: [email protected] And be sure to follow me on X : @caitlinoprysko .

A message from the Defense Credit Union Council:

DURBIN-MARSHALL CREDIT CARD MANDATES WILL HARM MILITARY FAMILIES The Defense Credit Union Council is sounding the alarm on the Durbin–Marshall credit card mandates. This proposal would increase fraud risk, restrict access to credit, eliminate rewards, and hand a massive windfall to corporate mega-retailers at the expense of consumers, small businesses, and community financial institutions. DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED —OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

ON THE AIRWAVES: The vaping industry’s main trade group, the Vapor Technology Association has launched an ad campaign on Trump’s favorite cable news networks prodding the president to make good on his campaign trail promise to “save” the flavored vaping industry.

— The weeklong ad buy from VTA will run online and on Fox News , Fox Business and Newsmax during key programming like “Fox and Friends,” “Kudlow” and “The Five,” and it follows an earlier appeal to Trump from the trade group earlier this year.

— “Mr. President, sir, vaping voters turned out for you by the hundreds of thousands,” multiple narrators identified as Trump voters say in the 30-second spot . “We trust you. We believe you. We delivered our promise to vote Trump. Now we need you to keep your promise to save the flavored vaping industry,” they continue, warning that the administration’s action is needed to save “millions of vapers and small businesses.”

— Though Trump signed into law a bill that raised the age for purchasing e-cigarettes from 18 to 21 and introduced some restrictions on vape flavors credited with the rise in youth vaping — which are currently before the Supreme Court — he backed away from a full ban on flavored e-cigarettes during his first term in office.

— Last year, The Washington Post reported that Trump’s sudden campaign promise to “save Vaping again!” followed a meeting with VTA executive director Tony Abboud , along with a flood of donations from the tobacco industry to Trump’s main super PAC. VTA also endorsed Trump’s selection of Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for HHS secretary, where Kennedy now oversees tobacco and e-cigarette regulation.

HOW DO YOU LOBBY A GUY LIKE ELON: “Washington’s lobbying class is grasping for an effective approach to an unprecedented challenge: how do you influence a mercurial outsider like Elon Musk who has immense but unofficial power and is the world’s richest person,” POLITICO ’s Sophia Cai and Daniel write.

— “Solving for Musk could pay huge dividends. If K Street can figure out how to lobby him, they can capitalize off the anxiety pervading Washington that drives companies and industries to sign six-figure retainers. ‘Washington is really used to deliberative processes where stakeholders get input,’ said Alex Conant , co-founder of Firehouse Strategies . ‘Musk doesn’t believe in any of that.’”

— “That frustration is shared across Washington, where private interests trying to protect their own projects — or nudging DOGE to target a competitor instead, sometimes through DOGE’s X account — are running into the same problem. Musk operates with a singular mission: cutting government waste at breakneck speed, with little patience for the conventional playbook.”

— “Lobbyists find they’re being asked not only to save a company from their fear of Musk’s unpredictable social media ire or a sweeping DOGE cut that would hit their industry or wipe out their contract.”

— “They’re also being queried about potential real estate investments from the General Services Administration’s plans to sell federal buildings and business opportunities arising from Musk’s effort to modernize government software. Lobbyists without direct ties to Musk’s inner circle are deploying other strategies such as working more conventional agency contacts or scouring the DOGE leader’s social media feed.”

THE BIGLAW REVIEW: As white shoe law firms scramble to get out of Trump’s crosshairs after a series of executive orders revoking some firms’ security clearances and targeting clients who hold contracts with the federal government, Semafor ’s Ben Smith , Liz Hoffman and Gina Chon report that “ Brad Karp , the chairman of Paul Weiss and one of the most powerful lawyers in New York, has been in Washington this week meeting with officials in President Donald Trump’s orbit, people familiar with the matter said.”

— Meanwhile, the Wall Street Journal ’s Richard Vanderford reports that Paul Weiss has been dropped by Steven Schwartz , a major client and former executive at Cognizant Technology Solutions who is facing foreign bribery charges, as a result of Trump’s attacks.

— “Schwartz is scheduled to go on trial next month over his alleged involvement in a scheme to pay $2 million in bribes in India to help obtain permission to build a corporate campus there, but the case is under review after Trump curbed enforcement of the U.S. law against foreign bribery.”

— “‘Mr. Schwartz is concerned that the firm’s continued representation of him may negatively affect his ability to obtain a favorable review of his case,’ Paul Weiss, which Schwartz had retained as lead counsel, wrote.”

MAKING NICE: “In October 2019, Amazon sued the Pentagon, alleging that President Donald Trump had blocked the company from securing a $10bn cloud-computing contract because of his animus towards The Washington Post and its owner Jeff Bezos — whom the US president derided as ‘Jeff Bozo,’” the Financial Times ’ Anna Nicolaou , Stephen Morris , Rafe Uddin and Alex Rogers write — one of many “near-constant skirmishes between Trump’s White House and corporate America.”

— “But the episode left an enduring mark on Bezos, the Amazon founder and the world’s second-richest person. Over the past year, Bezos has executed a sharp public reversal in his relationship with Trump — whom he previously criticised as a ‘threat to democracy’ — that has surprised even longtime associates and has stunned the Post’s newsroom.”

— The spate of recent moves by Bezos and his companies to accommodate Trump “are part of a marked shift in Bezos’s strategy towards Trump,” with Bezos’ associates framing him to FT as “a shrewd capitalist, making practical calculations to protect his businesses. But they also believe Bezos is operating with a dose of fear about Trump, as well as resentment towards what he considers to be the Democrats’ ‘vilification’ of Big Tech during the Biden administration.”

NO RAVE REVIEWS FROM TINSELTOWN: Major donors across Hollywood are shutting down the gravy train for Democratic politicians across the board after last year’s election drubbing, according to The Ankler ’s Matthew Frank . One donor adviser told Frank that “longtime donors who are ‘always in for everything’ … are now saying, ‘We’re not giving to anything.’ Not only that, but also ‘we’re not even attending anything. We’re not engaging in anything.’”

— And even though many of the industry’s top benefactors signaled they’ll likely be ready to open their wallets again by the time next year’s midterms roll around, “the Party is not making it easy for its supporters — especially its most consistent fundraising base in Hollywood.”

— “Even amid the private fuming — which has led to collective feelings of ‘disillusionment,’ ‘depression’ and being ‘angry,’ ‘frustrated’ and ‘kind of pissed off’ — some donors are seeking to be proactive. They’re using this moment to rethink how they interact with Democrats, moving away from being a no-strings-attached funding source and toward being more active participants in the political process.”

— Niketa Patel is now executive director and CEO of the Online News Association . She previously was senior director of leadership programs at the Craig Newmark Graduate School of Journalism at CUNY , and is a CNN and The 19th alum.

Biden energy diplomat launching critical minerals practice at McLarty

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO 

03/20/2025 07:28 PM EDT

Presented by

With Daniel Lippman

FIRST IN PI: Geoffrey Pyatt, the top U.S. diplomat for energy issues under former President Joe Biden, is joining global strategic advisory firm McLarty Associates to launch a new practice focused on helping companies navigate the increasingly fraught and complex geopolitical landscape for critical minerals and energy.

— Pyatt left the State Department earlier this year after more than three decades — during which he served as U.S. ambassador to Greece, Ukraine and, most recently, as assistant secretary for energy resources.

— “Few things will move markets or drive geopolitics more significantly in the next decade than energy and critical materials, and I’m looking forward to helping our clients succeed in this dynamic environment,” Pyatt said in a statement on the new practice, which he said will help clients with “market entry, energy resilience and advanced energy partnerships, and diversification of supply chains for key energy materials and technologies.”

— Even under President Donald Trump, who has railed against the electric vehicle industry for which the critical mineral supply chain is crucial, the sector has already played a massive role in the current administration’s diplomatic priorities. Trump signed an executive order just today aimed at boosting U.S. production of rare earth minerals, an arena currently dominated by China.

— Trump recently dispatched a congressional ally to the Democratic Republic of Congo, one of the world’s top producers of valuable minerals like copper, cobalt, diamonds and gold, to potentially discuss a minerals deal with the country’s leader. Greenland’s trove of rare earth minerals are also widely believed to play a role in Trump’s desire to take over the autonomous Danish territory.

— And last month’s Oval Office blow up between Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy was intended to be a precursor to the signing of a deal to grant U.S. access to Ukrainian rare earth minerals that are used in products like batteries and electronics. Trump told reporters this afternoon that the deal was back on track to be signed imminently.

— “Energy and critical minerals are remaking geopolitics and creating enormous economic competition and opportunity everywhere,” said Lee Feinstein, president of McLarty Associates, which was founded by former Bill Clinton chief of staff Mack McLarty and practices what it dubs “commercial diplomacy.”

Happy Thursday and welcome to PI, where your host is still rooting for the Dawgs to pull off an upset tonight. Send K Street tips and gossip: [email protected] And be sure to follow me on X: @caitlinoprysko.

A message from the Defense Credit Union Council:

DURBIN-MARSHALL CREDIT CARD MANDATES WILL HARM MILITARY FAMILIES The Defense Credit Union Council is sounding the alarm on the Durbin–Marshall credit card mandates. This proposal would increase fraud risk, restrict access to credit, eliminate rewards, and hand a massive windfall to corporate mega-retailers at the expense of consumers, small businesses, and community financial institutions. DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED—OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

ON THE AIRWAVES: The vaping industry’s main trade group, the Vapor Technology Association has launched an ad campaign on Trump’s favorite cable news networks prodding the president to make good on his campaign trail promise to “save” the flavored vaping industry.

— The weeklong ad buy from VTA will run online and on Fox News, Fox Business and Newsmax during key programming like “Fox and Friends,” “Kudlow” and “The Five,” and it follows an earlier appeal to Trump from the trade group earlier this year.

— “Mr. President, sir, vaping voters turned out for you by the hundreds of thousands,” multiple narrators identified as Trump voters say in the 30-second spot. “We trust you. We believe you. We delivered our promise to vote Trump. Now we need you to keep your promise to save the flavored vaping industry,” they continue, warning that the administration’s action is needed to save “millions of vapers and small businesses.”

— Though Trump signed into law a bill that raised the age for purchasing e-cigarettes from 18 to 21 and introduced some restrictions on vape flavors credited with the rise in youth vaping — which are currently before the Supreme Court — he backed away from a full ban on flavored e-cigarettes during his first term in office.

— Last year, The Washington Post reported that Trump’s sudden campaign promise to “save Vaping again!” followed a meeting with VTA executive director Tony Abboud, along with a flood of donations from the tobacco industry to Trump’s main super PAC. VTA also endorsed Trump’s selection of Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for HHS secretary, where Kennedy now oversees tobacco and e-cigarette regulation.

HOW DO YOU LOBBY A GUY LIKE ELON: “Washington’s lobbying class is grasping for an effective approach to an unprecedented challenge: how do you influence a mercurial outsider like Elon Musk who has immense but unofficial power and is the world’s richest person,” POLITICO’s Sophia Cai and Daniel write.

— “Solving for Musk could pay huge dividends. If K Street can figure out how to lobby him, they can capitalize off the anxiety pervading Washington that drives companies and industries to sign six-figure retainers. ‘Washington is really used to deliberative processes where stakeholders get input,’ said Alex Conant, co-founder of Firehouse Strategies. ‘Musk doesn’t believe in any of that.’”

— “That frustration is shared across Washington, where private interests trying to protect their own projects — or nudging DOGE to target a competitor instead, sometimes through DOGE’s X account — are running into the same problem. Musk operates with a singular mission: cutting government waste at breakneck speed, with little patience for the conventional playbook.”

— “Lobbyists find they’re being asked not only to save a company from their fear of Musk’s unpredictable social media ire or a sweeping DOGE cut that would hit their industry or wipe out their contract.”

— “They’re also being queried about potential real estate investments from the General Services Administration’s plans to sell federal buildings and business opportunities arising from Musk’s effort to modernize government software. Lobbyists without direct ties to Musk’s inner circle are deploying other strategies such as working more conventional agency contacts or scouring the DOGE leader’s social media feed.”

THE BIGLAW REVIEW: As white shoe law firms scramble to get out of Trump’s crosshairs after a series of executive orders revoking some firms’ security clearances and targeting clients who hold contracts with the federal government, Semafor’s Ben Smith, Liz Hoffman and Gina Chon report that “Brad Karp, the chairman of Paul Weiss and one of the most powerful lawyers in New York, has been in Washington this week meeting with officials in President Donald Trump’s orbit, people familiar with the matter said.”

— Meanwhile, the Wall Street Journal’s Richard Vanderford reports that Paul Weiss has been dropped by Steven Schwartz, a major client and former executive at Cognizant Technology Solutions who is facing foreign bribery charges, as a result of Trump’s attacks.

— “Schwartz is scheduled to go on trial next month over his alleged involvement in a scheme to pay $2 million in bribes in India to help obtain permission to build a corporate campus there, but the case is under review after Trump curbed enforcement of the U.S. law against foreign bribery.”

— “‘Mr. Schwartz is concerned that the firm’s continued representation of him may negatively affect his ability to obtain a favorable review of his case,’ Paul Weiss, which Schwartz had retained as lead counsel, wrote.”

MAKING NICE: “In October 2019, Amazon sued the Pentagon, alleging that President Donald Trump had blocked the company from securing a $10bn cloud-computing contract because of his animus towards The Washington Post and its owner Jeff Bezos — whom the US president derided as ‘Jeff Bozo,’” the Financial Times’ Anna Nicolaou, Stephen Morris, Rafe Uddin and Alex Rogers write — one of many “near-constant skirmishes between Trump’s White House and corporate America.”

— “But the episode left an enduring mark on Bezos, the Amazon founder and the world’s second-richest person. Over the past year, Bezos has executed a sharp public reversal in his relationship with Trump — whom he previously criticised as a ‘threat to democracy’ — that has surprised even longtime associates and has stunned the Post’s newsroom.”

— The spate of recent moves by Bezos and his companies to accommodate Trump “are part of a marked shift in Bezos’s strategy towards Trump,” with Bezos’ associates framing him to FT as “a shrewd capitalist, making practical calculations to protect his businesses. But they also believe Bezos is operating with a dose of fear about Trump, as well as resentment towards what he considers to be the Democrats’ ‘vilification’ of Big Tech during the Biden administration.”

NO RAVE REVIEWS FROM TINSELTOWN: Major donors across Hollywood are shutting down the gravy train for Democratic politicians across the board after last year’s election drubbing, according to The Ankler’s Matthew Frank. One donor adviser told Frank that “longtime donors who are ‘always in for everything’ … are now saying, ‘We’re not giving to anything.’ Not only that, but also ‘we’re not even attending anything. We’re not engaging in anything.’”

— And even though many of the industry’s top benefactors signaled they’ll likely be ready to open their wallets again by the time next year’s midterms roll around, “the Party is not making it easy for its supporters — especially its most consistent fundraising base in Hollywood.”

— “Even amid the private fuming — which has led to collective feelings of ‘disillusionment,’ ‘depression’ and being ‘angry,’ ‘frustrated’ and ‘kind of pissed off’ — some donors are seeking to be proactive. They’re using this moment to rethink how they interact with Democrats, moving away from being a no-strings-attached funding source and toward being more active participants in the political process.”

title: Energy lobbyist eyes run for Turner’s seat

FIRST IN PI — ENERGY LOBBYIST CONSIDERS CONGRESSIONAL RUN: Zoe Cadore, a director of federal and regulatory affairs for energy company Calpine , is considering running for the Houston-area congressional seat that has come open after the death of Democratic Rep. Sylvester Turner , two people familiar with the matter told Daniel.

A message from the Defense Credit Union Council:

DURBIN-MARSHALL CREDIT CARD MANDATES WILL HARM MILITARY FAMILIES The Defense Credit Union Council is sounding the alarm on the Durbin–Marshall credit card mandates. This proposal would increase fraud risk, restrict access to credit, eliminate rewards, and hand a massive windfall to corporate mega-retailers at the expense of consumers, small businesses, and community financial institutions. DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED —OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

— Cadore is having conversations with community and local leaders to decide if launching a campaign is the best course of action for herself and the district, according to one of the people. She served on Turner’s first transition team when he became Houston mayor in 2016 and volunteered on both of his mayoral campaigns. While in the energy industry, she has focused on workforce development and increasing diversity, equity and inclusion in the sector.

— If she runs, she would join an already crowded field that includes Harris County Attorney Christian Menefee , former Houston City Council member Amanda Edwards , and Isaiah Martin , a former senior advisor to the late Rep. Sheila Jackson Lee (D-Texas). The special election has not been scheduled yet by Texas Gov. Greg Abbott .

— Cadore, who previously was a policy adviser for the American Petroleum Institute, earlier in her career interned in the district office for Jackson Lee on veterans affairs, housing and immigration and was briefly a law clerk on voting rights and criminal justice reform for the House Judiciary Committee.

— When she was a Congressional Black Caucus Foundation API Energy Fellow almost a decade ago, Cadore worked on crafting a carbon capture and sequestration policy that made its way into the Bipartisan Infrastructure Law. Cadore, who was named Miss Houston in 2013, lives in the district and serves on the board of the Houston Ballet and the Ensemble Theatre . She declined to comment on a potential run.

TELEHEALTH PLATFORM LOBBIES UP: Hims & Hers Health has registered its first in-house lobbyist as the telehealth company continues to ramp up its footprint in Washington. Veteran drug lobbyist Sonya Elling — who has worked in-house for PhRMA , Eli Lilly , Bluebird Bio and, most recently, the advocacy group I Am ALS — is lobbying on “all matters” affecting telehealth providers, according to a disclosure filing.

— In addition to bringing on its first in-house lobbyist, Hims brought on two new outside firms since the start of this year: Kountoupes Denham Carr & Reid and Continental Strategy . The telehealth platform previously reshuffled its lobbying roster last summer, retaining Cassidy & Associates and parting ways with Tarplin Downs & Young and Horizon Government Affairs .

— The company specializes in selling direct-to-consumer treatments for issues like hair loss and erectile dysfunction and, as of last summer, weight loss — selling compounded GLP-1 injections featuring the same active ingredient as the weight-loss drugs Ozempic and Wegovy , thanks to regulatory flexibility afforded by FDA’s designation of the drugs as in shortage.

— That line of business began to take a hit last fall, however, when the FDA declared an end to the shortage of another weight-loss drug. A federal judge this month sided with the FDA in a lawsuit over the designation brought by drug compounders.

— Hims has been scaling up its political activity and gone on offense against the name-brand drug industry. The company launched a corporate PAC last summer, though FEC filings show it doled out less than $15,000 in contributions to lawmakers in 2024. But the platform donated $1 million to President Donald Trump ’s inauguration earlier this year. And it sparked controversy and protests from drug groups like PhRMA over a Super Bowl ad taking aim at the drug industry’s prices for weight-loss drugs in particular.

A message from the Defense Credit Union Council:

FIRST IN PI II — 1 MILLION LETTERS TO CONGRESS: Concerns about Social Security have driven more than 1 million AARP members to write lawmakers in less than two weeks as part of a campaign organized by the group to urge protections for the program, a spokesperson for the organization told PI.

— It’s a signal confirming the fears of some GOP lawmakers: that the party’s leaders making changes to entitlement programs — whether on the Hill or from the White House — could mean swift backlash from constituents.

— The drive comes amid the Trump administration’s announcement that it would end identity checks over the phone in search of fraud, and after Elon Musk ’s Department of Government Efficiency sought data from the Social Security Administration — though a judge blocked the move .

— Musk previously called the program “the biggest Ponzi scheme of all time.” The policy changes and suggestions of massive fraud come as Trump promised to “always protect” Social Security.

MUSK READ: Musk “took his campaign to cut the U.S. federal government into uncharted waters on Friday , holding an unprecedented top-level meeting at the Pentagon and calling for the prosecution of any Defense Department officials leaking ‘maliciously false information’ about his visit,” Reuters’ Phil Stewart , Idrees Ali and Nandita Bose write.

— “Musk, whose businesses have a number of Defense Department contracts, met U.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth for 80 minutes in his first such talks at the Pentagon, which is responsible for a large chunk of federal government spending.” The huddle followed a New York Times report last night that Musk was being briefed on the Pentagon’s secret blueprints for a war with China, which Trump and Musk furiously denied.

— Jonathan Fahey , a former federal prosecutor and senior DHS official during President Donald Trump ’s first administration, will work on the account along with Alex Vogel , Ali Khimji , Andrew Nehring and Hayden Jewett .

— Meanwhile, Marshall & Popp has signed five new clients. Among them is Abbott Laboratories , the maker of top baby formula brand Similac , which retained the firm last month to lobby on formula issues. In 2022, the shutdown of an Abbott plant triggered a widespread formula shortage.

— Last week, Trump revoked the Biden administration’s use of the Defense Production Act to speed up manufacturing of baby formula, which was invoked to help address that shortage. Also last week, HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. ordered a review of the ingredients in baby formula as well as labeling standards and supply chains.

— Eli Lilly , whose Alzheimer’s drug donanemab was approved by the FDA last year, also retained Marshall & Popp to lobby on Alzheimer’s treatment. Biotech company Grail hired the firm to lobby on issues related to cancer screenings, and Vertex Pharmaceuticals , which recently won FDA approval for its opioid alternative Journavx, brought the firm on to work on issues related to pain management, disclosure filings show.

A message from the Defense Credit Union Council:

MONUMENT ADDS DUFFY SPOX: Mark Bednar , a top spokesperson for multiple current or prospective members of the Trump administration, is joining Monument Advocacy as a principal. Bednar briefly served as communications director for former Sen. David Perdue (R-Ga.), whom Trump has nominated for ambassador to China, before spending two years as a communications director for Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy during his time in Congress.

— After working for Duffy, Bednar moved over to the office of future House Speaker Kevin McCarthy , where he served as strategic communications director. After leaving the Hill last year, Bednar served as vice president of communications for the American Exploration & Production Council .

CREEPY EASTER BUNNY COSTUME BROUGHT TO YOU BY …: “The White House, through an outside event production company called Harbinger , is soliciting corporate sponsors for this year’s Easter Egg Roll , which is prompting major concerns from ethics experts and shock from former White House officials from both parties,” CNN ’s Betsy Klein writes.

— “The sponsorship offers range from $75,000 to $200,000, with the promise of logo and branding opportunities,” as well as a private brunch with first lady Melania Trump , tickets to the event itself and a private tour of the White House available for some sponsors, according to a pitch document sent to potential sponsors.

— “But the solicitation for sponsorships marks an unprecedented offering of corporate branding opportunities on White House grounds running counter to long-established regulations prohibiting the use of public office for private gain.”

FORMER TRUMP AIDE HEADS BACK TO K STREET: Tiber Creek Group has hired Joe Russo , boosting the firm’s ties to the West Wing as well as its appropriations expertise. Russo was most recently coalitions director for the House Appropriations Committee and before that was an in-house lobbyist for the Association for Accessible Medicines , which represents generic drugmakers. During Trump’s first presidency, Russo worked as a special assistant to the president and served as a deputy director of the White House Office of Public Liaison.

LACIVITA FOLLOWS THROUGH: “Senior Trump political adviser Chris LaCivita has filed a defamation suit against The Daily Beast , alleging that the outlet published ‘malicious’ and ‘damag[ing] reporting about him during the 2024 campaign’ with reckless disregard for the truth,’” Axios’ Alex Isenstadt reports.

— The suit “centers on an October 2024 article by investigative reporter Michael Isikoff that originally asserted LaCivita had made $22 million off the Trump campaign. LaCivita, who was Trump’s co-campaign manager, has aggressively pushed back on the allegations, saying the vast majority of the money paid for advertising.”

title: Trump’s law feud hits the Hill
body_text:
LAW FIRM PRESSURE CAMPAIGN HITS CONGRESS: President Donald Trump ’s retribution tour against Big Law has arrived on Capitol Hill , Dasha Burns , Daniel and I report. An email circulated by a high-level Republican Senate staffer to GOP Senate offices Friday instructs them to pay heed to the lobbying clients of Covington & Burling and Perkins Coie, two prominent law firms that Trump has singled out for punishment.

— “We wanted to let you know that these firms also lobby the Senate and you can find a list of their lobbying clients at this link,” the missive obtained by POLITICO states. It provides a link to the Senate lobbying disclosure database along with instructions for how to navigate it.

— A person familiar with the email who was granted anonymity to speak freely said the goal was to signal “that maybe Senate Republican staffers should consider twice whether or not they should be helpful to these individuals [that hire Covington and Perkins Coie], given their affiliation with firms deemed to be anti-Trump.”

— The person predicted the impact could extend beyond Congress: “If you’re Google or Meta or Apple — you’re thinking, ‘Do I really want to use these firms?’ That could make it harder to work with the White House.”

— The effort to squeeze the firms may have limited impact — neither firm has lobbying practices on par with some of the top-earning law and lobbying shops on K Street — though Covington has several big-ticket clients, including PhRMA , SK Americas and an intellectual property arm of Samsung .

— One of the firm’s longest-running — and most lucrative — lobbying contracts is with software and semiconductor giant Qualcomm , which has paid the firm tens of millions of dollars since 2004. Covington’s quarterly lobbying fees for Qualcomm regularly break seven figures and are often among the largest, if not the largest, individual lobbying contracts in Washington each quarter.

— In comparison, Perkins Coie was registered to lobby for just three clients last quarter, and reported less than $55,000 in lobbying revenues last year between two of them.

— If the pressure campaign seems familiar, that’s because it has echoes of last year’s bipartisan threats to blacklist lobbying firms who represent certain Chinese military-linked companies. There was also a 2023 effort by a conservative nonprofit urging Hill aides to boycott meetings with the clients or lobbyists of firms that had hired former staffers on the House committee investigating the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol.

— It’s also reminiscent of yet another GOP-led effort to shape the activity of organizations working to influence federal policy. In 2002, The Washington Post reported that Republican lobbyists were “ researching the party affiliation and political contributions of hundreds of lobbyists in Washington, part of a campaign that could deny government access and prime lobbying jobs to Democrats.”

— The undertaking triggered a warning at the time from the heads of the Senate Ethics Committee, who warned in a “Dear Colleague” letter that determining access based solely on such information might violate the chamber’s ethics rules.

— “Identifying those seeking access to Members based on party affiliation, political contributions or past employment, or encouraging others to do so, suggests a motive to grant special access, or deny access, based on those criteria and tends to adversely affect public confidence in the Senate,” wrote the late panel Chair Harry Reid (D-Nev.) and ranking member Pat Roberts (R-Kan.). Roberts, who is now a lobbyist at Capitol Counsel , did not respond to a request for comment.

AI’S SEA CHANGE: “For just over two years, technology leaders at the forefront of developing artificial intelligence had made an unusual request of lawmakers. They wanted Washington to regulate them,” The New York Times’ Cecilia Kang writes.

— “The tech executives warned lawmakers that generative A.I., which can produce text and images that mimic human creations, had the potential to disrupt national security and elections, and could eventually eliminate millions of jobs.”

— Since Trump’s election, however, “tech leaders and their companies have changed their tune, and in some cases reversed course, with bold requests of government to stay out of their way, in what has become the most forceful push to advance their products.”

— “In recent weeks, Meta , Google , OpenAI and others have asked the Trump administration to block state A.I. laws and to declare that it is legal for them to use copyrighted material to train their A.I. models. They are also lobbying to use federal data to develop the technology, as well as for easier access to energy sources for their computing demands. And they have asked for tax breaks, grants and other incentives.”

ANNALS OF CAMPAIGN FINANCE: E-commerce giant Shein and digital identification company ID.me have both formed corporate PACs, a new step in each company’s growing political footprint ahead of next year’s midterms.

— The companies are newer on the Washington influence scene. Shein, which has faced scrutiny over its roots in China and trade practices, only registered its first lobbyists in 2022. And ID.me — which has partnered with agencies like the IRS, VA, HHS and FBI — has retained federal lobbyists consistently since 2020.

— A spokesperson for ID.me told PI that the PAC will “support candidates who share our vision of making it easier, more secure, and more accessible for Americans to seamlessly login and prove their identities online,” adding that the company’s PAC dollars will go to politicians from both parties. Trump’s law feud hits the Hill

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO 

03/25/2025 06:00 PM EDT

Presented by

LAW FIRM PRESSURE CAMPAIGN HITS CONGRESS: President Donald Trump’s retribution tour against Big Law has arrived on Capitol Hill, Dasha Burns, Daniel and I report. An email circulated by a high-level Republican Senate staffer to GOP Senate offices Friday instructs them to pay heed to the lobbying clients of Covington & Burling and Perkins Coie, two prominent law firms that Trump has singled out for punishment.

— “We wanted to let you know that these firms also lobby the Senate and you can find a list of their lobbying clients at this link,” the missive obtained by POLITICO states. It provides a link to the Senate lobbying disclosure database along with instructions for how to navigate it.

— A person familiar with the email who was granted anonymity to speak freely said the goal was to signal “that maybe Senate Republican staffers should consider twice whether or not they should be helpful to these individuals [that hire Covington and Perkins Coie], given their affiliation with firms deemed to be anti-Trump.”

— The person predicted the impact could extend beyond Congress: “If you’re Google or Meta or Apple — you’re thinking, ‘Do I really want to use these firms?’ That could make it harder to work with the White House.”

— The effort to squeeze the firms may have limited impact — neither firm has lobbying practices on par with some of the top-earning law and lobbying shops on K Street — though Covington has several big-ticket clients, including PhRMA, SK Americas and an intellectual property arm of Samsung.

— One of the firm’s longest-running — and most lucrative — lobbying contracts is with software and semiconductor giant Qualcomm, which has paid the firm tens of millions of dollars since 2004. Covington’s quarterly lobbying fees for Qualcomm regularly break seven figures and are often among the largest, if not the largest, individual lobbying contracts in Washington each quarter.

— In comparison, Perkins Coie was registered to lobby for just three clients last quarter, and reported less than $55,000 in lobbying revenues last year between two of them.

— If the pressure campaign seems familiar, that’s because it has echoes of last year’s bipartisan threats to blacklist lobbying firms who represent certain Chinese military-linked companies. There was also a 2023 effort by a conservative nonprofit urging Hill aides to boycott meetings with the clients or lobbyists of firms that had hired former staffers on the House committee investigating the Jan. 6 attack on the Capitol.

— It’s also reminiscent of yet another GOP-led effort to shape the activity of organizations working to influence federal policy. In 2002, The Washington Post reported that Republican lobbyists were “researching the party affiliation and political contributions of hundreds of lobbyists in Washington, part of a campaign that could deny government access and prime lobbying jobs to Democrats.”

— The undertaking triggered a warning at the time from the heads of the Senate Ethics Committee, who warned in a “Dear Colleague” letter that determining access based solely on such information might violate the chamber’s ethics rules.

— “Identifying those seeking access to Members based on party affiliation, political contributions or past employment, or encouraging others to do so, suggests a motive to grant special access, or deny access, based on those criteria and tends to adversely affect public confidence in the Senate,” wrote the late panel Chair Harry Reid (D-Nev.) and ranking member Pat Roberts (R-Kan.). Roberts, who is now a lobbyist at Capitol Counsel, did not respond to a request for comment.

title: Ford seeks help to save IRA tax credits
body_text:
NEW BUSINESS: Ford Motor Co. has enlisted the help of former Rep. Ryan Costello (R-Pa.) in lobbying his former colleagues to keep a key tax break to incentivize clean energy manufacturing from the chopping block in Republicans’ reconciliation bill.

— The automaker retained Costello last week to “advocate for protection of IRA 45X tax credit, Foreign Entity of Concern language considerations and related IRA provisions,” according to a disclosure filing. Costello, who left Congress in 2019, will also lobby for the automaker on trade and anticipated tariffs.

— The 45X tax credit, which was created under the Inflation Reduction Act, is aimed at incentivizing domestic manufacturing of clean energy technologies like components for wind turbines, solar panels and batteries like the ones that power electric vehicles, and is one of several provisions from the Democratic climate law that Republicans have mobilized to urge their colleagues against repealing repeal .

— Ford is one of over 40 Michigan-based companies that signed on to a letter sent to members of the state’s congressional delegation earlier this week. The letter identified a dozen different clean energy incentives from the IRA that the companies wrote “have helped us stay competitive in a rapidly evolving national and global market, where states and countries are making major investments to support automotive manufacturing, advanced energy, energy efficiency, and critical grid services.”

— “Without these critical incentives, our businesses will face significant challenges—hindering expansion, slowing job creation, and jeopardizing Michigan’s leadership in the future of energy and mobility,” warned the signatories, which also included General Motors , the Michigan arm of Caterpillar and the EV charging company ChargePoint .

— Meanwhile, defense and tech firm L3Harris Technologies has brought on Adam Howard of Baseline Strategies , a former chief of staff to House Armed Services member Mike Turner (R-Ohio). The firm began lobbying for L3Harris at the beginning of February, according to a disclosure filing — weeks before drawing flak from Elon Musk for the state of the communications system it provided for the FAA.

— And Florida-based Rubin, Turnbull & Associates has registered four more clients as part of the firm’s expansion into D.C. following Trump’s win last year. The firm has signed Weedmaps , which helps users find marijuana dispensaries and deals; sports betting company PrizePicks ; behavioral health company Acadia Healthcare ; and the Florida town of Bay Harbor Island.

— Rubin Turnbull, which also has a strategic partnership with Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck , has registered a dozen new federal clients — tripling its roster — since announcing in January that it would open an office in Washington helmed by Caroline Wiles , the daughter of White House chief of staff Susie Wiles .

BUCHANAN LD JOINS CROSSROADS: Stephen Voljavec , a former aide to one of the top House GOP tax writers, has left the Hill to join Crossroads Strategies as a senior vice president. Voljavec most recently served as legislative director for Rep. Vern Buchanan (R-Fla.), a vice chair on the House Ways and Means Committee and head of the panel’s health subcommittee. Before that, he worked for Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) and at BGR Group .

— Crossroads has also hired Jackson Stuteville , a former congressional liaison for the assistant secretary of Defense for mission capabilities, as a senior vice president, and promoted Scott Brenner , Jason Gleason , Brittany Hernandez , Chris Miller and Marc Numedahl to principals.

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO

NEW BUSINESS: Ford Motor Co. has enlisted the help of former Rep. Ryan Costello (R-Pa.) in lobbying his former colleagues to keep a key tax break to incentivize clean energy manufacturing from the chopping block in Republicans’ reconciliation bill.

— The automaker retained Costello last week to “advocate for protection of IRA 45X tax credit, Foreign Entity of Concern language considerations and related IRA provisions,” according to a disclosure filing. — The 45X tax credit, which was created under the Inflation Reduction Act, is aimed at incentivizing domestic manufacturing of clean energy technologies like components for wind turbines, solar panels and batteries like the ones that power electric vehicles, and is one of several provisions from the Democratic climate law that Republicans have mobilized to urge their colleagues against repealing repeal.

— Ford is one of over 40 Michigan-based companies that signed on to a letter sent to members of the state’s congressional delegation earlier this week. — “Without these critical incentives, our businesses will face significant challenges—hindering expansion, slowing job creation, and jeopardizing Michigan’s leadership in the future of energy and mobility,” warned the signatories, which also included General Motors, the Michigan arm of Caterpillar and the EV charging company ChargePoint.

— Meanwhile, defense and tech firm L3Harris Technologies has brought on Adam Howard of Baseline Strategies, a former chief of staff to House Armed Services member Mike Turner (R-Ohio). — Crossroads has also hired Jackson Stuteville, a former congressional liaison for the assistant secretary of Defense for mission capabilities, as a senior vice president, and promoted Scott Brenner, Jason Gleason, Brittany Hernandez, Chris Miller and Marc Numedahl to principals.

title: Real estate makes its play on carried interest
body_text:
CARRIED INTEREST FIGHT GETS REAL: A coalition of trade groups representing various corners of the real estate world is warning congressional tax writers that making tweaks to the current treatment of carried interest and capital gains taxes would be detrimental to efforts to address housing supply and affordability, laying down a marker as lawmakers begin working to pass a deficit-conscious extension of the 2017 tax cuts.

— “The tax code has never, and should never, limit the reward for risk-taking to taxpayers who have cash to invest,” more than a dozen trade associations wrote in a letter to the bipartisan heads of the Senate Finance Committee and House Ways and Means Committee on Wednesday. Among those signatories were the National Association of Realtors , National Multifamily Housing Council , American Hotel and Lodging Association , Mortgage Bankers Association and The Real Estate Roundtable .

— President Donald Trump has revived the prospect of eliminating the preferential treatment for carried interest — a tax break prized by a slew of deep-pocketed industries including private equity, venture capital and real estate investors — after the loophole evaded death during negotiations of 2022’s Inflation Reduction Act and escaped Trump’s 2017 tax law largely intact.

— And though it’s far from certain whether there’s an appetite for making further changes among congressional Republicans, industries with skin in the game clearly aren’t resting on their laurels . The real estate coalition pointed to the tax break’s recent history, praising lawmakers’ “thoughtful and well-designed reforms” to carried interest in 2017. “At this point, additional changes represent a solution in search of a problem,” the groups wrote.

body_text:
FIRST IN PI: TRUMP’S LAW CRUSADE SPREADS ON THE HILL — President Donald Trump ’s crusade against Big Law is coursing through Capitol Hill.

— A senior Republican House aide circulated a memo to GOP offices on Thursday instructing members to be wary of lobbying clients of Covington & Burling and Perkins Coie , two of the major law firms that have drawn Trump’s ire, according to the email obtained by Dasha.

— The missive follows a nearly identical one sent to Senate Republican offices last Friday, which was first reported by POLITICO . The email references POLITICO’s reporting on the Senate side, with the House aide writing: “I wanted to do the same and let you know these firms also lobby the House and you can find a list of their lobbying clients at this link .”

— The impact is already being felt. Qualcomm , which is a client of Covington & Burling, reached out to a D.C. lobbying firm this week asking about its rates and included POLITICO’s report on the Senate email, according to a lobbyist at the firm granted anonymity to discuss private matters.

— “Covington’s experienced practitioners, with both Republican and Democratic backgrounds, continue to engage with Members of Congress and congressional staff across the political spectrum,” a Covington spokesperson said in a statement. “We are proud to assist our clients in exercising their First Amendment rights to petition the government.”

— Spokespeople for Perkins Coie and Qualcomm didn’t respond to a request for comment. Read more from Dasha and your PI host here .

PERKINS COIE WITHSTANDING TRUMP BLACKLIST: “When President Trump signed an executive order attacking Perkins Coie, the white-shoe law firm did what most of its rivals have not,” the Wall Street Journal ’s Dana Mattioli and Erin Mulvaney report. “It fought back. And so far, its biggest clients and superstar lawyers are standing with it .”

— “Some of Perkins’s oldest and biggest clients, including Boeing , Microsoft , Google , Amazon , Intel and the National Football League ’s Seattle Seahawks team, have stuck by the firm so far, according to people familiar with the matter. And more important, so too have its top lawyers, including litigators Michael Huston, Katie O’Sullivan and David Perez .”

— “The firm has received cards and notes from clients who support its decision to sue and not back down. Some clients have even said they are looking for ways to send more work Perkins’s way. ... Amazon alone spends tens of millions of dollars a year on the firm — and has given Perkins more work since the executive order.”

DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED —OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

PARTS OF BIG LAW GROW A SPINE: “Two law firms targeted by President Donald Trump sued Friday to bar enforcement of his executive orders seeking to shut them out of government business and strip key lawyers of their security clearances,” POLITICO ’s Kyle Cheney and Daniel Barnes report.

— “In separate suits, Big Law firms Jenner & Block and WilmerHale say Trump’s effort to target them amounts to an unprecedented attack on the legal profession in retaliation for their work for past clients he doesn’t like and for past causes with which he disagrees. If carried out, they say, the orders would devastate their practices and have already begun to cause anxiety among their hundreds of clients with government business. … The lawsuit was filed on the firm’s behalf by California-based law firm Cooley LLP .”

BUT BUT BUT: “The White House has reached a deal with one of the largest law firms in the world to provide the equivalent of $100 million in free legal work to causes supported by the administration, President Donald Trump announced Friday afternoon,” per Daniel.

— “The law firm, Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom LLP , will also fund fellowships for law school graduates to work on causes in line with the administration’s priorities. The fellows ‘will represent a wide range of political views, including conservative ideals,’ the president said in a statement.”

— “No [executive] order had been signed targeting Skadden, however, the fifth-highest grossing law firm in the world according to Law.com, making this the first time a law firm has preemptively gone to the White House to negotiate with the administration.”

— He is on the internal Office of Legislative Affairs team interfacing with other components of the White House and agencies’ legislative affairs shops. Chalkey served in the first Trump White House as an associate director of OLA and an associate director of the National Economic Council. Chalkey, who is also a former deputy chief of staff for Rep. Nancy Mace (R-S.C.), didn’t respond to a request for comment.

FIRST IN PI — Amid looming tariffs and the tax reform debate, a number of top whiskey producers are launching the American Whiskey Association , a new trade group dedicated to promoting U.S.-made whiskey globally.

— A spokesperson for the association told PI that key priorities will include reducing tariffs in important markets around the world, addressing non-tariff trade barriers and finding marketing opportunities to promote the industry.

— Founding members of the association include the parent companies of Jack Daniel’s , Maker’s Mark , Pappy Van Winkle , Weller , Buffalo Trace , Jim Beam , Wild Turkey , Jefferson’s and Bulleit .

— “With several distinct challenges and growth opportunities on the horizon, it became clear our industry needed a unified voice that captured the breadth and depth of the dynamic American whiskey category,” Brett Hale , chair of the American Whiskey Association and chief corporate affairs officer for Suntory Global Spirits , said in a statement to PI. He said that the group has been in the works for a couple years.

ANNALS OF QATARI INFLUENCE: “Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) left some people scratching their heads on Thursday after he provided an impassioned defense for the Islamic nation of Qatar during a congressional hearing,” the Washington Examiner ’s Robert Schmad reports.

— “A Washington Examiner review of Foreign Agents Registration Act records found that the arguments Marshall made to defend Qatar matched talking points provided to his office by foreign agents working on behalf of the Qatari government.”

— “‘What was Qatar’s role in the hostage release of Americans?’ Marshall asked Charles Asher Small , director of the Institute for the Study of Global Antisemitism and Policy , during the hearing. When Small began to answer by pointing out that Qatar funds Hamas, Marshall cut him off by saying, ‘The Qataris were vastly responsible for the freeing of American hostages and many others.’”

AUDIENCE OF ONE: “About a dozen political groups, using unlimited and undisclosed donations, are running ads with twin goals: Boosting — and flattering — President Trump,” Axios ’ Alex Isenstadt reports. “The groups — separate from Trump’s official political operation — have combined to spend more than $20 million since his election .”

— “ America First Steel Alliance , one of the Trump-aligned outfits, is running spots praising his decision to impose steep tariffs on steel imports. … So far, the biggest-spending outfit has been Seniors 4 Better Care , which has aired more than $8.7 million worth of TV commercials, plus another $2.5 million in digital ads.”

— “ Chris LaCivita and Tony Fabrizio , who were top strategists on Trump’s campaign and are key players in the president’s official political apparatus, are behind some of the advocacy outfits. They help run Make America Affordable Again , a group that this week is launching a multimillion-dollar TV ad blitz supporting Trump’s plans to end ‘lawsuit abuse’ and blaming Biden for inflation.”

— “The newest Trump-aligned group is the Big Stick Project , which is overseen by LaCivita, Fabrizio and Republican strategist Chip Englander and is planning ads touting Trump’s energy policies.”

TRUMP ORG EYEING VIETNAM: “The Trump Organization and its partner in Vietnam are working on multiple investments worth billions of dollars in golf courses, hotels and real estate projects in the Southeast Asian country, a spokesman for the consortium” told Reuters ’ Francesco Guarascio .

— “The spokesman said the project, which includes three 18-hole golf courses and a residential complex, is the largest in East Asia for the Trump Organization. The first two courses are expected to be operational by mid-2027, he said. The group is also involved in two golf clubs in Indonesia, one of which is under construction.”

ICYMI — EYES EMOJI: “Rep. Cory Mills , a Florida Republican, allegedly held weapons contracts with the federal government while serving in Congress, according to a report from the Office of Congressional Conduct ,” POLITICO ’s Hailey Fuchs reports.

— “Mills was sworn into Congress in January 2023. Since that time, ‘ Pacem Defense/ALS ’ — the name of two entities tied to Mills and his wife — has received nearly $1,000,000 for munition and weapons for prisons, the report found. Another entity, Pacem Solutions , entered into a contract with the federal government last May for about $11,600.”

— “‘Congressman Mills is committed to complying with all laws and ethics rules and is pleased that the Federal Election Commission recently dismissed a complaint with similar allegations,’ said Jillian Anderson , a spokesperson for Mills, in a statement. ‘We trust the House Ethics Committee will come to a similar conclusion.’”

FAMILY MATTERS: “The Trump family’s latest cryptocurrency business venture is threatening to jeopardize bipartisan support for a GOP effort to lightly regulate the digital assets industry,” POLITICO ’s Jasper Goodman writes.

— “Republican lawmakers need Democratic support to pass long-promised crypto legislation that they are rushing to send to President Donald Trump’s desk. But an announcement this week that World Liberty Financial , a company started by Trump’s eldest sons, plans to launch a new digital asset could make it harder to get additional Democrats on board.”

— “The firm’s new stablecoin … could allow Trump family members to profit off the GOP-led legislation that would help legitimize the assets and enact industry-friendly rules for how they are overseen by regulators.”

FLY-INS: As part of the Distilled Spirits Council ’s annual conference in Washington, more than 150 distillers and spirits industry representatives made the rounds on Capitol Hill yesterday with more than 100 meetings with members of Congress and staff, according to a PI tipster. Among the members they met were Sens. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) and Rep. Diana Harshbarger (R-Tenn.), to discuss tariffs, taxes and how the industry contributes to the economy.

Knight previously was a senior research fellow at George Mason University ’s Mercatus Center . Nash previously was a corporate attorney at Richards, Layton & Finger .

title: Hogan Lovells nabs Sinema
body_text:
SINEMA HEADS DOWNTOWN: Former Sen. Kyrsten Sinema , the centrist dealmaker who wielded virtually unilateral veto power over the Biden administration’s legislative agenda, has landed on K Street , your host reports.

— The Arizona Democrat-turned-independent is joining the law and lobbying firm Hogan Lovells , where she will serve as a senior counsel in the global regulatory and intellectual property practice.

— The hire marks a jackpot for the firm, given Sinema’s intimate involvement in shaping some of the most significant pieces of legislation of the past four years, including the Inflation Reduction Act, bipartisan infrastructure law and the CHIPS and Science Act, in addition to landmark gun control and marriage equality legislation and a scrapped border security bill.

— Sinema said in an interview that she will not be registering to lobby, but instead will advise businesses across industries to “understand, anticipate and influence the shifting regulatory landscape” and help them “navigate the intersection of business and government.” Daniel Winkler , a longtime Sinema aide, is joining Hogan Lovells as well.

— Sinema, a former member of the Senate Banking, Commerce, Appropriations, Veterans Affairs and Homeland Security committees, told PI she’ll be working largely with clients in industries where she’s long “had interest and expertise,” including artificial intelligence and technology, fintech, crypto, and private equity. She was drawn to Hogan Lovells because of the firm’s growing global regulatory practice and its focus on leading-edge industries in the tech space, she said.

— Though her new role with Hogan Lovells is Sinema’s most significant step into the influence industry since leaving office earlier this year, it isn’t her first. In January, Sinema joined the global advisory council at crypto exchange Coinbase alongside Chris LaCivita , President Donald Trump ’s 2024 co-campaign manager. Sinema also formed the Arizona Business Roundtable , which retained Mehlman Consulting in January to lobby on tax issues.

— Sinema became known as a reliable ally of the business community, especially during her time in the Senate, with her votes against several of former President Joe Biden ’s labor nominees and her vote against increasing the federal minimum wage provoking the ire of the Democratic base.

— Sinema also singlehandedly rescued the carried interest loophole during IRA negotiations — a tax provision that proponents in private equity, real estate and venture capital are once again gearing up to protect .

— “I’ve really focused on helping people solve complex challenges and problems, bringing unlikely people together in a room to find unlikely outcomes,” Sinema said of her record from her 12 years in Congress and nearly a decade in the Arizona Legislature before that.

— Sinema isn’t the first 118th Congress alum to land a new lobbying or lobbying-adjacent job since leaving Congress this year. Others include former Rep. Drew Ferguson (R-Ga.), who joined Alston & Bird ; former Senate Agriculture Chair Debbie Stabenow (D-Mich.), who joined Liberty Partners Group ; former Rep. Larry Bucshon (R-Ind.), who joined Holland & Knight ; and former Rep. Blaine Luetkemeyer (R-Mo.), who’s now head of the American Consumer & Investor Institute .

— Sinema’s fellow former swing vote, Joe Manchin (I-W.Va.), joined the Australian government affairs firm Bondi Partners , while former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy has launched a public affairs partnership with Jeff Miller , and former House Financial Services Chair Patrick McHenry (R-N.C.) is advising several companies in the fintech space.

A BIG HEALTH TECH ACQUISITION: The American Telemedicine Association ’s lobbying arm, ATA Action , has acquired the Digital Therapeutics Alliance , Ben reports, a significant shake-up in digital health’s presence on K Street.

— The merger of two of the biggest names in their respective domains — telehealth and digital therapeutics, which are software-based medicines — will broaden ATA Action’s mandate as it has been focusing on artificial intelligence in health care in recent years. It’s also lobbying to continue and make permanent pandemic-era expanded access for patients to see their doctors virtually from their homes.

— “It’s expanding our reach vastly,” said Kyle Zebley , executive director of ATA Action, in an interview. “We want to be the face of the future of health care.”

— Digital therapeutics advocates have long struggled to get the government to pay for the technology through Medicare coverage but got a win last fall in final rules allowing the first-ever payment for digital mental health. Supporters have argued they have shown promise in mental health and addiction treatment, but skeptics say there isn’t sufficient evidence to support coverage amid rising health care costs.

— “Together, we are well-positioned to continue to lead policy and advocacy efforts that will remove the barriers and build the infrastructures to create permanent access to telehealth, broadly defined, and ensure that the global regulatory and reimbursement momentum continues for digital therapeutics,” said Andy Molnar , outgoing CEO of DTA, who will move to head of digital health at ATA Action, in a statement.

GET DOWN ON YOUR KNEES AND TELL ME YOU LOVE ME: “One after another, a parade of the wealthiest and most elite institutions in American life since last November have found themselves confronted by unprecedented demands” as a result of Trump’s revenge tour, John Harris and a slew of POLITICO colleagues write.

— “One after another, these establishment pillars have met these demands with the same response: capitulation and compliance. The details are varied but two themes are consistent. The first is an effort — far more organized and disciplined than any precedent from Trump’s first term — to bring institutions who have earned the president’s ire to heel.”

— “The second theme is even more surprising: The swiftness with which supposedly powerful and supposedly independent institutions have responded — with something akin to the trembling acquiescence of a child surrendering his lunch money to a big kid on the morning walk to school. Cumulatively, the cases represent an astonishing new chapter in the history of the American establishment: The Great Grovel.”

FLYING IN: The American Dental Association has kicked off its annual fly-in with dentists and dental students. More than 1,000 attendees will fan out across the Hill through Tuesday to discuss dental insurance reform, community water fluoridation and student debt.

— The Portland Cement Association will kick off its fly-in on Tuesday, with meetings on the Hill and with the Trump administration focused on permitting reform and reducing red tape to boost domestic manufacturing; reauthorizing federal surface transportation and infrastructure bills; and preserving key programs at the Energy Department while improving the industry’s environmental footprint.

— Among the lawmakers cement industry executives are slated to meet with are House Majority Whip Tom Emmer ; Reps. Jay Obernolte (R-Calif.) and Rick Larsen (D-Wash.); and Sens. Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), Steve Daines (R-Mont.) and Jerry Moran (R-Kan.).

WHAT’S NEXT FOR WHITEHOUSE-LEVINE: Miller Whitehouse-Levine , the former CEO of the DeFi Education Fund , has launched a new crypto advocacy group, the Solana Policy Institute , which he told Declan will aim to provide “a Solana-native voice” to the crypto policy landscape in Washington.

— “In D.C., people hear crypto and think of bitcoin and don’t think about anything else,” Whitehouse-Levine said. The Solana Policy Institute, he added, wants to focus on showing policymakers the variety of things that are being built on the Solana blockchain, which run the gamut from NFTs and meme coins to decentralized social networks. Whitehouse-Levine said the Solana Policy Institute has a “few backers” but declined to name them.

IF YOU MISSED IT OVER THE WEEKEND: “ Uber and DoorDash are pressing Republican lawmakers to expand President Trump’s no-tax-on-tips promise beyond employees to include independent contractors who drive ride-share vehicles and deliver food,” per The Wall Street Journal ’s Richard Rubin .

— “The leading tax-free tips proposal, from Sen. Ted Cruz (R., Texas) and Rep. Vern Buchanan (R., Fla.), would let many restaurant and casino workers claim the deduction. But Uber and other ride-share drivers are typically independent contractors, not employees,” and they wouldn’t be eligible under Cruz and Buchanan’s bill.

— “ Javi Correoso , Uber’s head of federal affairs, said the company was counting on lawmakers’ familiarity with its platform to get their drivers’ tips included. … ‘We’ve become a major component of how consumers tip,’ Correoso said. ‘If Congress is going to move in the direction of prioritizing this no-tax-on-tips concept, we’re engaged in asking lawmakers to support Uber drivers and UberEats couriers as a fairness issue.’”

— Lindsay Garcia is now a principal at Kountoupes Denham Carr & Reid . She most recently was clerk of the Senate Appropriations Energy and Water Development Subcommittee and is a Senate Republican Policy Committee alum.

— The Adwell Group has added Camille Torres as senior vice president and Les Umberger as creative director. Torres previously was incumbent protection director at the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee . Umberger previously was owner and creative director of Mod Creations .

— Kristen Edgreen Kaufman has joined the U.S. Council for International Business as senior vice president of sustainability. She was previously deputy commissioner in the New York City Mayor’s Office of International Affairs.

— Nora Kenney is now communications director at End Chronic Disease . She previously was communications director at the Manhattan Institute .

— John Etienne is joining Americans for Responsible Innovation as digital communications director, Morning Tech reports. Etienne most recently served as House Majority PAC ‘s digital director and prior to that was a senior digital media adviser at Third Way .

— Context Strategies has hired Michael Gehlken as deputy vice president. He was most recently at The Dallas Morning News and is a San Diego Union-Tribune and Las Vegas Review-Journal alum.

— Susan Buehler is now senior vice president of corporate communications at the Clean Energy Buyers Association , Morning Energy reports. Buehler was previously chief communications officer at the PJM Interconnection .

— Rachel Huxley-Cohen is now a senior director on Invariant ’s national security public affairs team. She previously was communications director for Sen. Jeanne Shaheen (D-N.H.), and is a Tammy Duckworth and Lois Frankel alum.

— Edward Holland is joining the Small Business Administration as director of policy, planning and intergovernmental affairs. He previously was director of government relations at Fiserv .

— Paolo Mastrangelo is now chief corporate affairs officer at Vial . He previously was co-founder of American Policy Ventures , where he’s now board chair and adviser.

— Ollie Hicks is now an account executive for BerlinRosen ’s NYC cities and public affairs team. He previously was press secretary/digital director for Rep. Susie Lee (D-Nev.).

LIBERATION DAY EVE ON THE RIGHT: Washington — and the globe — are waiting with bated breath for President Donald Trump to roll out a new tariff regime tomorrow, and conservative and free market groups are mounting a last-minute push for restraint from the White House.

— “Your leadership in pursuing lower taxes, regulatory relief, and pro-business policies has already spurred growth,” the heads of nine different advocacy groups wrote in a letter to Trump today, calling on the president to “[press] forward with tax relief, regulatory reform, and energy expansion” and stay away from across-the-board tariffs.

— “Long-term tariffs act as a hidden tax on American businesses and consumers, raising costs and reducing competitiveness. Any trade actions should be narrowly tailored to target specific abuses while minimizing collateral damage to American industries,” the letter continues. Its signatories include leaders from the Center for Freedom and Prosperity , the National Taxpayers Union , the Competitive Enterprise Institute and Hispanic Leadership Fund .

— As tariff day approaches, Advancing American Freedom , the nonprofit led by former Vice President Mike Pence , has put together a primer on the underlying trade investigations that will be used to justify Trump’s new tariffs, the potential details of which AAF has worked to puzzle out ahead of the rollout and will continue to track.

— The group is also backing a Senate Democratic push to block Trump’s Canadian tariffs. “The first Trump administration cut an excellent deal with Canada with USMCA,” AAF President Tim Chapman wrote in a post on X , arguing that Trump lacks the authority to unilaterally abandon the trade deal.

— Chapman then took the taunt a step further, tying Trump to the outcome of Canada’s snap election set for later this month. “This White House’s protectionist policies have saved Justin Trudeau ‘s Liberal Party from certain electoral defeat, making future negotiations with Canada even more difficult,” he argued.

END OF AN ERA: Kristin Smith , who has overseen the crypto industry’s premiere trade group since the outset of the Blockchain Association , will depart next month to join a new upstart crypto organization. She’ll join the Solana Policy Institute — a new group launched this week by the recently departed head of another digital asset trade group — as its president.

— Smith joined the Blockchain Association in 2018, before it even launched, and steered the group through the crypto industry’s transformation in Washington over the years — from being the new kid on the block to pariahs, and then back to having immense power and at the precipice of securing a number of substantial policy victories.

— Under Smith’s leadership, the Blockchain Association’s membership has grown to more than 125 members since its launch, while Smith has become a well-respected face of some of the biggest names in the industry before policymakers. In a post on LinkedIn reflecting on her time there, Smith said the trade group is now “stronger than ever.”

— BA’s board of directors has already begun a “comprehensive search” for Smith’s successor, whom it hopes to have in place by the time Smith formally steps down in May.

WHAT PHARMA WANTS: Drugmakers are lobbying Trump “to phase in tariffs on imported pharmaceutical products in hopes of reducing the sting from the charges and to allow time to shift manufacturing,” Reuters’ Maggie Fick and Michael Erman report, citing four sources familiar with the discussions.

— Though the sources “said it is their understanding that Trump will not announce specifics on any pharma tariffs on Wednesday … the largest multinational drug companies now expect U.S. tariffs targeting medical products are inevitable and hope to secure an incremental ramp-up to the 25% tariff the president has threatened, rather than 25% from day one.” Instead, Trump could announce “a study looking at how the industry-specific tariffs could be applied.”

FLY-IN SZN: Trump’s tariffs will also be a major discussion topic for the restaurant industry, which will kick off a two-day fly-in tomorrow with more than 300 Hill meetings on the books so far, according to the National Restaurant Association . The trade group will host 600 restaurateurs and industry leaders during the fly-in, which will also touch on swipe- fee legislation and the association’s top tax priorities.

— Hundreds more representatives of the travel industry will be on the Hill starting tomorrow to build on a campaign launched in February by the U.S. Travel Association to bulk up the U.S. travel system ahead of upcoming World Cup and Olympic hosting duties. Industry leaders are pushing for funding to upgrade airport security screening, efficient visa processing for next year’s World Cup and more.

— The Pilot Mental Health Campaign , which advocates for modernizing the FAA’s mental health policies and procedures, is holding its second annual fly-in this week. Attendees are set to meet with members of the Senate Commerce Committee and House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee to lobby for passage of the Mental Health in Aviation Act and the Aviation Medication Transparency Act.

— The Biotechnology Innovation Organization will also hit the Hill this week as part of a summit of the trade group’s Council of State Bioscience Associations . State bioscience associations and companies from 30 states will be in town and have over 150 meetings planned across the House and Senate, during which they’ll discuss the economic footprint of the biotech industry and push for the restoration of the research and development tax deduction and the reauthorization of the Small Business Innovation Research program.

THE FREE FILE TAXMAN COMETH: “The nation’s tax prep giants and Republican lawmakers are laser-focused on ensuring this is the last year the Internal Revenue Service offers free tax filing,” NOTUS’ Taylor Giorno reports. “[A]s the program has expanded its reach, it has simultaneously become the target of millions in lobbying dollars aimed at unravelling the federal government’s efforts to offer Americans a free way to directly file simple tax returns.”

— “‘We think [the IRS] ought to wind it down, and they ought to focus their attention on other key priorities like modernization,’ said David Ransom , a tax lobbyist at Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck who represents the American Coalition for Taxpayer Rights , an alliance of tax prep companies including TurboTax owner Intuit and H&R Block .”

— “Intuit and H&R Block currently dominate the consumer tax preparation market. Direct File could disrupt that dynamic by offering people a program to file their federal taxes for free directly with the Internal Revenue Service.”

— “Several tax prep giants have stepped up their lobbying at this pivotal moment. Intuit spent $3.7 million on federal lobbying in 2024, more money than it has ever spent on federal lobbying in a single year, according to the money in politics trackers at the nonpartisan nonprofit OpenSecrets. The American Coalition for Taxpayer Rights spent $390,000 on federal lobbying last year, more money than it has spent in a single year.”

ON THE AIRWAVES: “A major labor union launched a six-figure ad campaign on Tuesday featuring Tufts University Ph.D. student Rumeysa Ozturk decrying what it called an infringement on the First Amendment,” The Hill ’s Brett Samuels writes.

— “The Service Employees International Union (SEIU), which represents nearly 2 million members in the United States and Canada, is launching digital ads and projections on buildings in Washington, D.C., and other cities” in conjunction with a day of rallies in major cities to protest the detention of Ozturk and Lewelyn Dixon , another SEIU member who has been detained by immigration authorities.

— The Children’s Hospital Association , meanwhile, is launching a six-figure ad blitz aimed at curtailing Medicaid cuts. A digital ad campaign touting the benefits Medicaid provides for 37 million children will be accompanied by TV spots launching later this month around the Beltway.

— And Incubate , a coalition of investors, is putting up seven figures in an effort to persuade Congress to change the Inflation Reduction Act’s so-called pill penalty, under which small molecule drugs like pills become eligible for Medicare price negotiations sooner than large molecule drugs like biologics.

— Drugmakers, which oppose the drug price negotiations altogether, have argued the discrepancy will result in less investment in such treatments. The nationwide ad campaign includes a website tracking declines in research programs and drugs discontinued since passage of the IRA.
