— Aaron Davis has joined Navigators Global as vice president of risk and resilience. He was previously vice president of federal relations at the International Code Council and is a House T&I alum.

— Mindset has promoted Becca Alcorn to principal. She was previously a senior director at the firm.

— Bryan Hood is now digital political director for the RNC . He previously was a director at Flexpoint Media .

— Andrew Stevens has joined Thrivent Financial as its first full-time employee in D.C. covering federal government affairs. He previously was vice president of government and external affairs at Allianz .

— Cara Baldari will be director of advocacy at Family Promise . She previously was vice president of family economics, housing and homelessness policy at First Focus on Children .

— Nicola Wagner is the incoming director of executive appointments in Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker ’s office. She most recently was deputy director of employee engagement and leadership development in the Biden White House.

— Holtzman Vogel has added William Klimon as a partner and Patrick Sternal as of counsel in the D.C. office. They were both previously at Compass Legal Group .

— Darren Scher will become managing director of finance at Adfero . He was previously CEO. Adfero is also promoting Lauren Tyler to chief impact officer and is adding Paul Mavrikes as COO. Mavrikes most recently served as the director of business operations at Texas A&M ’s Bush School of Government and Public Service.

— Malvina Gasco has joined the Lincoln Electric Company as government affairs principal. She was most recently executive director of strategic engagement and industrial base policy at Boeing .

— Michael Considine is now a senior adviser in FGS Global ’s global public affairs practice. He previously was deputy assistant secretary of Energy for foreign investment and national security.

— Rolling out the measures today, Trump said “he will impose a baseline 10 percent tariff on imports from all countries, with a higher tariff on approximately 60 countries the United States believes have the most unfair trade relationships with the U.S.,” as POLITICO ’s Doug Palmer reports.

— “Needless to say, today’s announcement was complicated, and manufacturers are scrambling to determine the exact implications for their operations,” National Association of Manufacturers chief executive Jay Timmons said in a statement tonight.

— “The stakes for manufacturers could not be higher. Many manufacturers in the United States already operate with thin margins,” he added, and “the high costs of new tariffs threaten investment, jobs, supply chains and, in turn, America’s ability to outcompete other nations and lead as the preeminent manufacturing superpower.”

— Other industry groups echoed those somber warnings. “The President’s plan is not a targeted attempt to protect American innovation or national security but will hit every family’s budget. Americans cannot afford another round of price increases,” said Michael Hanson , the top lobbyist at the Retail Industry Leaders Association . Hanson urged the White House to reverse course “before lasting damage is done to the economy and family budgets.”

— A number of industries did win reprieves — in a roundabout way — from “double dipping,” meaning that the new tariffs won’t be stacked on top of existing duties for the auto, aluminum and steel industries, for example. And sectors where tariffs could be forthcoming, like copper, pharmaceuticals, semiconductors and lumber, were also exempted from today’s batch.

— The International Fresh Produce Association thanked Trump for excluding crops covered under the USMCA, but said it “remains concerned about the broader application of tariffs on global trading partners and the resulting disruptions to supply chains, market stability, and food prices worldwide.”

— Gary Shapiro , the head of the Consumer Technology Association , came in especially hot. “President Trump’s sweeping global and reciprocal tariffs are massive tax hikes on Americans that will drive inflation, kill jobs on Main Street, and may cause a recession for the U.S. economy,” he warned in a blistering rebuke.

— “This will not be a golden age — but a return to the global economic catastrophe of the Smoot-Hawley tariffs of the 1930s that will disproportionately hurt low income and hardworking Americans,” Shapiro continued. “Make no mistake: American consumers, families, and workers will feel real pain, and elected policymakers in Washington will be held accountable by voters.”

Happy Wednesday and welcome to PI . I want to know all your thoughts on Trump’s tariff announcement. What are you hearing from and telling clients? I’ll keep you anonymous! Add me on Signal , email me at [email protected] , and be sure to follow me on X : @caitlinoprysko .

BUT BUT BUT :There was a glimmer of hope among the tech industry that the new tariffs could batter a slew of U.S. allies across Europe and in Canada and India into relenting on punishing new rules and digital taxes targeting the tech industry on privacy, antitrust and more, as POLITICO ’s Brendan Bordelon and Gabby Miller reported earlier today.

— “We need to hold our trading partners accountable if they’re not giving our exporters a fair shake in markets abroad,” Matthew Schruers , president and CEO of the Computer & Communications Industry Association , told them.

— Their plan depends on whether Trump “actually sees this as a negotiating tactic, or if he just really likes tariffs,” but Brendan and Gabby write that “Trump has shown signals he sees the world this way as well, telling a Davos audience in January that EU fines against Apple , Google and Meta are ‘a form of taxation’ and that their laws are unfairly rigged against American companies.”

— The Information Technology Industry Council channeled to that wishful thinking tonight, praising Trump’s tariffs in a statement as “an available tool to shape international trade flows.” But Sean Murphy , one of the group’s top lobbyists, cautioned that trade penalties “should not be a substitute for a proactive U.S. trade strategy and market-opening negotiations with other governments,” urging the administration to find its way to ultimately reversing the tariffs announced today.

THE VIEW FROM ACROSS LAFAYETTE PARK: In the lead-up to Trump’s announcement today, U.S. Chamber of Commerce chief policy officer Neil Bradley picked apart the premise of tariff reciprocity in a memo to members .

— Depending on how they’re implemented, the concept “could generate an explosion in tariff complexity that officials will find impossible to administer,” while raising prices for U.S. consumers on goods not heavily produced in the U.S. and providing little actual reciprocal benefit, Bradley wrote. “Is this action aligned with the notion of a government cutting the bureaucracy and red tape that slows economic growth?”

— In an interview this morning on CNBC , Bradley was also cool on the idea of “picking winners and losers” through negotiations and exemptions for certain duties, as well as companies absorbing the full cost of the tariffs, which he argued would hurt retirement accounts by depressing stock prices.

— Bradley called the business lobby’s engagement with the administration and Congress “great” despite the sharp policy divergence on tariffs, and said the Chamber has sought to redirect policymakers’ focus to areas of agreement “that will grow the economy, that will lower prices — and let’s set aside this issue that economists across the spectrum — conservative, liberal, everyone in between — agrees will only serve to raise prices.”

RELATED TARIFF READING: “As retaliatory tariffs mount, recyclers worry what goes around, comes around,” by NBC News’ Alexandra Byrne .

THE RICH GET RICHER: The gusher of new business flowing to lobbying firms with ties to the White House isn’t letting up, according to a flurry of new disclosures filed following the end of Q1. Ballard Partners has registered to lobby for more than a dozen new clients just in the past week — a list that includes PBS , which Trump accused on Tuesday of being among “RADICAL LEFT ‘MONSTERS’ THAT SO BADLY HURT OUR COUNTRY!”, JPMorgan Chase , SAP America and the precision health care arm of GE .

— Michael Best Strategies has disclosed eight new clients this week, including Norfolk Southern , the Mortgage Bankers Association , DraftKings , Westinghouse Electric and the Business Council of Canada . Checkmate Government Relations has registered to lobby for UNC Chapel Hill and drugmakers Eli Lilly and Regeneron , disclosures show.

— Alumni of the first Trump administration at CGCN Group have registered a pair of new clients in recent days — Cisco and Booking Holdings — and Mercury Public Affairs has signed computing giant Qualcomm and building materials supplier Cosentino Global .

MORE NEW BUSINESS: Those aren’t the only new lobbying registrations that caught our eye over the past few days. Booking added another new outside firm, bringing on a team of lobbyists at the Duberstein Group that includes Ben Howard and Katherine Winkler Keating , both alumni of Trump’s first administration.

— Honeywell International has retained Arnold & Porter Kaye Scholer to lobby on nuclear fuel issues, including the Price-Anderson Act, which governs liability issues for both nuclear power companies and the general public and which has been invoked against the company in ongoing litigation.

— And Brown University became one of the latest elite institutions to bring on lobbying help amid the Trump administration’s offensive on higher education and a potential increase in the excise tax on university endowments. The Ivy hired GOP lobbying firm AxAdvocacy Government Relations last week as a subcontractor to Providence-based law firm Nixon Peabody , according to a disclosure filing.

— Meanwhile, the chipmaker Nvidia registered its first in-house lobbyists this week. Ned Finkle , Nvidia’s longtime vice president of external affairs, and Stewart Barber , who joined the semiconductor giant in January and was an aide to the president during Trump’s first term, will lobby on a litany of issues, including computing, artificial intelligence, trade and export controls, semiconductor policy, research and development, energy and workforce development.

PLANNED PARENTHOOD STARES INTO THE ABYSS: “ Planned Parenthood is closing clinics and facing more financial strains as Republican control of Washington opens new avenues for weakening the abortion provider ,” per The Wall Street Journal ’s Jennifer Calfas , Mariah Timms and Jess Bravin .

— “The organization went before the Supreme Court on Wednesday for a case that will help determine whether states can kick healthcare providers that offer abortions out of their Medicaid programs, a move that would further imperil the organization’s presence in conservative states.”

— “Republicans who control Congress and the White House are using cuts to federal spending to target progressive groups. Antiabortion leaders are making a push to get GOP lawmakers in the coming weeks to strip some $700 million in Medicaid and other federal funding that Planned Parenthood receives for nonabortion healthcare services. Already the Trump administration has frozen about $20 million in family-planning grants to Planned Parenthood clinics in about a dozen states.”

— “Any loss of funding would exacerbate the organization’s financial challenges. A burst in fundraising after the overturning of Roe v. Wade nearly three years ago has dissipated, and Planned Parenthood is operating at a loss and treating fewer patients, according to the most recent publicly available financial reports.”

WHAT THE ZUCK: “ Mark Zuckerberg is lobbying President Trump and White House officials to agree to a settlement that would prevent Meta Platforms from facing an antitrust trial later this month,” people familiar with the matter tell WSJ’s Josh Dawsey , Rebecca Ballhaus and Dana Mattiol .

— “Meta and its representatives have met with the president and his senior advisers ahead of an April 14 Federal Trade Commission trial that could force the company to unwind its acquisition of the messaging platform WhatsApp and image-sharing app Instagram. The terms of a potential settlement weren’t immediately clear.

— “Zuckerberg, Meta’s chief executive, was at the White House on Wednesday, his third visit during Trump’s presidency, the people said. Some of Trump’s aides have grown frustrated at the company’s lobbying strategy, believing it has been too aggressive, some of the people said.”

— “Trump hasn’t yet decided whether the administration will settle with the company over accusations that it bought Instagram and WhatsApp to quash its competition, according to a person with direct knowledge of his thinking,” but the overtures have “followed an extensive effort by Zuckerberg to make inroads with Trump and improve a relationship that has been rocky for years.”

MORE ZUCK READS: Zuckerberg “is the latest billionaire to shell out tens of millions of dollars for a pricey outpost in Donald Trump’s gilded capital,” per POLITICO ’s Michael Schaffer . “For a month, neighbors in Washington’s upscale Woodland Normanstone neighborhood have speculated about the unidentified buyer who paid $23 million in cash for a 15,000-square-foot mansion.”

— “The sale was the third-most expensive in city history and was shrouded in secrecy, with real estate agents muzzled by non-disclosure agreements. Soon after the deal went through in early March, images of the house became pixelated on Google Maps.”

— “But on Monday, the same day flight-tracking web sites revealed that the Meta CEO’s private jet had landed at Dulles Airport, observers on the quiet block not far from the Naval Observatory noticed an uptick in action at the house, which had been largely dark for months.”

— So why did Zuckerberg pony up now? “I think it’s proximity and being here,” Tom Daley , a longtime veteran of Washington’s high-end real-estate game, told Michael. “It’s the ultimate bow to the man in the White House. To me, it’s a little reminiscent of when the Trump Hotel was the Trump Hotel. He notices who’s there. It’s an easy way to say, ‘Hey, we’re with ya. Here we are.’ I’m sure he takes it as the ultimate compliment.”

Jobs report

— The Institute for Critical Infrastructure Technology has named Brett Freedman its inaugural senior director of emerging technology. Freedman is a senior adviser at WestExec , adviser at the Washington Office and is a DOJ, NSA and Senate Intel alum.

— Julie Margetta Morgan has been named the next president of The Century Foundation . She previously was associate director of research, monitoring and regulations at the CFPB, and is an Education Department alum.

— Mike Frosolone is now a principal at JM2 , a Democratic direct mail firm. He previously was Michigan campaign manager for the Harris campaign and is a DLCC and Cory Booker alum.

— Molly Wilkinson is joining Onebrief as head of government relations. She most recently was vice president and head of regulatory and international government affairs at American Airlines .

— Terry Neal is joining DDC Public Affairs as executive vice president for earned and strategic media. He most recently has been president of Neal Communication Strategies , and is a WaPo alum.

— Rachael Dean Wilson is joining Anduril as communications director. She previously was a managing director at the German Marshall Fund and is a John McCain alum.

— Morgan Hook has joined Bluejacket Strategies as partner and head of the Albany office. He most recently launched and then led the Albany office for SKDK and also co-led its energy and clean tech vertical.

— Human Rights First has announced Uzra Zeya as its new president and CEO. Zeya served as under secretary of state for civilian security, democracy, and human rights in the Biden administration.

— Caterpillar Inc. has hired Christine Gomes as manager of government affairs and Katie Webster as manager of CATPAC and government affairs. Gomes was most recently with the Commerce Department and Webster was previously with Growth Energy .

— Former undersecretary of Homeland Security for intelligence and analysis Ken Wainstein has joined Mayer Brown as a partner in Washington. He served as homeland security adviser to President George W. Bush .

— Tom Wackman is joining DHS in the Office of Public Affairs. He was previously at CRC Advisors .

— Former acting Defense Secretary Christopher Miller has joined the defense advisory board at Applied Intuition .

— HB Strategies has hired Brad Kiesling as a managing principal to lead its Arizona state advocacy office in Phoenix. He most recently served as director of government affairs for Republic Services .

— Rebecca Matwijkow has joined ROKK Solutions as vice president of digital and paid media. She was previously a director at Purple Strategies .

title: ‘Bedlam’ breaks out on K Street after Trump tariffs
body_text:
PICKING UP THE PIECES: The dust is still far from settled 24 hours after President Donald Trump ’s move to unleash punishing new tariffs on U.S. trade partners around the globe, and lobbyists across K Street have been scrambling to decode the new levies’ ramifications for various clients and begin formulating a game plan to win their clients relief.

— “Every CEO in the industry is having a Maalox moment,” Gary Shapiro , CEO of the Consumer Technology Association , told Daniel, referring to the antacid used to treat heartburn and indigestion.

— “It’s been bedlam, in the sense of, clients are freaking out,” said one lobbyist close to the administration, who like others was granted anonymity to speak candidly about what’s been unfolding since last night’s announcement.

— Still, there’s also been a grim sense of relief in finally having concrete information to latch on to, from how this latest batch of tariffs would be structured to who they would hit and how hard.

— “To some extent, they’re all happier today than they were a week ago,” argued another lobbyist close to the White House. “Now we know this is what it looks like, and now we can start to plan more today than we could four days ago, because four days ago we didn’t know anything.”

— “It’s been a ‘what if’ exercise, and now it is a ‘here’s what will happen’ exercise,” a third Republican lobbyist echoed. “Now everybody’s trying to run the numbers internally. And most of the numbers come back really, really ugly.”

— And “the fact that the reciprocal tariffs are not stackable with some of the existing tariffs, like the Section 232 steel and aluminum tariffs, make them easier to swallow for companies that were having a lot of heartburn about this announcement,” Vogel Group ‘s Samir Kapadia added.

— Even now, though, the influence industry is scrambling to answer a new set of questions — namely, whether the tariffs really are here for the long haul (as opposed to serving as a jumping off point for trade negotiations) as well as whether tailored relief from the duties is even on the table — and if so, what that might look like.

— Lobbyists are also puzzling out what’s in store for industries like the pharmaceutical sector, for example, that were spared by Wednesday’s tariffs but which the administration has suggested aren’t in the clear yet.

— The lobbyist close to the administration said that while the White House initially had been privately adamant there would be no exemptions, they did signal the possibility of leniency on products not made or as readily available in the U.S. But the broad-based nature of the new tariffs had K Street feeling somewhat confident throughout today that there will be some wiggle room for interested parties — even as the White House has declared otherwise in spite of today’s post-announcement stock market freefall.

— “Right now, the administration said no exclusions,” said the second lobbyist close to the administration. “But you know, at some point, we’re hoping to be able to gather enough information to make the case that there ought to be.”

— Winning carveouts from the tariffs will require a delicate touch though, as industries and companies in search of exemptions try to convey the strain tariffs will cause without ending up with a target on their backs, with multiple lobbyists stressing that clients need to be cognizant of the fact that Trump is doing what he’s long campaigned on.

— “I think a lot of business leaders are very frustrated that the process of getting here was opaque, and that the decision points are so starkly black and white, and … that they’re not dealing with situations with more nuance,” the third GOP lobbyist told PI, before adding: “I’m trying to say something profound without getting a call from the White House that ‘You’re next.’”

— “What’s the Japanese proverb? The nail sticking up gets hammered down. On K Street, there’s no value in being the nail sticking up right now,” they cautioned.

— As a result, expect the business community to lean heavily on members of Congress to carry their flag with Trump. Job No. 1 for companies “lucky enough to have Republicans in your delegation” should be to sit those lawmakers down and convey “the real world impacts at the plant in your district or at the stores we have in your state,” the third lobbyist argued.

— Already, four Republican senators voted last night to help Democrats pass a resolution that would nullify the emergency powers Trump invoked last month to levy 25 percent tariffs on Canadian imports. And Sen. Chuck Grassley — a senior Republican whose home state of Iowa stands to be hit hard in a trade war — introduced legislation today aimed at clawing back congressional control of tariff policy.

— It’s especially lucky, then, that trade associations with plenty of skin in the game, including the National Restaurant Association, the Information Technology Industry Council and the National Retail Federation all had members in town this week getting face time with lawmakers — with small businesses from the latter group slated to meet with 85 Hill offices today, including Grassley’s.

Happy Thursday and welcome to PI . How are you helping clients process the tariff news? Add me on Signal , email me at [email protected] , and be sure to follow me on X : @caitlinoprysko .

FIRST IN PI — GIORNO AND MILO TO HELP CONGO: The Democratic Republic of the Congo, facing a strong Rwanda-backed insurgency trying to access its mineral wealth, has hired a new lobbying firm started by Trump 2016 campaign alum Karen Giorno with a six-month, $5 million contract, Daniel reports.

— She recently started a lobbying and PR firm called Earhart Turner , where she is joined by senior partner Milo Yiannopoulos, a former far-right Breitbart journalist who will be helping on the Congo account with PR and influencer marketing.

— The work for Congo includes advocacy before Congress, the executive branch, and other government agencies, strategic communications and public affairs help and policy research and analysis, according to a copy of the contract filed with FARA.

— Giorno was a senior adviser on the Trump 2016 campaign and previously worked in operations for first lady Laura Bush , former President George H.W. Bush and former Florida Gov. Rick Scott .

— Congo has tried to lure the Trump administration into making a deal to get the U.S. access to its vast store of critical minerals. Massad Boulos , the father-in-law of Tiffany Trump and Trump’s senior adviser for Africa, is going on a diplomatic trip to Congo, Rwanda and other parts of east Africa this week. Congo also employs Ballard Partners , which recently upped its fee for the country, as well as the law and lobbying firm Von Batten-Montague-York , Dickens & Madson Canada and FGS Global .

— Giorno’s new firm also includes Vish Burra , a former firebrand aide to ex-Rep. George Santos (R-N.Y.) and Ron Coleman , who previously worked for Harmeet Dhillon ’s law firm.

BLAGO’S NEW GIG: “ Rod Blagojevich has a new job: representing the interests of an ultranationalist politician known as the ‘Bosnian Bear’ who has ties to Russian President Vladimir Putin ,” per POLITICO ’s Gregory Svirnovskiy and Shia Kapos .

— “The former Illinois governor, who was pardoned in February by President Donald Trump, has agreed to lobby on behalf of the Republic of Srpska, a Serb-majority territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina long mired in the bitter ethnic tensions of the region.”

— “ RRB Strategies , Blagojevich’s firm, ‘will provide communications and public affairs support on behalf of the Republic of Srpska,’” according to DOJ filings. Bosnia and Herzegovina is held together by the Dayton Agreement, a 1995 treaty that ended the Bosnian War and unified the country. Blagojevich told POLITICO on Wednesday that he hopes to “use whatever ability I have to persuade the decision-makers that we need to take another look at the Dayton Agreement and bring it in line with the realities of today.”

YOU GOTTA DO META THAN THAT: “Senators are probing Meta for its work to develop a presence in China , even in the wake of the company’s moves to boost its Republican credentials” during Trump 2.0, per POLITICO ’s Hailey Fuchs .

— “The Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Crime and Counterterrorism will hold a hearing to scrutinize the parent company of Facebook and Instagram next Wednesday, which will be titled, ‘A Time for Truth: Oversight of Meta’s Foreign Relations and Representations to the United States Congress.’ Sen. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.), the chair of the subcommittee, joined the leadership of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations to ask Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg for a host of internal records relating to the company’s work in China.”

NEW BUSINESS: “A former head of the Department of Energy’s energy efficiency office is now lobbying for companies regulated by that office ,” E&E News’ Tim Cama reports. Dan Simmons , who served as assistant secretary for energy efficiency and renewable energy during Trump’s first term, registered to lobby this week for the Association of Home Appliance Manufacturers .

— “It’s the first lobbying arrangement for Simmons, who established the firm Simmons Energy and Environmental Strategies after Trump left office in 2021. Paperwork filed with Congress says only that Simmons is lobbying on ‘appliance standards.’” The hire comes as Trump’s new administration begins rolling back stricter efficiency standards imposed by the Biden administration.

— Already, four Republican senators voted last night to help Democrats pass a resolution that would nullify the emergency powers Trump invoked last month to levy 25 percent tariffs on Canadian imports. And Sen. Chuck Grassley — a senior Republican whose home state of Iowa stands to be hit hard in a trade war — introduced legislation today aimed at clawing back congressional control of tariff policy.

— It’s especially lucky, then, that trade associations with plenty of skin in the game, including the National Restaurant Association, the Information Technology Industry Council and the National Retail Federation all had members in town this week getting face time with lawmakers — with small businesses from the latter group slated to meet with 85 Hill offices today, including Grassley’s.

— “The former Illinois governor, who was pardoned in February by President Donald Trump, has agreed to lobby on behalf of the Republic of Srpska, a Serb-majority territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina long mired in the bitter ethnic tensions of the region.”

— “RRB Strategies, Blagojevich’s firm, ‘will provide communications and public affairs support on behalf of the Republic of Srpska,’” according to DOJ filings. title: Why Trump’s tariff critics are scared straight
body_text:
— “There is zero incentive for any company or brand to be remotely critical of this administration,” said a public affairs operative, who, like others interviewed was granted anonymity to speak freely. “It destroys your ability to work with the White House and advance your policies, period.”

— An official in the energy industry echoed that sense of fear. “Hearing angst and frustration from all quarters,” the official said via text message, “but no one wants to be first out of the box saying anything negative about Trump’s decision-making.”

— The paralysis reflects the broader mood of Trump’s second administration, in which he’s targeted and threatened to destroy institutions that cross him, including law firms , universities and more .

— With his tight grip on Washington, Trump has faced no meaningful resistance to policies that are upending the global economy, tearing up America’s relationships with its closest allies and making deep, unilateral cuts to the federal government. Leaders have quickly learned that however harmful they think a Trump policy might be, publicly contradicting the president could be worse.

— “There is absolutely a sense that the administration is keeping a list, and no one on K Street wants to be on it,” said one executive at a trade group downtown.

— Now with the Trump administration doubling down on tariffs and trying to sell the country on short-term pain for long-term gain, it’s unclear what the breaking point will be for officials and lobbyists representing the most-impacted constituencies .

— Even those close to Trump expected louder pushback, with a White House ally close to the president’s inner circle pointing out that there is a question about whether the administration’s tariffs are legal, predicting the White House is “gonna be sued off their asses for this as soon as it happens,” the person said, “by trade associations, companies, industry groups.”

— A person close to the administration, however, argued that companies aren’t being fearful about speaking out; rather, they’re trying to be strategic about how to engage with the president.

— Even on Capitol Hill, which lobbyists were hoping would be a key avenue for influencing the president without provoking his ire, fear is spreading among GOP lawmakers as the market hemorrhages trillions of dollars. But so far, most Republicans are unwilling to call on Trump to back down, even as they field a wave of distressed phone calls from industry leaders and constituents in their states.

TGIF and welcome to PI . We made it folks. Drop me a line with all your piping hot tea on lobbying moves, tariffs, reconciliation or whatever else lighting up your group chats these days. Add me on Signal , email me at [email protected] , and be sure to follow me on X : @caitlinoprysko .

SPEAKING OF SPOOKS: “In both Washington and in California, a narrative has quickly emerged about [ Elon ] Musk ’s assault on the federal government: This is what happens when you bring the Silicon Valley playbook to D.C.,” POLITICO Magazine ’s Issie Lapowsky writes.

— “As Musk’s young lackeys rifle through sensitive databases, conk out in makeshift bedrooms set up in government buildings and gut entire agencies, the implication seems to be that this is how it’s done in tech. And there is obviously a very loud corner of the tech sector that agrees .”

— “But in an industry whose workforce overwhelmingly donated to Democrats, in a region whose voters overwhelmingly backed Kamala Harris , there are also a lot of people in tech who view Musk’s handiwork as not just dangerous, but totally antithetical to running a healthy business, let alone the government. They’re just increasingly terrified to say that out loud.”

LAYOFFS HIT AXIOM: Axiom Strategies , the major Republican consulting firm owned by Jeff Roe , on Friday laid off 10 percent of the employees of the firm, Daniel reports.

— Since Trump’s victory in the 2024 primaries, Roe has faced blowback for his role as a key architect of the super PAC that backed Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis in that campaign. Key Trump world figures have pressured down-ballot Republican candidates not to hire Roe or Axiom — a consulting goliath which, as of early 2024, said it had nearly 400 employees across almost 20 individual firms. Now after the layoffs, the firm says it has more than 200 full-time employees.

— Former Trump co-campaign manager Chris LaCivita , who has had a long-running feud with Roe, said in an X post on Thursday : “Today is Liberation Day for many of @jeffroe’s employees who word on the street is will be unceremoniously sacked. Fear not ! when one door closes, another one opens — feel free to reach out for expanding opportunity!”

— In awkward timing, the cuts come a few days before Axiom’s Nashville retreat, celebrating its 20th anniversary. The three-day event features a black tie optional gala dinner at the Country Music Hall of Fame , as well as group activities like “Urban Cowboy Line Dancing,” “Goo Goo Clusters Candy Making” and more. There are also three opportunities to get new headshots.

— “They have promoted it as a ‘family reunion’ for months with the company philosophy being that employees should retire with the company and have their children work here too,” said the current Axiom employee.

— Until 2:30 p.m. on Friday, Roe had not addressed the layoffs with all the staff, according to the employee, even though he gave an interview to Bloomberg on Friday in which he told the outlet that he’s cutting the firm by 10 percent. Once all departing employees were notified, he sent out a memo saying that the firm was still growing and that the firm has more employees today than last Election Day.

— AxAdvocacy , Roe’s lobbying arm, was among his firms that got hit with layoffs today, according to a former Axiom employee with direct knowledge of the matter. Four AxAdvocacy employees were let go Friday, and another recently resigned, according to the person.

GOP POLLSTER RELOCATING TO D.C. : GrayHouse , the polling and data analytics firm founded by Arizona-based political strategist Landon Wall that has become a go-to pollster for Senate Republicans, is relocating its headquarters from Phoenix to Washington, per POLITICO ’s Dasha Burns .

— The move follows a seven-figure investment from moneyed conservatives. Wall has worked with the NRSC and congressional campaigns over the last two cycles and does work for a nonprofit supporting Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.). He has also worked with Eli Lilly Company and Coalition for App Fairness , a group funded by Spotify .

IN HIS OWN WORDS: “The State Department last week released a letter that Hunter Biden wrote while his father was serving as vice president in which he sought assistance from the U.S. government for the Ukrainian energy company Burisma ,” per The New York Times’ Ken Vogel , offering new details about outreach previously uncovered by the Times.

— “In the previously unpublished June 2016 letter on Burisma letterhead to the U.S. ambassador to Italy, Mr. Biden requested ‘support and guidance’ in arranging a meeting with an Italian official to resolve regulatory hurdles to geothermal energy projects Burisma was pursuing in the Tuscany region.”

— “In a response letter also released by the State Department last week, the ambassador, John R. Phillips , indicated that he had dispatched a Commerce Department official to assist with the request.”

ON THE AIRWAVES: Koch-funded conservative advocacy group Americans for Prosperity has launched another wave of ads to marshal pressure on congressional Republicans and highlight what they say is the urgency to extend the 2017 tax cuts in time for voters to feel the effect by next year’s midterms.

— The seven-figure ad blitz is part of a larger $20 million commitment by the group to help get tax legislation over the finish line before a slew of key provisions begin to expire. The national and Beltway-specific digital and radio ads are pegged to Tax Day in a few weeks, by which time congressional leaders have pledged to squeeze their requisite budget resolutions through and formally kick off the reconciliation process.

— “Tax Day is always a pain. Next year could be a nightmare,” the nationwide spot says , warning that “if Congress fails to extend Trump’s tax cuts, middle class families will get hit with a huge tax increase.”

— In addition to the ads, state chapters of AFP will hold grassroots rallies, with a particular focus on California, Georgia, Michigan, Ohio, Maine, Texas and Washington and will meet with lawmakers to drive that point home.

— “Congress needs to act quickly and get the policy right, so businesses have the certainty they need to invest, and Americans feel the benefits well before the next election,” Brent Gardner , AFP’s chief government affairs officer, said in a statement. “With everything packed into one big reconciliation bill, the entire agenda is on the line.”

FLYING IN: Members of the Small Business Payments Alliance , an offshoot of the Electronic Payments Coalition , were on the Hill this week to tout the importance of credit cards and lobby against the swipe fee bill that Sens. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) and Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) are preparing to reintroduce. The fly-in coincided with the launch of a new video campaign featuring small business owners who oppose the Credit Card Competition Act.

IS IT COLD IN HERE OR IS IT JUST US?: Capitol Hill Republicans, corporate America and White House allies are terrified about what’s next in President Donald Trump’s escalating trade war. But they fear Trump’s wrath even more, your host reports along with more than half a dozen colleagues in a look at the chill that has fallen over Washington in the aftermath of this week’s tariffs.

— “There is zero incentive for any company or brand to be remotely critical of this administration,” said a public affairs operative, who, like others interviewed was granted anonymity to speak freely. “It destroys your ability to work with the White House and advance your policies, period.”

— An official in the energy industry echoed that sense of fear. “Hearing angst and frustration from all quarters,” the official said via text message, “but no one wants to be first out of the box saying anything negative about Trump’s decision-making.”

— The paralysis reflects the broader mood of Trump’s second administration, in which he’s targeted and threatened to destroy institutions that cross him, including law firms, universities and more.

— With his tight grip on Washington, Trump has faced no meaningful resistance to policies that are upending the global economy, tearing up America’s relationships with its closest allies and making deep, unilateral cuts to the federal government. Leaders have quickly learned that however harmful they think a Trump policy might be, publicly contradicting the president could be worse.

— “There is absolutely a sense that the administration is keeping a list, and no one on K Street wants to be on it,” said one executive at a trade group downtown.

— Now with the Trump administration doubling down on tariffs and trying to sell the country on short-term pain for long-term gain, it’s unclear what the breaking point will be for officials and lobbyists representing the most-impacted constituencies.

— Even those close to Trump expected louder pushback, with a White House ally close to the president’s inner circle pointing out that there is a question about whether the administration’s tariffs are legal, predicting the White House is “gonna be sued off their asses for this as soon as it happens,” the person said, “by trade associations, companies, industry groups.”

— A person close to the administration, however, argued that companies aren’t being fearful about speaking out; rather, they’re trying to be strategic about how to engage with the president.

— Even on Capitol Hill, which lobbyists were hoping would be a key avenue for influencing the president without provoking his ire, fear is spreading among GOP lawmakers as the market hemorrhages trillions of dollars. But so far, most Republicans are unwilling to call on Trump to back down, even as they field a wave of distressed phone calls from industry leaders and constituents in their states.

SPEAKING OF SPOOKS: “In both Washington and in California, a narrative has quickly emerged about [Elon] Musk’s assault on the federal government: This is what happens when you bring the Silicon Valley playbook to D.C.,” POLITICO Magazine’s Issie Lapowsky writes.

— “As Musk’s young lackeys rifle through sensitive databases, conk out in makeshift bedrooms set up in government buildings and gut entire agencies, the implication seems to be that this is how it’s done in tech. And there is obviously a very loud corner of the tech sector that agrees.”

— “But in an industry whose workforce overwhelmingly donated to Democrats, in a region whose voters overwhelmingly backed Kamala Harris, there are also a lot of people in tech who view Musk’s handiwork as not just dangerous, but totally antithetical to running a healthy business, let alone the government. They’re just increasingly terrified to say that out loud.”

LAYOFFS HIT AXIOM: Axiom Strategies, the major Republican consulting firm owned by Jeff Roe, on Friday laid off 10 percent of the employees of the firm, Daniel reports.

— Since Trump’s victory in the 2024 primaries, Roe has faced blowback for his role as a key architect of the super PAC that backed Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis in that campaign. Key Trump world figures have pressured down-ballot Republican candidates not to hire Roe or Axiom — a consulting goliath which, as of early 2024, said it had nearly 400 employees across almost 20 individual firms. Now after the layoffs, the firm says it has more than 200 full-time employees.

— Former Trump co-campaign manager Chris LaCivita, who has had a long-running feud with Roe, said in an X post on Thursday: “Today is Liberation Day for many of @jeffroe’s employees who word on the street is will be unceremoniously sacked. Fear not ! when one door closes, another one opens — feel free to reach out for expanding opportunity!”

— In awkward timing, the cuts come a few days before Axiom’s Nashville retreat, celebrating its 20th anniversary. The three-day event features a black tie optional gala dinner at the Country Music Hall of Fame, as well as group activities like “Urban Cowboy Line Dancing,” “Goo Goo Clusters Candy Making” and more. There are also three opportunities to get new headshots.

— “They have promoted it as a ‘family reunion’ for months with the company philosophy being that employees should retire with the company and have their children work here too,” said the current Axiom employee.

— Until 2:30 p.m. on Friday, Roe had not addressed the layoffs with all the staff, according to the employee, even though he gave an interview to Bloomberg on Friday in which he told the outlet that he’s cutting the firm by 10 percent. Once all departing employees were notified, he sent out a memo saying that the firm was still growing and that the firm has more employees today than last Election Day.

— AxAdvocacy, Roe’s lobbying arm, was among his firms that got hit with layoffs today, according to a former Axiom employee with direct knowledge of the matter. Four AxAdvocacy employees were let go Friday, and another recently resigned, according to the person.

GOP POLLSTER RELOCATING TO D.C.: GrayHouse, the polling and data analytics firm founded by Arizona-based political strategist Landon Wall that has become a go-to pollster for Senate Republicans, is relocating its headquarters from Phoenix to Washington, per POLITICO’s Dasha Burns.

— The move follows a seven-figure investment from moneyed conservatives. Wall has worked with the NRSC and congressional campaigns over the last two cycles and does work for a nonprofit supporting Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.). He has also worked with Eli Lilly Company and Coalition for App Fairness, a group funded by Spotify.

IN HIS OWN WORDS: “The State Department last week released a letter that Hunter Biden wrote while his father was serving as vice president in which he sought assistance from the U.S. government for the Ukrainian energy company Burisma,” per The New York Times’ Ken Vogel, offering new details about outreach previously uncovered by the Times.

— “In the previously unpublished June 2016 letter on Burisma letterhead to the U.S. ambassador to Italy, Mr. Biden requested ‘support and guidance’ in arranging a meeting with an Italian official to resolve regulatory hurdles to geothermal energy projects Burisma was pursuing in the Tuscany region.”

— “In a response letter also released by the State Department last week, the ambassador, John R. Phillips, indicated that he had dispatched a Commerce Department official to assist with the request.”

ON THE AIRWAVES: Koch-funded conservative advocacy group Americans for Prosperity has launched another wave of ads to marshal pressure on congressional Republicans and highlight what they say is the urgency to extend the 2017 tax cuts in time for voters to feel the effect by next year’s midterms.

— The seven-figure ad blitz is part of a larger $20 million commitment by the group to help get tax legislation over the finish line before a slew of key provisions begin to expire. The national and Beltway-specific digital and radio ads are pegged to Tax Day in a few weeks, by which time congressional leaders have pledged to squeeze their requisite budget resolutions through and formally kick off the reconciliation process.

— “Tax Day is always a pain. Next year could be a nightmare,” the nationwide spot says, warning that “if Congress fails to extend Trump’s tax cuts, middle class families will get hit with a huge tax increase.”

— In addition to the ads, state chapters of AFP will hold grassroots rallies, with a particular focus on California, Georgia, Michigan, Ohio, Maine, Texas and Washington and will meet with lawmakers to drive that point home.

— “Congress needs to act quickly and get the policy right, so businesses have the certainty they need to invest, and Americans feel the benefits well before the next election,” Brent Gardner, AFP’s chief government affairs officer, said in a statement. “With everything packed into one big reconciliation bill, the entire agenda is on the line.”

Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) and Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) are preparing to reintroduce. The fly-in coincided with the launch of a new video campaign featuring small business owners who oppose the Credit Card Competition Act.

WHAT THE NUMBERS MEAN: Six months into President Donald Trump ’s second term was all it took for a handful of newer firms with ties to the president or his administration to overtake many of the more established firms on K Street. Ballard Partners vaulted all the way to the top of the revenue rankings in the second quarter with an astonishing haul of $20.6 million — up from $14 million in Q1 and more than four times what the firm brought in during the same period a year ago.

— Miller Strategies and Mercury Public Affairs , meanwhile, jumped into the top 10 earners on K Street last quarter, while Continental Strategy debuted at No. 15 in the rankings in Q2.

— More broadly, the second Trump administration has ushered in a gold rush across K Street, as haggling over the GOP megabill, tariff and trade whiplash and more drove record-breaking business to firms around town.

— “There’s certainly a hunger for information, and then analysis to help predict and plan for the future,” Will Moschella , who co-leads the Brownstein’s lobbying practice, told PI. Though the firm lost the top spot in the rankings to Ballard, Brownstein’s $18.5 million in lobbying revenues last quarter broke the firm’s previous quarterly record set in Q2 of 2024.

— BGR Group , meanwhile, leapfrogged Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld en route to the firm’s own quarterly record of $17.7 million in Q2. “We’re sort of looking through all the numbers and trying to make some observations about it and the wild thing is … there’s no one single issue that drove our growth,” Loren Monroe , the co-head of BGR’s lobbying practice, told PI. “It’s across the board with multiple issues at the same time.”

FARA FRIDAY, ON TUESDAY: Testimony from David Weiss , the former U.S. attorney tasked with investigating and prosecuting Hunter Biden , revealed prosecutors lacked the evidence needed to bring charges against the former first son under FARA, the New York Post ’s Josh Christenson writes.

— Weiss admitted to House Judiciary Committee members June 6 that he “personally” considered bringing charges that Biden acted as a foreign agent, but was unable to back up the charges, according to a transcript released by House Republicans Monday.

— Biden’s foreign business deals were uncovered amid House Republicans’ efforts to impeach Joe Biden. They found that Hunter Biden would often invoke his father’s name to secure deals with clients in Ukraine, Kazakhstan, Mexico, Russia and China. Weiss had previously hinted at FARA violations last August, citing an instance in which Biden attempted to lobby State Department officials amidst a probe of Romanian businessperson Gabriel Popoviciu during his father’s vice presidency.

ON THE AIRWAVES: MAHA Action , a 501(c)(4) organization, is launching an ad campaign in support of the Trump administration’s MAHA agenda. The campaign, which begins Tuesday and runs through Aug. 12, features an ad titled “ A New Day in America ” focused on the “health revolution” enacted by President Donald Trump and HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The ad will run on cable outlets and online in the D.C. area and nationwide.

— A spokesperson for MAHA Action told PI that while there are no specific markets for nationwide buys, the ad buy is in the high six figures.

— The campaign seeks to highlight the growing public support behind Trump and Kennedy’s MAHA agenda, specifically citing Kennedy’s push to reform the food industry and dietary guidelines.

— “MAHA Action will amplify the voices demanding an end to the corruption that has led to the chronic disease epidemic, to an existential health crisis,” MAHA Action President Tony Lyons said in a news release.

—“Their mix of wonky policy talk and mentions of their affluent lifestyles has gained so much cachet that cabinet secretaries and senators now frequently join. On Wednesday, President Trump is expected to deliver a major address at a summit on “winning the AI race” that “All-In” is co-hosting with bipartisan group Hill & Valley Forum.”

— “The foursome are in some ways a media manifestation of the MAGA movement’s ties to tech—a place where DOGE cuts, AI and crypto are celebrated. The hosts’ proximity to power can draw big-name guests such as Jared Isaacman , whose nomination as NASA administrator Trump had withdrawn, Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. ”

WHAT THE NUMBERS MEAN: Six months into President Donald Trump’s second term was all it took for a handful of newer firms with ties to the president or his administration to overtake many of the more established firms on K Street. Ballard Partners vaulted all the way to the top of the revenue rankings in the second quarter with an astonishing haul of $20.6 million — up from $14 million in Q1 and more than four times what the firm brought in during the same period a year ago.

— Miller Strategies and Mercury Public Affairs, meanwhile, jumped into the top 10 earners on K Street last quarter, while Continental Strategy debuted at No. 15 in the rankings in Q2.

— More broadly, the second Trump administration has ushered in a gold rush across K Street, as haggling over the GOP megabill, tariff and trade whiplash and more drove record-breaking business to firms around town.

— “There’s certainly a hunger for information, and then analysis to help predict and plan for the future,” Will Moschella, who co-leads the Brownstein’s lobbying practice, told PI. Though the firm lost the top spot in the rankings to Ballard, Brownstein’s $18.5 million in lobbying revenues last quarter broke the firm’s previous quarterly record set in Q2 of 2024.

— BGR Group, meanwhile, leapfrogged Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld en route to the firm’s own quarterly record of $17.7 million in Q2. “We’re sort of looking through all the numbers and trying to make some observations about it and the wild thing is … there’s no one single issue that drove our growth,” Loren Monroe, the co-head of BGR’s lobbying practice, told PI. “It’s across the board with multiple issues at the same time.”

FARA FRIDAY, ON TUESDAY: Testimony from David Weiss, the former U.S. attorney tasked with investigating and prosecuting Hunter Biden, revealed prosecutors lacked the evidence needed to bring charges against the former first son under FARA, the New York Post’s Josh Christenson writes.

— Weiss admitted to House Judiciary Committee members June 6 that he “personally” considered bringing charges that Biden acted as a foreign agent, but was unable to back up the charges, according to a transcript released by House Republicans Monday.

— Biden’s foreign business deals were uncovered amid House Republicans’ efforts to impeach Joe Biden. They found that Hunter Biden would often invoke his father’s name to secure deals with clients in Ukraine, Kazakhstan, Mexico, Russia and China. Weiss had previously hinted at FARA violations last August, citing an instance in which Biden attempted to lobby State Department officials amidst a probe of Romanian businessperson Gabriel Popoviciu during his father’s vice presidency.

ON THE AIRWAVES: MAHA Action, a 501(c)(4) organization, is launching an ad campaign in support of the Trump administration’s MAHA agenda. The campaign, which begins Tuesday and runs through Aug. 12, features an ad titled “A New Day in America” focused on the “health revolution” enacted by President Donald Trump and HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The ad will run on cable outlets and online in the D.C. area and nationwide.

— A spokesperson for MAHA Action told PI that while there are no specific markets for nationwide buys, the ad buy is in the high six figures.

— The campaign seeks to highlight the growing public support behind Trump and Kennedy’s MAHA agenda, specifically citing Kennedy’s push to reform the food industry and dietary guidelines.

— “MAHA Action will amplify the voices demanding an end to the corruption that has led to the chronic disease epidemic, to an existential health crisis,” MAHA Action President Tony Lyons said in a news release.

—“Their mix of wonky policy talk and mentions of their affluent lifestyles has gained so much cachet that cabinet secretaries and senators now frequently join. On Wednesday, President Trump is expected to deliver a major address at a summit on “winning the AI race” that “All-In” is co-hosting with bipartisan group Hill & Valley Forum.”

SPOOKED SEASON: Major American companies have arguably the most to lose from President Donald Trump ’s tariffs. — The U.S. Chamber of Commerce opted against bringing its own case against Trump’s tariff powers, but the powerful business lobby filed an amicus brief with the Consumer Technology Association arguing that Trump lacks the power to impose the tariffs — joining a chorus of mostly smaller businesses and other legal or advocacy groups.

— While most business groups have remained on the sidelines of the legal fight, they continue to push back against the tariffs in less headline-grabbing ways. “We haven’t had the type of loud, aggressive lobbying you would have seen in past administrations, or on other issues, for obvious reasons. That doesn’t mean business hasn’t been engaged,” said one person familiar with trade association lobbying efforts on tariffs.

— “I’m trying to think of a more heavily lobbied issue this year, and I don’t know of one,” said Gary Shapiro , CTA’s president. But while Shapiro, whose organization has been among the most vocal critics of Trump’s tariffs from the beginning, said that there are many trade associations of the same mind downtown, “people are concerned about speaking out.”

— “I thought we’d have a lot more people on, who wanted to be on, but they had internal decision-making [and] decided they wouldn’t,” Shapiro said of the effort to recruit more names for the amicus brief. He declined to name any of the other groups who decided not to sign on. “We’ve seen a general quiet of people who generally speak” out on policy issues “since Jan. 20,” he added.

title: Paramount Skydance’s first lobbying hire
body_text:
MAKING MOVES: Paramount Skydance Corporation , the entity formed by one of the most high-profile media acquisitions of the second Trump administration, has made its first outside lobbying hire as the deal faces scrutiny on Capitol Hill. Paramount Skydance retained Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck at the beginning of October to provide work on tax and competition issues, according to a disclosure filing.

— Nadeam Elshami , who isn’t working on the account but who co-leads Brownstein’s lobbying practice, told PI that tax issues could come up as part of a future reconciliation bill. The entertainment industry is also staring down the expiration this year of a prized domestic production tax incentive.

— Among those who are working on the account are Democratic lobbyists Al Mottur , Alice Lugo and Andrew Usyk , Republican Greta Joynes and competition experts Will Moschella and Allen Grunes .

— Last week, a pair of House Democrats accused the new company of “stonewalling congressional oversight” of the $8 billion deal. It was approved by regulators only after Paramount-owned CBS News agreed to pay $16 million to settle a lawsuit filed by President Donald Trump , appoint an ombudsman at the network to eliminate “bias” against the president, and nix diversity, equity and inclusion initiatives. Trump also said at the time that the company had agreed to provide millions more in free advertising or PSAs.

— In a letter to Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison Wednesday, House Energy & Commerce ranking member Frank Pallone (D-N.J.) and House Judiciary ranking member Jamie Raskin (D-Md.) rebuked the company’s “inadequate and incomplete response” to an August letter seeking documents about the merger.

— “Given the lack of meaningful responses to our requests, your letter calls into question whether your company intends to cooperate with our investigation,” they wrote.

— Paramount already had a half-dozen outside lobbying firms on retainer before the merger, including FGS Global , Ballard Partners , Capitol Tax Partners and Capitol Counsel . Meanwhile Ellison’s Skydance Media retained Convergence Strategies last year to lobby for the merger’s approval. That contract was terminated last month, disclosures show.

Micah Ketchel , who was most recently a senior adviser in the State Department’s Bureau of International Organization Affairs, is joining the firm as a partner.

— Before moving to State earlier this year, Ketchel was chief of staff to former national security adviser Mike Waltz when Waltz was in the House. Ketchel followed Waltz to the White House, where he served as a senior adviser on the National Security Council.

— At Ballard, he’ll help the firm capitalize on Trump’s interest in striking deals related to the production of critical minerals across the globe — part of an effort to undercut Chinese dominance of the global supply chain for the minerals. title: Dems probe K Street ballroom fundraising
body_text:
BALLROOM BLITZ: A trio of Senate Democrats want more information about the lobbyists reportedly helping raise money for President Donald Trump ’s White House ballroom project from corporate America and other donors with business before Trump’s administration.

— In letters to Ballard Partners ’ Brian Ballard , Miller Strategies ’ Jeff Miller and Michael Best Strategies ’ Reince Priebus , the lawmakers request that the Trump-tied lobbyists turn over documents and respond to a slew of questions outlining their role in the ballroom fundraising project. Those include how and when the lobbyists got involved; the donors from whom lobbyists have solicited donations; whether the lobbyists received any guidance about who they should or shouldn’t raise money from; and whether a contribution was intended to be made anonymously.

— Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) demanded to know whether the firms in question “made any representations that the prospective donor would be more likely to secure favorable action from the federal government if it made a donation” or offered anything in exchange for donations or pledges, such as access to administration officials or invites to White House events. The senators posed similar questions to Meredith O’Rourke , Trump’s primary fundraiser.

— The inquiry follows reports that Ballard and Miller —both top Trump fundraisers — and Priebus, Trump’s first White House chief of staff, have been among those heavily involved in fundraising for the ballroom.

— An analysis out today from the watchdog group Public Citizen found that of the known corporate donors to the ballroom project, two-thirds are clients of at least one of the three firms the senators reached out to. Several donors retain two of the three firms, including Palantir (Ballard and Miller) Hard Rock International (Ballard and Michael Best) and Ripple (Ballard and Michael Best).

— Ballard and Priebus declined to comment, while Miller and O’Rourke did not respond to requests for comment.

— Blumenthal, Warren and Schiff also point to an earlier analysis from Public Citizen that found corporate ballroom donors had been awarded $279 billion in government contracts in the last five years. Meanwhile, more than half of the disclosed donors are either currently facing enforcement actions from the federal government or had enforcement actions paused by Trump, according to the analysis.

— The senators requested a response from the lobbyists and O’Rourke by the first week of December.

— Last night, Musk “made his first public appearance in Washington since he left the capital in May, attending a formal dinner that Mr. Trump threw for Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia.”

— “In the period since Mr. Musk left Washington in a rage … he has largely backed down from his feud with the president,” and has signaled he is likely to spread around some of his largesse ahead of the midterms next year — even as associates tell the Times he “has not been closely following Republican politics since leaving Washington.”

BALLROOM BLITZ: A trio of Senate Democrats want more information about the lobbyists reportedly helping raise money for President Donald Trump’s White House ballroom project from corporate America and other donors with business before Trump’s administration.

— In letters to Ballard Partners’ Brian Ballard, Miller Strategies’ Jeff Miller and Michael Best Strategies’ Reince Priebus, the lawmakers request that the Trump-tied lobbyists turn over documents and respond to a slew of questions outlining their role in the ballroom fundraising project. Those include how and when the lobbyists got involved; the donors from whom lobbyists have solicited donations; whether the lobbyists received any guidance about who they should or shouldn’t raise money from; and whether a contribution was intended to be made anonymously.

— Sens. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) demanded to know whether the firms in question “made any representations that the prospective donor would be more likely to secure favorable action from the federal government if it made a donation” or offered anything in exchange for donations or pledges, such as access to administration officials or invites to White House events. The senators posed similar questions to Meredith O’Rourke, Trump’s primary fundraiser.

— The inquiry follows reports that Ballard and Miller —both top Trump fundraisers — and Priebus, Trump’s first White House chief of staff, have been among those heavily involved in fundraising for the ballroom.

— An analysis out today from the watchdog group Public Citizen found that of the known corporate donors to the ballroom project, two-thirds are clients of at least one of the three firms the senators reached out to. Several donors retain two of the three firms, including Palantir (Ballard and Miller) Hard Rock International (Ballard and Michael Best) and Ripple (Ballard and Michael Best).

— Ballard and Priebus declined to comment, while Miller and O’Rourke did not respond to requests for comment.

— Blumenthal, Warren and Schiff also point to an earlier analysis from Public Citizen that found corporate ballroom donors had been awarded $279 billion in government contracts in the last five years. Meanwhile, more than half of the disclosed donors are either currently facing enforcement actions from the federal government or had enforcement actions paused by Trump, according to the analysis.

PARAGUAYAN POLITICS: The former Paraguayan vice president and an associate of his who have been banned from entering the United States since 2022 have hired Florida-based Corcoran Partners to lobby on “issues around visas,” according to disclosure reports .

— Hugo Velazquez , who left office in 2023, was accused by State Department officials of attempting to thwart a Paraguayan investigation that threatened his financial interests by offering a $1 million bribe to a public official. The bribe was allegedly offered via an intermediary, Juan Carlos Duarte , a personal friend of Velazquez’s who served as legal counsel for the entity that controls the Yacyreta Dam on the border of Paraguay and Argentina.

— Both men and their families were banned from traveling to the U.S. as a result of the designation. Velazquez was later additionally sanctioned by the Treasury Department under the Magnitsky Act, cutting him off from U.S. banks and prohibiting him from doing business with U.S. companies. The recently filed disclosure report for Velazquez also mentions “issues related to OFAC [Office of Foreign Assets Control] sanctions and removal policies.”

— A third individual, former Paraguayan Minister of Agriculture Rodolfo Max Friedmann , has also hired Corcoran Partners to lobby on visa issues . Friedmann resigned in 2020 after being hit with corruption and money laundering charges related to his time as governor of Paraguay’s Guaira Department. PI could not immediately determine if Friedmann had also been designated as an individual involved in corruption. The State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

— On the accounts for Corcoran Partners are Carlos San Jose and Steve Bovo . As PI reported last month , Bovo is a close ally of Secretary of State Marco Rubio from their time in Florida politics. Bovo’s wife, Viviana Bovo , currently works under Rubio at the State Department, according to The Miami Herald .

In other words, roughly 1 in every 13 dollars spent in last year’s national elections was donated by a handful of the country’s richest people.”

FUNDING AMERICA FIRST: DonorsTrust , a leading conservative dark money nonprofit, gave more than $25 million in 2024 to two Trump-aligned organizations founded by current administration officials, Taylor Giorno reports for NOTUS .

— America First Legal Foundation , founded by Trump’s deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller , received nearly $21.3 million from DonorsTrust, a massive increase from the $3.2 million AFLF received in 2023.

— America First Policy Institute , founded by Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins , got more than $4.4 million, an amount more than 20 times higher than the $159,200 AFPI received from DonorsTrust in 2023.

— “Overall, DonorsTrust is booming, disclosing nearly $1.4 billion in ‘net assets or fund balances’ at the end of 2024, up from $1.3 billion at the end of 2023. In all, DonorsTrust gave out $284.1 million in grants in 2024, its second-biggest year since its founding in 1999.”

FAMILY BUSINESS: As Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick pushes for foreign investment in U.S. industrial projects like data centers, his sons Kyle and Brandon are cashing in on those projects to the benefit of their portfolio of family businesses, Eric Lipton , Michael Rothfeld , David Yaffe-Bellany and Ana Swanson report for The New York Times .

— New data centers, driven by the AI boom, are particularly ripe targets for foreign investment, the kind of which is being heavily encouraged by Lutnick and the Trump administration. One of the Lutnick family companies, Newmark, recently announced it had completed more than $25 billion in data center deals in the past year, earning millions in fees.

— “The data center boom is ‘a modern-day gold rush,’ Chad Lavender, a top Newmark executive, said in a podcast interview. …’We’re seeing a ton of activity.’ Now Mr. Lutnick is helping foster that activity from Washington. The Commerce Department is seeking to accelerate data center construction with tax breaks, grants and permits to build new power sources to fuel the facilities.”

— “The White House and the Commerce Department said in statements that Mr. Lutnick had fulfilled his ethics requirements and took them seriously.”

CLUB PENGUIN: Wondering why Rep. William Timmons ’ (R-S.C.) profile picture on X is a chubby blue penguin ? It all comes back to crypto.

— Pudgy Penguins , a brand that spans NFTs, cryptocurrency, mobile games, toys and collectables was on the Hill this week meeting with members about crypto issues. The brand arrived in Washington in September, when it hired Invariant to lobby lawmakers on crypto legislation like the GENIUS Act, the STABLE Act and the CLARITY act.

— As a part of this week’s Hill visit, Pudgy Penguins created penguin versions of the nine members they met with. Timmons posted his penguin on X and promised to make it his profile picture if the post received 10,000 likes. Timmons should keep the profile picture through the end of the month, assuming he abides by the results of an X poll he posted yesterday.

— No other members followed Timmons in changing their profile pictures, but you can see penguin Rep. Mike Collins (R-Ga.) here .

Bendler’s lawyers wrote in sentencing paperwork that he believed BGR had completed the required FARA paperwork on his behalf. In a statement to PI, BGR said that Bendler never consulted with the firm about registering.

— “Registering under FARA is the responsibility of individuals who do work that falls under its requirements,” said Jeff Birnbaum , president of BGR Public Relations. “Dale Bendler, who was a BGR independent contractor years ago, agreed in writing to abide by all applicable laws including the Foreign Agents Registration Act. Bendler did not consult with BGR about registration and recently — after he was indicted and pled guilty to a variety of offenses including misuse of secret documents — registered retroactively.”

— “BGR fully cooperated with investigators as a witness in the case. We understand that BGR was never the subject or target of this investigation and, importantly, has never been charged with any wrongdoing. It is not surprising that Mr. Bendler’s attorney would now attempt to blame anyone other than his client for his guilt to get a lighter sentence.”

TO BAN OR NOT TO BAN: A Chinese-founded electronics manufacturer facing bipartisan calls for an investigation into its relationship with the Chinese government has hired former Donald Trump campaign adviser Bryan Lanza of Mercury Public Affairs to lobby Congress and the administration, according to a newly filed disclosure report .

— TP-Link , maker of smart home devices like wireless routers, smart doorbells, security cameras and more, hired Lanza in October to “educate policymakers, federal agencies and Congress” on the company’s U.S. operations and “compliance with U.S. data security and supply chain requirements,” according to the disclosure report. On the account with Lanza are John Lonergan and James Messner .

— Founded by two brothers in China in 1996, TP-Link completed a corporate restructuring last year that spun off its U.S. business, creating a split between China-based TP-Link Technologies and U.S.-based TP-Link Systems. One brother maintains control of the China-based company while the other fully controls the newly-established U.S. company.

— The separation has not assuaged China hawks in Washington. Earlier this year, a group of GOP senators led by Tom Cotton (R-Ark.) sent a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick asking him to ban the company’s wireless routers from sale in the U.S. And earlier this month, a bipartisan group of 23 lawmakers sent a letter to Lutnick asking him to investigate, and if necessary, ban sale of TP-Link smart devices like security cameras and baby monitors.

— “Right now, nothing stops CCP-tied companies from spying on Americans through internet-connected cameras in our homes,” the lawmakers wrote. “The Chinese Communist Party can capture and exploit these videos to track, blackmail, or extort U.S. citizens — including top government and military officials.”

— While no official action has been taken on TP-Link, there are signs the administration is taking those concerns seriously. At the end of October, The Washington Post reported that multiple federal agencies had reviewed the matter and backed a proposal to ban TP-Link routers. Separately, Bloomberg reported in April that the Justice Department is conducting a criminal antitrust investigation into the company’s pricing strategies.

— “TP-Link Systems Inc. emphatically objects to any allegation it is tied to the Communist Party of China, dependent on the Chinese government, or otherwise subject to interference under Chinese national security laws,” a company spokesperson told PI. “TP-Link will continue to work with the U.S. Department of Commerce to ensure we understand and can respond to any concerns the government has.”

— “Despite unsourced media reports regarding a Department of Justice antitrust probe, TP-Link has received no inquiries from the DOJ,” the spokesperson added.

— As skepticism of TP-Link rises in Washington, so too has the company’s spending. In the summer of 2024, the company made Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld its first lobbying hire, paying the firm $380,000 that year. In the first three quarters of this year, the company has shelled out nearly $1 million to Akin, Vernonburg Group and Ballard Partners .
