MENDING BRIDGES: “Building America’s Future, a dark-money group that has been supported by Elon Musk, is shelling out more than a million dollars to promote recent White House wins, including a GOP domestic policy package the Tesla CEO and former Trump administration employee once called ‘a disgusting abomination,’” POLITICO’s Gregory Svirnovskiy reports.

— “The 30-second ad, titled ‘Independence,’ is set to run nationally on Fox News and will congratulate President Donald Trump on the passage of Republicans’ ‘One Big, Beautiful Bill,’ which extends his 2017 tax cuts alongside other GOP wins at the expense of nearly $1 trillion in coming Medicaid cuts.”

— “Musk, who has donated extensively to BAF, assailed the megabill when it reached Congress,” and threatened to bankroll primary challenges against every Republican who voted for the measure.

— “But the group that Musk has backed doesn’t agree with his assessment of the megabill. ‘President Trump, Leader John Thune, and Speaker Mike Johnson all showed tremendous strength and vision to get historic tax cuts for working families across the finish line this summer, and their remarkable achievement will put America on a path to prosperity for years to come,’ said Generra Peck, senior advisor to the group.”

BEHIND THE LOBBYING FIGHT OVER FACIAL RECOGNITION BILL: “Senate GOP privacy hawks are stewing over the derailment of a bill … that would limit face scanning technologies — and blaming the TSA for interference in an under-the-radar legislative battle,” per POLITICO’s Benjamin Guggenheim.

— “On the surface, Senate Commerce Chair Ted Cruz had to cancel consideration of the bipartisan bill that would put guardrails on the airport security screening tool due to intense lobbying from the travel industry, which had sowed seeds of doubt among committee members.”

— “Privately, though, Republicans who support the measure say it was the TSA itself, with the encouragement of its politically appointed leadership, that assumed a critical role in orchestrating the lobbying campaign that grew opposition and forced the legislation to be scrapped at the last minute from the markup docket.”

— The lobbying effort may imperil the potential confirmation prospects for Ha Nguyen McNeill, the current acting TSA chief who Trump is expected to nominate to fill the role full-time. McNeill was previously an executive at Pangiam, which provides airports with AI-powered facial recognition software that the company boasts can match a photo against a gallery of millions of mugshots in a matter of milliseconds.

— TSA’s opposition to the facial recognition bill pits McNeill against Kristi Noem, who as DHS secretary is McNeill’s superior and who supports the bill, per Ben. And even though travel and biometrics industry groups reiterated their opposition last week, “lawmakers who have been trying to push the bill forward are saying that TSA was the real driving force behind the legislation’s withdrawal, with the agency using industry lobbyists as conduits to relay dissatisfaction and mar the measure’s chances.”

ANNALS OF INFLUENCE PEDDLING: Campaign finance reports filed last week by Trump’s super PAC are helping shed new light on the ways “lobbyists, political consultants and others in the influence industry have capitalized on Mr. Trump’s aggressive fund-raising while in office to deliver for clients and earn chits with a president who keeps close tabs on who is delivering cash and listens to their appeals,” The New York Times’ Ken Vogel and David Yaffe-Bellany reported over the weekend.

— “MAGA Inc.’s report included donations from a mother seeking a pardon for her son, as well as people who had been, or would later be, appointed to posts in his administration and companies in industries seeking more lenient treatment than they had gotten under” the Biden administration.

— “It is not just MAGA Inc. that benefits. Since Mr. Trump’s election last fall, fund-raisers and lobbyists have been steering corporations and donors to a buffet of options for unlimited giving, some of which are less overtly political or allow anonymous donations, that can bring access to the president.” The options included Trump’s inaugural committee, which shattered fundraising records, as well as the Trump-affiliated dark money group Securing American Greatness. “Even the White House Historical Association has become a vehicle for lobbyists and favor seekers,” the Times reports.

FRIENDS IN HIGH PLACES: AECOM, the infrastructure firm tapped by the White House to lead the engineering team for the construction of the $200 million White House ballroom being built with private money, is a lobbying client of Ballard Partners, which previously employed Trump administration officials like as White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and Attorney General Pam Bondi, per Daniel.

— AECOM hired Ballard a week after Trump’s win in November, and has paid the firm $120,000 to lobby the White House and Congress so far this year. Wiles, who left Ballard years before it signed AECOM, told Daniel in an email that she didn’t “know how they were selected, but I was never lobbied about any of the contractors or involved in any way.” Ballard declined to comment. Spokespeople for AECOM didn’t respond to a request for comment.

— AECOM has received numerous federal contracts since the start of the Trump administration, including an Air Force contract worth up to $1.5 billion and at least two major contracts from the Army Corps of Engineers. title: Layoffs at top women’s legal group
body_text:
FIRST IN PI — REDUCTION IN FORCE: The National Women’s Law Center recently laid off a fifth of its staff as it tries to weather a downturn in funding for progressive nonprofits, Daniel L. reports.

— The more than 50-year-old organization let go 32 employees in early September, with the cuts affecting all its teams, including reproductive health, workplace justice, education and communications, according to four people familiar with the organization. The development team, critical to addressing the financial issues facing NWLC, was also affected despite exceeding its fundraising targets in the last year, according to two of the people.

— There is anger at the organization that none of NWLC’s vice presidents and C-suite executives took pay cuts to try to reduce the number of layoffs, according to the four people. NWLC CEO Fatima Goss Graves makes $550,000 annually, including benefits, per the organization’s tax records.

— “When we asked why, we were told it would have been ‘symbolic’ to take a pay cut,” said one of the people.

— Another said that such an action would have signaled that leadership was taking some “accountability” to make up for having “spent a little too much money and not properly anticipated what the funding landscape would be.”

— Economic volatility has caused a wave of layoffs in the nonprofit space this year, with the sector losing at least 23,000 full-time jobs from President Donald Trump ’s inauguration to June 30, according to the Chronicle of Philanthropy . Earlier this year, for instance, the Human Rights Campaign also laid off a fifth of its employees .

— Employees knew that it wasn’t good news when they were called to a mandatory staff Zoom on 30-minutes notice and most of the VPs were in the office, according to three of the people. Earlier in the year, the organization had talked about prioritizing staff retention, according to the people.

— “It just really felt so sudden,” the person said. It “felt very similar to DOGE tactics that we were so vocal against since the beginning of the year.”

— One executive said the organization tried to carry out the layoffs as humanely as possible. Affected employees were given at least three months pay and help with finding a new job and temporary health coverage. Goss Graves told employees that a slowdown in donations had caused the layoffs.

— “To ensure the organization’s long-term sustainability amid economic volatility for many nonprofits, we were forced to make the incredibly difficult decision to reduce the size of our workforce,” spokesperson Uma M. Iyer told PI. “This decision was made only after carefully evaluating all other options, and to ensure we can continue leading the fight for gender justice.”

BARNES HANGS A SHINGLE: Tori Barnes , who stepped down in August as the top lobbyist for the U.S Travel Association , has launched her own shop, Anchor Solutions . The trade association is one the first clients for whom Barnes registered to lobby this week on issues including the new $250 “visa integrity fee” that went into effect on Wednesday. The fee, created under the GOP megabill that became law in July, has sparked industry concerns that it could curtail travel ahead of next year’s FIFA World Cup.

— Barnes has also signed hotel giant Hilton Worldwide , for which she will lobby on issues related to corporate taxes, hospitality and travel issues. And she’s been named executive director of the Great American Road Trip , an initiative sponsored by U.S. Travel, Chase Travel , Toyota , the Philadelphia Convention and Visitors Bureau and building materials group CRH to promote America’s semiquincentennial next year.

NEW CLIENTS FOR BRIDENSTINE, BERNHARDT: Two former agency heads under President Donald Trump have registered to lobby for a batch of new clients this week. Among the new clients for The Artemis Group , which was founded by former GOP congressmember and NASA Administrator Jim Bridenstine , is commercial weather data company PlanetiQ .

— Last month, NOAA awarded PlanetiQ a $24 million contract “for satellite data services, the largest contract for such services ever granted to a private-sector firm,” per E&E News’ Daniel Cusick . The Artemis Group began lobbying for PlanetiQ weeks earlier on issues related to weather, space and appropriations.

— Bridenstine and his firm also began lobbying at the beginning of September for the space startups Portal Space Systems and ExLabs — the latter of which won a $1.9 million contract from the Space Force earlier this week. The hires bring the total number of new lobbying clients for Artemis Group this year to 14, according to a PI analysis of disclosure filings.

— The Bernhardt Group , which was started earlier this year by former Interior Secretary David Bernhardt , disclosed a trio of new clients this week as well, including 5E Advanced Materials , which supplies products derived from boron and has been lobbying for its inclusion in the U.S. Geological Survey’s next list of critical minerals.

HATCHING A PROBLEM: “Agencies across the federal government are explicitly blaming Democrats for the government shutdown — from banners on top of public websites to suggested out-of-office messages for federal employees — in an unusually overt show of partisan messaging that some ethics experts say may violate federal law ,” POLITICO ’s Faith Wardwell writes.

WARNING SIGNS FOR AIPAC: “With American support for the Israeli government’s management of the conflict in Gaza undergoing a seismic reversal, and Democratic voters’ support for the Jewish state dropping off steeply, AIPAC is becoming an increasingly toxic brand for some Democrats on Capitol Hill,” The New York Times’ Annie Karni writes.

— The latest evidence of the Democratic realignment on unconditional support for Israel came last month when House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries , a longtime staunch AIPAC ally, accepted the endorsement of the center-left pro-Israel J Street for the first time.

— “Some Democrats who once counted AIPAC among their top donors have in recent weeks refused to take the group’s donations. Its annual trip to Israel, a formative experience for many lawmakers that once drew a majority of first-term members, has seen a drop-off in Democratic attendance. And a majority of the Senate Democratic Caucus has voted in recent months for legislation opposed by AIPAC to cut off weapons sales to Israel.”

— “AIPAC has long been a force on Capitol Hill, able to spend seemingly whatever it took to defeat lawmakers it viewed as hostile to Israel. Last year, for instance, the group spent more than $23 million to defeat former Representatives Cori Bush of Missouri and Jamaal Bowman of New York, two progressives who vocally opposed unconditional U.S. aid to Israel.”

HE’S MAKING A LIST: The White House is “enlisting powerful business and labor groups to push Senate Democrats to end the government shutdown,” per Axios’ Alex Isenstadt , as Trump “play[s] an inside game by cultivating support from influential D.C. interests — a tactic he typically dismissed during his first administration.”

— “White House officials tell Axios they’ve had about 400 calls with a range of interest groups in recent weeks to press them on the shutdown — even as Trump was publicly musing that it would give his team an opportunity to slash Democratic priorities .”

— “White House officials insist they haven’t been explicitly pressuring groups to oppose the shutdown, but have strongly nudged them toward Trump’s corner. They have, for example, conveyed to the Chamber of Commerce and the Business Roundtable that if they want to continue to engage with the administration, they have to show they can ‘play ball,’ one Trump aide said.”

— Many of D.C.’s most powerful industry groups generally disavow government shutdowns as a matter of course. But it’s worth noting that ahead of the Senate’s failure to pass a stopgap funding bill again today, Business Roundtable CEO Josh Bolten blasted out a statement calling on Congress “to immediately pass a clean continuing resolution.

— “A fully functional government is essential for American businesses, workers and consumers while policymakers continue working on a full-year funding package and other pressing issues,” Bolten added.

— And the Chamber is adopting a strategy similar to its response to Trump’s tariff policies , urging small businesses to share their stories of how the shutdown is affecting their organizations.

ANNALS OF FUNDRAISING: “Liberal activist David Hogg ‘s political group is off to a shaky start in his mission to knock out Democratic incumbents and usher in a new generation of leaders,” per Axios’ Alex Thompson and Holly Otterbein .

— Hogg said earlier this year that his PAC, Leaders We Deserve , would pump $20 million into races backing younger candidates or primarying Democratic incumbents in safe seats. But the group “hasn’t endorsed any challengers to Democratic incumbents in Congress and has been successful in just one of three contests this year.”

— And though Hogg “ has accused Democrats of being overly reliant on political consultants … his group is spending most of its money on such companies, according to campaign finance reports.”

— “Leaders We Deserve and its allies argue they need to invest in a grassroots fundraising infrastructure now to compete against incumbent Democrats next year. … But even progressives who support Hogg’s plan are growing impatient.”

— Bridenstine and his firm also began lobbying at the beginning of September for the space startups Portal Space Systems and ExLabs — the latter of which won a $1.9 million contract from the Space Force earlier this week. The hires bring the total number of new lobbying clients for Artemis Group this year to 14, according to a PI analysis of disclosure filings.

— The Bernhardt Group, which was started earlier this year by former Interior Secretary David Bernhardt, disclosed a trio of new clients this week as well, including 5E Advanced Materials, which supplies products derived from boron and has been lobbying for its inclusion in the U.S. Geological Survey’s next list of critical minerals.

HATCHING A PROBLEM: “Agencies across the federal government are explicitly blaming Democrats for the government shutdown — from banners on top of public websites to suggested out-of-office messages for federal employees — in an unusually overt show of partisan messaging that some ethics experts say may violate federal law,” POLITICO’s Faith Wardwell writes.

WARNING SIGNS FOR AIPAC: “With American support for the Israeli government’s management of the conflict in Gaza undergoing a seismic reversal, and Democratic voters’ support for the Jewish state dropping off steeply, AIPAC is becoming an increasingly toxic brand for some Democrats on Capitol Hill,” The New York Times’ Annie Karni writes.

— The latest evidence of the Democratic realignment on unconditional support for Israel came last month when House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, a longtime staunch AIPAC ally, accepted the endorsement of the center-left pro-Israel J Street for the first time.

— “Some Democrats who once counted AIPAC among their top donors have in recent weeks refused to take the group’s donations. Its annual trip to Israel, a formative experience for many lawmakers that once drew a majority of first-term members, has seen a drop-off in Democratic attendance. And a majority of the Senate Democratic Caucus has voted in recent months for legislation opposed by AIPAC to cut off weapons sales to Israel.”

— “AIPAC has long been a force on Capitol Hill, able to spend seemingly whatever it took to defeat lawmakers it viewed as hostile to Israel. Last year, for instance, the group spent more than $23 million to defeat former Representatives Cori Bush of Missouri and Jamaal Bowman of New York, two progressives who vocally opposed unconditional U.S. aid to Israel.”

HE’S MAKING A LIST: The White House is “enlisting powerful business and labor groups to push Senate Democrats to end the government shutdown,” per Axios’ Alex Isenstadt, as Trump “play[s] an inside game by cultivating support from influential D.C. interests — a tactic he typically dismissed during his first administration.”

— “White House officials tell Axios they’ve had about 400 calls with a range of interest groups in recent weeks to press them on the shutdown — even as Trump was publicly musing that it would give his team an opportunity to slash Democratic priorities.”

— “White House officials insist they haven’t been explicitly pressuring groups to oppose the shutdown, but have strongly nudged them toward Trump’s corner. They have, for example, conveyed to the Chamber of Commerce and the Business Roundtable that if they want to continue to engage with the administration, they have to show they can ‘play ball,’ one Trump aide said.”

— Many of D.C.’s most powerful industry groups generally disavow government shutdowns as a matter of course. But it’s worth noting that ahead of the Senate’s failure to pass a stopgap funding bill again today, Business Roundtable CEO Josh Bolten blasted out a statement calling on Congress “to immediately pass a clean continuing resolution.

— “A fully functional government is essential for American businesses, workers and consumers while policymakers continue working on a full-year funding package and other pressing issues,” Bolten added.

— And the Chamber is adopting a strategy similar to its response to Trump’s tariff policies, urging small businesses to share their stories of how the shutdown is affecting their organizations.

ANNALS OF FUNDRAISING: “Liberal activist David Hogg‘s political group is off to a shaky start in his mission to knock out Democratic incumbents and usher in a new generation of leaders,” per Axios’ Alex Thompson and Holly Otterbein.

— Hogg said earlier this year that his PAC, Leaders We Deserve, would pump $20 million into races backing younger candidates or primarying Democratic incumbents in safe seats. But the group “hasn’t endorsed any challengers to Democratic incumbents in Congress and has been successful in just one of three contests this year.”

— And though Hogg “has accused Democrats of being overly reliant on political consultants … his group is spending most of its money on such companies, according to campaign finance reports.”

— “Leaders We Deserve and its allies argue they need to invest in a grassroots fundraising infrastructure now to compete against incumbent Democrats next year. … But even progressives who support Hogg’s plan are growing impatient.”

title: How Trump 2.0 is blowing up lobbying
body_text:
LDA WEEK AMUSE-BOUCHE: After decades of revolving-door culture, Washington is grappling with a new normal for how influence works in the capital, your host reports with Brendan Bordelon and Amanda Chu . Conversations with several dozen lobbyists, industry officials and public relations professionals revealed a transformation far more disruptive than the typical churn that comes with a new administration.

— In Trump 2.0, American policy influence has shifted from its previous channels — agency officials, top lawmakers and staffers on key congressional committees — to a new reality where change comes suddenly from the top.

— President Donald Trump and a handful of lieutenants have seized full control over policies once considered the remit of Congress and experts at agencies, including hyperspecific issues like tariff rates, high-skilled visa fees and funding freezes. The president’s gravitational pull has forced CEOs to act as their companies’ top lobbyists, plying the president with gifts and concessions to secure their policy priorities.

— The new dynamic has transformed the business of Washington influence, shutting out many veteran lobbyists and excluding even longtime experts from the most important policy fights in Washington. With Congress and the agencies often sidelined, outside lobbying firms and in-house specialists — many with decades of policy experience and cross-party relationships — are declining in importance.

— From K Street’s point of view, there’s only one lever consistently worth pulling — and it sits in the Oval Office.

— Lobbyists who can’t get clients in front of the president are struggling to adapt. Longtime lobbying heavyweights with extensive policy chops and Hill acumen are facing greater competition from newer firms with direct lines to Trump and his aides, or pouring resources into public affairs campaigns with the hopes of getting their message in front of the right audience. And industry trade associations, once the crucial eyes and ears of member companies, are largely flying blind.

Happy Monday and welcome to PI . How has the influence industry changed for you during Trump’s second term? And what are you watching for in tonight’s LDA dump? Let us know. Caitlin is on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 and email her at coprysko@politico.com . Daniel is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com . Also follow us on X : @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns .

A message from the Defense Credit Union Council:

DURBIN-MARSHALL CREDIT CARD MANDATES WILL HARM MILITARY FAMILIES The Defense Credit Union Council is sounding the alarm on the Durbin–Marshall credit card mandates. This proposal would increase fraud risk, restrict access to credit, eliminate rewards, and hand a massive windfall to corporate mega-retailers at the expense of consumers, small businesses, and community financial institutions. DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED —OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

OMIDYAR HIRES ALPINE GROUP: The Omidyar Network , the philanthropic and investment group started by eBay founder — and Big Tech critic — Pierre Omidyar , has hired Alpine Group Partners to work on tech issues in D.C., ending a brief lobbying hiatus at the federal level.

— The organization has funded several prominent watchdog groups working to limit the influence of Silicon Valley tech giants, including the Tech Transparency Project and Accountable Tech , which shut its doors in August . The Omidyar Network hired its first federal lobbyists, the Democratic lobbying and PR firm NVG LLC , in 2020.

— But that contract lapsed at the end of last year. The network parted ways with Keefe Strategies at the beginning of 2024, meaning the network had no federal lobbyists on its roster until retaining Alpine Group in September.

MORE NEW BUSINESS: Here’s a quick round-up of several other registrations that caught our eye ahead of tonight’s Q3 filing deadline. Sargento Cheese retained Wisconsin-based Michael Best Strategies back in July to lobby on an industry-backed bill that would establish a statutory definition for “natural cheese,” according to a newly filed disclosure.

— Newly filed disclosures revealed several other hires from this summer, including that UPS retained Cornerstone Government Affairs in July to work on the GOP megabill and that 3M retained Holland & Hart to lobby on chemical and industrial manufacturing operations.

— More recently, design software Figma hired Invariant last month to work on AI issues, and the AI fintech firm Cleo hired Federal Hall Policy Advisors at the beginning of October to lobby on fintech regulations. Tire titan Goodyear hired Covington & Burling last month to work on “issues related to manufacturing facilities and policies in the U.S.”

FLYING IN: Advocacy group Small Business Majority will hit the Hill starting tomorrow for a two-day fly-in focused on a range of issues, from health care to tariffs to immigration. A group of 20 small business owners from states like Alabama, Georgia, Texas and Illinois are slated to meet with nearly three dozen congressional offices on both sides of the Hill, including staff of Sens. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), Katie Britt (R-Ala.) and Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Reps. Susie Lee (D-Nev.), Carol Miller (R-W.Va.) and Tony Gonzales (R-Texas).

SHUTDOWN DOUBLE DOWN: “Influential conservative groups with deep pockets are pushing Republicans to demand steep concessions from Democrats in exchange for extending health care subsidies, a move that risks prolonging a US government shutdown now in its 20th day,” Bloomberg ’s Emily Birnbaum and Erik Wasson report.

— “Activists on the right, including a powerful political advocacy group funded by billionaire Charles Koch , are running ads and holding meetings to pressure Republicans to stave off Democrats’ demands. If they must negotiate, some of the groups argue, Republicans should at least leverage any health care talks to score political wins on abortion and other priorities resisted by Democrats. Their push comes as congressional Republicans are divided over how to handle the expiring Obamacare premium subsidies at the center of the shutdown fight.”

— “Conservative stalwarts like Grover Norquist of the anti-tax group Americans for Tax Reform , who have long opposed Obamacare and view the Covid-era subsidies as costly handouts, are determined to make sure the attention Democrats have focused on the expiring subsidies doesn’t weaken Republican will.”

— “ Americans for Prosperity , the Koch-funded group, is running a six-figure ad campaign encouraging Congress to allow the subsidies to expire, emphasizing that they are a vestige of the pandemic and the Biden administration. … At weekly meetings in Washington, advocates are sharing intelligence and fact sheets to spread to Republicans considering deals to renew the subsidies.”

WHO’S BACKING MAHA: “Major U.S. soft-drink and snack-food corporations are waging a coordinated campaign that aims to pit Donald Trump’s Maga faithful against Robert F. Kennedy Jr. ’s Make America Healthy Again movement” in order to “stymie the Maha-led effort to curb Americans’ consumption of soda and ultra-processed foods,” Josh Voorhees writes for The Guardian .

— “To carry out the plan, the companies have turned to a partially formalized network of for-hire pollsters, strategists and political financiers with deep ties to the national Republican party – several of whom have taken steps that obscure their connection to the effort and to one another. In the process, the industry has also been aided less directly by a loose coalition of free-market ideologues who have previously worked to advance Trump’s deregulatory agenda.”

— “The effort features Maga influencers hired by a firm that promotes ‘anti-woke’ movies; an obscure research group Lee Zeldin was working for when Donald Trump picked him to lead the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency; and a media outlet backed by rightwing billionaires Leonard Leo and Charles Koch, among others.”

How Trump 2.0 is blowing up lobbying

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO 

10/20/2025 06:42 PM EDT

Updated 10/22/2025 09:48 AM EDT

2025-10-22T09:48-0400

Presented by

With help from Daniel Lippman

LDA WEEK AMUSE-BOUCHE: After decades of revolving-door culture, Washington is grappling with a new normal for how influence works in the capital, your host reports with Brendan Bordelon and Amanda Chu. Conversations with several dozen lobbyists, industry officials and public relations professionals revealed a transformation far more disruptive than the typical churn that comes with a new administration.

— In Trump 2.0, American policy influence has shifted from its previous channels — agency officials, top lawmakers and staffers on key congressional committees — to a new reality where change comes suddenly from the top.

— President Donald Trump and a handful of lieutenants have seized full control over policies once considered the remit of Congress and experts at agencies, including hyperspecific issues like tariff rates, high-skilled visa fees and funding freezes. The president’s gravitational pull has forced CEOs to act as their companies’ top lobbyists, plying the president with gifts and concessions to secure their policy priorities.

— The new dynamic has transformed the business of Washington influence, shutting out many veteran lobbyists and excluding even longtime experts from the most important policy fights in Washington. With Congress and the agencies often sidelined, outside lobbying firms and in-house specialists — many with decades of policy experience and cross-party relationships — are declining in importance.

— From K Street’s point of view, there’s only one lever consistently worth pulling — and it sits in the Oval Office.

— Lobbyists who can’t get clients in front of the president are struggling to adapt. Longtime lobbying heavyweights with extensive policy chops and Hill acumen are facing greater competition from newer firms with direct lines to Trump and his aides, or pouring resources into public affairs campaigns with the hopes of getting their message in front of the right audience. And industry trade associations, once the crucial eyes and ears of member companies, are largely flying blind.

Happy Monday and welcome to PI. How has the influence industry changed for you during Trump’s second term? And what are you watching for in tonight’s LDA dump? Let us know. Caitlin is on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 and email her at coprysko@politico.com. Daniel is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com. Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns.

OMIDYAR HIRES ALPINE GROUP: The Omidyar Network, the philanthropic and investment group started by eBay founder — and Big Tech critic — Pierre Omidyar, has hired Alpine Group Partners to work on tech issues in D.C., ending a brief lobbying hiatus at the federal level.

— The organization has funded several prominent watchdog groups working to limit the influence of Silicon Valley tech giants, including the Tech Transparency Project and Accountable Tech, which shut its doors in August. The Omidyar Network hired its first federal lobbyists, the Democratic lobbying and PR firm NVG LLC, in 2020.

— But that contract lapsed at the end of last year. The network parted ways with Keefe Strategies at the beginning of 2024, meaning the network had no federal lobbyists on its roster until retaining Alpine Group in September.

MORE NEW BUSINESS: Here’s a quick round-up of several other registrations that caught our eye ahead of tonight’s Q3 filing deadline. Sargento Cheese retained Wisconsin-based Michael Best Strategies back in July to lobby on an industry-backed bill that would establish a statutory definition for “natural cheese,” according to a newly filed disclosure.

— Newly filed disclosures revealed several other hires from this summer, including that UPS retained Cornerstone Government Affairs in July to work on the GOP megabill and that 3M retained Holland & Hart to lobby on chemical and industrial manufacturing operations.

— More recently, design software Figma hired Invariant last month to work on AI issues, and the AI fintech firm Cleo hired Federal Hall Policy Advisors at the beginning of October to lobby on fintech regulations. Tire titan Goodyear hired Covington & Burling last month to work on “issues related to manufacturing facilities and policies in the U.S.”

FLYING IN: Advocacy group Small Business Majority will hit the Hill starting tomorrow for a two-day fly-in focused on a range of issues, from health care to tariffs to immigration. A group of 20 small business owners from states like Alabama, Georgia, Texas and Illinois are slated to meet with nearly three dozen congressional offices on both sides of the Hill, including staff of Sens. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.), Ron Wyden (D-Ore.), Katie Britt (R-Ala.) and Ted Cruz (R-Texas) and Reps. Susie Lee (D-Nev.), Carol Miller (R-W.Va.) and Tony Gonzales (R-Texas).

SHUTDOWN DOUBLE DOWN: “Influential conservative groups with deep pockets are pushing Republicans to demand steep concessions from Democrats in exchange for extending health care subsidies, a move that risks prolonging a US government shutdown now in its 20th day,” Bloomberg’s Emily Birnbaum and Erik Wasson report.

— “Activists on the right, including a powerful political advocacy group funded by billionaire Charles Koch, are running ads and holding meetings to pressure Republicans to stave off Democrats’ demands. If they must negotiate, some of the groups argue, Republicans should at least leverage any health care talks to score political wins on abortion and other priorities resisted by Democrats. Their push comes as congressional Republicans are divided over how to handle the expiring Obamacare premium subsidies at the center of the shutdown fight.”

— “Conservative stalwarts like Grover Norquist of the anti-tax group Americans for Tax Reform, who have long opposed Obamacare and view the Covid-era subsidies as costly handouts, are determined to make sure the attention Democrats have focused on the expiring subsidies doesn’t weaken Republican will.”

— “Americans for Prosperity, the Koch-funded group, is running a six-figure ad campaign encouraging Congress to allow the subsidies to expire, emphasizing that they are a vestige of the pandemic and the Biden administration. … At weekly meetings in Washington, advocates are sharing intelligence and fact sheets to spread to Republicans considering deals to renew the subsidies.”

WHO’S BACKING MAHA: “Major U.S. soft-drink and snack-food corporations are waging a coordinated campaign that aims to pit Donald Trump’s Maga faithful against Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again movement” in order to “stymie the Maha-led effort to curb Americans’ consumption of soda and ultra-processed foods,” Josh Voorhees writes for The Guardian.

— “To carry out the plan, the companies have turned to a partially formalized network of for-hire pollsters, strategists and political financiers with deep ties to the national Republican party – several of whom have taken steps that obscure their connection to the effort and to one another. In the process, the industry has also been aided less directly by a loose coalition of free-market ideologues who have previously worked to advance Trump’s deregulatory agenda.”

— “The effort features Maga influencers hired by a firm that promotes ‘anti-woke’ movies; an obscure research group Lee Zeldin was working for when Donald Trump picked him to lead the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency; and a media outlet backed by rightwing billionaires Leonard Leo and Charles Koch, among others.”

title: Scalise’s chief heads downtown
body_text:
HOTELIERS PICK UP HORTON: Brett Horton , who has served for the past decade as chief of staff to House Majority Leader Steve Scalise , is leaving the Hill to become the top lobbyist at the American Hotel & Lodging Association . Horton has worked in Scalise’s office since 2010, seeing the Louisiana Republican through his rise up the leadership ranks, which also included surviving an assassination attempt and a cancer diagnosis.

— Horton will join AHLA in December in the newly created role of chief advocacy officer. As part of the role, he’ll oversee the trade group’s direct lobbying efforts as well as its PAC strategy, grassroots engagement, coalition building and issue advocacy campaigns at both the federal and state levels.

— He leaves the Hill having had a front-row seat to countless political fights over the last decade and a half. They include the passage of this year’s reconciliation package through the narrowest House majority in almost a century and what looks to be the longest-ever shutdown.

— In an interview, Horton said his decision to leave the Hill came down to simply being ready for a new challenge. While he fielded several other offers downtown, Horton said he felt the strongest alignment with the culture at AHLA, which represents some of the world’s biggest hotel brands, including Marriott , IHG and Hilton .

— Horton said that one of the most crucial skills he’ll take to AHLA is coalition building. “You can do anything in the House if you have a majority, but getting a majority is incredibly hard,” he added. “That’s the same if you have 245 Republicans, or if you have 220 Republicans … building consensus is never easy,” and “that’s a skill that you absolutely have to hone if you’re gonna be successful here.”

— “There are few people that know Capitol Hill better than Brett Horton,” Scalise said in a statement provided by AHLA. The majority leader went on to hail Horton as “instrumental in every major policy victory of the last decade” and said his outgoing chief will be an “incredible asset to the hotel industry.”

— As Punchbowl News — which first reported Horton’s departure — notes, Horton is the fourth top Scalise aide to decamp for K Street this year: former floor director Ben Napier joined the government affairs team at Andreessen Horowitz , former deputy chief of staff Bart Reising is now with Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck , and former communications director Lauren Fine is now on the policy comms team at Google .

Happy Wednesday and welcome to PI. Send K Street tips. Caitlin is on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 and email her at coprysko@politico.com . Daniel is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com . Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns .

FLY-INS AREN’T SHUT DOWN: Trade associations and advocacy groups have continued trekking through the halls of Congress the past four weeks to find a captive audience for their fly-ins despite a shutdown that’s had the rest of Washington at a standstill.

— This afternoon, Goldman Sachs ’ 10,000 Small Businesses initiative kicked off its annual Washington summit, which is expected to draw more than 2,000 small business owners from across the country. They include business leaders like Goldman chief executive David Solomon and policymakers such as Sens. Katie Britt (R-Ala.), Ben Ray Luján (D-N.M.) and Dave McCormick (R-Pa.) and SBA Administrator Kelly Loeffler .

— Organizers for groups that have elected to go ahead with their fly-ins in spite of the shutdown said their policy concerns are too urgent to wait for the government to open back up.

— “The issues that are hanging in the balance at the heart of the government shutdown are innately small business issues,” said Alexis D’Amato , the director of government affairs for Small Business Majority , which hosted a fly-in for small business leaders last week. “As Congress debates key policies that impact Main Street businesses including the expiring enhanced ACA tax credits, access to government programs and loan options, and the impact of tariffs, it’s more important than ever that lawmakers hear from small businesses.”

— “Tariffs continue to be a hugely disruptive factor for our small businesses, especially ahead of the holiday season, and many of them are going to be completely tied up in … the holiday selling season starting in November,” added Meghan Cruz , vice president of advocacy and engagement at the National Retail Federation .

— The NRF brought more than a dozen small business owners to Washington for a fly-in last week that Cruz said largely went off without a hitch. While lawmakers’ willingness to take meetings varied from office to office, she noted that the vast majority of NRF’s meeting requests were accepted — even with one chamber of Congress out of session.

— In fact, Cruz added, NRF’s members were able to secure extended face time with key committee staff and senators even as the pace of hearings and votes has slowed considerably.

— The only real logistical hiccup organizers have been seeing is longer wait times at security checkpoints to get into the Capitol.

— Among the other organizations that have hosted fly-ins during the shutdown are the U.S. Chamber of Commerce , the American Society of Travel Advisors , the American Public Transportation Association , the Small Business Payments Alliance , the Associated Equipment Distributors and the National Star Route Mail Contractors Association .

FRIENDS IN HIGH PLACES: “The Trump administration on Wednesday lifted sanctions against a Serbian nationalist leader who had been accused of undermining a U.S.-brokered peace agreement that ended bloody sectarian fighting in the 1990s in the Balkans,” The New York Times’ Ken Vogel reports.

— “The sanctions relief for Milorad Dodik , who had served until earlier this month as president of a small self-governing territory in Bosnia and Herzegovina called Republika Srpska, was a victory for the politician and for a pricey influence campaign mounted on his behalf by several allies of President Trump,” including lobbyist Marc Zell , former New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani , former national security adviser Michael Flynn , fundraiser Caroline Wren , far-right influencer Laura Loomer and former Illinois Mayor Rod Blagojevich .

— “The removal of the sanctions could allow Mr. Dodik, who is still the leader of the ruling party in Srpska and has closely allied himself with President Vladimir V. Putin of Russia, to remain influential in the Serb-controlled region even without a formal role in the government.”

— “The Treasury Department did not provide an explanation for the sanctions relief in its announcement , and a spokesman declined to comment. The State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.”

TALLY IT UP: “Major accounting firms have largely hiked lobbying spending amid the Republican overhaul of tax policy and changes in contracting under the Trump administration,” POLITICO ’s Danny Nguyen reports.

— “ Ernst & Young , Deloitte and KPMG — three of the ‘big four’ accounting firms that offer tax and financial advisory services for some of the biggest public companies in the world — have increased lobbying spending during the third quarter of the Trump administration, according to newly released lobbying disclosure files POLITICO reviewed.”

— “Deloitte, the London-based accounting and consulting firm, increased lobbying spending by a whopping 92 percent from the third quarter of 2024 compared to the same time in 2025, raising it to $480,000 from $250,000.”

— “KPMG, based in the Netherlands, similarly rocketed lobbying spending, by 64 percent, over that period, to $590,000 from $360,000. And from the beginning of the year to Sept. 30, both accounting firms increased lobbying spending by over 20 percent.”

FLATTERY GETS YOU EVERYWHERE: “ Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang turned his company’s annual artificial intelligence conference into a chance to lavish praise on President Donald Trump on Tuesday,” POLITICO ’s Gabby Miller reports.

— “In his keynote remarks at the Walter E. Washington Convention Center, Huang said Trump ‘deserves enormous credit’ for recognizing the U.S. tech sector needs more energy to win the AI race, and for pushing tech companies to bring production back to America. ‘If this didn’t happen, we could have been in a bad situation, and I want to thank President Trump,’ Huang said of the administration’s agenda.”

— The chipmaker, which became the first company in the world to reach a $5 trillion valuation this morning on the back of the global AI boom, “has been one of the largest beneficiaries of the Trump administration’s policies.”

— Earlier this year, Nvidia won the right to sell one of its chips to China in exchange for sharing part of its revenues with the federal government. The company may be on the verge of another major breakthrough, after Trump signaled an openness today to allowing China access to Nvidia’s most powerful AI processor in order to close a trade deal with Beijing.

— In Washington on Tuesday, “Huang’s speech was notable for its sharp political turn,” even borrowing from Trump’s campaign slogan at its conclusion.

— “But Huang has spent the past year working to ingratiate himself with Trump’s Washington, making appeals to the president at $1 million-per-head dinners at Mar-a-Lago and joining Trump on official state visits to the Gulf region and United Kingdom, where the president unveiled multibillion-dollar tech deals.”

CLICKER: Sludge and the liberal digital media outlet More Perfect Union partnered to launch a searchable database to track all of the disclosed corporate donors to Trump’s inaugural fund and White House ballroom project. The database also highlights the return on those donors’ investments, whether in the form of legal or regulatory relief from the Trump administration, favorable administration appointments or some other kind of major policy achievement.

HIGH TIMES: Earlier this week, more than three dozen state attorneys general asked Congress to close a loophole in the 2018 farm bill that allowed the sale of synthetic THC products. The products, which are derived from legal hemp, have similar intoxicating effects as marijuana but are not scheduled under the Controlled Substances Act.

— A legislative effort to close that loophole is being led by Sen. Mitch McConnell and Rep. Andy Harris (R-Md.), who say the growth of the market for hemp-derived synthetic THC was an unintended consequence of the 2018 bill. But their effort has run into stiff opposition from fellow Kentucky Republican Sen. Rand Paul , who has said efforts to recriminalize hemp would “devastate” a multi-billion dollar industry . Paul has said he’s prepared to block government funding legislation containing language that would crack down on the hemp industry.

— Now, amid the burgeoning intra-Kentucky delegation fight , Hemp Industry & Farmers of America has hired Kentucky-based firm Babbage Cofounder to advocate on the industry’s behalf.

— Former Kentucky Secretary of State Bob Babbage was hired on Oct. 1 to “maintain the status of hemp cultivation and manufacturing as expressed in the current Farm Bill law in the next update of the Farm Bill,” according to a new disclosure report .

— It’s just the latest hire by the hemp industry, which appears to be staffing up on the Hill as pressure builds to close the regulatory loophole that has allowed hemp-based THC products to be sold in states where marijuana remains illegal. Since July, Lobbyit , Crossroads Strategies and Williams and Jensen have been hired to represent the National Industrial Hemp Council , the Hemp Beverage Alliance and the U.S. Hemp Roundtable , respectively.

SAY ALOHA: Ballard Partners is headed to Hawaii, hiring defense contracting specialist Bernice Glenn Kissinger to lead the firm’s new Honolulu office where she will focus on military and national security issues in the Indo-Pacific region.

— The new office is the latest addition to Ballard Partners’ global presence, which now spans nearly 20 offices across the U.S., Israel, Turkey, Nigeria and Saudi Arabia. Domestically, Ballard now has an office in five states plus Washington.

— Kissinger is a long-time defense technology expert, whose career has focused on building bilateral defense programs with U.S. allies in Asia. Ballard has signed a number of clients with defense industry ties since President Donald Trump’s reelection, including Safe Pro Group , OceanSound Partners and Solonian Resources .

title: Airline industry presses for end to shutdown
body_text:
AIRPLANE BLUES: With flights across the country being canceled by the hundreds at undermanned airports, the airline industry is ratcheting up efforts to convince lawmakers to end the government shutdown, Daniel B. reports .

— Widespread flight reductions are scheduled to take effect at airports on Friday, giving many air travelers their first real-life taste of the shutdown. Industry officials who’ve been pressing Congress and the White House think that could be what it takes to finally break the impasse after more than five weeks.

— “While it wasn’t the purpose of [Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy ’s] actions” — referring to an order to cut flights by 10 percent across 40 airports — it “has hopefully gotten folks on Capitol Hill to realize that there has to be something that gets things moving forward,” Airlines for America CEO and former New Hampshire governor Chris Sununu told PI. A4A is the industry’s main trade group in Washington.

— Major airlines, industry trade associations and labor unions have been calling for an end to the shutdown for weeks, pushing senators to pass a clean continuing resolution already approved by the House to open the government. And top airline CEOs have been working the phones since the shutdown began, Sununu said, leaning on personal relationships with lawmakers from their states to advocate for a resolution.

— “The health care fight’s important,” he said, referring to Democratic demands to extend expiring Obamacare subsidies. “But that’s not the fight of keeping the government open, that’s completely separate.”

— Air traffic controllers, TSA agents and other essential federal employees have been working without pay for more than a month, leading to concerns that aviation safety could be compromised as labor shortages increase and the Thanksgiving travel rush approaches.

— On Wednesday, Duffy announced the nationwide flight restrictions, calling them a safety precaution. Potentially affected airports include major hubs around Atlanta and Chicago as well all major airports around Washington and New York City.

— “We’re in a new world after last night’s announcement,” said a person familiar with airline industry lobbying efforts granted anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak publicly. “The clean [continuing resolution] is the quickest way to get back to normal operations.”

— “They’ve said ‘no’ to keeping the government open 14 times . [The] fifteenth time is the charm,” Sununu said. “To wait until things really get bad to force action in Washington is just a terrible sign of the times in terms of what it takes to get things done.”

Happy Thursday and welcome to PI. Have you had a flight for tomorrow canceled? Let us know at dbarnes@politico.com and coprysko@politico.com or on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and caitlinoprysko.17 . And don’t forget to follow us on X at @dnlbrns and @caitlinoprysko .

DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED —OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

DARE TO DREAM: The business community has reason for optimism that the Supreme Court will rule in industry’s favor when it comes to Trump’s emergency tariff authorities. But even before yesterday’s oral arguments kicked off, work was already underway downtown to help companies navigate the post-SCOTUS landscape no matter how it looks.

— “All of our clients are anticipating how to collect back tariffs that they might have paid in the past,” said Samir Kapadia , who leads the trade practice at the Vogel Group . Clients have been poring over case studies for similar duty or tax liability programs in the past to get a sense of what a reimbursement process might look like, he told PI — or whether it will be worth the headache.

— Consumer Technology Association President Gary Shapiro , whose association submitted an amicus brief in the case, reiterated today that the government should “keep it simple and ensure that retailers and importers get their tariff payments refunded swiftly and with as few hoops to jump through as possible.”

— But lobbyists and clients are preparing for the likelihood that the administration has contingency plans to try and impose tariffs using other authorities, while at the same time working to minimize the impact of a slew of separate ongoing tariff probes.

— When it comes to the tariffs before the court, “we’ve been conditioned to that,” Kapadia said. “That’s just the way the world is. Hey, if we get our money back on that, fantastic. But I’m already looking ahead, and I can see that I’ve got all these other things that are coming at me.”

— “How it gets paid back is not as significant as whether [tariffs] will come back a different way,” argued Justin Sayfie , a partner at Ballard Partners . If the court strikes down the tariffs, those details may be pertinent to some clients. But the more urgent question will be “are tariffs gone forever or are they coming back another way?” he added. “The answer to that question has massive impact on investment decisions and business planning.”

WENSTRUP TO CGCN: Former Ohio Rep. Brad Wenstrup has joined all-Republican firm CGCN Group as a strategic partner, Taylor Giorno scoops for NOTUS .

— Wenstrup, who spent 12 years on the Hill before retiring in January, remains subject to a mandatory “cooling off” period and won’t register to lobby, he told NOTUS. He plans on maintaining his consulting firm, Ubiquitous Strategies Alliance , and will continue to serve on President Donald Trump’s Intelligence Advisory Board .

SMALL BUSINESS FEELING THE PINCH: Seventy percent of small business owners surveyed by the National Small Business Association over the past week say their companies have been impacted by the government shutdown, according to a new survey released today .

— However, the bad vibes revealed in the survey extend beyond the impact of the government shutdown. Fifty-three percent of respondents reported feeling worse about the economy than they did six months ago, a trend that rewarded Democrats in elections across the country earlier this week.

— Small business owners surveyed don’t anticipate things getting better any time soon. Thirty-eight percent told NSBA they anticipate the economy remaining flat over the next year and 40 percent said they expect a recession.

BIG DATA: The growing need for data centers, the hulking warehouses containing thousands of computer servers to support AI and other cloud computing, is contributing to a lobbying boom, Carolyn Neugarten writes for OpenSecrets .

— “ The Data Center Coalition , a trade association representing the interests of data center developers, spent $123,000 on lobbying during the first quarter of 2025 and $125,000 in the second quarter — and then more than doubled those numbers, spending $360,000 in the third quarter. The coalition’s membership includes many of the tech giants powering the AI revolution, including Amazon , Google , Microsoft and Meta , as well as major infrastructure and data center operators like Stack Infrastructure and Oracle .”

ELECTRIC BILL: All those data centers require electricity — a lot of electricity. Those needs are, in turn, driving a lobbying boom for the utilities industry, which is on track to spend $150 million on lobbying this year, a 14 percent increase over last year, Josh Saul reports for Bloomberg .

— “U.S. utilities spent almost $108 million in the first three quarters of 2025, compared with about $99 million for the same period last year. Southern Co . spent the most with more than $8 million, followed by the trade group Edison Electric Institute , Duke Energy , NextEra Energy and PG&E Corp .”

Airline industry presses for end to shutdown

By DANIEL BARNES and CAITLIN OPRYSKO 

11/06/2025 08:23 PM EST

Presented by

AIRPLANE BLUES: With flights across the country being canceled by the hundreds at undermanned airports, the airline industry is ratcheting up efforts to convince lawmakers to end the government shutdown, Daniel B. reports.

— Widespread flight reductions are scheduled to take effect at airports on Friday, giving many air travelers their first real-life taste of the shutdown. Industry officials who’ve been pressing Congress and the White House think that could be what it takes to finally break the impasse after more than five weeks.

— “While it wasn’t the purpose of [Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy’s] actions” — referring to an order to cut flights by 10 percent across 40 airports — it “has hopefully gotten folks on Capitol Hill to realize that there has to be something that gets things moving forward,” Airlines for America CEO and former New Hampshire governor Chris Sununu told PI. A4A is the industry’s main trade group in Washington.

— Major airlines, industry trade associations and labor unions have been calling for an end to the shutdown for weeks, pushing senators to pass a clean continuing resolution already approved by the House to open the government. And top airline CEOs have been working the phones since the shutdown began, Sununu said, leaning on personal relationships with lawmakers from their states to advocate for a resolution.

— “The health care fight’s important,” he said, referring to Democratic demands to extend expiring Obamacare subsidies. “But that’s not the fight of keeping the government open, that’s completely separate.”

— Air traffic controllers, TSA agents and other essential federal employees have been working without pay for more than a month, leading to concerns that aviation safety could be compromised as labor shortages increase and the Thanksgiving travel rush approaches.

— On Wednesday, Duffy announced the nationwide flight restrictions, calling them a safety precaution. Potentially affected airports include major hubs around Atlanta and Chicago as well all major airports around Washington and New York City.

— “We’re in a new world after last night’s announcement,” said a person familiar with airline industry lobbying efforts granted anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak publicly. “The clean [continuing resolution] is the quickest way to get back to normal operations.”

— “They’ve said ‘no’ to keeping the government open 14 times. [The] fifteenth time is the charm,” Sununu said. “To wait until things really get bad to force action in Washington is just a terrible sign of the times in terms of what it takes to get things done.”

Happy Thursday and welcome to PI. Have you had a flight for tomorrow canceled? Let us know at dbarnes@politico.com and coprysko@politico.com or on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and caitlinoprysko.17. And don’t forget to follow us on X at @dnlbrns and @caitlinoprysko.

DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED—OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

DARE TO DREAM: The business community has reason for optimism that the Supreme Court will rule in industry’s favor when it comes to Trump’s emergency tariff authorities. But even before yesterday’s oral arguments kicked off, work was already underway downtown to help companies navigate the post-SCOTUS landscape no matter how it looks.

— “All of our clients are anticipating how to collect back tariffs that they might have paid in the past,” said Samir Kapadia, who leads the trade practice at the Vogel Group. Clients have been poring over case studies for similar duty or tax liability programs in the past to get a sense of what a reimbursement process might look like, he told PI — or whether it will be worth the headache.

— Consumer Technology Association President Gary Shapiro, whose association submitted an amicus brief in the case, reiterated today that the government should “keep it simple and ensure that retailers and importers get their tariff payments refunded swiftly and with as few hoops to jump through as possible.”

— But lobbyists and clients are preparing for the likelihood that the administration has contingency plans to try and impose tariffs using other authorities, while at the same time working to minimize the impact of a slew of separate ongoing tariff probes.

— When it comes to the tariffs before the court, “we’ve been conditioned to that,” Kapadia said. “That’s just the way the world is. Hey, if we get our money back on that, fantastic. But I’m already looking ahead, and I can see that I’ve got all these other things that are coming at me.”

— “How it gets paid back is not as significant as whether [tariffs] will come back a different way,” argued Justin Sayfie, a partner at Ballard Partners. If the court strikes down the tariffs, those details may be pertinent to some clients. But the more urgent question will be “are tariffs gone forever or are they coming back another way?” he added. “The answer to that question has massive impact on investment decisions and business planning.”

He plans on maintaining his consulting firm, Ubiquitous Strategies Alliance, and will continue to serve on President Donald Trump’s Intelligence Advisory Board.

SMALL BUSINESS FEELING THE PINCH: Seventy percent of small business owners surveyed by the National Small Business Association over the past week say their companies have been impacted by the government shutdown, according to a new survey released today.

— However, the bad vibes revealed in the survey extend beyond the impact of the government shutdown. Fifty-three percent of respondents reported feeling worse about the economy than they did six months ago, a trend that rewarded Democrats in elections across the country earlier this week.

— Small business owners surveyed don’t anticipate things getting better any time soon. Thirty-eight percent told NSBA they anticipate the economy remaining flat over the next year and 40 percent said they expect a recession.

BIG DATA: The growing need for data centers, the hulking warehouses containing thousands of computer servers to support AI and other cloud computing, is contributing to a lobbying boom, Carolyn Neugarten writes for OpenSecrets.

— “The Data Center Coalition, a trade association representing the interests of data center developers, spent $123,000 on lobbying during the first quarter of 2025 and $125,000 in the second quarter — and then more than doubled those numbers, spending $360,000 in the third quarter. The coalition’s membership includes many of the tech giants powering the AI revolution, including Amazon, Google, Microsoft and Meta, as well as major infrastructure and data center operators like Stack Infrastructure and Oracle.”

title: How some lobbyists view the Mike Johnson mess
body_text:
A HOUSE DIVIDED: K Street is keeping a close eye on Speaker Mike Johnson as his grip on his conference appears to be weakening — and raising the possibility that the dysfunction in the House could stall their clients’ legislative interests.

— “[Johnson] has been doing a high-wire act since the beginning, and did a remarkable job under the circumstances, but it does seem like something has changed,” one Republican lobbyist granted anonymity to speak candidly told PI.

— A chaotic majority is nothing new for Johnson, who ascended to the speakership in 2023 after former Speaker Kevin McCarthy was ousted in an effort led by fellow Republican Matt Gaetz . Criticism from within his own party has mounted in recent weeks following the longest government shutdown in history and a spate of electoral losses for Republicans. In an interview this week, Rep. Elise Stefanik told the Wall Street Journal Johnson no longer has the votes to remain speaker were a new election to be held.

— “The honeymoon is over,” another GOP lobbyist said. “We’re turning into the end of a very, very tumultuous year with the rough waters of the Trump presidency — the fast pace, the political fallout and ramifications, and the anticipation and anxiety of what might be a difficult election next year. No one could master and weather that perfectly, because it’s incredibly difficult.”

— Any attempt to remove Johnson would eat up valuable legislative time and, if successful, could derail the work of Congress for weeks. It took the House 22 days to select Johnson after McCarthy’s ouster. And time at the start of 2026 will be extra valuable for legislative work before members shift their attention to campaigning for the midterms.

— “Lets face it, Congress isn’t great at getting stuff done under the best of circumstances, so if you take away a lot of time it’s going to be difficult,” the first lobbyist said. “We may have a very tight window in the very beginning of the year to really get in anything related to appropriations or the NDAA or anything like that.”

— Even absent an effort to replace Johnson as speaker, dissatisfied Republican members are hindering leadership’s ability to bring bills to the floor. Yesterday, leadership postponed a scheduled vote on the SCORE Act , a bill supported by the White House that would create new regulations for compensating student athletes.

— Still, chaos in the House is largely business as usual, lobbyists say. And with the way Donald Trump governs, Congress is often not the best route for advancing clients’ goals.

— “More and more, the administration and the agency work is way more important to our clients, and setting up for the moments in a presidency when they do get to do their one priority,” said Sam Geduldig , a Republican lobbyist at CGCN . “You need years to set it up so you can get your provisions included in that big bill, whatever it might be, whoever the administration, whatever party. And that’s why you lobby Congress, to set the frame for when that moment happens.”

BUDD’S CHIEF TO BALLARD: Tucker Knott , chief of staff to North Carolina Republican Sen. Ted Budd , will leave the Hill in January to join Ballard Partners as a partner in the Washington office.

— Knott, who spent the last three years in Budd’s office, previously served as chief of staff to former Rep. George Holding (R-N.C.) for more than six years. He briefly left the Hill in 2019 to serve as a senior director at Pfizer .

— Knott told PI he decided to join Ballard after meeting with Brian Ballard and hearing about the firm’s desire to strengthen its operations outside of the Trump administration.

WHITE-COLLAR WARNING: The Justice Department’s second in command warned white-collar lawyers this morning they may have a harder time getting deals for their clients if they have publicly accused the Justice Department of being soft on white-collar crime, POLITICO’s Josh Gerstein reports .

— “If folks in this room are going to be honest brokers when counseling clients, posting on LinkedIn or writing client alerts, the public narrative should match the private one. If you publicly claim we are not enforcing white-collar crime aggressively enough, but privately insist that your clients are the victims of overreach, we notice that inconsistency,” Blanche told the attendees of a conference focused on the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act.

BALLROOM DONATIONS: Senate Democrats are adding to the chorus of lawmakers demanding more details on corporate donations to Trump’s White House ballroom project, sending requests for information to Nvidia , Apple , Microsoft , Amazon , Meta and others, Ken Thomas scoops for The Wall Street Journal .

— The letters, signed by Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.), Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) and a group of eight House Democrats, mention the various interests the companies have before the federal government and question if the donations were made to secure favorable treatment. Last month, senators sent similar requests for information to lobbyists who have reportedly helped solicit donations for the ballroom.

Laura Friedman (D-Calif.), Kevin Mullin (D-Calif.), Rick Allen (R-Ga.) and Nick Begich (R-Alaska).

— Also flying in this week was The Battery Advocacy for Technology Transition (BATT) , a coalition representing domestic producers of battery materials, asking lawmakers to adopt a ban on battery materials from China that are used in U.S. military electronics.

FIRST IN PI — FINDING THEIR WAY: A pair of lobbyists with roots in Hawaii Democratic politics have teamed up with the former chief lobbyist for Nike to launch a firm with offices in Honolulu and Washington. They will offer guidance on state and federal government relations, communications and marketing services.

— The Wayfinder Group is a collaboration between Andy Winer , John White and Jesse McCollum , all of whom previously served as chiefs of staff on Capitol Hill. Winer, who will lead the Washington office, spent more than six years as chief to Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii). White, who will lead the Honolulu office, previously served as chief of staff to Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawaii) when she was a freshman in the House. Winer and White spent the last six years as colleagues at West Coast-based Strategies 360 .

— McCollum, who previously worked as chief of staff for former Rep. Ron Klein (D-Fla.), will serve as managing partner of The Wayfinder Group. McCollum founded his own firm, Tidal Basin Advisors , in 2023 after spending more than a decade helming government affairs for sports-giant Nike . His clients, which include satellite TV service provider Dish Network Corporation , are expected to follow to the new firm.

— Rounding out the firm’s staff are six alums from Strategies 360: Alex Hetherington , Lambros Syrmos , Nate Wyatt , Allicia Thompson , Kristine Reitan and Raelyn Batacan .

— “The federal government is very important to the state of Hawaii just based on where it is geographically and how important it is from a national security perspective and a transportation and communications perspective as well,” McCollum told PI, adding that he anticipates clients with appropriations interests before the federal government will also drive business for the new firm.

— The Wayfinder Group’s Honolulu office will also offer state government relations services, leaning on Winer’s previous experience as a senior adviser to Hawaii Gov. Josh Green .

“Any Fortune 100 company has state government affairs offices or has state government needs, so they’re all potential clients, as are localities and counties and things like that before the state government,” McCollum said. “So you really have two different ways, frankly, of building a business.”

ANNALS OF ANTITRUST: The next big antitrust fight is here. Streaming service Netflix announced today it has reached an agreement to purchase Warner Bros. Discovery ’s film studio, television network HBO and streaming service HBO Max . The deal does not include news network CNN , which, along with other Discovery television networks, will remain under the control of a new corporate entity, Discovery Global .

— News of the deal set off bipartisan calls for regulators to stop the $82.7 billion purchase that would combine two of the biggest names in streaming content.

— “This deal looks like an anti-monopoly nightmare,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) said on social media . “The Justice Department must enforce our nation’s anti-monopoly laws fairly and transparently — not use the Warner Bros. deal review to invite influence-peddling and bribery.”

— Former Rep. Matt Gaetz , President Donald Trump ’s initial pick for attorney general, called on the president to stop the deal, predicting that the Justice Department will view it as an “anti-trust violation” that is “deeply harmful to the marketplace.”

— Complicating matters is Paramount Skydance , Netflix’s main rival in pursuing Warner Bros. Lawyers for Paramount sent a letter to Warner Bros. Discovery leadership Thursday, complaining that the bid process appeared rigged in favor of Netflix. Paramount’s chair and CEO, David Ellison (son of billionaire Trump donor Larry Ellison ) reportedly visited Washington earlier this week to lobby against the Netflix bid.

PARDON ME: Trump’s eyebrow raising pardon of convicted cocaine trafficker Juan Orlando Hernández earlier this week came after the former Honduran president spent years building relationships with MAGA figures and American business leaders, Vera Bergengruen , Alex Leary , José de Córdoba , and Josh Dawsey report for The Wall Street Journal .

— “Trump has privately told advisers in recent days that he decided to grant the pardon after his allies in Florida, including longtime confidant Roger Stone and members of his Mar-a-Lago club, pushed for it, according to a person who spoke to him.”

— In addition to Stone, Gaetz worked to elevate Hernández’s case, giving his wife airtime on radio and television to argue that her husband was “a victim of the DOJ’s Biden lawfare agenda.”

— Stone also cast Hernández as a “crucial conservative ally” in Latin America and contended that freeing him would be a way to undercut Honduras’ current leftist President Xiomara Castro . In announcing Hernández’s pardon last week, Trump also endorsed Castro’s conservative opponent in the country’s Nov. 30 presidential election. That race remains too close to call.

NEW GOP FUNDRAISING PLATFORM: Dominant Republican fundraising platform WinRed is facing new competition from a Trump-aligned platform called Impact , Alex Isenstadt scoops for Axios .

— The new platform is led in part by Alex Bruesewitz , a key Trump adviser from the 2024 campaign who maintains good relationships with the White House. Impact promises to take a smaller cut of donations processed through the platform than WinRed. “People familiar with Impact’s plans say its goal is to break the stranglehold of WinRed, which processed contributions for more than 5,000 campaigns and committees in 2024.”

MILLIONS FOR SCHOOL CHOICE: One of the richest men in the world believes taxpayer-funded school choice programs would benefit millions of students and he’s willing to spend anything to make those programs a reality, Laura Meckler, Beth Reinhard and Clara Ence Morse report for The Washington Post .

— Billionaire Jeff Yass , co-founder of trading firm Susquehanna International Group , has donated hundreds of millions of dollars to politicians in recent years with the sole goal of realizing his vision of taxpayer funded school choice, or voucher programs that would allow families to opt out of public schools and send their children to private, charter or religious schools at no extra cost.

— Yass’ goal has led him to an alliance with Trump, whom he describes as a “true champion” of school choice. He’s donated to the Trump transition committee, gave millions to a Trump-aligned super PAC and recently contributed to Trump’s White House ballroom project.

PhRMA DOLLARS: Consumer advocacy group the National Consumers League started criticizing foes of the pharmaceutical industry after receiving approximately $2 million from PhRMA between 2020 and 2024, Robert Schmad reports for the Washington Examiner .

— “The National Consumers League, America’s oldest consumer advocacy organization, accepted no funding from Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America between 2018 and 2019. — “NCL receives support from a diverse set of stakeholders, and our policy positions are our own,” a spokesperson for the organization told the Examiner. “We retain complete editorial control over all content, and our agreements explicitly safeguard that independence.”
