WHO’S WORKING FOR WHO: Lobbying armies are being amassed in real time as the media giants vying to purchase Warner Bros. Discovery — Netflix and Paramount Skydance — game out the Washington landscape in pursuit of their prize.

— Netflix’s nearly $83 billion deal to acquire the legendary Hollywood studio was already facing scrutiny from leaders in Washington before Paramount Skydance upped the ante this morning with a hostile takeover bid of its own .

— While Netflix CEO Ted Sarandos has lobbied President Donald Trump personally to support the streaming giant’s bid for WBD, the president told reporters at the Paramount-hosted Kennedy Center Honors last night that the Netflix deal “could be a problem.” Trump said he’d be involved in the transaction — one of many wrinkles for the army of lobbyists already working for parties involved in or affected by the deal.

— Besides his mid-November meeting with Trump, Sarandos went to the White House again Tuesday, three days before the announcement, according to three people familiar with the visit, including a person who saw him. Clete Willems , Netflix’s chief global affairs officer, accompanied Sarandos to the White House, according to that person.

— A Netflix spokesperson said that Sarandos didn’t meet with Trump last Tuesday. Asked if Trump met with Sarandos during his visit, an official said the White House does not comment “on private meetings that may or may not have happened.”

— Both parties jockeying to buy Warner Bros. Discovery already have serious lobbying firepower. Netflix brought on Willems, a deputy director of the National Economic Council during Trump’s first term, in April. On Monday, Netflix announced another new hire with ties to the White House. Virginia Boney Moore , who served as special assistant to the president in Trump’s first Office of Legislative Affairs, joined the company from Amazon as director for federal affairs.

— Netflix has already spent $2.3 million lobbying Washington through the first three quarters of 2025, up from an annual record of $1.9 million last year, disclosures show. The streamer’s roster of outside lobbyists includes Monument Advocacy , Mehlman Consulting and Miller & Chevalier .

— Paramount, which has spent nearly $4.6 million on federal lobbying so far this year, also added two other outside lobbying firms to its roster in 2025: Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck and Telemedia Policy Corp . The company’s stable of outside firms also includes Capitol Tax Partners , Becker & Poliakoff , Capitol Counsel and FGS Global , according to disclosure filings.

— And though Paramount’s longtime chief lobbyist announced last week that she plans to step down next month, the media giant in October hired Makan Delrahim , who ran DOJ’s antitrust division during Trump’s first term, to be its new chief legal officer. Delrahim, who worked as an antitrust attorney at Brownstein for more than a decade, oversees Paramount’s government relations efforts as part of his new role.

— One lobbying powerhouse has an interest on both sides: Ballard Partners represents Netflix and Paramount, as well as the Motion Picture Association , of which both entertainment giants are members. Attorney General Pam Bondi , who is poised to wield influence over the antitrust review of any deal to buy Warner, is among several Ballard alumni now in the Trump administration.

— Paramount hired Ballard Partners days before Trump’s second term began and has paid the firm $270,000 through the first three quarters of the year, disclosures show. Netflix hired Ballard in March and has paid the firm $120,000 through the first three quarters of the year.

— “Our firm has had the privilege of representing many of the world’s leading entertainment companies on crucial issues such as copyright, tax, and trade matters,” Brian Ballard , the firm’s founder, told PI in a statement. “Given our nearly 1,000 clients, conflicts occasionally arise when their business decisions place them in competition with one another. In such instances, we address the situation directly with the affected clients to find a mutually agreeable resolution.”

— Both Netflix and Paramount have courted the services of Jason Miller , a close ally of the Trump administration and veteran of all three Trump campaigns, according to a person familiar with the matter, granted anonymity to speak about confidential personnel discussions. But he recently started providing communications advice for an investor with an interest in Paramount taking over WBD, according to the person.

— Miller, who has posted numerous times on X in recent days against the Netflix deal or in favor of Paramount honcho David Ellison ’s bid, declined to comment.

— Warner Bros. Discovery has also brought on former Trump co-campaign manager Chris LaCivita as a consultant to help deal with the transaction, according to a person familiar with the matter. LaCivita declined to comment.

— The entertainment giant has four outside lobbying firms on retainer as well, including Tiber Creek Group , Capitol Tax Partners , Intersect Public Affairs and BG Advocacy . Though WBD reported spending a record of more than $3.1 million lobbying Washington last year, through the first nine months of 2025, that sum is just $1.7 million.

title: Turning to K Street to save Christmas
body_text:
DESPERATELY SEEKING SANTA EXEMPTIONS: President Donald Trump ’s move to slap tariffs on imports from around the globe may have been a lump of coal for purveyors of Christmas cheer, but the scramble to roll those tariffs back has been a huge gift for K Street, Caitlin reports .

— Trade groups and companies representing manufacturers and retailers of everything from Christmas trees and decor to toys and spices — like virtually every other sector of the economy — have bolstered their lobbying operations in D.C., dropping massive sums as they jockeyed for tariff relief.

— Lobbying outlays by the Toy Association — which in April warned of devastation for toymakers if an initial 145 percent tariff on Chinese imports were to stand — skyrocketed to $510,000 through the first nine months of the year. That’s up from $40,000 in all of 2024 and the most spent since 2015. In preparation for Trump’s tariffs, the association brought on Ballard Partners last December for guidance on the matter, lobbying disclosures show.

— The association also retained its former top lobbyist Ed Desmond at the beginning of the year, and in February the Toy Association brought on Ridgeline Advocacy Group to work on a number of issues in addition to the tariffs, including consumer protection, sustainability and taxes.

— Detentes between Beijing and Washington gradually lowered tariffs on Chinese toy imports to 20 percent by the end of the year. But toymakers are closely tracking the Supreme Court decision on Trump’s so-called reciprocal tariffs and the prospect of seeing tariff payments refunded.

— Trump’s tariffs have prompted some holiday brands to turn to K Street for the first time. They include the Christmas Trade Group , a coalition of holiday retailers like the ornament and decor purveyors Kurt Adler and Old World Christmas , and artificial tree makers National Tree Company and Puleo . The coalition also includes holiday florists, lighting companies and even one commercial decorator whose portfolio includes the Trump International Hotel in New York.

— The trade group has paid Williams & Jensen $90,000 since March to build ties with the Trump administration and lawmakers on the key congressional committees that oversee trade. It has also lobbied for an exemption on products like Christmas lights similar to the one issued during Trump’s first administration.

— Artificial tree behemoth Balsam Brands , meanwhile, has spent $210,000 on lobbying through the first three quarters of the year — including $110,000 in Q3 alone. That’s less than the $420,000 Balsam Brands spent in 2019, but is the most by far for the company since the end of its three-year lobbying hiatus in 2023.

— Beyond the producers of holiday decor and goods, the retailers that sell those products have been some of the most vocal tariff critics in Washington this year. The National Retail Federation , whose members include Walmart , Target and Macy’s , is on track for its second-highest lobbying expenditures ever. NRF has dropped more than $8.5 million on lobbying so far this year, already more than the $8.3 million spent in all of 2024.

Happy Wednesday and welcome to the final PI of the year . Thank you all for reading and sending tips — we couldn’t have made it through this whirlwind of a year without you. We’ll be back in your inboxes on Jan. 5, but feel free to send us influence tips to chase down in the New Year. You can reach Caitlin on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 or at coprysko@politico.com . Daniel B. is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com . Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns .

YOU CAN’T HANDLE THE TRUTH: “K Street’s current playbook for clients avoiding President Donald Trump’s wrath on Truth Social is four words long: ‘Don’t poke the bear.’ That’s how one Democratic lobbyist described their advice to clients,” NOTUS’ Taylor Giorno writes. “Several other lobbyists have told NOTUS — on condition of anonymity so as not to ‘poke the bear’ — that playing defense has become an essential lobbying strategy early in Trump’s second term.”

— “A NOTUS analysis of every Trump Truth Social post since Jan. 20 indicates they have cause for concern. Trump has used the platform — his Trump Media & Technology Group owns it — to call out companies, colleges and other corporations and organizations at least 177 times across at least 129 posts.”

— “Asked where getting called out by Trump on Truth Social falls on a scale ranging from inconvenient to five-alarm fire, one Republican lobbyist told NOTUS it’s a ‘nine out of 10.’”

JANE STREET LANDS ON K STREET: “ Jane Street Group has hired lobbyists for the first time in 20 years, and top executives have been proactively meeting with lawmakers,” per Bloomberg ’s Katherine Doherty , Chiranjivi Chakraborty and Todd Gillespie .

— “In some cases, those appointments have been pitched as simple, get-to-know-Jane-Street conversations, part of an effort to explain how the privately-held firm makes markets and is generating trading hauls greater than many of the world’s largest investment banks in the process.”

— But Jane Street’s decision to enlist Hogan Lovells comes as regulators in India are probing “additional trading strategies Jane Street used, including allegedly manipulating the country’s biggest index to make money with an options strategy commonly known as a ‘short straddle,’ according to people familiar with the investigation.” Jane Street has denied any wrongdoing in India and is appealing a July decision to boot the firm from the country’s financial markets.

— In the U.S., Jane Street has paid Hogan Lovells $160,000 from July to September, and firm representatives have met with officials at Treasury, Commerce and in the Executive Office of the President “to discuss Jane Street’s operations in India, according to the lobbying disclosures and the people familiar with the matter, who asked not to be named discussing non-public information. Separately, Jane Street co-founder Rob Granieri has also met with lawmakers, the people said.”

FAMILY MATTERS: The New York Times’ Teddy Schleifer is out today with a look at the tag-team effort by David and Larry Ellison to build out their media empire via the family’s hostile takeover bid for Warner Bros. Discovery , including Larry Ellison’s overtures to Trump, whose administration would need to green-light any deal.

— “Larry Ellison has taken the lead in making the case to the president for why Paramount and not Netflix, its rival bidder, should win control of Warner Bros., two of the people said. Mr. Trump has pledged to be ‘involved’ in any decision about whether to approve a deal,” per the Times.

— Trump, meanwhile, “has privately said Larry Ellison assured him that he would turn CBS News , which the Ellisons took over when they bought Paramount, into a more conservative outlet, two people with knowledge of the president’s comments said.”

PARDON ME: The new approach to presidential pardons adopted during Trump’s second term “has spawned a pardon-shopping industry where lobbyists say their going rate is $1 million” in order to fast-track their clients’ shot at freedom , The Wall Street Journal ’s Rebecca Ballhaus , Josh Dawsey and C. Ryan Barber

— “Administration officials and lobbyists describe two playbooks that have emerged. There is the official track, which involves pardon czar Alice Johnson , Justice Department pardon attorney Ed Martin and the White House Counsel’s Office.”

— “Applicants usually go through one of the three, and ultimately White House counsel Dave Warrington reviews the application and makes a recommendation to Trump. The two men meet every few weeks to discuss pardons, administration officials said.”

— “The second track is riskier but can be much faster. If an applicant can find Trump at Mar-a-Lago or a White House event and ask for a pardon directly, Trump is often inclined to be helpful, administration officials said—particularly if someone says the magic words: “unjust persecution.”

— “Many of Trump’s most controversial pardons—including for [ Binance founder Changpeng ] Zhao and the Honduran ex-president—have gone through the latter track, which some senior administration officials said worried them. Another senior White House official said the ‘vast majority’ of pardons have gone through the proper channels. Driving up the price for well-connected lobbyists and lawyers is the sense that they can pursue only a few pardons, given the political capital they need to expend to fast-track a case.”

Jobs report

— The Heritage Foundation is adding Stewart Whitson as chief of staff to President Kevin Roberts . He previously worked at the Foundation for Government Accountability and was the GOP nominee in a Virginia special congressional election this year. Peter St. Onge is returning to Heritage as senior economist, and the think tank promoted Jay Richards to vice president of social and domestic policy, Allen Mendenhall to research fellow at the Thomas A. Roe Institute for Economic Policy Studies and Roger Severino to vice president of economic and domestic policy.

In preparation for Trump’s tariffs, the association brought on Ballard Partners last December for guidance on the matter, lobbying disclosures show.

— The association also retained its former top lobbyist Ed Desmond at the beginning of the year, and in February the Toy Association brought on Ridgeline Advocacy Group to work on a number of issues in addition to the tariffs, including consumer protection, sustainability and taxes.

— Detentes between Beijing and Washington gradually lowered tariffs on Chinese toy imports to 20 percent by the end of the year. But toymakers are closely tracking the Supreme Court decision on Trump’s so-called reciprocal tariffs and the prospect of seeing tariff payments refunded.

— Trump’s tariffs have prompted some holiday brands to turn to K Street for the first time. They include the Christmas Trade Group, a coalition of holiday retailers like the ornament and decor purveyors Kurt Adler and Old World Christmas, and artificial tree makers National Tree Company and Puleo. The coalition also includes holiday florists, lighting companies and even one commercial decorator whose portfolio includes the Trump International Hotel in New York.

— The trade group has paid Williams & Jensen $90,000 since March to build ties with the Trump administration and lawmakers on the key congressional committees that oversee trade. It has also lobbied for an exemption on products like Christmas lights similar to the one issued during Trump’s first administration.

— Artificial tree behemoth Balsam Brands, meanwhile, has spent $210,000 on lobbying through the first three quarters of the year — including $110,000 in Q3 alone. That’s less than the $420,000 Balsam Brands spent in 2019, but is the most by far for the company since the end of its three-year lobbying hiatus in 2023.

— Beyond the producers of holiday decor and goods, the retailers that sell those products have been some of the most vocal tariff critics in Washington this year. The National Retail Federation, whose members include Walmart, Target and Macy’s, is on track for its second-highest lobbying expenditures ever. NRF has dropped more than $8.5 million on lobbying so far this year, already more than the $8.3 million spent in all of 2024.

Happy Wednesday and welcome to the final PI of the year. Thank you all for reading and sending tips — we couldn’t have made it through this whirlwind of a year without you. We’ll be back in your inboxes on Jan. 5, but feel free to send us influence tips to chase down in the New Year. You can reach Caitlin on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 or at coprysko@politico.com. Daniel B. is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com. Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns.

— “A NOTUS analysis of every Trump Truth Social post since Jan. 20 indicates they have cause for concern. Trump has used the platform — his Trump Media & Technology Group owns it — to call out companies, colleges and other corporations and organizations at least 177 times across at least 129 posts.”

— “Asked where getting called out by Trump on Truth Social falls on a scale ranging from inconvenient to five-alarm fire, one Republican lobbyist told NOTUS it’s a ‘nine out of 10.’”

— “In some cases, those appointments have been pitched as simple, get-to-know-Jane-Street conversations, part of an effort to explain how the privately-held firm makes markets and is generating trading hauls greater than many of the world’s largest investment banks in the process.”

— But Jane Street’s decision to enlist Hogan Lovells comes as regulators in India are probing “additional trading strategies Jane Street used, including allegedly manipulating the country’s biggest index to make money with an options strategy commonly known as a ‘short straddle,’ according to people familiar with the investigation.” Jane Street has denied any wrongdoing in India and is appealing a July decision to boot the firm from the country’s financial markets.

Discovery, including Larry Ellison’s overtures to Trump, whose administration would need to green-light any deal.

Ryan Barber

— “Administration officials and lobbyists describe two playbooks that have emerged. There is the official track, which involves pardon czar Alice Johnson, Justice Department pardon attorney Ed Martin and the White House Counsel’s Office.”

MILLER STAFFS UP: Former Rep. Trey Gowdy (R-S.C.) is joining Miller Strategies , the lobbying shop led by top GOP fundraiser Jeff Miller , as of counsel. The former federal prosecutor served four terms in the House, including as chair of the House Oversight Committee and Benghazi Committee, before retiring in 2019.

— Shortly after leaving office, Gowdy rejoined his former law firm, Nelson Mullins Riley & Scarborough , as a partner in the white collar defense and government investigations practice. He was briefly tapped to be a member of President Donald Trump ’s defense team during his first impeachment, and lobbied the president for a pardon of an entertainment executive over a round of golf last year.

— More recently, Gowdy has been the host of “Sunday Night in America with Trey Gowdy” on Fox News and is one of several political power players who works for the law firm Oberheiden P.C. It’s unclear whether he will register to lobby at Miller Strategies.

— Miller Strategies has also added another Trump White House alum to its roster. Natalie McIntyre , who most recently worked in the White House’s legislative affairs office, has joined the firm as a principal. McIntyre served in Trump’s first term as well, along with her new Miller colleagues George Caram , Ashley Gunn , Jonny Hiler , Stefan Passantino and Luke Wallwork .

IF YOU MISSED IT OVER THE BREAK: Netflix brought on a prominent GOP antitrust lobbyist last month as the streaming giant works to fend off competition concerns related to its proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery ’s studios and streaming assets.

— The Gibson Group ’s Joseph Gibson , who previously worked in DOJ’s Antitrust Division in addition to serving as a top lawyer for the House Judiciary Committee, began working on tech antitrust issues for the streamer on Dec. 12, according to a disclosure filed last week. That was days after reports of the Netflix-WBD merger set off alarm bells across Washington .

— Gibson will join an outside lobbying team for Netflix that includes Monument Advocacy , Miller & Chevalier and Ballard Partners. Ballard is working to help Netflix win regulatory approval despite also being registered to lobby for Paramount Skydance , which has mounted a hostile takeover bid for WBD.

— Netflix’s in-house roster includes Clete Willems , a deputy director of the National Economic Council during Trump’s first term, and Emma Rindels-Hill , a former Kevin McCarthy aide. Virginia Boney Moore , who served as special assistant to the president in Trump’s first Office of Legislative Affairs, also joined Netflix last month.

5 YEARS LATER: In the wake of the attack on the Capitol five years ago today, dozens of major corporations announced plans to halt or review their political donations to the 147 Republican lawmakers who voted against certifying Joe Biden ’s victory in the 2020 election.

— Half a decade later, just 10 of those companies have upheld their pledges to stop contributing to congressional election objectors via their corporate PACs, according to Popular Information ’s Judd Legum , Rebecca Crosby and Noel Sims , who have been tracking this issue over the years.

— That group includes Farmers Insurance , Clorox , Whirlpool and Expedia Group , which all said they would suspend all political contributions after the Jan. 6 attack. (Whirlpool shuttered its corporate PAC in 2023.)

— Meanwhile Airbnb , Nike , Lyft , Qurate Retail (now known as QVC ) and Eversource Energy have all upheld their initial pledges to cut off donations specifically to election objectors, per Popular Information. Holland & Hart , the law and lobbying firm that employs former Trump EPA chief Andrew Wheeler , has similarly stuck to its promise not to donate to any of the election objectors.

UNLEASH THE WALL STREET EXECS: Lobbyists for banks and cryptocurrency companies have been brawling for months over a landmark bill that would overhaul how digital assets are regulated. Now, bank CEOs from around the country are about to wade into the fight, per our friends at Morning Money .

— The clash centers on whether crypto exchanges should be allowed to pay an annual percentage yield via rewards programs to customers who hold stablecoins. In a new twist, the American Bankers Association is now trying to harness the political capital of its members by urging bank leaders to press lawmakers for bill language that would ban crypto exchanges from doing so.

— The issue “demands immediate action from every bank leader in the country,” ABA President Rob Nichols wrote in a letter to CEOs . “We need you — along with your staff and, where appropriate, your customers — to contact Congress and make our voices heard.”

— The intensifying lobbying push — and pointed language — is notable coming from the ABA, which represents a huge array of banking institutions that are often at odds with each other over financial policy. The group tends to shy away from taking hardline stances on hot-button issues, and its approach to the yield fight illustrates that there is unity across the banking sector on the matter.

— Digital asset firms, an increasingly powerful force in Washington, are fighting back.

A coalition of crypto companies led by the Blockchain Association wrote in a letter to senators last month that proposals to crack down on exchanges’ rewards programs “would reopen a settled issue, undermine a carefully negotiated compromise, reduce consumer choice, suppress competition, and inject uncertainty into the implementation of a new law before regulations have even been proposed.”

HEADS UP: “Longtime climate advocate Sen. Ed Markey is demanding answers from President Donald Trump over the role that oil companies might have played in his decision to attack Venezuela and arrest its president,” E&E News’ Amelia Davidson reports.

title: Vance-linked firm sets up shop in DC

FIRST IN PI: New Jersey-based government affairs shop MAD Global Strategy is expanding to D.C. The firm, which was founded in 2021 by GOP operative Mike DuHaime and has offices in Ohio, New York and West Virginia, has tapped veteran energy and transportation lobbyist Mimi Braniff to steer its new outpost. It will serve as a full-service extension of work the firm has already been doing at the state level and for its existing national clients.

— Braniff has spent the past four years with Exxon Mobil , where she was most recently head of federal government and regulatory affairs. Before that, she was an in-house lobbyist for Delta Air Lines , an aide to Sen. Lisa Murkowski (R-Alaska) and a lobbyist for NRG Energy .

— In an interview, Braniff said the new office is currently a one-woman operation and that while she expects an initial heavy focus on energy and transportation policy issues given her background, MAD Global’s D.C. shop will eventually expand into other policy arenas. Braniff plans on registering to lobby for the firm as part of her new role.

— The firm has close ties to Vice President JD Vance . Jai Chabria , an Ohio-based partner at MAD Global, is a longtime Vance adviser who served as the chief strategist for Vance’s 2022 Senate campaign. (Chabria is also helping choreograph Vivek Ramaswamy ’s Ohio gubernatorial bid and ran Patrick Morrissey ’s successful West Virginia gubernatorial campaign in 2024.) Taylor Van Kirk , a longtime Vance spokesperson who joined him at the White House, is a MAD Global alum.

But now he is starting to feel the squeeze ” after a social media post ribbing billionaires who were threatening to flee California over a proposed one-time wealth tax in the state, according to The New York Times ’ Teddy Schleifer .

— Khanna “easily won re-election in 2024 and has loyal support from his district’s South Asian community. He sits on almost $15 million in campaign cash that even a candidate backed by wealthy tech donors would struggle to compete against. But the anger toward him … reflects the tense relationship between Silicon Valley and the Democratic Party, particularly its progressive wing.”

FLYING IN: The U.S. Chamber of Commerce hit the Hill today with more than 50 business and association leaders to try to regain momentum for a permitting overhaul after the House passed a package of reforms before skipping town last year.

— A policy forum this morning featured remarks from Senate Environment and Public Works Chair Shelley Moore Capito (R-W.Va.), House Natural Resources Chair Bruce Westerman (R-Ark.), Rep. Jared Golden (D-Maine), Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.) and Emily Domenech , who chairs the Trump administration’s permitting council. Participants then headed to meetings across the Hill to emphasize the urgency of passing permitting reform as bipartisan negotiations teeter .

— The event included leaders from individual energy and infrastructure companies as well as from the American Road & Transportation Builders Association , the Data Center Coalition , American Electric Power , the National Stone, Sand & Gravel Association , the American Cement Association , the American Gas Association , the Association of American Railroads , the American Chemistry Council , the Bipartisan Policy Center , the National Mining Association and more.

TRUMP SETS UP SHOWDOWN WITH PRIVATE EQUITY: “President Donald Trump on Wednesday said he will move to ban large investors from acquiring more single-family homes and called on Congress to back the initiative, in a bid to bring down the cost of housing,” POLITICO ’s Victoria Guida , Sam Sutton and Katherine Hapgood report.

— “I am immediately taking steps to ban large institutional investors from buying more single-family homes, and I will be calling on Congress to codify it,” Trump wrote in a post on Truth Social, adding that he would elaborate on the proposal at the World Economic Forum in Davos later this month.

— “The president’s broadside against institutional investors echoes previous Democratic-led efforts to restrict the private equity industry’s involvement in the housing market, and it’s likely to face considerable pushback from an industry that has a long history of beating back Washington-led efforts to rein in its activities,” Victoria, Sam and Katherine note.

— “But the public’s fury over the cost of housing and rising consumer prices has positioned the ‘affordability crisis’ as a central theme of the upcoming midterm elections,” and it comes as Vance “has been sharply critical of the asset management world’s growing role in housing.”

CRUZIN’ FOR A BRUISIN’: “Senate Commerce Committee Chair Ted Cruz (R-Texas) on Tuesday said Ford CEO Jim Farley was scared to testify before Congress, a day after Cruz postponed the hearing due to Farley’s refusal to appear,” POLITICO ’s Chris Marquette reports.

— “Cruz popped off on Farley, whose reluctance to appear delayed what was set to be a marquee hearing with the leaders of the Big Three Detroit automakers and a top engineer at Tesla . Cruz also bashed Farley on a since-scrapped plan by the automaker that would have let dealers continue to offer the $7,500 electric vehicle tax credit on leases, even after the benefit expired.”

— Cruz, who demurred on whether he would issue a subpoena to compel Farley to testify, pledged to hold a hearing focused on affordability and the upcoming surface transportation reauthorization with or without Ford’s input. A spokesperson for the automaker said Ford was “committed to appropriately engaging on issues that impact our company, our employees and the industry and we look forward to continuing to work with leaders such as Senator Cruz.”

SWEET HOME ALABAMA: Public affairs firm Seven Letter is expanding nationwide, opening new offices in Los Angeles, New York City and Huntsville, Alabama, the firm announced today . The move is the firm’s largest expansion to date, raising its total number of offices to five from its current two locations in Washington and Boston.

— The decision to open an office in Huntsville, an area which has become a major hub for the aerospace industry and hosts a variety of Defense Department, Justice Department and NASA components at the Army’s Redstone Arsenal base, is reflective of the firm’s existing client base in the national security sector, CEO Erik Smith told PI.

— “In the aerospace and national security spheres, if people know we have a presence in Huntsville, and a significant one, that shows them we understand their business and we understand where the business is going,” he said.

— Firm veteran Holly Jackson will lead the Huntsville office. She will partner with Blair Taylor , an alum of former Alabama Sen. Richard Shelby’s office and the former communications director for the Senate Appropriations Committee. Also boosting the firm’s work for national security clients is recent hire Sabrina Singh , who served as deputy press secretary at the Pentagon during the Biden administration.

— Helming the Los Angeles office will be new hire Brandon Shaw , who previously worked as a vice president for Disney and Hulu and led his own firm B. Shaw Communications , which has been acquired by Seven Letter. Casey Hernandez , currently a partner in the firm’s Washington office, will move to Los Angeles to assist in launching the new office.

— Previous fellow at the firm Marley Hambourger is returning as a director to launch the New York office located in Manhattan. In addition to the new locations, the firm has hired Camille Cherney to serve as a content specialist in the Boston office.

FROM THE WHITE HOUSE TO MERCURY: Special Assistant to the President and Deputy Director of the White House Office of Public Liaison Brette Powell has left the West Wing to join Mercury Public Affairs , the firm announced today. She will serve as a managing director in the firm’s government relations team.

— Powell’s White House career started with a 2018 internship that led to subsequent positions during the first Trump administration. At the time Trump left office in 2021, she was serving as the president’s lead press advance representative. Following a stint in the private sector, she joined the Trump campaign in 2022 as director of external affairs.

— Powell is the latest in a string of White House aides who have decamped to K Street during the first year of the second Trump administration. Trump staffers Harrison Fields , Trent Morse and May Davis Mailman all exited the administration for K Street gigs in 2025. It is unclear if Powell will register to lobby.

title: Ballard name gets pulled into Mangione case
body_text:
IN THE COURTS: Lawyers for Luigi Mangione, the accused murderer of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson, are making a novel argument to get their client’s death penalty case thrown out: They’re claiming that Attorney General Pam Bondi’s previous employment with Ballard Partners has created a conflict of interest.

— Mangione appeared in a New York courtroom today for a hearing where a federal judge set a potential trial date and ruled on an evidentiary issue. But the judge did not address the defense’s tenuous argument that Bondi’s six years at Ballard, which registered to lobby for UnitedHealthcare in 2024, is sufficient grounds to dismiss Mangione’s indictment.

— Ballard signed UnitedHealthcare as a client while Bondi was still working at the firm in August 2024, four months before Thompson’s murder. Citing that timeline, Mangione’s defense team accuses Bondi of having a “personal financial interest” due to a retirement account administered by Ballard, and seeking to “avenge the death of the CEO of her former firm’s client.”

— Prosecutors blasted the defense’s argument in a separate filing this week , calling the description of Bondi’s financial ties to Ballard “incomplete and misleading” and clarifying that the firm has not contributed to her 401(k) since her departure.

— “There is nothing in the Attorney General’s financial disclosure form that suggests receipt

of any ongoing income, distributions, partnership draws, or remuneration from Ballard Partners in any form,” prosecutors wrote. They added that there is “no factual basis” to claim that corporate interests influenced the decision to seek the death penalty and the defense’s “insinuations otherwise rest on an inaccurate financial narrative.”

— Ballard Partners, currently the top lobbying firm in Washington by revenue, declined to comment.

title: Ballard launches Western Hemisphere practice
body_text:
WILD WILD WEST: Ballard Partners has launched a new practice group dedicated to helping clients navigate the geopolitical upheaval under way across the Western Hemisphere, along with a dedicated working group focused on Venezuela specifically following the Trump administration’s military operation to depose Nicolás Maduro.

— Both groups will include Micah Ketchel and Thomas Boodry , both of whom have worked for the National Security Council under President Donald Trump as well as for top national security officials like Mike Waltz or Marco Rubio ; and Tracie Pough , the longtime former chief of staff to Rep. Debbie Wasserman-Schultz (D-Fla.), whose district includes the highest concentration of Venezuelans living in the U.S.

— Jose Felix Diaz , a former Florida legislator and attorney with extensive experience in international trade issues; Scott Wagner , an attorney specializing in business, maritime and aviation law; and Tucker Knott , who previously served as chief of staff to Sen. Ted Budd (R-N.C.), will also work with the new practice groups, which will provide clients with strategic advice related to Latin America, Mexico, Canada and Greenland.

— Ballard already represents Chevron , which is the only U.S. oil company licensed to operate in Venezuela after the Trump administration reinstated the company’s permission to do so last year. And though other U.S. oil giants have expressed varying degrees of skepticism about diving headfirst into Venezuela, Ballard has recently registered to lobby for Maha Capital , a Swedish company with rights to another Venezuelan oil project that is seeking U.S. approval for partnerships.

— While K Street has been fielding questions from clients about potential business opportunities in Venezuela in the wake of Maduro’s ouster, lobbyists have cautioned that there are still many unknowns. Trump’s new Western-focused foreign policy agenda “will create plentiful opportunities for clients in the Hemisphere, but they require immediate and strategic engagement in a manner that is aligned with U.S. national interests,” Ballard’s Justin Sayfie told PI.

— The firm’s new offerings are aimed at “ensuring our clients have access to the deep regional expertise and bipartisan institutional knowledge required to succeed in these critical markets,” founder Brian Ballard said in a statement.

FIRST IN PI — AMAZON LOBBYIST JOINS ATLAS: Atlas Crossing has hired Bobby Parmiter as a principal. Parmiter has spent the past three years at Amazon , where he represented the e-commerce giant before Congress on issues ranging from artificial intelligence and data privacy to tax and trade policy. He also chaired the government relations committee and PAC board of the industry group Security Industry Association .

— Before that, Parmiter spent more than a decade on the Hill, serving as general counsel for the House Intelligence Committee under chairs Devin Nunes (R-Calif.) and Mike Turner (R-Ohio). He’s also a House Judiciary, Doug Collins and DOJ alum.

MERCURY ADDS ANOTHER TRUMP ALUM: Brian Hughes , who most recently served as chief of staff at NASA, has joined Mercury Public Affairs as a partner leading the firm’s Tallahassee office. He also plans on registering to lobby at the federal level and work with the firm’s D.C. clients, further reinforcing the firm’s deep ties to the Trump administration.

— Before joining NASA last year, Hughes was a deputy national security adviser for strategic communications at the White House and was a senior adviser and Florida campaign director for Trump’s 2024 campaign.

— Hughes also has extensive political experience in the Sunshine State, having served in then-Gov. Rick Scott ’s administration and as chief administrative officer for the city of Jacksonville and chief of staff to former Mayor Lenny Curry . (Curry now works for Florida powerhouse Ballard Partners.)

— Hughes is the latest person to head through the revolving door between Mercury and Trump’s orbit. Last week, the firm hired former special assistant to the president and deputy director of the White House Office of Public Liaison Brette Powell , and Mercury is also home to Trump adviser Bryan Lanza . And prior to joining the White House as chief of staff last year, Susie Wiles worked at Mercury as a co-chair.

WHAT THE EPC IS READING: “President Donald Trump is taking on Wall Street as he pushes his message of making life more affordable for Americans. Capitol Hill Republicans may be his biggest obstacle ,” POLITICO ’s Aiden Reiter , Katherine Hapgood and Jordain Carney report.

— “On Friday, the president called for a one-year 10-percent cap on credit card interest rates, and early Tuesday morning he endorsed the Credit Card Competition Act, a bill that would subject credit card companies to more oversight and could lower costs for merchants who accept cards.”

— “Both proposals have drawn sharp opposition from the financial sector. And both would likely require action in Congress, where Republicans have stymied similar efforts in the past, even as they have been championed by Democrats. That sets up an election-year clash between Trump and other Republicans over the president’s new populist policy agenda.”

BET ON IT: The newly launched alliance of online prediction markets has landed a pair of high-ranking former congressmembers to help the industry navigate Washington. The Coalition for Prediction Markets , whose members include Kalshi , Crypto.com , Robinhood , Coinbase and Underdog , has tapped former Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney (D-N.Y.) as its president and CEO, while former Rep. Patrick McHenry (R-N.C.) will join the group as a senior adviser.

— Maloney lost reelection in 2022 after five terms in office, which included a stint leading House Democrats’ campaign arm. McHenry, meanwhile, retired last year after two decades in the House, during which he served as chair of the powerful House Financial Services Committee as well as chief deputy whip and even, briefly, speaker pro tempore. Since leaving office, McHenry has also joined the crypto arm of venture capital firm a16z — a Kalshi investor — as a senior adviser.

— The hires come as prediction markets face increasing scrutiny from both sides of the aisle in Washington, where critics have called for additional guardrails to stem concerns about potential insider trading as well as the industry’s foray into sports betting.

WHAT TECH COMPANIES SAID ABOUT THEIR BALLROOM CHECKS: Congressional Democrats on Monday released responses from half a dozen tech companies to their questions about the tech giants’ donations to the project to erect a White House ballroom.

— The replies from Meta , Microsoft , Nvidia , Amazon , Apple and Comcast , which were shared by Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Rep. Dave Min (D-Calif.), varied in length — Meta’s response , for instance, was just a single paragraph — but some did shed new light on the ballroom fundraising process, which Warren, Min and nine other Democrats have sought to frame as potential quid-pro-quo arrangements.

— Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld ’s Karen Elizabeth Christian , responding to the Democratic inquiry on behalf of Microsoft, told lawmakers that the company was contacted last fall by an unnamed fundraiser for the ballroom project and confirmed a donation to the nonpartisan nonprofit Trust for the National Mall in September.

— “Microsoft’s donation was offered without any intent to influence or affect any issue, proceeding or business Microsoft has before the federal government,” Christian wrote, adding that “the benefits of this project will redound not only to this presidency, but presidencies to come, as they welcome guests to the White House on behalf of the American people.”

— Comcast told lawmakers that its donation was made with no restrictions or conditions on how it was to be used and echoed the responses of Apple and Amazon in emphasizing the company’s “extensive history of philanthropic efforts” around D.C. Nvidia noted that D.C. landmarks such as the Washington Monument, Lincoln Memorial, Jefferson Memorial and more were all funded by private donations.

Last week, the firm hired former special assistant to the president and deputy director of the White House Office of Public Liaison Brette Powell, and Mercury is also home to Trump adviser Bryan Lanza. And prior to joining the White House as chief of staff last year, Susie Wiles worked at Mercury as a co-chair.

WHAT THE EPC IS READING: “President Donald Trump is taking on Wall Street as he pushes his message of making life more affordable for Americans. Capitol Hill Republicans may be his biggest obstacle,” POLITICO’s Aiden Reiter, Katherine Hapgood and Jordain Carney report.

— “On Friday, the president called for a one-year 10-percent cap on credit card interest rates, and early Tuesday morning he endorsed the Credit Card Competition Act, a bill that would subject credit card companies to more oversight and could lower costs for merchants who accept cards.”

— “Both proposals have drawn sharp opposition from the financial sector. And both would likely require action in Congress, where Republicans have stymied similar efforts in the past, even as they have been championed by Democrats. That sets up an election-year clash between Trump and other Republicans over the president’s new populist policy agenda.”

BET ON IT: The newly launched alliance of online prediction markets has landed a pair of high-ranking former congressmembers to help the industry navigate Washington. The Coalition for Prediction Markets, whose members include Kalshi, Crypto.com, Robinhood, Coinbase and Underdog, has tapped former Rep. Sean Patrick Maloney (D-N.Y.) as its president and CEO, while former Rep. Patrick McHenry (R-N.C.) will join the group as a senior adviser.

— Maloney lost reelection in 2022 after five terms in office, which included a stint leading House Democrats’ campaign arm. McHenry, meanwhile, retired last year after two decades in the House, during which he served as chair of the powerful House Financial Services Committee as well as chief deputy whip and even, briefly, speaker pro tempore. Since leaving office, McHenry has also joined the crypto arm of venture capital firm a16z — a Kalshi investor — as a senior adviser.

— The hires come as prediction markets face increasing scrutiny from both sides of the aisle in Washington, where critics have called for additional guardrails to stem concerns about potential insider trading as well as the industry’s foray into sports betting.

WHAT TECH COMPANIES SAID ABOUT THEIR BALLROOM CHECKS: Congressional Democrats on Monday released responses from half a dozen tech companies to their questions about the tech giants’ donations to the project to erect a White House ballroom.

— The replies from Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, Amazon, Apple and Comcast, which were shared by Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) and Rep. Dave Min (D-Calif.), varied in length — Meta’s response, for instance, was just a single paragraph — but some did shed new light on the ballroom fundraising process, which Warren, Min and nine other Democrats have sought to frame as potential quid-pro-quo arrangements.

— Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld’s Karen Elizabeth Christian, responding to the Democratic inquiry on behalf of Microsoft, told lawmakers that the company was contacted last fall by an unnamed fundraiser for the ballroom project and confirmed a donation to the nonpartisan nonprofit Trust for the National Mall in September.

— “Microsoft’s donation was offered without any intent to influence or affect any issue, proceeding or business Microsoft has before the federal government,” Christian wrote, adding that “the benefits of this project will redound not only to this presidency, but presidencies to come, as they welcome guests to the White House on behalf of the American people.”

— Comcast told lawmakers that its donation was made with no restrictions or conditions on how it was to be used and echoed the responses of Apple and Amazon in emphasizing the company’s “extensive history of philanthropic efforts” around D.C. Nvidia noted that D.C. landmarks such as the Washington Monument, Lincoln Memorial, Jefferson Memorial and more were all funded by private donations.

MEA CULPA: This morning’s newsletter misstated the former title for American Policy Venture’s Valerie Shen and the new title for APV’s Ari Gerstman. Shen is a program manager at Renaissance Philanthropy, and Gerstman will be a vice president. PI regrets the error.

title: Kalshi opens a DC office
body_text:
FIRST IN PI : Kalshi has opened an office in D.C. as the online betting giant continues to grow its footprint in the nation’s capital. The betting platform has tapped Biden administration and Hill alum John Bivona as its first head of federal government relations.

— Bivona most recently worked for Kalshi’s newest outside lobbying firm, Intersection Government Relations . Before that, he worked at Rasky Partners following a stint as DHS’ White House liaison during the Biden administration and on the Biden campaign. He also served as chief of staff to Antonio Delgado , who served in the House before becoming New York’s lieutenant governor in 2022.

— Kalshi’s expansion in D.C. began during the Biden administration when the platform’s regulator, the CFTC, sought to clamp down on so-called event contracts, which allow prediction markets to take wagers on everything from awards shows to elections and, increasingly, sports. A 2024 court ruling opened the floodgates for prediction markets, and the sector has flourished under President Donald Trump .

— That popularity has sparked a fight with casinos and critics in state and federal government who have sought to challenge the industry’s incursion into sports betting. Late last year, companies including Kalshi, Crypto.com , Coinbase and Robinhood launched the Coalition for Prediction Markets , and earlier this month the coalition hired former Reps. Sean Patrick Maloney (D-N.Y.) and Patrick McHenry (R-N.C.) as its president and senior adviser, respectively.

— Kalshi registered its first in-house lobbyist over the summer, and the platform reported dropping $615,000 on federal lobbying last year — down from $670,000 the year before.

FIRST IN PI II — WHAT’S IN A NAME: Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck is revamping its leadership hierarchy to elevate top leaders of the law and lobbying firm’s government relations practice. The firm has named eight of its top lobbyists as principals of public policy, a new title that is the equivalent of an equity shareholder for non-attorneys — though without an ownership stake or fee-sharing arrangement.

— Though the American Bar Association generally bars non-lawyers from holding ownership stakes in a law firm, Brownstein’s lobbying practice brings in “a significant percentage” of the firm’s overall revenues, which firm leaders wanted to recognize, said Will Moschella , who co-leads the federal lobbying practice.

— The new principals — who will take on an expanded role in strategic planning for the firm — include Moschella’s co-leader atop the lobbying practice, Nadeam Elshami . Samantha Carl-Yoder and former Rep. Ed Royce , who co-chair Brownstein’s international practice, are also among the new principals, as are financial services practice co-chairs Zach Pfister and Brian McGuire ; tech and telecom practice leader Greta Joynes ; Sacramento managing director Greg Hayes and Democratic fundraiser David Reid .

— Given the dominance of Brownstein’s lobbying arm and its contributions to the firm’s bottom line, the new titles are an effort to “signify in the marketplace” that the new principals are on par with equity shareholders like Moschella, he told PI.

— They’re also aimed at helping the firm remain competitive in a bustling D.C. influence scene. “We understand that we’re competing against a lot of non-law firms as well, and so these titles are reflective of these individuals’ status … within our law firm,” Moschella added.

MINNESOTA BIZ LEADERS SPEAK UP AFTER KILLING: Chief executives from more than five dozen companies based in Minnesota called for a deescalation on Sunday after protests of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in Minneapolis turned deadly for the second time this month.

— “The recent challenges facing our state have created widespread disruption and tragic loss of life,” the CEOs said in an open letter following Saturday’s shooting of 37-year-old Alex Pretti by a federal immigration agent in Minneapolis. “We are calling for an immediate deescalation of tensions and for state, local and federal officials to work together to find real solutions.”

— Members of Minnesota’s business community have been backchanneling for weeks with officials including Gov. Tim Walz , Vice President JD Vance , the White House and local mayors, the executives said, adding that “there are ways for us to come together to foster progress.” Signatories included the heads of Target , Cargill , 3M , Ameriprise Financial , Best Buy , UnitedHealth Group , U.S. Bancorp , Mayo Clinic and more.

— The letter doesn’t explicitly criticize the Trump administration’s actions in Minneapolis or those protesting the immigration crackdown. Still, it represents notable pushback from the business community during an administration characterized by Trump’s willingness to punish his critics, and preceded the first signs of a pivot from the White House.

ANOTHER ALLY SPEAKS OUT: Amid criticism on the right for Pretti’s decision to carry a gun to Saturday’s protests, conservatives “ are facing pushback from an unlikely quarter : gun-rights groups that traditionally have largely sided with the GOP,” The Wall Street Journal ’s Cameron McWhirter reports.

— “‘The first thing that politicians want to do is blame the gun,’ said Taylor Rhodes , spokesperson for the National Association for Gun Rights , based in Greenville, S.C. Rhodes said he has attended hundreds of protests and rallies over the years, always with a gun. He said a thorough investigation is needed, but judging from videos of the shooting, ‘I don’t think it looks good on the ICE agents.’”

— “For Second Amendment activists, the conversation around Pretti’s shooting intersects with an argument they have long made: Gun owners have a constitutional right to carry their firearms in public.”

MARSHALL BACKS DOWN ON SWIPE FEES : “Sen. Roger Marshall agreed not to offer an amendment aimed at cracking down on credit card swipe fees during a Senate Agriculture markup of cryptocurrency legislation on Thursday,” POLITICO ’s Jasper Goodman and Meredith Lee Hill report.

— “The Kansas Republican filed an amendment to Senate Ag’s crypto bill last week that seeks to force payment networks to compete on swipe fees. But he agreed in private conversations on Saturday not to call up the provision, which is similar to legislation dubbed the Credit Card Competition Act that he has pushed for years along with Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.).”

— “White House officials have gotten involved in the matter, according to several people with knowledge of the internal deliberations. The Marshall amendment would have ‘jeopardized’ passage of the crypto bill, which the White House is pressing to pass out of committee, according to one of the people.”

— Durbin, meanwhile, is “not currently expected to offer the amendment at the markup, according to a person with knowledge of the matter, though no final decision has been made. A spokesperson for the Illinois Democrat declined to comment.”

RIVERA MAY CALL WILES, RUBIO: Defense attorneys for former Rep. David Rivera , who is set to go on trial later this spring for charges of acting as an unregistered foreign agent of the Venezuelan government under recently ousted leader Nicolás Maduro , are seeking testimony in the upcoming trial from top Trump administration officials, including White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and Secretary of State Marco Rubio , the Miami Herald ’s Jay Weaver writes, potentially ramping up the stakes of the trial further.

— Rivera and his co-defendant, political consultant Esther Nuhfer , “have strongly denied the allegations, and hope to undercut the government’s case by showing they were not doing Maduro’s bidding but rather were attempting to get him removed from power.”

— “They also want to show that Wiles’ former lobbying firm was attempting to lobby Trump, on behalf of [wealthy Venezuelan businessman Raul Gorrin ] to bring about a regime change in Venezuela. The lead federal prosecutor, Harold Schimkat , said at a Miami federal court hearing last week that the government will try to quash Wiles’ subpoena, saying: ‘We don’t see her connection to this case at all.’”

— “But defense attorneys for Rivera and Nuhfer wrote a letter to the White House seeking Wiles as a witness, saying they want to question the former Ballard lobbyist about her ‘extensive communications’ regarding the firm’s $50,000-a-month representation of Gorrin in 2017 and 2018.”

Kalshi opens a DC office

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO and DANIEL BARNES 

01/26/2026 07:39 PM EST

Presented by

With Daniel Lippman

FIRST IN PI: Kalshi has opened an office in D.C. as the online betting giant continues to grow its footprint in the nation’s capital. The betting platform has tapped Biden administration and Hill alum John Bivona as its first head of federal government relations.

— Bivona most recently worked for Kalshi’s newest outside lobbying firm, Intersection Government Relations. Before that, he worked at Rasky Partners following a stint as DHS’ White House liaison during the Biden administration and on the Biden campaign. He also served as chief of staff to Antonio Delgado, who served in the House before becoming New York’s lieutenant governor in 2022.

— Kalshi’s expansion in D.C. began during the Biden administration when the platform’s regulator, the CFTC, sought to clamp down on so-called event contracts, which allow prediction markets to take wagers on everything from awards shows to elections and, increasingly, sports. A 2024 court ruling opened the floodgates for prediction markets, and the sector has flourished under President Donald Trump.

— That popularity has sparked a fight with casinos and critics in state and federal government who have sought to challenge the industry’s incursion into sports betting. Late last year, companies including Kalshi, Crypto.com, Coinbase and Robinhood launched the Coalition for Prediction Markets, and earlier this month the coalition hired former Reps. Sean Patrick Maloney (D-N.Y.) and Patrick McHenry (R-N.C.) as its president and senior adviser, respectively.

— Kalshi registered its first in-house lobbyist over the summer, and the platform reported dropping $615,000 on federal lobbying last year — down from $670,000 the year before.

FIRST IN PI II — WHAT’S IN A NAME: Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck is revamping its leadership hierarchy to elevate top leaders of the law and lobbying firm’s government relations practice. The firm has named eight of its top lobbyists as principals of public policy, a new title that is the equivalent of an equity shareholder for non-attorneys — though without an ownership stake or fee-sharing arrangement.

— Though the American Bar Association generally bars non-lawyers from holding ownership stakes in a law firm, Brownstein’s lobbying practice brings in “a significant percentage” of the firm’s overall revenues, which firm leaders wanted to recognize, said Will Moschella, who co-leads the federal lobbying practice.

— The new principals — who will take on an expanded role in strategic planning for the firm — include Moschella’s co-leader atop the lobbying practice, Nadeam Elshami. Samantha Carl-Yoder and former Rep. Ed Royce, who co-chair Brownstein’s international practice, are also among the new principals, as are financial services practice co-chairs Zach Pfister and Brian McGuire; tech and telecom practice leader Greta Joynes; Sacramento managing director Greg Hayes and Democratic fundraiser David Reid.

— Given the dominance of Brownstein’s lobbying arm and its contributions to the firm’s bottom line, the new titles are an effort to “signify in the marketplace” that the new principals are on par with equity shareholders like Moschella, he told PI.

— They’re also aimed at helping the firm remain competitive in a bustling D.C. influence scene. “We understand that we’re competing against a lot of non-law firms as well, and so these titles are reflective of these individuals’ status … within our law firm,” Moschella added.

MINNESOTA BIZ LEADERS SPEAK UP AFTER KILLING: Chief executives from more than five dozen companies based in Minnesota called for a deescalation on Sunday after protests of the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in Minneapolis turned deadly for the second time this month.

— “The recent challenges facing our state have created widespread disruption and tragic loss of life,” the CEOs said in an open letter following Saturday’s shooting of 37-year-old Alex Pretti by a federal immigration agent in Minneapolis. “We are calling for an immediate deescalation of tensions and for state, local and federal officials to work together to find real solutions.”

— Members of Minnesota’s business community have been backchanneling for weeks with officials including Gov. Tim Walz, Vice President JD Vance, the White House and local mayors, the executives said, adding that “there are ways for us to come together to foster progress.” Signatories included the heads of Target, Cargill, 3M, Ameriprise Financial, Best Buy, UnitedHealth Group, U.S. Bancorp, Mayo Clinic and more.

— The letter doesn’t explicitly criticize the Trump administration’s actions in Minneapolis or those protesting the immigration crackdown. Still, it represents notable pushback from the business community during an administration characterized by Trump’s willingness to punish his critics, and preceded the first signs of a pivot from the White House.

ANOTHER ALLY SPEAKS OUT: Amid criticism on the right for Pretti’s decision to carry a gun to Saturday’s protests, conservatives “are facing pushback from an unlikely quarter: gun-rights groups that traditionally have largely sided with the GOP,” The Wall Street Journal’s Cameron McWhirter reports.

— “‘The first thing that politicians want to do is blame the gun,’ said Taylor Rhodes, spokesperson for the National Association for Gun Rights, based in Greenville, S.C. Rhodes said he has attended hundreds of protests and rallies over the years, always with a gun. He said a thorough investigation is needed, but judging from videos of the shooting, ‘I don’t think it looks good on the ICE agents.’”

— “For Second Amendment activists, the conversation around Pretti’s shooting intersects with an argument they have long made: Gun owners have a constitutional right to carry their firearms in public.”

MARSHALL BACKS DOWN ON SWIPE FEES: “Sen. Roger Marshall agreed not to offer an amendment aimed at cracking down on credit card swipe fees during a Senate Agriculture markup of cryptocurrency legislation on Thursday,” POLITICO’s Jasper Goodman and Meredith Lee Hill report.

— “The Kansas Republican filed an amendment to Senate Ag’s crypto bill last week that seeks to force payment networks to compete on swipe fees. But he agreed in private conversations on Saturday not to call up the provision, which is similar to legislation dubbed the Credit Card Competition Act that he has pushed for years along with Sen. Dick Durbin (D-Ill.).”

— “White House officials have gotten involved in the matter, according to several people with knowledge of the internal deliberations. The Marshall amendment would have ‘jeopardized’ passage of the crypto bill, which the White House is pressing to pass out of committee, according to one of the people.”

— Durbin, meanwhile, is “not currently expected to offer the amendment at the markup, according to a person with knowledge of the matter, though no final decision has been made. A spokesperson for the Illinois Democrat declined to comment.”

RIVERA MAY CALL WILES, RUBIO: Defense attorneys for former Rep. David Rivera, who is set to go on trial later this spring for charges of acting as an unregistered foreign agent of the Venezuelan government under recently ousted leader Nicolás Maduro, are seeking testimony in the upcoming trial from top Trump administration officials, including White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, the Miami Herald’s Jay Weaver writes, potentially ramping up the stakes of the trial further.

— Rivera and his co-defendant, political consultant Esther Nuhfer, “have strongly denied the allegations, and hope to undercut the government’s case by showing they were not doing Maduro’s bidding but rather were attempting to get him removed from power.”

— “They also want to show that Wiles’ former lobbying firm was attempting to lobby Trump, on behalf of [wealthy Venezuelan businessman Raul Gorrin] to bring about a regime change in Venezuela. The lead federal prosecutor, Harold Schimkat, said at a Miami federal court hearing last week that the government will try to quash Wiles’ subpoena, saying: ‘We don’t see her connection to this case at all.’”

— “But defense attorneys for Rivera and Nuhfer wrote a letter to the White House seeking Wiles as a witness, saying they want to question the former Ballard lobbyist about her ‘extensive communications’ regarding the firm’s $50,000-a-month representation of Gorrin in 2017 and 2018.”

title: Biofuels use Iowa visit to woo Trump
body_text:
ETHANOL FRUSTRATIONS: As President Donald Trump travels to Iowa today to speak about energy and the economy, “ tensions remain high over the future of ethanol sales ” after the collapse last week of an eleventh-hour push to allow year-round sales of E15 as part of Congress’ spending bill, per POLITICO ’s Grace Yarrow .

— “The failed effort left lobbyists feeling betrayed by the White House and farm-state lawmakers feeling frustrated with a key agriculture industry group, according to three people granted anonymity to discuss behind-the-scenes conversations. The National Corn Growers Association rankled Midwestern Republicans on Wednesday when it dismissed the effectiveness” of a new working group set up by House Republicans as a consolation.

— “During a House Agriculture GOP member meeting the following day, several lawmakers said they felt thrown under the bus by NCGA’s reaction to E15 being excluded from the funding package, calling the statement ‘unhinged,’ according to two of the people familiar with the talks.”

— Iowa ethanol advocates appealed directly to the president ahead of his trip today, warning in a letter that corn farmers are at a “breaking point” and that “without immediate policy intervention to create new demand, we are looking at an avoidable decline in Iowa’s rural economy.”

— “Removing the outdated regulatory hurdle for E15 is exactly the type of government efficiency you’ve worked for,” leaders of the Iowa Corn Growers Association and the Iowa Renewable Fuels Association wrote to Trump. The trade groups also took out a full-page ad in today’s Des Moines Register reminding Trump of his previous support for E15 and declaring that “in Iowa, the intersection of economy and energy occurs at a place called E15.” (In what advocates are surely hoping is a good sign, the president slapped his autograph on a copy of the ad, per Reuters’ Jarrett Renshaw .)

— The overtures from the ethanol industry come on the heels of tens of millions of dollars dropped by biofuels advocates last year, in part to win year-round E15 sales. Top biofuel and ethanol producers including Bayer , POET , Koch Industries and Archer Daniels Midland collectively spent almost $28.4 million on federal lobbying last year, disclosures show.

— The National Corn Growers Association spent around $370,000 lobbying Washington in 2025, up from $330,000 a year prior. Ethanol trade group Growth Energy shelled out close to $2.5 million in 2025, compared with $2.3 million the year before, meanwhile fellow biofuel lobby Renewable Fuels Association spent almost $1.1 million — down from nearly $1.6 million in 2024.

Happy Tuesday and welcome to PI. Send K Street tips and gossip. You can reach Caitlin on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 or at coprysko@politico.com . Daniel B. is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com . Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns .

FRIENDS IN HIGH PLACES: Fresh off the nursing home industry’s victory in scoring a 10-year moratorium on a Biden administration rule requiring increased staffing levels last summer, industry executives began looking further down the line to try to have the rule — aimed at reducing patient neglect — dropped permanently. So they “ turned to a tool that has proved successful in getting President Trump’s attention,” The New York Times’ Ken Vogel and Christina Jewett report: money.

— “Starting in early August, the industry began making donations that over the course of weeks would eventually total nearly $4.8 million to MAGA Inc. , a super PAC devoted to Mr. Trump and run by his allies. Later that same month, a handful of nursing home executives who had given the biggest donations joined industry lobbyists at Mr. Trump’s golf club in suburban Washington to plead their case, according to campaign finance filings and people familiar with the meeting.”

— “Less than one month after the lunch meeting, Trump administration lawyers quietly stopped defending the pending staffing rule in court against challenges from the industry. Complete victory came a couple of months after that, when the White House approved a full revocation,” sparking an outcry from patient groups.

— There is no evidence linking the donations to the repeal of the rule, which the White House and HHS defended and which “was already facing uncertain prospects before the August meeting. … But the industry’s fund-raising for MAGA Inc. highlights the eagerness of corporate America to curry favor with a president who has repeatedly used the levers of government to reward donors and allies — and to punish critics.”

BERNHARDT GROUP ADDS BUDGET STAFFER: Tamzin Astani has joined the Bernhardt Group , the lobbying firm founded last year by former Interior Secretary David Bernhardt , as a policy director. Astani has worked since 2023 for House Budget Chair Jodey Arrington (R-Texas), most recently serving as a professional staff member and coalition’s deputy director for the budget panel.

ANNALS OF CAMPAIGN FINANCE: “The Justice Department under the Biden administration opened an investigation into Representative Ilhan Omar , Democrat of Minnesota, in 2024 to scrutinize her finances, campaign spending and interactions with a foreign citizen,” people with knowledge of the matter tell the Times’ Glenn Thrush and Annie Karni .

— “The inquiry, initiated by the U.S. attorney’s office in Washington and the department’s public integrity unit in June of that year, appears to have stalled for lack of evidence, according to one of the people who requested anonymity to discuss internal department matters.”

— “The investigation appeared to be thrust into the public spotlight on Monday, when President Trump blindsided department officials by posting about it on Truth Social , singling out Ms. Omar. It was part of a rambling statement announcing a shake-up of the team overseeing immigration raids in Ms. Omar’s Minneapolis district that misspelled her name.”

Q STREET ELECTS NEW BOARD: Q Street , the professional association for LGBTQ+ policy and political professionals, has reelected Yesenia Alvarado Henninger of Helion Energy as president, Stu Malec of the Progressive Policy Institute as secretary and Brendan Neal of Neal Strategies as treasurer.

— David Reid of Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck and Rob Curis of Lowe’s will return as board members alongside new members Abigail Harris of Honeywell and Alex Catanese of the American Bankers Association .

— Andrew Ting has joined the American Bankers Association as deputy general counsel and executive vice president. He was most recently chief legal officer and corporate secretary at Panorama Education .

Caitlin Oprysko covers lobbying for POLITICO and writes the Influence newsletter. She was previously a breaking news reporter for POLITICO, covering the 2018 midterms, 2020 election and everything (seriously) in between. Caitlin is originally from the Atlanta area and graduated from the University of Georgia, where she covered state and local news and worked for the student-run newscast Grady Newsource.

By DANIEL LIPPMAN , CAITLIN OPRYSKO and DANIEL BARNES

01/28/2026 06:12 PM EST

Presented by

FIRST IN PI : The debate about banning members of Congress from trading stocks has jumped to the campaign trail. Former Rep. Colin Allred (D-Texas), who is in a heated primary against Rep. Julie Johnson , has bragged about how he never traded any stocks during his six years in Congress, Daniel L. reports.

— His spokesperson said Johnson’s more of a Johnny-come-lately on the issue. “Colin Allred never traded a single stock while serving in Congress — not because anyone required it, but because he believes public service demands putting the people’s interests ahead of personal gain,” Sandhya Raghavan said in a statement. “Meanwhile, Julie Johnson has actively traded stocks throughout her six years in the Texas Legislature and continued to do so as a member of Congress.”

— At a Jan. 14 House Administration Committee markup for congressional stock trading legislation, Johnson said she chose to divest, “not because the law required it, but because earning the trust of my constituents demands it.”

— She continued: “Full divestment is the only way to truly eliminate conflicts of interest, and that is why I took that step myself.”

— But Johnson, who was a successful small business owner and attorney before entering Congress last year, only fully started divesting her holdings in September after a bipartisan group of House lawmakers, including Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) and Chip Roy (R-Texas), introduced the Restore Trust in Congress Act , which would ban congressional stock trading. Ocasio-Cortez recently endorsed Johnson .

— Johnson also gained attention last spring for making dozens of stock sales the day before President Donald Trump ’s tariff “Liberation Day” which sent stock markets temporarily reeling. Her office didn’t respond to questions at the time about the sales.

— Her new vocal stance against stock trading in September was a reversal from Johnson’s practice of buying individual stocks the previous month; a spokesperson at the time called it an “ongoing process” to get rid of her holdings. She made almost 350 purchases, sales or exchanges of stock last year, which gave the lawmaker the unwanted distinction of being in the top 2 percent of all congressional traders.

— Johnson said in a statement to PI that her stock holdings are managed by independent third parties and that her divestment began last March and that she fully divested at the end of last year.

— “I came to Congress after years as a small business owner and attorney with complex, pre-existing financial holdings,” she added. “The law did not require me to divest—but I chose to do so because earning the trust of my constituents matters more than personal convenience. Divestment is a process, not a moment, and I completed it fully.”

Happy Wednesday and welcome to PI. Send K Street tips and gossip. You can reach Caitlin on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 or at coprysko@politico.com . Daniel B. is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com . Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns .

THE BRITISH ARE COMING: Prominent British strategic advisory firm Hanbury Strategy is planting a flag in D.C. Laura Dooley , the former longtime global lobbying chief for StubHub , will lead the new D.C. office.

— Hanbury was founded a decade ago by former David Cameron aide Ameet Gill and Paul Stephenson , a top spokesperson for the Brexit campaign. The firm is led by CEO Emilie Oldknow , a former executive director of the U.K.’s Labour Party and a former leader with the labor group UNISON . The firm, which has 130 staff across the globe, represents clients such as Blackstone , Coinbase , Epic Games , Workday , Microsoft , Nvidia , Spotify , Samsung and more.

— Though this will be the first outpost in the U.S. for Hanbury Strategy, their sister data and research firm Stack Data Strategy has done work here for years, including for the NRSC during the 2022 and 2024 cycles, according to FEC filings. Stack Data Strategy will continue to support Hanbury’s U.S. offerings.

ANNALS OF FUNDRAISING: The network of super PACs funded by the crypto industry “said Wednesday it has grown its war chest to more than $190 million ahead of this fall’s midterm elections, a haul intended to push lawmakers to support industry-friendly legislation that is struggling to advance in the Senate,” POLITICO ’s Jasper Goodman reports.

— The trio of industry-backed super PACs, Fairshake , Protect Progress and Defend American Jobs , pulled in a $25 million contribution from Ripple and $24 million from venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz . “Its $193 million total, set to be reported in federal campaign finance filings that are due at the end of the month, also includes previously reported contributions from the crypto exchange Coinbase that total $50 million since the 2024 election,” per Jasper, marking the latest signal that the PAC network plans to remain a major player in this year’s midterms after funneling tens of millions of dollars into the 2024 election.

ANNALS OF FUNDRAISING II : “Just six months ago, most congressional Republicans kept their distance from Elon Musk after the tech mogul’s messy political breakup with President Donald Trump and his feverish attempt to kill their signature megabill. Musk is persona non grata no longer , thanks to his mega checkbook and mega platform — both of which he is now using to influence the future of the GOP,” POLITICO ’s Meredith Lee Hill, Mia McCarthy and Jordain Carney write.

— “Republicans see his recent donation to a Kentucky Senate candidate as an encouraging sign that Musk will make good on his promises to back the GOP, and top House leaders are elated — especially those in charge of defending their razor-thin majority. Musk spent more than $260 million in the last election helping to elect Trump and Republicans.”

SIKE-EDELIC: “People who think psychedelic drugs are the key to treating intractable mental illness could not have been more psyched when Donald Trump named one of their own to lead the government’s health agencies. A year into his tenure, Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has yet to expand access to the mind-altering drugs and advocates are starting to lose patience ,” POLITICO ’s Amanda Chu reports.

— “The advocates had every reason to expect quick action. Kennedy once put the drugs at the top of his list of unheralded treatments he planned to promote at the Health and Human Services Department, alongside ‘anything else that advances human health and can’t be patented by Pharma.’”

— “Since, Kennedy has occasionally reiterated his ambition, but hasn’t taken concrete steps to achieve it,” prompting worries among advocates that “their goals have been overshadowed by other Kennedy agenda items, related to food and vaccines, and that a chance to get psychedelic drugs to people who need them could be slipping away.”
