MEDIA MOVES: A pair of prominent media outlets have new leaders for their government relations shops in D.C. TelevisaUnivision has tapped Bernadette Carrillo to lead its D.C. office as senior vice president of government relations, filling a role that had been vacant for nearly two years following the departure of Steve Haro in 2024.

— Carrillo was most recently a managing director at the New York consultancy Tusk Strategies , where she helped launch its Washington office and stood up a CHIPS Act practice and Latino outreach practice at the firm. She previously served as director of intergovernmental affairs for former Commerce Secretary Gina Raimondo and in the White House Office of Presidential Personnel under former President Joe Biden .

— Meanwhile, Versant , the new parent company of MS NOW , CNBC , E! , USA Network and more, has hired Jonathan Kott as senior vice president of government affairs, where he will oversee the company’s public policy efforts. Kott was most recently a partner at Capitol Counsel , and before that he wore a number of different hats on the Hill, including simultaneously working for former Sen. Joe Manchin (I-W.Va.) and Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.).

AV STAKEHOLDERS LOBBY UP: A handful of autonomous vehicle stakeholders have added new lobbying muscle since the beginning of the year, according to newly filed disclosures. AV trade group the Autonomous Vehicle Industry Association retained Mehlman Consulting last month to work on issues related to the industry as well as “access to critical technologies,” ahead of a Feb. 4 Senate hearing featuring industry leaders and the trade group’s chief executive.

— Meanwhile BlackSea Technologies , which manufactures unmanned boats, brought on American Defense International to lobby on federal “unmanned surface vehicle programs and industrial base,” according to a disclosure. And autonomous submarine manufacturer Albacore hired Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck earlier this month — the company’s second lobbying hire since retaining Crossroads Strategies last summer.

Kevin Yoder (R-Kan.), who will lobby for the aviation giant on a host of issues, including quality and safety, supply chains, commercial aviation and commercial and aftermarket operations.

title: Crypto optimistic for compromise with banks
body_text:
CRYPTO DENTENTE: Cryptocurrency companies and big banks may finally be approaching a compromise on stablecoin yield payments that could clear the way for a crypto regulation bill currently stalled in the Senate.

— The crypto industry and banks have fought for months on the issue of stablecoin yields, a practice where crypto exchanges pay stablecoin holders interest via rewards programs. Banks strongly oppose the practice, which competes with traditional interest-paying accounts, and have previously called for Congress to close a loophole in the GENIUS Act that makes such payments possible.

— The back and forth has stalled progress on what would be a landmark crypto regulation bill, the Digital Asset Market Clarity Act , currently before the Senate Banking Committee. Brian Armstrong , CEO of crypto exchange Coinbase and one of the industry’s biggest proponents for stablecoin interest payments, publicly denounced a draft version of the bill last month. Now, he’s changing his tune.

— “There’s now a path forward where we can get a win-win-win outcome here,” Armstrong told CNBC yesterday . “Win for the crypto industry, a win for the banks and a win for the American consumer to get President Trump’s crypto agenda through to the finish line so we can make America the crypto capital of the world.”

— “There’s a small list of remaining open items and I think that if a compromise can be found this will get to the president’s desk for a signature in a few months,” he added. In the same interview, Banking Committee member Sen. Bernie Moreno (R-Ohio) predicted passage “hopefully by April.”

— The apparent progress comes a week after a White House meeting between the two sides. During that meeting, banks proposed an outright ban on stablecoin yield payments. That’s a suggestion the crypto industry is unlikely to acquiesce to, and based on Amrstrong’s latest optimism, may no longer be on the table.

title: Tariffs struck down but trade fights continue
body_text:
TA-TA TO TARIFFS: President Donald Trump’s sweeping tariffs are no longer in effect after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled today that the emergency economic powers law cited by the White House last year doesn’t actually permit the president to impose tariffs.

— Trade associations across Washington quickly praised the ruling and cast the decision as an opportunity for the president to work with businesses that have been shaken by volatile trade policies during the first year of the administration.

— “The Supreme Court’s decision … opens the door for the administration to engage industry more closely on trade policy to create the stability and predictability American retailers and consumers need,” Brian Dodge , president and CEO of the Retail Industry Leaders Association , said in a statement.

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce , one of the few major business groups to file legal briefs opposing the tariffs, called the decision “welcome news for business and consumers.”

— “We encourage the administration to use this opportunity to reset overall tariff policy in a manner that will lead to greater economic growth, larger wage gains for workers, and lower costs for families,” Neil Bradley , the chamber’s chief policy officer, said in a statement.

— The administration doesn’t appear to share the associations’ desire for a reset. Hours after the court released its opinion, Trump announced a new 10 percent global tariff, instituted under a different authority than the one evaluated by the justices. This new tariff will remain in effect for 150 days, unless extended by Congress.

— The question of whether the government will be required to refund businesses that already paid the now-illegal tariffs also remains unsettled . That question was not addressed by the justices, likely leaving the matter up to lower courts to decide.

— “Now, the government must act quickly to refund retailers and importers without red tape or delay,” Consumer Technology Association executive chair and CEO Gary Shapiro said in a statement.

— Trump doesn’t appear inclined to grant refunds, complaining to reporters at the White House about the court’s lack of guidance on the matter.

— “I guess it has to get litigated for the next two years,” he said.

TA-TA TO TARIFFS: President Donald Trump’s sweeping tariffs are no longer in effect after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled today that the emergency economic powers law cited by the White House last year doesn’t actually permit the president to impose tariffs.

— Trade associations across Washington quickly praised the ruling and cast the decision as an opportunity for the president to work with businesses that have been shaken by volatile trade policies during the first year of the administration.

— “The Supreme Court’s decision … opens the door for the administration to engage industry more closely on trade policy to create the stability and predictability American retailers and consumers need,” Brian Dodge, president and CEO of the Retail Industry Leaders Association, said in a statement.

The U.S. Chamber of Commerce, one of the few major business groups to file legal briefs opposing the tariffs, called the decision “welcome news for business and consumers.”

— “We encourage the administration to use this opportunity to reset overall tariff policy in a manner that will lead to greater economic growth, larger wage gains for workers, and lower costs for families,” Neil Bradley, the chamber’s chief policy officer, said in a statement.

— The administration doesn’t appear to share the associations’ desire for a reset. Hours after the court released its opinion, Trump announced a new 10 percent global tariff, instituted under a different authority than the one evaluated by the justices. This new tariff will remain in effect for 150 days, unless extended by Congress.

— The question of whether the government will be required to refund businesses that already paid the now-illegal tariffs also remains unsettled. That question was not addressed by the justices, likely leaving the matter up to lower courts to decide.

— “Now, the government must act quickly to refund retailers and importers without red tape or delay,” Consumer Technology Association executive chair and CEO Gary Shapiro said in a statement.

— Trump doesn’t appear inclined to grant refunds, complaining to reporters at the White House about the court’s lack of guidance on the matter.

— “I guess it has to get litigated for the next two years,” he said.

— Berger Action Fund is affiliated with the eponymous foundation run by the Swiss-born Wyss, who has increasingly become the target of scrutiny and conservative complaints about dark and foreign money in liberal politics.

— Several of the groups funded by Berger Action Fund have dropped boatloads of cash to help elect Democrats or support Democratic ballot initiatives. title: K Street’s tariff work is far from over
body_text:
IT NEVER ENDS: President Donald Trump ’s tariffs may be no longer , but that doesn’t mean K Street’s cash cow is going to fade away after last week’s Supreme Court ruling. There’s still immense interest from the business community about where trade policy goes from here, as evidenced by a webinar on the ruling hosted by the trade team at Squire Patton Boggs this morning, which drew more than 400 attendees.

— “We’re fielding calls from clients opposed to tariffs who are acting like it’s V-E day,” said Hunter Morgen , a trade lobbyist at Ballard Partners , adding that he’s advised clients this is “a short blip.”

— Clients across K Street are clamoring for intel on what the refund process will look like . There are also questions about the fate of the country-specific trade deals already struck by the Trump administration and the alternative tariff authorities the Trump administration plans to lean on to try and recreate the duties struck down by the court Friday. ( Mehlman Consulting ’s Bruce Mehlman has a helpful graphic on his Substack illustrating how many different avenues the administration still has in its toolbox.)

— That includes Section 232 tariffs that have already been levied on products like aluminum, steel and auto parts, with pending investigations focused on everything from critical minerals to pharmaceuticals and semiconductors, as well as Section 301 tariffs on goods from China.

— “If you’re a company, this decision is very problematic, because now there is no predictability into how the layering of other authorities can impact supply chain strategy,” said Samir Kapadia , who leads the trade practice at The Vogel Group . Some clients, he said, may have been happier with Trump’s International Emergency Economic Powers Act tariff regime “because it’s clean, it’s understandable. … Now I’ve got to worry about three different authorities and how they all work together. Pain in the butt, that’s what companies are saying.”

— On the other hand, “the fact that [tariffs] can’t just be dropped on some of these guys just out of nowhere and there’s a defined process is a little more comforting for those in the business community,” Morgen said.

— Lobbyists are already gaming out how to approach this process, which arguably has much higher stakes. “Those programs are super durable, and frankly, once they’re put into place, they’re very hard to roll back,” Kapadia said of trade authorities like Section 301 and 232.

— “If you don’t raise objections then the investigation may not take into account your [or] consider your particular situation, so being on the record is important,” Everett Eissenstat , a trade lobbyist at Squire Patton Boggs, cautioned during today’s webinar.

— Morgen said that his firm “has engagement ideas and engagement strategies based on every possible option or opportunity that the administration can put forward,” But, he added, “we have to see the details surrounding the executive actions before we can really turn the key on anything.”

K Street’s tariff work is far from over

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO and DANIEL BARNES 

02/23/2026 07:15 PM EST

Presented by

IT NEVER ENDS: President Donald Trump’s tariffs may be no longer, but that doesn’t mean K Street’s cash cow is going to fade away after last week’s Supreme Court ruling. There’s still immense interest from the business community about where trade policy goes from here, as evidenced by a webinar on the ruling hosted by the trade team at Squire Patton Boggs this morning, which drew more than 400 attendees.

— “We’re fielding calls from clients opposed to tariffs who are acting like it’s V-E day,” said Hunter Morgen, a trade lobbyist at Ballard Partners, adding that he’s advised clients this is “a short blip.”

— Clients across K Street are clamoring for intel on what the refund process will look like. There are also questions about the fate of the country-specific trade deals already struck by the Trump administration and the alternative tariff authorities the Trump administration plans to lean on to try and recreate the duties struck down by the court Friday. (Mehlman Consulting’s Bruce Mehlman has a helpful graphic on his Substack illustrating how many different avenues the administration still has in its toolbox.)

— That includes Section 232 tariffs that have already been levied on products like aluminum, steel and auto parts, with pending investigations focused on everything from critical minerals to pharmaceuticals and semiconductors, as well as Section 301 tariffs on goods from China.

— “If you’re a company, this decision is very problematic, because now there is no predictability into how the layering of other authorities can impact supply chain strategy,” said Samir Kapadia, who leads the trade practice at The Vogel Group. Some clients, he said, may have been happier with Trump’s International Emergency Economic Powers Act tariff regime “because it’s clean, it’s understandable. … Now I’ve got to worry about three different authorities and how they all work together. Pain in the butt, that’s what companies are saying.”

— On the other hand, “the fact that [tariffs] can’t just be dropped on some of these guys just out of nowhere and there’s a defined process is a little more comforting for those in the business community,” Morgen said.

— Lobbyists are already gaming out how to approach this process, which arguably has much higher stakes. “Those programs are super durable, and frankly, once they’re put into place, they’re very hard to roll back,” Kapadia said of trade authorities like Section 301 and 232.

— “If you don’t raise objections then the investigation may not take into account your [or] consider your particular situation, so being on the record is important,” Everett Eissenstat, a trade lobbyist at Squire Patton Boggs, cautioned during today’s webinar.

— Morgen said that his firm “has engagement ideas and engagement strategies based on every possible option or opportunity that the administration can put forward,” But, he added, “we have to see the details surrounding the executive actions before we can really turn the key on anything.”

title: Downtown has some ideas for Trump on affordability
body_text:
WHAT’S IN A NAME: When President Donald Trump takes the stage tonight for the first State of the Union address of his second term , there are a slew of issues the business community will be looking to hear from him on — which has many groups couching their pet policy priorities in language that the president will surely recognize.

— “We’ll be watching to see whether the President connects economic affordability with America’s leadership in financial innovation,” Blockchain Association chief Summer Mersinger told PI in a statement.

— Mersinger touted digital assets as a tool to help with “reducing costs, expanding economic access, and giving Americans more control over their financial lives” and arguing that “the right regulatory framework can protect consumers while ensuring these technologies are developed and scaled here in the United States, not overseas.”

— The U.S. Chamber of Commerce , meanwhile, is hoping that Trump will use his bully pulpit to talk about “how we take on frivolous lawsuits,” Chamber president and CEO Suzanne Clark told CNBC this morning. “We’ve got trial lawyers clogging up the courts and costing American families $4,200 a year,” she said. “States that have tackled it are seeing decreasing insurance costs and housing costs. We’d like to hear the president go after it too.”

— Also on the Chamber’s wishlist is the implementation of a federal regulatory framework for artificial intelligence and passage of a surface transportation reauthorization ahead of its expiration in September.

— And multiple industry groups — including the Business Roundtable , the National Association of Manufacturers , the American Petroleum Institute , the American Chemistry Council and the Chamber — want to hear Trump beat the drum on permitting reforms, which Clark noted would help Trump build on last summer’s tax cuts and his administration’s broader deregulation push.

— “American oil and natural gas production is at record levels, and energy is critical to affordability and economic growth,” API President and CEO Mike Sommers said in a statement, adding that “the challenge before us is not supply but the infrastructure to deliver it.”

— Business groups are also anxiously awaiting Trump’s next moves on tariffs in the wake of last week’s Supreme Court decision. Austen Jensen , senior executive vice president of public affairs at the Retail Industry Leaders Association , said in a statement that “the time is optimal for President Trump and Congress to work together to chart a trade policy that will achieve the administration’s goals to grow the economy, create jobs and protect our national security.”

— Beyond trade policy, retailers want to hear Trump nudge Congress on the contentious swipe fee legislation that the president endorsed last month as part of a midterm-focused affordability push. “By bringing more stability to the trade landscape and ensuring competition in the payments system, Congress and the president can deliver solutions that will help Americans,” Jensen argued.

— Clark echoed RILA’s emphasis on Congress’ role in implementing tariffs, which she suggested would go a long way toward improving much-needed certainty for businesses. BRT’s Joshua Bolten , meanwhile, stressed that an extension of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement along with “duty-free North American trade” would be a huge boon for “domestic manufacturing, supporting American farmers and workers, and keeping costs down for families.”

— On the health care front, drugmakers will be listening to see how Trump proposes building on the pharmacy benefit manager reforms he signed into law this month, “particularly steps to rein in insurer and PBM consolidation, curb excessive coverage denials, and bring more transparency and accountability to the 340B program,” said PhRMA spokesperson Chanse Jones . The trade group is also reiterating the importance of policies that help maintain U.S. leadership in drug development.

The campaign comes ahead of ACU’s annual fly-in next week, during which credit union leaders will raise their opposition to the Credit Card Competition Act with lawmakers in person.

— In the lead up to the fly-in, ACU will run digital ads in more than 70 congressional districts, along with radio ads and newsletter sponsorships that urge viewers to contact their congressional representatives about the bill. The ad campaign will pivot to the Beltway as ACU’s fly-in kicks off next week.

FLY-IN SZN: The Blockchain Association was on the Hill today to tout the crypto group’s newly released tax policy framework. — BA members will head back to the Hill on Thursday for another fly-in focused on the stalled crypto market structure bill, with two dozen meetings planned with staff from the Senate Banking and Agriculture committees.

— More than 400 early childhood educators and advocates from across the country headed to the Hill today for a fly-in organized by the National Association for the Education of Young Children . The group had more than 200 meetings slated with offices on both sides of the aisle and members of key committees in both chambers, during which participants planned to push for increased federal funding for child care and early learning programs.

— Executives and other representatives from members of the Semiconductor Industry Association were also on the Hill today. The industry had 75 meetings on the books with members and staff from personal offices and leaders of key congressional committees to discuss a range of issues, including research and development incentives for chip manufacturing, taxes, export controls, supply chains, trade, workforce development, immigration and energy.

AI TAKEOVER: “More than one in four federal lobbyists are now pushing AI-related agendas , according to a new report from Public Citizen — and they are overwhelmingly working for corporate interests seeking to influence federal AI policy, or block state rules over the industry,” Sludge ’s David Moore reports.

— “According to the report … 3,570 federal lobbyists — comprising 26% of all registered lobbyists in 2025 — reported lobbying on artificial intelligence issues last year. The vast majority of the lobbying disclosures analyzed by the watchdog group specifically mentioned AI, with the remainder mentioning autonomous systems or data centers.”

— “Public Citizen researchers found that between 2022 and 2025, the number of lobbyists working on AI issues has exploded, rising by 168%. The surge comes as the AI industry makes an aggressive push for federal preemption in Congress, aiming to override a rise in bipartisan state-level regulations of the technology in areas like deepfake imagery, algorithmic discrimination, biometric surveillance, consumer deception and more.”

— “While polling suggests the data center debate is far from being a top-tier midterm subject, the issue is bubbling up as a wedge for lesser-known candidates looking to differentiate themselves from the pack,” especially as more high-profile Democrats shift their positions on the issue.

— Still, “it’s unclear how much traction the data center discussion will give underdog candidates. Despite deep concern in certain communities, voters’ views about data centers appear far from settled.”

Downtown has some ideas for Trump on affordability

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO and DANIEL BARNES 

02/24/2026 07:04 PM EST

Presented by

With Daniel Lippman

WHAT’S IN A NAME: When President Donald Trump takes the stage tonight for the first State of the Union address of his second term, there are a slew of issues the business community will be looking to hear from him on — which has many groups couching their pet policy priorities in language that the president will surely recognize.

— “We’ll be watching to see whether the President connects economic affordability with America’s leadership in financial innovation,” Blockchain Association chief Summer Mersinger told PI in a statement.

— Mersinger touted digital assets as a tool to help with “reducing costs, expanding economic access, and giving Americans more control over their financial lives” and arguing that “the right regulatory framework can protect consumers while ensuring these technologies are developed and scaled here in the United States, not overseas.”

— The U.S. Chamber of Commerce, meanwhile, is hoping that Trump will use his bully pulpit to talk about “how we take on frivolous lawsuits,” Chamber president and CEO Suzanne Clark told CNBC this morning. “We’ve got trial lawyers clogging up the courts and costing American families $4,200 a year,” she said. “States that have tackled it are seeing decreasing insurance costs and housing costs. We’d like to hear the president go after it too.”

— Also on the Chamber’s wishlist is the implementation of a federal regulatory framework for artificial intelligence and passage of a surface transportation reauthorization ahead of its expiration in September.

— And multiple industry groups — including the Business Roundtable, the National Association of Manufacturers, the American Petroleum Institute, the American Chemistry Council and the Chamber — want to hear Trump beat the drum on permitting reforms, which Clark noted would help Trump build on last summer’s tax cuts and his administration’s broader deregulation push.

— “American oil and natural gas production is at record levels, and energy is critical to affordability and economic growth,” API President and CEO Mike Sommers said in a statement, adding that “the challenge before us is not supply but the infrastructure to deliver it.”

— Business groups are also anxiously awaiting Trump’s next moves on tariffs in the wake of last week’s Supreme Court decision. Austen Jensen, senior executive vice president of public affairs at the Retail Industry Leaders Association, said in a statement that “the time is optimal for President Trump and Congress to work together to chart a trade policy that will achieve the administration’s goals to grow the economy, create jobs and protect our national security.”

— Beyond trade policy, retailers want to hear Trump nudge Congress on the contentious swipe fee legislation that the president endorsed last month as part of a midterm-focused affordability push. “By bringing more stability to the trade landscape and ensuring competition in the payments system, Congress and the president can deliver solutions that will help Americans,” Jensen argued.

— Clark echoed RILA’s emphasis on Congress’ role in implementing tariffs, which she suggested would go a long way toward improving much-needed certainty for businesses. BRT’s Joshua Bolten, meanwhile, stressed that an extension of the U.S.-Mexico-Canada Agreement along with “duty-free North American trade” would be a huge boon for “domestic manufacturing, supporting American farmers and workers, and keeping costs down for families.”

— On the health care front, drugmakers will be listening to see how Trump proposes building on the pharmacy benefit manager reforms he signed into law this month, “particularly steps to rein in insurer and PBM consolidation, curb excessive coverage denials, and bring more transparency and accountability to the 340B program,” said PhRMA spokesperson Chanse Jones. The trade group is also reiterating the importance of policies that help maintain U.S. leadership in drug development.

FIRST IN PI: Adam Suess is returning to K Street, joining Squire Patton Boggs as a principal following a yearlong stint working for Interior Secretary Doug Burgum. Suess was most recently a senior counselor in Burgum’s office, and before that he served as principal deputy assistant secretary and acting assistant secretary for lands and minerals management in the department.

— Prior to joining the Trump administration, Suess worked as counsel and vice president of government and external affairs for energy and hospitality conglomerate REH Company. He’ll take on a similar dual legal and public policy role at Squire Patton Boggs, Suess told PI.

— While he plans on registering to lobby and expects to work on a wide range of public policy issues, Suess said that on the legal side of the coin, “it’ll be a strong focus on energy to continue to deliver on the administration’s and the President’s agenda of resource production and affordable, reliable and abundant energy supply in an era of spectacular demand.”

Dick Durbin (D-Ill.) and Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) in the wake of Trump’s surprise endorsement. The campaign comes ahead of ACU’s annual fly-in next week, during which credit union leaders will raise their opposition to the Credit Card Competition Act with lawmakers in person.

— In the lead up to the fly-in, ACU will run digital ads in more than 70 congressional districts, along with radio ads and newsletter sponsorships that urge viewers to contact their congressional representatives about the bill. The ad campaign will pivot to the Beltway as ACU’s fly-in kicks off next week.

FLY-IN SZN: The Blockchain Association was on the Hill today to tout the crypto group’s newly released tax policy framework. Members of the association were slated to huddle with staff from around two dozen offices of House Ways and Means members, who are working to craft a crypto tax bill ahead of next year’s filing season.

— BA members will head back to the Hill on Thursday for another fly-in focused on the stalled crypto market structure bill, with two dozen meetings planned with staff from the Senate Banking and Agriculture committees.

— More than 400 early childhood educators and advocates from across the country headed to the Hill today for a fly-in organized by the National Association for the Education of Young Children. The group had more than 200 meetings slated with offices on both sides of the aisle and members of key committees in both chambers, during which participants planned to push for increased federal funding for child care and early learning programs.

— Executives and other representatives from members of the Semiconductor Industry Association were also on the Hill today. The industry had 75 meetings on the books with members and staff from personal offices and leaders of key congressional committees to discuss a range of issues, including research and development incentives for chip manufacturing, taxes, export controls, supply chains, trade, workforce development, immigration and energy.

AI TAKEOVER: “More than one in four federal lobbyists are now pushing AI-related agendas, according to a new report from Public Citizen — and they are overwhelmingly working for corporate interests seeking to influence federal AI policy, or block state rules over the industry,” Sludge’s David Moore reports.

— “According to the report … 3,570 federal lobbyists — comprising 26% of all registered lobbyists in 2025 — reported lobbying on artificial intelligence issues last year. The vast majority of the lobbying disclosures analyzed by the watchdog group specifically mentioned AI, with the remainder mentioning autonomous systems or data centers.”

— “Public Citizen researchers found that between 2022 and 2025, the number of lobbyists working on AI issues has exploded, rising by 168%. The surge comes as the AI industry makes an aggressive push for federal preemption in Congress, aiming to override a rise in bipartisan state-level regulations of the technology in areas like deepfake imagery, algorithmic discrimination, biometric surveillance, consumer deception and more.”

— Still, “it’s unclear how much traction the data center discussion will give underdog candidates. Despite deep concern in certain communities, voters’ views about data centers appear far from settled.”

title: Another White House aide heads downtown
body_text:
ANOTHER ONE: Taylor LaJoie has left the White House, where he most recently served in the legislative affairs office, to join Alpine Group as a vice president. LaJoie has been serving as a special assistant to President Donald Trump as well as one of the West Wing’s liaisons to the Senate, where he previously worked for Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) and now-Vice President JD Vance .

— LaJoie is also an alum of the Tax Foundation , and worked on the 2017 GOP tax cuts under Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah). More recently, he was a key intermediary for the Trump administration on last year’s reconciliation bill, placing him among a growing crowd of new K Streeters who worked on the GOP megabill.

— He’s also the latest White House aide to cash in on their time in the administration with a new gig downtown, a group that includes fellow leg affairs alum Natalie McIntyre , now at Miller Strategies , former spokesperson Harrison Fields , now at CGCN Group ; former economic adviser Robin Colwell , now at Intel ; Brette Powell and Brian Hughes , now at Mercury Public Affairs ; former national security advisers Micah Ketchel and Thomas Boodry , now at Ballard Partners ; and May Davis Mailman and Trent Morse , who started their own firms.

REVIEWS ARE IN: Hats off to all of you who stayed up for all of last night’s record-breaking stem-winder , which shed a little more light on what Trump plans to do next on tariffs, but has left lobbyists scrambling for more details about the pledge tech companies are set to sign at the White House next week aimed at forcing Silicon Valley to shoulder more of the financial burden of AI data centers.

— While the speech was “heavy on patriotism, party divide, pageantry, and performance,” it was not “a call to action for a refreshed policy agenda,” the team at Invariant noted in its breakdown of everything the president did (and didn’t) touch on during his address. (POLITICO is a client of Invariant.)

— “On the issues, even the ‘controversial’ items for K street were cursory and shallow,” said John Stanford , a partner and CEO of the consulting firm Novel Strategies .

— One other thing Trump’s speech was shockingly light on? Corporate callouts. “This is the SOTU that corporate PR pros dreamt of: no name checking of the Fortune 100,” Stanford noted. “That’s a big departure from the past and a key objective of their teams in Washington,” he added. Generally speaking though, “that’s as much calm [as] K Street can hope for,” he said.

Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) and John Shimkus (R-Ill.).

SARANDOS TO THE WHITE HOUSE: Netflix CEO Ted Sarandos is set to head to the White House tomorrow as his deal to merge with Warner Bros. Discovery faces new headwinds in Washington, POLITICO ’s Yasmin Khorram reports.

— Though it’s not clear whether Sarandos will have any facetime with the president himself, the visit follows Sarandos’ rejection of Trump’s demand that Netflix fire Democrat Susan Rice from its board earlier this week. It also comes amid an intensifying bidding war for WBD between Netflix and Paramount Skydance .

— “Warner Bros. has said a revised bid from Paramount — now increased to $31 a share from $30 — could outbid Netflix’s current offer, raising the prospect that political pressure and a bidding war are colliding in real time,” Yasmin notes. “Just hours after his studio raised its bid, Paramount CEO David Ellison appeared at the State of the Union as a guest of Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), a close Trump ally.”

— Netflix’s deal to acquire Warner Bros. is already under scrutiny from regulators, and the streaming giant has quickly amassed a small army of veteran antitrust lobbyists to help fend off competition concerns stemming from the deal.

— Adding to that pressure, nearly a dozen Republican state attorneys general came out against the merger, calling on the Justice Department today to conduct “a thorough and exacting review” of the deal’s potential effects on competition in streaming services and entertainment.

FOOD INDUSTRY VS. MAHA: One of Washington’s most powerful lobbies is escalating its fight against HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. ’s Make America Healthy Again movement’s targeting of ultraprocessed foods, per Amanda.

— The National Association of Manufacturers warns in a new video and report that the food industry is “under increasing strain” and federal and state proposals to restrict ingredients are undermining Trump’s efforts to boost manufacturing and lower prices.

— “Anytime that you’re increasing the regulatory burden … you end up driving up the cost of the product,” Jay Timmons , chief executive of NAM, told Amanda. “We want to unleash the potential of the sector here in the United States,” he added. “Any small change in costs or potential costs can be extraordinarily disruptive. It can result in a lack of food supply. It can result in a lack of additional investment.”

— The video features statements from major food lobbies, including FMI, The Food Industry Association , the Consumer Brands Association , the American Beverage Association and the American Frozen Food Institute .

— More than a hundred state bills were introduced last year to crack down on food ingredients, a five-fold increase from the previous year, according to a POLITICO analysis in August. NAM’s campaign is the latest salvo from the food industry against the state bills. It underscores how companies leverage GOP vulnerabilities on the economy to push their agenda ahead of the November midterm elections, which will shape Trump’s influence for the remainder of his term.

— Last fall, more than three dozen food companies and trade associations, including NAM, launched a coalition, Americans for Ingredient Transparency , which warns that the patchwork of state laws would increase grocery bills and calls for a national standard. Eight members of AFIT appeared in NAM’s video.

GATES’ EPSTEIN MEA CULPA: “ Bill Gates apologized to staff of the Gates Foundation over his ties to Jeffrey Epstein , admitting he made mistakes that had cast a cloud over the philanthropic group while insisting he didn’t participate in Epstein’s crimes,” per The Wall Street Journal ’s Emily Glazer .

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO and DANIEL BARNES

With help from Daniel Lippman and Amanda Chu

ANOTHER ONE: Taylor LaJoie has left the White House, where he most recently served in the legislative affairs office, to join Alpine Group as a vice president. LaJoie has been serving as a special assistant to President Donald Trump as well as one of the West Wing’s liaisons to the Senate, where he previously worked for Sen. Roger Marshall (R-Kan.) and now-Vice President JD Vance.

— LaJoie is also an alum of the Tax Foundation, and worked on the 2017 GOP tax cuts under Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah). More recently, he was a key intermediary for the Trump administration on last year’s reconciliation bill, placing him among a growing crowd of new K Streeters who worked on the GOP megabill.

— He’s also the latest White House aide to cash in on their time in the administration with a new gig downtown, a group that includes fellow leg affairs alum Natalie McIntyre, now at Miller Strategies, former spokesperson Harrison Fields, now at CGCN Group; former economic adviser Robin Colwell, now at Intel; Brette Powell and Brian Hughes, now at Mercury Public Affairs; former national security advisers Micah Ketchel and Thomas Boodry, now at Ballard Partners; and May Davis Mailman and Trent Morse, who started their own firms.

REVIEWS ARE IN: Hats off to all of you who stayed up for all of last night’s record-breaking stem-winder, which shed a little more light on what Trump plans to do next on tariffs, but has left lobbyists scrambling for more details about the pledge tech companies are set to sign at the White House next week aimed at forcing Silicon Valley to shoulder more of the financial burden of AI data centers.

— While the speech was “heavy on patriotism, party divide, pageantry, and performance,” it was not “a call to action for a refreshed policy agenda,” the team at Invariant noted in its breakdown of everything the president did (and didn’t) touch on during his address. (POLITICO is a client of Invariant.)

— “On the issues, even the ‘controversial’ items for K street were cursory and shallow,” said John Stanford, a partner and CEO of the consulting firm Novel Strategies.

— One other thing Trump’s speech was shockingly light on? Corporate callouts. “This is the SOTU that corporate PR pros dreamt of: no name checking of the Fortune 100,” Stanford noted. “That’s a big departure from the past and a key objective of their teams in Washington,” he added. Generally speaking though, “that’s as much calm [as] K Street can hope for,” he said.

SARANDOS TO THE WHITE HOUSE: Netflix CEO Ted Sarandos is set to head to the White House tomorrow as his deal to merge with Warner Bros. Discovery faces new headwinds in Washington, POLITICO’s Yasmin Khorram reports.

— Though it’s not clear whether Sarandos will have any facetime with the president himself, the visit follows Sarandos’ rejection of Trump’s demand that Netflix fire Democrat Susan Rice from its board earlier this week. It also comes amid an intensifying bidding war for WBD between Netflix and Paramount Skydance.

— “Warner Bros. has said a revised bid from Paramount — now increased to $31 a share from $30 — could outbid Netflix’s current offer, raising the prospect that political pressure and a bidding war are colliding in real time,” Yasmin notes. “Just hours after his studio raised its bid, Paramount CEO David Ellison appeared at the State of the Union as a guest of Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), a close Trump ally.”

— Netflix’s deal to acquire Warner Bros. is already under scrutiny from regulators, and the streaming giant has quickly amassed a small army of veteran antitrust lobbyists to help fend off competition concerns stemming from the deal.

— Adding to that pressure, nearly a dozen Republican state attorneys general came out against the merger, calling on the Justice Department today to conduct “a thorough and exacting review” of the deal’s potential effects on competition in streaming services and entertainment.

FOOD INDUSTRY VS. MAHA: One of Washington’s most powerful lobbies is escalating its fight against HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Make America Healthy Again movement’s targeting of ultraprocessed foods, per Amanda.

— The National Association of Manufacturers warns in a new video and report that the food industry is “under increasing strain” and federal and state proposals to restrict ingredients are undermining Trump’s efforts to boost manufacturing and lower prices.

— “Anytime that you’re increasing the regulatory burden … you end up driving up the cost of the product,” Jay Timmons, chief executive of NAM, told Amanda. “We want to unleash the potential of the sector here in the United States,” he added. “Any small change in costs or potential costs can be extraordinarily disruptive. It can result in a lack of food supply. It can result in a lack of additional investment.”

— The video features statements from major food lobbies, including FMI, The Food Industry Association, the Consumer Brands Association, the American Beverage Association and the American Frozen Food Institute.

— More than a hundred state bills were introduced last year to crack down on food ingredients, a five-fold increase from the previous year, according to a POLITICO analysis in August. NAM’s campaign is the latest salvo from the food industry against the state bills. It underscores how companies leverage GOP vulnerabilities on the economy to push their agenda ahead of the November midterm elections, which will shape Trump’s influence for the remainder of his term.

— Last fall, more than three dozen food companies and trade associations, including NAM, launched a coalition, Americans for Ingredient Transparency, which warns that the patchwork of state laws would increase grocery bills and calls for a national standard. ‘That’s bad for him to say’: Trump puts Paxton on notice in Texas Senate primary

By DANIEL LIPPMAN , DANIEL BARNES and CAITLIN OPRYSKO

02/26/2026 08:09 PM EST

Presented by

FIRST IN PI — Republicans are poised to make the Democratic mayor of Scranton, Pennsylvania’s support for a local bank a top issue in one of the nation’s most competitive House races, Daniel L. reports.

— While Mayor Paige Cognetti has hit her opponent Rep. Rob Bresnahan over his stock trading while in office, she is now facing scrutiny for helping secure a multimillion-dollar state grant for a new Fidelity Bank headquarters at the same time her uncle-in-law sat on the board of the company.

— She also received $14,600 in campaign contributions from Fidelity board members months before getting the city to purchase Fidelity’s old Scranton branch building last year.

— “By the end of the campaign, each and every voter in Northeast Pennsylvania will be acutely aware that Paige is an unelectable, corrupt, poll-constructed fraud,” Reilly Richardson , a spokesperson for the National Republican Congressional Committee, said in a statement to PI when asked about the reporting.

— Cognetti, whom the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee on Monday put on its “Red to Blue” list , is running against Bresnahan, one of Democrats’ primary targets this cycle.

— “Mayor Paige Cognetti’s record of delivering for Scranton is unimpeachable,” a Cognetti spokesperson said in a statement when asked about her dealings with Fidelity.

— Cognetti has served as mayor since 2020 and in her 2019 campaign, she ran on fighting political corruption within the local Democratic apparatus, using the campaign slogan “Paige Against the Machine.” One of her top issues she’s using against Bresnahan is his many Wall Street transactions of last year, including the sale of Pennsylvania health care-related bonds and stock in Medicaid providers around the time he voted on Medicaid cuts. Bresnahan’s team has said his financial adviser did all the trading without his prior knowledge, but he has since suspended the activity.

— In 2022, Fidelity Bank, which has been in the region for more than a century, announced it had bought the historic Electric Building in downtown Scranton but left it vacant because it needed extensive renovations. In 2024, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro gave Fidelity a $5 million grant to help renovate the building, which is expected to eventually house 165 Fidelity employees. In 2022, after they purchased the building and were counting on state government support for a renovation, Fidelity thanked Cognetti for her support for the project , calling it “vital to making the Bank’s vision a reality.”

— The next year, on April 29, 2025, all nine members of Fidelity’s board of directors at the time, including her uncle-in-law and Fidelity board secretary John Cognetti , gave $1,500 each to Cognetti’s mayoral campaign, according to Pennsylvania campaign finance records.

— John Cognetti didn’t respond to a request for comment. Bresnahan spokesperson Peter Brath did not respond when asked if Bresnahan supported the new Fidelity Bank headquarters renovation project.

— Seven months later after the donations, council members learned that Cognetti had added an item to the budget requesting the city purchase Fidelity’s old headquarters to convert it into an extension of City Hall, despite a recent costly renovation. Cognetti’s advocacy for the project came after the CEO of Fidelity said the city was interested in buying the building. The extension will be used for public safety purposes including a Police Department real-time crime center facility; Scranton’s police chief called the project “a gold mine for us” because of its potential to improve public safety.

— Two members of the City Council expressed major opposition to the purchase, with Mark McAndrew saying : “If I was to vote yes, then I would vote yes to a conflict and a behavior that I am uncomfortable with.” Council member Thomas Schuster raised questions about the fiscal responsibility of the purchase, asking about the loss of tax revenue from the building, a possible pricey renovation and uncertain operating costs. Incoming City Council member Sean McAndrew also voiced concerns about the purchase. The city ended up purchasing the building for slightly lower than the assessed value . The proposal to buy the building ultimately passed the City Council by only a 3-2 margin.

— The Cognetti spokesperson defended her actions in the matter by touting her mayoral tenure. “She has breathed new life into the city by creating good-paying union jobs, upgrading Scranton’s credit rating to A- level status, and investing millions of dollars in policing,” the spokesperson said. “Every decision Paige has made as mayor has been with the goal of benefiting the people – never herself.” The spokesperson pointed out that there are 186 Cognettis in the region and many of them have donated to her.

— DCCC spokesperson Eli Cousin also hit back against Republicans raising concerns about Cognetti’s Fidelity dealings by saying in a statement “they are resorting to desperate, laughable lies.”

— Bresnahan, who owns between $15,001 and $50,000 in Fidelity stock, has also praised the bank’s presence in Scranton, saying in 2022 , “I love having Fidelity there.” (In April 2024, Bresnahan also received a $3,300 donation from James Clemente , who joined the Fidelity Bank board last month. Clemente didn’t respond to a request for comment.) In recent months, Bresnahan has tried to make crime an issue in the race although Brath, his spokesperson, did not respond to a question when asked whether he supports the new police facility. But Brath said Bresnahan “is a steadfast supporter of our brave police” and had recently secured a half million grant for officer safety in Scranton.

— Fidelity spokesperson Tara Smith said in a statement that the restoration of the Scranton Electric Building was supported by numerous leaders at the government level and that it was grateful for the support of Cognetti and other elected officials for the project.

— “As for individual campaign contributions, Fidelity Bank does not direct or coordinate political giving,” Smith said. “Board members, like any private citizens, may support candidates of their choosing in their personal capacity. … Our focus remains on strengthening the communities we serve and continuing to invest in the economic vitality of Scranton and the region.”

REFUND FIGHT : The Trump administration is working overtime to come up with a strategy that would allow the government to keep billions of dollars in tariff revenue collected before the Supreme Court struck down the president’s IEEPA tariffs last week, our colleagues Megan Messerly and Daniel Desrochers report . But officials are likely to run into a wall of opposition from Big Business, which is eager for refunds following the court’s ruling.

— Business groups across Washington publicly called for the administration to begin issuing refunds last week and at least one major company, FedEx , has filed a lawsuit demanding its money back. Administration officials have so far taken a hostile approach to the idea of paying out refunds, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling the idea the “ultimate corporate welfare.”

— Companies are bracing for a drawn-out fight, Megan and Daniel report. Trade lawyers have advised clients to quickly file lawsuits to claim their tariff refunds, anticipating a complicated process.

— “Nobody is expecting a quick answer to the refunds,” Tami Overby , a partner at DGA Government Relations, told Megan and Daniel. “Trump said he expected lawsuits for years and, to me, that means the government’s not going to make it easy.”

HOWARD’S HEADACHE: The recent success of Cantor Fitzgerald , has caused some tension between the Commerce secretary and the president, Daniel L. and our colleague Sophia Cai report in a wide-ranging look at Howard Lutnick’s standing within the administration.

— The financial firm, which has been run by Lutnick’s sons Brandon and Kyle since he joined the administration, had a banner year in 2025, posting an all-time high revenue of approximately $2.5 billion.

— Trump has been upset that Lutnick’s family is profiting so aggressively off his popularity and he confronted Lutnick directly about it during an episode at Mar-a-Lago over the winter holiday, two people familiar with the exchange told Daniel L. and Sophia.

— “There definitely is this thing where a lot of people in business … just want to do deals with whoever is closer to the administration,” one of the officials said.

CAUTIONARY TALE : Our London Influence counterpart, John Johnston , is out today with a behind the scenes look at how former British Ambassador Peter Mandelson ’s connection to Jeffrey Epstein brought down the U.K. lobbying firm Mandelson founded 16 years ago.

— The firm, Global Counsel , announced last week that it was closing its doors following the release of new documents appearing to show Mandelson previously sent Epstein an internal British government email regarding the 2009 economy. Mandelson, who hasn’t been involved with running the firm since 2024, has since been arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office.

— “Staff initially hoped the Mandelson backlash would be limited to a series of gruesome headlines. But those hopes were dashed when a host of household names — including Tesco, Bank of America and Barclays — called time on their relationship with the firm,” John reports.

— While Mandelson’s friendship with Epstein has brought down the firm, that stain doesn’t appear to extend to the firm’s rank-and-file, with several staffers already securing new jobs. “One staff member at rival firm FGS Global said … the lobbying agency is planning a hiring spree, with as many as two dozen ex-Global Counsel staff being lined up for new gigs. Those are expected to include a raft of senior staffers who’d been working on financial services and private equity briefs,” John reports.

HERE COMES THE SUN: Katie Miller , wife of Stephen Miller and MAGA operative turned podcast host, has posted several times this month in support of solar energy, causing some to wonder if she has been paid to promote the decidedly non-MAGA solar industry, Catherine Boudreau reports for Latitude Media .

— “Solar energy is the energy of the future. Giant fusion reactor up there in the sky — we must rapidly expand solar to compete with China,” Miller posted earlier this month.

— Paying conservative influencers for supportive posts isn’t a new practice for the solar industry. The former president and CEO of the Solar Energy Industries Association , Abigail Ross Hopper , last week acknowledged paying for pro-solar content during negotiations over the One Big Beautiful Bill.

— Another possible explanation is Miller’s link to Elon Musk , whose companies like Tesla and SpaceX are investing in solar energy. Miller served as the spokesperson for Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency at the start of the second Trump administration and left government with him for a position at Musk’s artificial intelligence company.

Pennsylvania Dem candidate’s bank ties come under scrutiny in top House race

By DANIEL LIPPMAN, DANIEL BARNES and CAITLIN OPRYSKO 

02/26/2026 08:09 PM EST

Presented by

FIRST IN PI — Republicans are poised to make the Democratic mayor of Scranton, Pennsylvania’s support for a local bank a top issue in one of the nation’s most competitive House races, Daniel L. reports.

— While Mayor Paige Cognetti has hit her opponent Rep. Rob Bresnahan over his stock trading while in office, she is now facing scrutiny for helping secure a multimillion-dollar state grant for a new Fidelity Bank headquarters at the same time her uncle-in-law sat on the board of the company.

— She also received $14,600 in campaign contributions from Fidelity board members months before getting the city to purchase Fidelity’s old Scranton branch building last year.

— “By the end of the campaign, each and every voter in Northeast Pennsylvania will be acutely aware that Paige is an unelectable, corrupt, poll-constructed fraud,” Reilly Richardson, a spokesperson for the National Republican Congressional Committee, said in a statement to PI when asked about the reporting.

— Cognetti, whom the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee on Monday put on its “Red to Blue” list, is running against Bresnahan, one of Democrats’ primary targets this cycle.

— “Mayor Paige Cognetti’s record of delivering for Scranton is unimpeachable,” a Cognetti spokesperson said in a statement when asked about her dealings with Fidelity.

— Cognetti has served as mayor since 2020 and in her 2019 campaign, she ran on fighting political corruption within the local Democratic apparatus, using the campaign slogan “Paige Against the Machine.” One of her top issues she’s using against Bresnahan is his many Wall Street transactions of last year, including the sale of Pennsylvania health care-related bonds and stock in Medicaid providers around the time he voted on Medicaid cuts. Bresnahan’s team has said his financial adviser did all the trading without his prior knowledge, but he has since suspended the activity.

— In 2022, Fidelity Bank, which has been in the region for more than a century, announced it had bought the historic Electric Building in downtown Scranton but left it vacant because it needed extensive renovations. In 2024, Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro gave Fidelity a $5 million grant to help renovate the building, which is expected to eventually house 165 Fidelity employees. In 2022, after they purchased the building and were counting on state government support for a renovation, Fidelity thanked Cognetti for her support for the project, calling it “vital to making the Bank’s vision a reality.”

— The next year, on April 29, 2025, all nine members of Fidelity’s board of directors at the time, including her uncle-in-law and Fidelity board secretary John Cognetti, gave $1,500 each to Cognetti’s mayoral campaign, according to Pennsylvania campaign finance records.

— John Cognetti didn’t respond to a request for comment. Bresnahan spokesperson Peter Brath did not respond when asked if Bresnahan supported the new Fidelity Bank headquarters renovation project.

— Seven months later after the donations, council members learned that Cognetti had added an item to the budget requesting the city purchase Fidelity’s old headquarters to convert it into an extension of City Hall, despite a recent costly renovation. Cognetti’s advocacy for the project came after the CEO of Fidelity said the city was interested in buying the building. The extension will be used for public safety purposes including a Police Department real-time crime center facility; Scranton’s police chief called the project “a gold mine for us” because of its potential to improve public safety.

— Two members of the City Council expressed major opposition to the purchase, with Mark McAndrew saying: “If I was to vote yes, then I would vote yes to a conflict and a behavior that I am uncomfortable with.” Council member Thomas Schuster raised questions about the fiscal responsibility of the purchase, asking about the loss of tax revenue from the building, a possible pricey renovation and uncertain operating costs. Incoming City Council member Sean McAndrew also voiced concerns about the purchase. The city ended up purchasing the building for slightly lower than the assessed value. The proposal to buy the building ultimately passed the City Council by only a 3-2 margin.

— The Cognetti spokesperson defended her actions in the matter by touting her mayoral tenure. “She has breathed new life into the city by creating good-paying union jobs, upgrading Scranton’s credit rating to A- level status, and investing millions of dollars in policing,” the spokesperson said. “Every decision Paige has made as mayor has been with the goal of benefiting the people – never herself.” The spokesperson pointed out that there are 186 Cognettis in the region and many of them have donated to her.

— DCCC spokesperson Eli Cousin also hit back against Republicans raising concerns about Cognetti’s Fidelity dealings by saying in a statement “they are resorting to desperate, laughable lies.”

— Bresnahan, who owns between $15,001 and $50,000 in Fidelity stock, has also praised the bank’s presence in Scranton, saying in 2022, “I love having Fidelity there.” (In April 2024, Bresnahan also received a $3,300 donation from James Clemente, who joined the Fidelity Bank board last month. Clemente didn’t respond to a request for comment.) In recent months, Bresnahan has tried to make crime an issue in the race although Brath, his spokesperson, did not respond to a question when asked whether he supports the new police facility. But Brath said Bresnahan “is a steadfast supporter of our brave police” and had recently secured a half million grant for officer safety in Scranton.

— Fidelity spokesperson Tara Smith said in a statement that the restoration of the Scranton Electric Building was supported by numerous leaders at the government level and that it was grateful for the support of Cognetti and other elected officials for the project.

— “As for individual campaign contributions, Fidelity Bank does not direct or coordinate political giving,” Smith said. “Board members, like any private citizens, may support candidates of their choosing in their personal capacity. … Our focus remains on strengthening the communities we serve and continuing to invest in the economic vitality of Scranton and the region.”

REFUND FIGHT: The Trump administration is working overtime to come up with a strategy that would allow the government to keep billions of dollars in tariff revenue collected before the Supreme Court struck down the president’s IEEPA tariffs last week, our colleagues Megan Messerly and Daniel Desrochers report. But officials are likely to run into a wall of opposition from Big Business, which is eager for refunds following the court’s ruling.

— Business groups across Washington publicly called for the administration to begin issuing refunds last week and at least one major company, FedEx, has filed a lawsuit demanding its money back. Administration officials have so far taken a hostile approach to the idea of paying out refunds, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent calling the idea the “ultimate corporate welfare.”

— Companies are bracing for a drawn-out fight, Megan and Daniel report. Trade lawyers have advised clients to quickly file lawsuits to claim their tariff refunds, anticipating a complicated process.

— “Nobody is expecting a quick answer to the refunds,” Tami Overby, a partner at DGA Government Relations, told Megan and Daniel. “Trump said he expected lawsuits for years and, to me, that means the government’s not going to make it easy.”

HOWARD’S HEADACHE: The recent success of Cantor Fitzgerald, has caused some tension between the Commerce secretary and the president, Daniel L. and our colleague Sophia Cai report in a wide-ranging look at Howard Lutnick’s standing within the administration.

— The financial firm, which has been run by Lutnick’s sons Brandon and Kyle since he joined the administration, had a banner year in 2025, posting an all-time high revenue of approximately $2.5 billion.

— Trump has been upset that Lutnick’s family is profiting so aggressively off his popularity and he confronted Lutnick directly about it during an episode at Mar-a-Lago over the winter holiday, two people familiar with the exchange told Daniel L. and Sophia.

— “There definitely is this thing where a lot of people in business … just want to do deals with whoever is closer to the administration,” one of the officials said.

CAUTIONARY TALE: Our London Influence counterpart, John Johnston, is out today with a behind the scenes look at how former British Ambassador Peter Mandelson’s connection to Jeffrey Epstein brought down the U.K. lobbying firm Mandelson founded 16 years ago.

— The firm, Global Counsel, announced last week that it was closing its doors following the release of new documents appearing to show Mandelson previously sent Epstein an internal British government email regarding the 2009 economy. Mandelson, who hasn’t been involved with running the firm since 2024, has since been arrested on suspicion of misconduct in public office.

— “Staff initially hoped the Mandelson backlash would be limited to a series of gruesome headlines. But those hopes were dashed when a host of household names — including Tesco, Bank of America and Barclays — called time on their relationship with the firm,” John reports.

— While Mandelson’s friendship with Epstein has brought down the firm, that stain doesn’t appear to extend to the firm’s rank-and-file, with several staffers already securing new jobs. “One staff member at rival firm FGS Global said … the lobbying agency is planning a hiring spree, with as many as two dozen ex-Global Counsel staff being lined up for new gigs. Those are expected to include a raft of senior staffers who’d been working on financial services and private equity briefs,” John reports.

HERE COMES THE SUN: Katie Miller, wife of Stephen Miller and MAGA operative turned podcast host, has posted several times this month in support of solar energy, causing some to wonder if she has been paid to promote the decidedly non-MAGA solar industry, Catherine Boudreau reports for Latitude Media.

— “Solar energy is the energy of the future. Giant fusion reactor up there in the sky — we must rapidly expand solar to compete with China,” Miller posted earlier this month.

— Paying conservative influencers for supportive posts isn’t a new practice for the solar industry. The former president and CEO of the Solar Energy Industries Association, Abigail Ross Hopper, last week acknowledged paying for pro-solar content during negotiations over the One Big Beautiful Bill.

— Another possible explanation is Miller’s link to Elon Musk, whose companies like Tesla and SpaceX are investing in solar energy. Miller served as the spokesperson for Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency at the start of the second Trump administration and left government with him for a position at Musk’s artificial intelligence company.

title: Here’s where K Street sent its money in the Texas Dem Senate primary
body_text:
DEEP IN THE HEART: Today’s primary elections in Texas feature a number of heated races, but the marquee contests revolve around the fight for the Senate. While both of the Texas Senate primaries have attracted a gusher of outside spending bankrolled by industry titans, they’ve also, naturally, drawn interest from Washington’s influence industry.

— On the Democratic side of the ticket, where state Rep. James Talarico is facing off against U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett , Talarico pulled in the larger checks of the two from K Street, according to a PI analysis of FEC filings. That includes a max donation of $7,000 from Cornerstone Government Affairs managing principal Michael Smith . Democratic strategist Guy Cecil , the former head of the marquee super PAC Priorities USA , kicked in around $7,000 as well.

— Anthony Harrington of Albright Stonebridge Group and Mary Stanton of Invariant both donated $3,500 to Talarico, while Airbnb global policy chief Laura Spanjian and Cornerstone principal Todd Webster cut him checks for $2,500, and the Daschle Group ’s Tom Daschle kicked in $2,000. (POLITICO is a client of Invariant.)

— Talarico’s K Street haul also included $1,000 from Allyson Baker of Paul Hastings , David Pore of Hance Scarborough , Estefania Rodriguez of theGROUP , Chris Coffey of Tusk Strategies , Richard Carbo of Cornerstone and David Perry of Jake Perry + Partners .

— Crockett, meanwhile, brought in $2,500 from Jennifer Stewart of Stewart Strategies & Solutions and ShaShrina Thomas of Reynolds American , along with $2,750 from Ervin Policy Group managing director Frank Ervin . Crockett also took in four-figure checks from Invariant ’s Nicole Venable and Justin Gray of Gray Global Advisors .

— Even more K Streeters made smaller contributions in the race. Talarico got $500 from Edward Ayoob of Barnes & Thornburg , Ted Dean of DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group , Tim Wolfmeyer of Cornerstone, John Gonzalez of Tiber Creek Group and Oscar Ramirez of Fulcrum Public Affairs .

— Crockett received $500 from nearly a dozen lobbyists, including Christopher Davis of Capitol Hill Consulting , John Mason of Altria , Keenan Austin Reed of the Alpine Group , Alane Dent of TruStage , Colette Honorable of Exelon , Megan Moore of FGS Global , Ebony Simpson of Stewart Strategies, Alexander Washington of Entergy and Kimberly Afoakwah of Home Depot .

WALKING BACK THE WALKBACK: The Justice Department told a federal appeals court Tuesday that the administration intends to continue defending President Donald Trump ’s executive orders targeting law firms — a surprising reversal less than 24 hours after the department informed the same court it no longer wished to defend the orders, Daniel B. and Josh Gerstein write.

— DOJ lawyers did not provide an explanation for their change in posture, which came via a short Tuesday filing . DOJ declined to comment on the reversal.

— Judges in four cases last year struck down as unconstitutional Trump’s executive orders seeking to punish law firms affiliated with his political opponents. The Justice Department appealed those losses in June and was set to deliver its opening brief to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit on Friday. But in a Monday evening filing, the department declared it no longer wished to pursue the appeal and moved to voluntarily dismiss it.

— “Under no circumstances should the government’s unexplained about-face provide a basis for an extension of its brief,” lawyers representing the targeted firms — Perkins Coie , Jenner & Block , WilmerHale and Susman Godfrey — stated in their filing.

THE AI GOLD RUSH: “Disrupting jobs, fueling a data center boom, even killing off this em dash—artificial intelligence is the conversation policymakers, and the rest of us, just can’t escape. That’s especially the case in Washington, where spending on federal AI influence hit an all-time high last year,” Bloomberg ’s Kate Ackley , John Woolley and Ava Mandoli report.

— “Lobbying firms reported a record $37.2 million in earnings from AI-related influence peddling in the fourth quarter alone, a 38% jump from a year earlier, according to a Bloomberg Government analysis.”

— “For the full year, Washington lobbyists received almost $130 million for work related to AI, as Microsoft Corp. , Meta Platforms Inc. and Alphabet Inc. ’s Google led the spending blitz. Some of the biggest jumps came from frontier labs OpenAI Inc. and Anthropic PBC , two of the highest valued startups in history vying to shape the AI industry’s future and most recently engulfed in a dispute over its use within the US military.”

BROWNSTEIN ADDS A DEFENSE APPROPS LOBBYIST: John Lucio is joining Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck as of counsel, expanding the firm’s defense and national security practices with quite perfect timing. Lucio was most recently an in-house lobbyist with defense contractor BWX Technologies , and before that he was a senior vice president at Ervin Graves Strategy Group .

— Lucio also spent more than half a decade on the Hill, where he was a professional staff member on the Senate Appropriations subcommittee that oversees defense spending. That process will take on even more importance given everything happening in the Middle East.

— “There’s enough emerging efforts going on right now that how you figure out what the new priorities might or might not be over the next several months” will be lobbyists’ latest challenge, Lucio told PI.

THE ROOM WHERE IT HAPPENED: Democratic Sens. Elizabeth Warren (Mass.) and Richard Blumenthal (Conn.) and California Democratic Rep. Sam Liccardo want Attorney General Pam Bondi and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles to spill the details of their meeting with Netflix boss Ted Sarandos last week.

— The meetings were intended to help assuage antitrust concerns holding up Netflix’s bid to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery . But instead, the streaming giant walked away from the deal, leaving Paramount Skydance one step closer to victory in its hostile takeover bid.

— “Your conversations with Mr. Sarandos taint the Warner Bros. bidding process by raising suspicions that the Trump administration’s DOJ is making merger review decisions based on politicized favoritism rather than the law or the facts,” the lawmakers wrote in a letter to Bondi and Wiles on Monday.

— The reported meetings “look even more disturbing because the meetings occurred just days after the politicized ouster of Antitrust Division Chief Gail Slater and amidst increasing lobbyist influence over DOJ’s antitrust work,” the Democrats added, nodding to the uptick in antitrust lobbying work flooding into administration-aligned firms like Ballard Partners , which lobbies for both Netflix and Paramount and which previously employed both Bondi and Wiles.

— Blumenthal, Warren and Liccardo — whose district includes Netflix’s Los Gatos headquarters — asked Bondi and Wiles to respond to a series of questions about last week’s meetings about the deal or any other conversations involving Netflix, Paramount or Ballard representatives.

SPEAKING OF: It’s Paramount’s turn to bring on antitrust lobbying heft . The media giant retained Matt Sandgren of Innovative Policy back in January to work on a slew of issues, including “competition in the media and entertainment sector, the subscription video online streaming market, and policies governing artificial intelligence, copyright, and other intellectual property rights,” according to a disclosure filing.

— Sandgren was previously chief of staff to the late Sen. Orrin Hatch (R-Utah) and served as a senior counsel on the Senate Judiciary Committee, of which Hatch was a former chair.

DEEP IN THE HEART: Today’s primary elections in Texas feature a number of heated races, but the marquee contests revolve around the fight for the Senate. While both of the Texas Senate primaries have attracted a gusher of outside spending bankrolled by industry titans, they’ve also, naturally, drawn interest from Washington’s influence industry.

— On the Democratic side of the ticket, where state Rep. James Talarico is facing off against U.S. Rep. Jasmine Crockett, Talarico pulled in the larger checks of the two from K Street, according to a PI analysis of FEC filings. That includes a max donation of $7,000 from Cornerstone Government Affairs managing principal Michael Smith. Democratic strategist Guy Cecil, the former head of the marquee super PAC Priorities USA, kicked in around $7,000 as well.

— Anthony Harrington of Albright Stonebridge Group and Mary Stanton of Invariant both donated $3,500 to Talarico, while Airbnb global policy chief Laura Spanjian and Cornerstone principal Todd Webster cut him checks for $2,500, and the Daschle Group’s Tom Daschle kicked in $2,000. (POLITICO is a client of Invariant.)

— Talarico’s K Street haul also included $1,000 from Allyson Baker of Paul Hastings, David Pore of Hance Scarborough, Estefania Rodriguez of theGROUP, Chris Coffey of Tusk Strategies, Richard Carbo of Cornerstone and David Perry of Jake Perry + Partners.

— Crockett, meanwhile, brought in $2,500 from Jennifer Stewart of Stewart Strategies & Solutions and ShaShrina Thomas of Reynolds American, along with $2,750 from Ervin Policy Group managing director Frank Ervin. Crockett also took in four-figure checks from Invariant’s Nicole Venable and Justin Gray of Gray Global Advisors.

— Even more K Streeters made smaller contributions in the race. Talarico got $500 from Edward Ayoob of Barnes & Thornburg, Ted Dean of DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group, Tim Wolfmeyer of Cornerstone, John Gonzalez of Tiber Creek Group and Oscar Ramirez of Fulcrum Public Affairs.

— Crockett received $500 from nearly a dozen lobbyists, including Christopher Davis of Capitol Hill Consulting, John Mason of Altria, Keenan Austin Reed of the Alpine Group, Alane Dent of TruStage, Colette Honorable of Exelon, Megan Moore of FGS Global, Ebony Simpson of Stewart Strategies, Alexander Washington of Entergy and Kimberly Afoakwah of Home Depot.

WALKING BACK THE WALKBACK: The Justice Department told a federal appeals court Tuesday that the administration intends to continue defending President Donald Trump’s executive orders targeting law firms — a surprising reversal less than 24 hours after the department informed the same court it no longer wished to defend the orders, Daniel B. and Josh Gerstein write.

— DOJ lawyers did not provide an explanation for their change in posture, which came via a short Tuesday filing. DOJ declined to comment on the reversal.

— Judges in four cases last year struck down as unconstitutional Trump’s executive orders seeking to punish law firms affiliated with his political opponents. The Justice Department appealed those losses in June and was set to deliver its opening brief to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit on Friday. But in a Monday evening filing, the department declared it no longer wished to pursue the appeal and moved to voluntarily dismiss it.

— “Under no circumstances should the government’s unexplained about-face provide a basis for an extension of its brief,” lawyers representing the targeted firms — Perkins Coie, Jenner & Block, WilmerHale and Susman Godfrey — stated in their filing.

THE AI GOLD RUSH: “Disrupting jobs, fueling a data center boom, even killing off this em dash—artificial intelligence is the conversation policymakers, and the rest of us, just can’t escape. That’s especially the case in Washington, where spending on federal AI influence hit an all-time high last year,” Bloomberg’s Kate Ackley, John Woolley and Ava Mandoli report.

— “Lobbying firms reported a record $37.2 million in earnings from AI-related influence peddling in the fourth quarter alone, a 38% jump from a year earlier, according to a Bloomberg Government analysis.”

— “For the full year, Washington lobbyists received almost $130 million for work related to AI, as Microsoft Corp., Meta Platforms Inc. and Alphabet Inc.’s Google led the spending blitz. Some of the biggest jumps came from frontier labs OpenAI Inc. and Anthropic PBC, two of the highest valued startups in history vying to shape the AI industry’s future and most recently engulfed in a dispute over its use within the US military.”
