FS Vector lobbyist jumps into Georgia House primary

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO 

07/21/2025 07:00 PM EDT

Presented by

With Daniel Lippman

FIRST IN PI: The crowded Democratic primary to unseat longtime Georgia Rep. David Scott just gained a new contender who hails from K Street. Pierre Whatley, a former Democratic Hill aide who now works as a principal at the financial services-focused lobbying firm FS Vector, filed paperwork over the weekend to run for the safe blue seat in east metro Atlanta. He will launch his campaign officially tomorrow.

— Whatley joins eight other Democrats challenging the 80-year-old, 12-term incumbent, who lost his post as the top Democrat on the House Agriculture Committee last year amid concerns about his health and a wider Democratic reckoning over age.

— Whatley joined FS Vector in 2021 after working for the House Financial Services Committee and as an economic policy aide to Sen. Raphael Warnock (D-Ga.). His lobbying clients last quarter included Navy Federal Credit Union, Intuit, the Investment Company Institute, the Digital Energy Council, Stellar Development Foundation and Citizens Bank, according to disclosure filings. Whatley also works for the Free Speech Coalition, a trade group representing the adult entertainment industry that was at the center of this year’s Supreme Court case challenging Texas’ age restrictions on porn sites.

— Whatley told PI he joined the race because, while he respects Scott and has worked with him on the Hill, it’s “time for more engaged, more present leadership” in Washington. “I think there’s a duty of service to do more [for the community] when it’s such a safe blue seat,” he said.

— Whatley argued that his understanding of how Congress works as a former Hill staffer distinguishes him from the other challengers. He said he won’t hide from his work as a lobbyist.

— “Everyone deserves an advocate, No. 1,” he said. But Whatley also defended his clients as entities helping underrepresented communities — whether they’re racial minorities, small businesses or those working in the adult entertainment industry — maintain access to financial services.

— Before his time on the Hill, Whatley also worked for Deloitte, Buckley Sandler, the Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland, the CFPB and the SEC.

— Whatley isn’t the only K Streeter with an eye on joining Congress. Zoe Cadore, a former director of federal and regulatory affairs for energy company Calpine, announced a run this year for the Houston-area seat opened up by the death of Democratic Rep. Sylvester Turner in March.

Happy Monday and welcome to PI. What are you watching for in tonight’s LDA filing deadline? Add me on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17, email me at [email protected], and be sure to follow me on X: @caitlinoprysko.

WHAT WALL STREET IS READING: “In late January, the CEO of the pro-business American Legislative Exchange Council told right-wing operatives and officials that they need a ‘scalp’ from one of two supposedly woke CEOs of major Wall Street firms,” per Rolling Stone’s Lauren Windsor.

— “Lisa Nelson, who leads ALEC, was discussing Larry Fink of BlackRock, the world’s largest asset manager, and Brian Moynihan of Bank of America, the second largest bank in the country. She appeared to be speaking metaphorically, as she struggled to refer to an unknown movie. Nelson made the comments at the Consumers’ Research Summit in Sea Island, Georgia” from which Rolling Stone obtained audio and documents.

— “Nelson noted she had spoken about this at breakfast. ‘Whether it’s Larry Fink or Brian Moynihan, we have got to take one of these guys out,’ she said, presumably another metaphor. She added, ‘Brian Moynihan is the guy, or Larry Fink is the guy that we should have their scalp.’”

— “ALEC is a powerful ‘bill mill’ that brings corporations, conservative advocates, and state legislators together to hash out right-wing, pro-business legislation that is then introduced nationwide, with a focus on red states.”

— While the organization doesn’t disclose a full list of its members (or its donors), ALEC’s Private Enterprise Advisory Council includes operatives with ties to Leonard Leo as well as executives from the American Bankers Association and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. Bank of America cut ties with ALEC in 2012, but a source told Rolling Stone that the bank was represented at ALEC’s annual meeting last week. A spokesperson for ALEC declined to comment on Nelson’s remarks, while a BlackRock spokesperson defended the company.

MORE CROWELL LOBBYISTS JOIN BROWNSTEIN: Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck has hired away three more members of Crowell & Moring’s government affairs practice after bagging half a dozen of the firm’s lobbyists earlier this month, including the former head of Crowell’s lobbying shop, Jim Flood.

— Energy and environmental lobbyist Tracy Tolk is coming over to Brownstein as a policy director, while health care experts Tim Shadyac and Stephen Holland are joining the firm as a senior policy adviser and senior counsel, respectively.

— Tolk previously spent 16 years at Van Ness Feldman before moving to Crowell, and is a Jay Inslee and Jim Davis alum. Shadyac was a lobbyist for Avalere Health and Sanofi before joining Crowell, while Holland previously spent more than a decade on the Hill, including as senior health counsel for the House Energy and Commerce Committee.

SIGNAL GROUP DECODES CONSERVATIVE MEDIA: Signal Group is building out its resources for helping clients break through a fractured media environment in the age of Donald Trump with a new service focused on paid media campaigns in conservative media.

— “The world of conservative media, especially conservative opinion, is complex and vast,” Signal’s Rob Bole writes in a new tipsheet on the topic, with “dozens of viable radio programs, hundreds of relevant podcasts, and thousands of video commentators and social influencers with significant audiences” that clients can use to reach key decisionmakers with their messages.

— “We are living through a moment in time where effective paid media and messaging tactics are integral to break through the noise, reach new audiences, communicate concisely with clarity, and drive real change in Washington,” Bole, who leads Signal Group’s innovation and strategy teams, said in a statement. The new offering builds off a master conservative media map and master conservative messaging guide Signal Group released earlier this year.

— Signal has also added a slate of new staffers, including bringing on Allison Kimble as senior vice president of digital. Kimble previously led digital strategy and content creation at Weber Shandwick and Rational 360. The firm has also added Emmy Keene as creative content manager, Preethi Murthy as health care manager and Rachel Martin as health care senior associate and promoted Mary Lieb to director.

PHRMA ADDS 4: PhRMA’s public affairs team has added Elise Shutzer as vice president, Mark Allen as deputy vice president, Cait DeBaun as chief of staff and Kristen Booze as senior director. Shutzer was previously at ExxonMobil, Allen was previously at Purple Strategies, DeBaun was previously at the American Beverage Association and Booze was previously at FDA.

A SHOT ACROSS THE BOW: “For decades, the prices Medicare pays doctors for different medical services have been largely decided not by Medicare itself, but by a powerful industry group, the American Medical Association,” The New York Times’ Reed Abelson and Margot Sanger-Katz write.

— “And for decades, critics have complained that this process unfairly rewards surgeons and other specialists, at the expense of primary care physicians and other generalists. … But a change buried inside a 1,803-page proposed regulation published last Monday suggests the Trump administration would like to move away from this longstanding system. If finalized, it could begin overturning a process that has entrenched pay advantages for certain kinds of doctors.”

— The proposal, which a CMS official told the Times would improve Medicare “by correcting outdated assumptions,” has already sparked backlash from the AMA, which said it would “ultimately harm patients.”

BUTLER’S NEW CLIENT: “Former Sen. Laphonza Butler is now advising OpenAI, her first known client since the California Democrat left Congress and landed at the global public affairs firm Actum,” POLITICO’s Christine Mui reports.

— “Tapped by Gov. Gavin Newsom to fill the late Sen. Dianne Feinstein’s seat, Butler served just over a year in the Senate to complete the term before returning to her roots as a behind-the-scenes power broker and becoming a partner at Actum. The California Democrat is barred from lobbying for a year as a former member of Congress.”

— “It’s not clear what issues Butler will be providing guidance on for the AI developer,” but the former labor leader and EMILY’s List head’s work with OpenAI comes as the firm “is facing an inflection point in its plans for future growth, hoping contentious changes to a more conventional corporate structure will help the company raise money to keep ahead of cash-slinging competitors.” This isn’t Butler’s first time advising a tech startup, having previously consulted for Uber and Airbnb at the California firm now known as Bearstar Strategies.

IN MEMORIAM: Ed Feulner, a founder, trustee and the longest serving president of The Heritage Foundation, has died, Heritage President Kevin Roberts announced. After founding the organization in 1973, Feulner served as president for 37 years, and “what started as a small outpost for conservative ideas became — under Ed’s tireless leadership — the intellectual arsenal for the Reagan Revolution and the modern conservative movement,” Roberts said in a statement, adding: “His legacy is not just the institution he built, but the movement he helped grow — a movement rooted in faith, family, freedom, and the founding.”

title: K Street goes to bat for the MLB
body_text:
MLB LOBBIES UP: Major League Baseball has added some more depth to its bullpen of outside help in Washington. The league retained Forbes Tate Partners and Cornerstone Government Affairs beginning yesterday to lobby on a slew of issues including taxes, game broadcasts, drones and stadium security and visas for athletes, disclosure filings show.

— More than a dozen lobbyists between the two firms are set to work on the accounts, including Jeff Forbes and Zach Williams of Forbes Tate and David Planning , Chris Hodgson and Mike Smith of Cornerstone.

— Cornerstone and Forbes Tate are the second and third additions to the MLB’s bench this year. In January, MLB brought on PhronesisDC , the firm started by veteran GOP tax lobbyist Brendan Dunn , to work on tax issues ahead of Republicans’ reconciliation push.

— The league has four other outside firms — Ballard Partners , Hogan Lovells , the Duberstein Group and Washington Council Ernst & Young — on retainer, but MLB’s lobbying hires this year were its first since 2019, disclosure filings show.

MORE NEW BUSINESS: Bayer added new lobbying heft last month prior to a series of significant wins in the form of a watered-down MAHA Commission report from HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and the inclusion of a prized liability shield in a GOP spending bill.

— According to a newly filed disclosure, Bayer brought on Mercury Public Affairs’ Bryan Lanza and John Lonergan at the beginning of September to lobby on “issues related to the importance of crop protection tools and related supply chains for U.S. agricultural production.”

— Meanwhile sports betting giant FanDuel has retained Mehlman Consulting to lobby on sports gambling and tax issues. The hire came amid the gaming industry’s push for a legislative fix to language in the GOP reconciliation package that advocates said would hike taxes on gamblers.

— And embattled Chinese drone company DJI Technologies brought on new lobbying help as the company stares down threats to its U.S. business from across the federal government. The drone giant hired MO Strategies’ Marty Obst , a longtime adviser to former Vice President Mike Pence , and Robert Goad , who served as DHS’ liaison to Congress and as a special assistant to the president during Trump’s first term, to “facilitate discussions on border security and technology” at the beginning of September, per a disclosure filing.

— A provision in last year’s defense authorization bill called for an automatic FCC ban on Chinese drone companies like DJI beginning in December unless cleared by a national security review. DJI has sought to rally its users ahead of the deadline. Adding to the pressure, a federal judge last week rejected DJI’s bid for removal from a Pentagon blacklist of companies with alleged ties to the Chinese military.

Happy Thursday and welcome to PI . Send lobbying tips and gossip. Caitlin is on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 and email her at coprysko@politico.com . Daniel is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com . Also follow us on X : @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns .

ARNOLD & PORTER ADDS 2 : Brian Bombassaro is returning to the firm’s international trade group at Arnold & Porter Kaye Scholer after his third stint on the Hill as international trade counsel for the Senate Finance Committee under a new GOP chair.

— The firm has also hired Bree Raum as a senior policy adviser. She was most recently executive director of government affairs for the Americas at Air Products and Chemicals , and previously lobbied for a slew of energy and environmental companies and trade groups, including BP America, the American Clean Power Association and its predecessor the American Wind Energy Association ; the American Gas Association and the National Propane Gas Association .

PATEL NIXES ADL PARTNERSHIP: “The FBI said on Wednesday it cut ties with the Anti-Defamation League , a Jewish group that tracks antisemitism, after conservatives criticized the group for including slain activist Charlie Kirk ‘s organization in a glossary on extremism,” per Reuters’ Kanishka Singh .

— “In a social media post, FBI Director Kash Patel said the bureau ‘won’t partner with political fronts masquerading as watchdogs.’ The ADL said it took note of Patel’s announcement and ‘has deep respect’ for the FBI.

— “Patel’s announcement followed criticism of the ADL by right-wing voices, including billionaire Elon Musk , over its inclusion of Kirk’s Turning Point USA in a ‘Glossary of Extremism and Hate.’ … After that criticism, the ADL removed the entire glossary from its website. The glossary had said Turning Point USA had a history of ‘bigoted statements,’ a charge the group rejects.”

— “ADL’s website says it ‘works closely with federal, state and local law enforcement’ in fighting extremism and hate. It also notes the FBI had turned to it for data and research as far back as the 1940s.”

HO, MAN: “The first time a Pennsylvania consultant named Charles Sowell connected with border czar Tom Homan was when Sowell reached out on LinkedIn in 2021, looking for advice about border contracting work” following Homan’s stint as acting ICE director, ProPublica ’s Avi Asher-Schapiro , Jeff Ernsthausen and Mica Rosenberg report.

— “By 2023, the men had gone into business together. Sowell was paying Homan as a consultant to his boutique firm, SE&M Solutions , which advised companies — in some cases for a fee of $20,000 a month — seeking contracts from the agencies where Homan had once worked. In 2024, Sowell became chair of the board of Homan’s foundation, Border911 , which championed tougher border security.”

— Homan said when he was appointed border czar following Trump’s win that he would recuse himself from contracting work. But “several industry executives who spoke with ProPublica said at least half a dozen companies vying for a slice of the $45 billion Congress has allocated for immigration detention work had hired Sowell because he had led them to believe his connections to Homan would help their chances of winning government work.”

Jobs report

— Keeley Hanlon is now a managing director in FTI Consulting ’s public affairs practice. She previously worked at Purple Strategies .

— Madison Smith has joined Ridge Path Strategies as a principal. He was previously a senior principal at Cozen O’Connor Public Strategies and is an AWS and John Cornyn alum.

— Hadley Heath Manning is joining the Independent Women’s Forum as a senior fellow for family and culture. She’s leaving her role as executive vice president of the Steamboat Institute , where she’ll remain a senior Tony Blankley fellow and fellowship director.

— Andrew Rohrbach is now a partner at Jenner & Block in their investigations, compliance and defense practice. He most recently worked for the U.S. Attorney’s Office for the Southern District of New York.

— Sarah Curtis is now director of U.S. federal public policy at Moderna . She most recently was chief of staff for then-Rep. Kathy Manning (D-N.C.).

— Deborah Rowe is joining the government relations team at the Port of Long Beach . She most recently was a director of public policy at Alpine Group and is a Steny Hoyer alum.

— Tom Sundlof is now a partner at Blank Rome . He most recently worked in the FDA’s Office of the Chief Counsel.

— Katie Kingsley is now director of government and political affairs at the National Mining Association . She previously worked for Rep. Russ Fulcher (R-Idaho).

— Ashley Forbes has joined enCore Energy Corp . as vice president of permitting and regulatory affairs, per Morning Energy . Forbes was previously the deputy director of the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality’s Radioactive Materials Division.

— The Alliance for Safe Online Pharmacies has named Matthew Strait to its board of directors, Morning Pulse reports. Strait is the owner and principal adviser of Controlled Substance Strategies and is a 26-year veteran of the DEA.

— Annie Butler is now a director on Targeted Victory ’s public affairs team. She previously worked for Rep. Nick Langworthy (R-N.Y.).

— Harold Kim has been named principal-in-charge at KPMG ’s office of government affairs and public policy. He previously worked at the U.S. Chamber of Commerce .

— Paul Teller has launched his own consulting firm, Teller Strategies . He previously was at Advancing American Freedom .

— Christian Curto is now executive vice president of advertising at TAG Strategies . He previously worked at Targeted Victory and is a Campaign Solutions alum.

— Paul Iskajyan is now comms director for New Democrat Coalition . He previously worked for Rep. Scott Peters (D-Calif.).

MANATT SIGNS MORE HOLLAND & KNIGHT CLIENTS: Manatt, Phelps & Phillips has registered to lobby for a half-dozen local government clients previously represented by lobbyists who decamped for the firm from Holland & Knight last year. They include Florida’s Jacksonville Transportation Authority , the government of Des Moines, Iowa, and the Los Angeles County Metropolitan Transportation Authority .

— Several other new clients signed with Manatt as subcontractors of Holland & Knight, such as Florida’s Hillsborough Area Regional Transit Authority , California’s Orange County Fire Authority , the Orlando Housing Authority and the North Tampa Housing Development Authority .

— Eve O’Toole , Leslie Pollner , Lisa Barkovic , Joe O’Brien and Adrianna Williams , all members of Holland & Knight’s local governments lobbying group, left the firm in October to join Los Angeles-based Manatt. In all, Manatt has registered to lobby for nearly three dozen current or former Holland & Knight clients in the last year, according to a PI analysis of disclosures.

Happy Monday and welcome to PI. Send K Street tips. You can reach Caitlin on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 or at coprysko@politico.com . Daniel B. is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com . Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns .

NO CAP: Wall Street doesn’t know how President Donald Trump ’s proposed temporary 10 percent cap on credit card interest rates would work, but banks and credit card companies are coming out forcefully against the idea floated Friday in a social media post.

— The Electronic Payments Coalition , which includes top banks and credit card issuers like Visa and Mastercard , pushed out a study Monday criticizing a bill from Sens. Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) and Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) that would cap credit card rates at 10 percent indefinitely. It said that anywhere from 82 percent to 88 percent of open credit card accounts would “lose their credit card as they know it today,” either through account closures or having their credit limits rolled back.

— “In essence, the credit card would become a very nice bookmark,” EPC executive director Richard Hunt said on a press call Monday, maintaining that an interest rate cap would simply create too much risk for many credit card issuers.

— “I understand the president is trying to make sure Americans can afford to make ends meet, and we support that,” he said. “This study is to show them the draconian effects that would happen to his voters and to the Senate and the House members’ constituents. This is serious stuff. This isn’t campaign rhetoric.”

— Hunt said he wasn’t aware of where Trump’s 10 percent number came from — or Trump’s vow for the interest rate cap to last only a year. And he added that he didn’t believe there was any mechanism for Trump to impose such a cap without congressional action, which appears unlikely. But the industry rushed to condemn the idea regardless.

— Trump’s proposal would be “devastating for millions of American families and small business owners who rely on and value their credit cards, the very consumers this proposal intends to help,” the Consumer Bankers Association , Bank Policy Institute , American Bankers Association , Financial Services Forum and Independent Community Bankers of America said in a joint statement Friday night. They pledged to work with Trump but warned that a cap “would only drive consumers toward less regulated, more costly alternatives.”

THE OTHER KIND OF INFLUENCER: “Trump’s return to the White House has transformed the federal government and upended the business of lobbying, creating a new class of Washington operatives that blur the lines between consulting, advocacy and journalism,” the Wall Street Journal ’s Maggie Severns , Natalie Andrews , Josh Dawsey and Eliza Collins write.

— “Corporate and foreign interests that used to rely primarily on paid lobbyists to pitch their case to lawmakers and administration officials are instead pouring money into trying to get their cause promoted by a group of young, conservative influencers known to be close to Trump’s staff.”

— “A camera-ready pack of Gen-Z social-media natives — many of whom were too young to vote when Trump announced his first run for office — are reaping the rewards. They don’t work for traditional news outlets and are thus unshackled from newsroom ethics rules, such as the typical ban on accepting gifts worth more than $25.”

— “They don’t have to follow the disclosure laws that apply to big-money super PACs or lobbyists. And they have large followings eager to hear pro-Trump views, a gold mine for those looking to sway both Washington and the public.”

A message from the Defense Credit Union Council:

DURBIN-MARSHALL CREDIT CARD MANDATES WILL HARM MILITARY FAMILIES The Defense Credit Union Council is sounding the alarm on the Durbin–Marshall credit card mandates. This proposal would increase fraud risk, restrict access to credit, eliminate rewards, and hand a massive windfall to corporate mega-retailers at the expense of consumers, small businesses, and community financial institutions. DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED —OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

DRONE LOBBYIST: Holland & Knight is boosting its expertise at the intersection of transportation, aviation and technology as the Trump administration vows to “unleash American drone dominance.” Matthew Satterley , the former head of global policy for Alphabet -owned drone delivery company Wing , has joined Holland & Knight as a senior policy adviser in the firm’s public policy and regulation practice group.

— Before joining Wing in 2019, Satterley was head of federal policy and government affairs for the shuttered drone traffic management company AirMap . He previously served as legislative director for former Rep. Frank LoBiondo (R-N.J.), who chaired the House Transportation & Infrastructure Aviation Subcommittee.

MORE NEW BUSINESS: Battery maker Duracell retained ArentFox Schiff in late November to lobby on federal funding for domestic battery materials processing and battery production, according to a newly filed disclosure.

— The hire came a little over a month after the Energy Department canceled more than $700 million in grants for advanced battery manufacturing projects issued by the Biden administration with funds from the 2021 bipartisan infrastructure law.

— And Capital One has brought on Venable , the credit card company’s first new outside firm since 2024. Venable previously lobbied for Discover Financial Services , which completed its merger with Capital One in May.

— Venable’s Thomas Boyd , Sarah Donovan , Josh Raymond , Chris Scribner and Timothy Ursprung began working for the card issuer at the beginning of the year on general banking policy, including issues related to data privacy and payment networks, disclosures show.

IF YOU MISSED IT OVER THE WEEKEND: Americans for Prosperity said on Friday that it will yank support for Republican lawmakers who voted in favor of restoring expired Affordable Care Act subsidies, POLITICO ’s Amanda Chu reports.

— “First on the group’s blacklist are the 17 House Republicans who broke from the party Thursday to join Democrats in passing legislation that would revive and extend the Obamacare subsidies for three years. … AFP said it was pausing current and future grassroots activity in those 17 districts, as well as advertisements in them promoting the domestic policy package that Republicans enacted in July and that is their foremost legislative achievement.”

TAKING STOCK: “GOP Rep. Rob Bresnahan last year bought stock in a major supplier for data centers that subsequently boomed in value — at the same time he was encouraging data centers to be built in his Pennsylvania district,” Daniel L. reports.

— “In June, Bresnahan bought between $1,001 and $15,000 of stock in Credo Technology , a company that provides electric cables and chips for data centers, according to a House report he filed in July. Bresnahan spokesperson Hannah Pope said the purchase totaled $1,454. Since then, the share price of Credo stock has risen about 109 percent — joining the set of AI companies ballooning in value.”

— “The trade, which has not been previously reported, comes as data centers have become an increasingly hot-button political issue and his Democratic opponent has sought to make Bresnahan’s stock trading a top issue in the campaign.”

META GETS TRUMPIER: “ Meta named former Trump adviser Dina Powell McCormick to serve as president and vice chair Monday, further cementing the company’s growing ties to Republicans” and the White House, POLITICO ’s Brendan Bordelon writes.

— “In addition to a long career on Wall Street, Powell McCormick served as Trump’s deputy national security adviser during his first term. She was also a member of the George W. Bush administration,” and is married to Sen. David McCormick (R-Pa.).

— Powell McCormick has served on Meta’s board since last April, as “part of a broader play by the social media and artificial intelligence giant to hire Republicans following Trump’s election,” Brendan notes. That push has included elevating Republican Joel Kaplan to serve as its head of global affairs and adding former Republican FCC Chair Kevin Martin as Kaplan’s deputy.

— Right on cue, Trump praised the move in a post on Truth Social on Monday that praised Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg for making a “great choice.” The president called Powell McCormick “a fantastic, and very talented, person, who served the Trump Administration with strength and distinction!”

He previously served as a senior research fellow at The Heritage Foundation . Bill Hansen is joining DFI’s board of directors. Hansen is currently the CEO of Building Hope Holdings .

title: Senate Judiciary advances effort to limit foreign influence

FOREIGN INFLUENCE: The Senate Judiciary Committee voted today to advance a bill that would ban former senior government officials from lobbying for foreign “countries of concern” like Russia and China.

— The bipartisan Conflict-free Leaving Employment and Activity Restrictions, or CLEAR, Path Act seeks to limit the impact of foreign influence in Washington by prohibiting former agency heads, their deputies and other former Senate-confirmed employees from lobbying the federal government on behalf of geopolitical adversaries. “Countries of concern” under the bill would initially include China, Russia, Iran, North Korea, Cuba and Syria. Adding or removing a country from that list would require a proposal from the secretary of state and the attorney general plus sign off from Congress.

— “Foreign adversaries with ill intentions should not wield influence on American policymaking, nor should they exploit our own citizens to intercede on their behalf,” said the bill’s sponsor Sen. John Cornyn (R-Texas).

— The bill, which has drawn bipartisan support from co-sponsors Sens. Peter Welch (D-Vt.), James Risch (R-Idaho) and Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), is just the latest Senate effort to reduce the influence of foreign lobbying. In December, the Senate passed two bills aimed at improving transparency around lobbying efforts with foreign connections that aren’t required to be reported to the Justice Department under the Foreign Agents Registration Act. The House has not taken any action on those measures.

FOCUS ON FRAUD: Jenner & Block has hired former Justice Department fraud chief Glenn Leon as a partner in the firm’s investigations, compliance and defense practice. Leon, who until recently served as the leader of the DOJ criminal division’s fraud section, has spent years investigating and prosecuting major health care fraud, securities and commodities fraud and other similar cases.

— His hiring comes as the Trump administration is telegraphing an enhanced focus on federal fraud prosecutions. Last week, Vice President JD Vance announced the creation of a new assistant attorney general position focused solely on fraud to investigate allegations that federal aid money had been widely misused in Minnesota. The new AAG for fraud would eventually investigate fraud nationwide, Vance said, adding that the new prosecutor would directly report to himself and the president.

— Leon alluded to those developments in a statement to PI, saying his experience would be “particularly valuable to clients navigating the evolving regulatory environment shaped by recent changes to federal enforcement priorities and Executive Orders.”

WICKER MAN HANGS UP A SHINGLE : John Keast , a top aide to Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.) for more than 30 years and a central figure in national security legislating, is launching a new firm with RTX as one of his first clients — just as the defense heavyweight finds itself in President Donald Trump’s crosshairs.

— Keast has formed the lobbying and consulting firm Keast Strategic Solutions , and he identified RTX as a client at a farewell reception Wednesday evening hosted by BGR Group . He is expected to file disclosure paperwork on Tuesday.

— The announcement comes as Trump has stepped up public criticism of major defense contractors, including RTX, injecting new uncertainty into the industry’s relationship with the White House even as Congress presses ahead with a $1.5 trillion budget proposal for 2027.

— Trump’s salvo included an executive order directing scrutiny of stock buybacks and executive compensation at defense contractors, all as the administration pushes companies to reinvest more aggressively in expanding U.S. munitions production capacity.

— Keast most recently served as staff director of the Senate Armed Services Committee. He spent more than a decade at Cornerstone Government Affairs before rejoining Wicker’s staff in 2018 as the GOP staff director of the Senate Commerce, Science and Transportation Committee.

— Wicker, in a recent floor speech marking Keast’s departure, praised him as a master of Senate process and policy, crediting him with playing a central role in National Defense Authorization Act negotiations, acquisition reform and industrial base issues.

— Wicker called out Keast’s work on the CHIPS and Science Act and credited him with delivering more than $1 billion in infrastructure and broadband funding to Mississippi and nationwide through Commerce Committee work.

ALL EYES ON GREENLAND : President Trump has set his sights on acquiring Greenland, and at least one company with interests in the Danish territory is positioning itself in Washington to seize the moment.

— Eclipse Metals , an Australian mining exploration company with holdings in Greenland, signed BGR Government Affairs in December to lobby on issues related to the company’s efforts to “unleash Greenland’s rare-earths potential in a manner consistent with the state commercial priorities of President Trump and the Administration,” according to a newly filed disclosure report .

— “Eclipse believes its Greenland holdings, licenses and interests can contribute to U.S. and allied resilience against disruptions in minerals critical to defense, advanced manufacturing, and AI-enabling technologies,” the report further states.

— Though Trump has emphasized national security reasons for obtaining the territory in recent weeks, the island’s rich deposits of critical minerals offer an additional explanation for the importance the administration has placed on the matter.

— BGR founding partner Ed Rogers will handle the account, joined by former BP top lobbyist Joe Ellis and former ExxonMobil senior adviser Collin Janich .

NETFLIX NEW HIRE : Netflix has added an additional hired gun to its Washington lobbying roster as it works to close the deal for its proposed acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery ’s studios and streaming platforms while fending off Paramount Skydance ’s attempt at a hostile takeover of WBD.

— Avoq registered to lobby for the streamer on Dec. 15, according to a disclosure report , on “issues related to the media and telecommunications industry.” Working on the account will be a bipartisan team of Barry LaSala , Natalie Farr Harrison and Joseph Orlando .

— The team at Avoq joins the growing list of firms hired by Netflix, which currently includes The Gibson Group , Monument Advocacy, Miller & Chevalier and Ballard Partners .

TRUMPCARE: The Trump administration has unveiled a proposed blueprint for health care reform that bashes private industry players that have long been considered GOP allies, POLITICO’s Amanda Chu , David Lim , Robert King and Kelly Hooper reported yesterday.

— “Republicans, on their heels after letting Obamacare premiums spike this month, sounded ready to embrace a plan to drive down costs that puts the blame on private industry,” they write. “Trump’s plan, notably, does not include free-market ideas in a bill House Republicans passed in December. That bill, for example, would have allowed small businesses to band together to drive harder bargains with insurers.”

— While Trump’s plan is scant on details, it marks a clear change in the Republican position on health care that for years has been largely defined by opposition to the Affordable Care Act.

— “The Paul Ryan Republican conference … was repeal and replace, and there was no other plan. … In terms of health care, this Republican Party looks a lot more innovative, a lot more open, and a lot more, quite frankly, forward-looking and aspirational,” Lauren Stewart , senior federal affairs liaison at Americans for Prosperity , told POLITICO.

PARDON ME : The president quietly issued a new slate of pardons this week, including a pardon for a convicted fraudster who had previously received clemency from Trump during his first term, Kenneth Vogel and Suzanne Craig report for The New York Times .

— Also pardoned this week was a man whose daughter donated millions to MAGA Inc. , the Trump-supporting super PAC. The man, a banker convicted on charges that he bribed the former governor of Puerto Rico, was represented by Christopher Kise , one of the president’s former criminal defense lawyers.

— Adriana Camberos , who was granted clemency by Trump in the final days of his first term and later convicted on new fraud charges, received a new pardon after hiring the same lawyers who secured her original commutation: former deputy White House counsel Stefan Passantino and former Rudy Giuliani defense lawyer Adam Katz .

SPENDING ON CIVIL RIGHTS : Civil rights groups upped their spending in Washington in 2025, according to an analysis by Jonathan Salant for OpenSecrets .

— The NAACP Legal Defense and Educational Fund reported spending $180,000 during the first three quarters of the year, nearly doubling its lobbying spending during the same period of 2024.

— The Leadership Conference on Civil and Human Rights spent nearly $1.7 million during the same time last year. That was a $200,000 increase from the group’s spending during the same time period in 2024.

— “It is an unfortunate reality, the defensive posture every civil rights organization finds itself in at the moment,” Cedric Haynes , vice president, policy & legislative affairs for the NAACP , told Salant.

title: Meet the new TikTok, same as the old TikTok

UNDER NEW MANAGEMENT: The new American-owned version of TikTok has registered to lobby and appears to be continuing to focus on the same issues as its former parent company ByteDance , according to a new filing .

— TikTok USDS Joint Venture , as the new U.S. entity is known, submitted its registration on Jan. 22, the same date the company was formed to comply with the bi-partisan law requiring Chinese-owned ByteDance to divest itself of the app’s U.S. operations or face a ban. The new company is owned by a consortium of investors led by Silver Lake , Oracle and MGX , each of whom hold 15 percent of the company. ByteDance retains a 19.9 percent stake.

— The joint venture will lobby on “issues related to internet technology and learning-enabled content platforms, including data protection and privacy, algorithm security and integrity, content moderation, software assurance, online safety, interoperability of global platforms, and small business and the economic impact of TikTok,” according to the registration.

— Another constant appears to be TikTok’s public policy and government affairs staff, nearly all of whom previously appeared on ByteDance filings. Mac Abrams , Michael Bloom , Albert Calamug and Derrick Dockery , will continue lobbying under the new joint venture.

— There is one new addition to the team: Nicole Nason , former head of the Federal Highway Administration, has been appointed as the joint venture’s head of public policy, according to her LinkedIn . TikTok USDS did not respond to a request for comment on Nason’s appointment or the new registration.

— It’s too soon to know how much the new TikTok is prepared to spend in Washington, but Nason’s hiring and the many similarities between this registration and previous ByteDance disclosure reports suggests it could be a similar amount. ByteDance reported spending $8.3 million on in-house lobbying alone last year.

ANTHROPIC OUT: All federal agencies have been directed to completely cease using Anthropic products and the company has been designated a supply-chain risk to national security following a breakdown in talks between the company and the Pentagon about the military’s use of Anthropic’s AI model, our colleague Brendan Bordelon reports .

— “The Leftwing nut jobs at Anthropic have made a DISASTROUS MISTAKE trying to STRONG-ARM the Department of War, and force them to obey their Terms of Service instead of our Constitution,” President Donald Trump posted this afternoon , warning of “major civil and criminal consequences” for the company if it is not “helpful” during a six month “phase out period.”

— That was followed by a post from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announcing that “no contractor, supplier, or partner that does business with the United States military may conduct any commercial activity with Anthropic.” The announcement marks a major change to Anthropic’s relationship with the federal government, which just last year awarded the company a $200 million Pentagon contract . Anthropic has not responded to a request for comment from Politico.

PARAMOUNT WINS: Paramount Skydance has emerged as the victor in its battle against Netflix to acquire WarnerBros Discovery , leaving regulator approval as the final hurdle to creating what would be a massive media empire controlled by a strong ally of the president.

— Netflix’s decision yesterday to pull out of the race came hours after its CEO met with Attorney General Pam Bondi and Trump, seeking facetime with the officials who would’ve needed to approve the streamer’s acquisition of Warner Bros and assurances that government review of the prospective deal would be handled fairly, our colleagues Yasmin Khorram and Sophia Cai reported .

— But despite receiving such assurances, Netflix chief Ted Sarandos announced his company would not seek to match Paramount’s latest offer, ceding its attempt to acquire the HBO Max streaming service and Warner Bros. studios. Paramount’s deal to acquire Warner Bros. includes all of the company’s properties, including CNN .

MAKING SOLAR GREAT AGAIN : Yesterday, PI told you about the questions that had been raised by Katie Miller’s sudden and mysterious push for solar energy. Thanks to POLITICO’s Kelsey Brugger , Zack Colman and Pavan Acharya , that mystery has been solved .

— Miller’s pro-solar posts are the result of an initiative by the American Clean Power Association to engage conservative influencers to promote solar energy, according to a strategy memo obtained by our colleagues. The “American Energy First” campaign plans to expand in the coming weeks and will include polling data gathered by Kellyanne Conway’s firm, paid media partnerships with podcasts and paid content placed in right-leaning publications.

— Miller has denied being paid by ACP for her solar posts. “I do not have a paid partnership with them,” she said in a statement. ACP declined to comment on whether it paid or partnered with Miller.

— The memo says the campaign is “not directly associated with ACP’s multi-technology brand,” and in a statement, the trade group’s spokesperson, Artealia Gilliard , said “American Energy First is supported and led by a small number of ACP member companies that deploy utility scale solar across the U.S.”

AIPAC’S NEXT TEST : The upcoming Illinois primary will be closely watched by those wondering how much sway the American Israel Public Affairs Committee still has in modern Democratic politics, Leah Askarinam , Maya Sweedler and Matt Brown report for the Associated Press .

— The leading pro-Israel advocacy group has invested at least $1.9 million in political ads in the race to replace retiring Rep. Danny Davis (D-Ill.). “Other organizations that critics believe are tied to AIPAC are also spending heavily in Illinois, a source of bitterness and recriminations in a state already known for its bare knuckled brand of politics,” they report.

— This comes after AIPAC invested nearly $2 million on attacking moderate Democrat Tom Malinowski in the recent Democratic primary for New Jersey’s upcoming special election, which resulted in the victory of an even harsher Israel critic, Analilia Mejia .

— AIPAC appears unbothered. “We expect to be involved in dozens of races both in primaries and general elections this cycle,” Patrick Dorton , a spokesperson for AIPAC’s affiliated super PAC, the United Democracy Project, told the AP.

— “The Leftwing nut jobs at Anthropic have made a DISASTROUS MISTAKE trying to STRONG-ARM the Department of War, and force them to obey their Terms of Service instead of our Constitution,” President Donald Trump posted this afternoon, warning of “major civil and criminal consequences” for the company if it is not “helpful” during a six month “phase out period.”

— That was followed by a post from Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announcing that “no contractor, supplier, or partner that does business with the United States military may conduct any commercial activity with Anthropic.” The announcement marks a major change to Anthropic’s relationship with the federal government, which just last year awarded the company a $200 million Pentagon contract. Anthropic has not responded to a request for comment from Politico.

PARAMOUNT WINS: Paramount Skydance has emerged as the victor in its battle against Netflix to acquire WarnerBros Discovery, leaving regulator approval as the final hurdle to creating what would be a massive media empire controlled by a strong ally of the president.

— Netflix’s decision yesterday to pull out of the race came hours after its CEO met with Attorney General Pam Bondi and Trump, seeking facetime with the officials who would’ve needed to approve the streamer’s acquisition of Warner Bros and assurances that government review of the prospective deal would be handled fairly, our colleagues Yasmin Khorram and Sophia Cai reported.

— But despite receiving such assurances, Netflix chief Ted Sarandos announced his company would not seek to match Paramount’s latest offer, ceding its attempt to acquire the HBO Max streaming service and Warner Bros. studios. Paramount’s deal to acquire Warner Bros. includes all of the company’s properties, including CNN.

IT’S NICE TO HAVE A FRIEND: No one in Washington has prepared for this moment as long as the Mojahedin-e-Khalq , an organization of Iranian exiles who have been fighting for decades to turn their homeland into a democracy.

— While supporters of Reza Pahlavi , the son of the deposed shah who hopes to return to Iran as its next leader, have assembled a broad network of enthusiastic exiles, the MEK has focused on an inside game in Western capitals. It recruited some of the most prominent figures in American politics, including former House Speaker Newt Gingrich and former Democratic National Committee chair Howard Dean , initially with the goal of getting the State Department to shed the MEK’s longstanding designation as a terrorist group .

— Now the MEK, which has been accused by critics of operating like a cult, sees an opening it has never had before. After this weekend’s killing of Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei by Israeli and U.S. airstrikes, France-based MEK leader Maryam Rajavi announced the formation of a secular provisional government.

— Rajavi’s announcement was celebrated by a ready-made echo chamber of American political figures, including several with close ties to the Trump administration. Former Secretary of State Mike Pompeo declared that “Iran’s democratic opposition is ready to step up and lead.” Former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani spent the weekend attacking Pahlavi, a longtime MEK rival, as “destabilizing” and “a formula for disaster.”

— “The only way to see an end to the threat of the Iran regime is to end the role of the dictatorship in Iran, and that’s, of course, the responsibility of the people of Iran,” said Alireza Jafarzadeh , deputy director of the U.S. branch of MEK’s political arm, the National Council of Resistance of Iran .

— Since MEK won removal of the terrorist designation in 2012, the council has paid more than $2.7 million to a lobbying firm run by former Sen. Robert Torricelli (D-N.J.), according to records filed with the Justice Department. Rosemont Associates worked to set up meetings with U.S. diplomats and lawmakers about various issues affecting Iranian refugees abroad, as well as promoting media appearances and signing onto letters or penning op-eds defending MEK and its leadership.

— Others registered to represent NCRI under FARA include Robert Joseph , a former undersecretary of State for arms control and international security, and former Attorney General Michael Mukasey , who have touted MEK talking points in op-eds and media interviews. The group also retains the booking agency Special Guests , DOJ filings show.

— MEK shows its political muscle during its annual “Free Iran” conferences in Washington and other global summits it has put on in locations across Europe. Pompeo addressed the group’s most recent summit in November alongside former U.S. Ambassador to Denmark Carla Sands , conservative commentator Guy Benson , and former Rep. Patrick Kennedy (D-R.I.). John Bercow , the former speaker of the British House of Commons, also participated.

— Many of the speakers are paid lavishly for their participation. Former Vice President Mike Pence received more than $400,000 in speaking fees from NCRI and affiliate groups after leaving office in 2021, according to financial disclosures filed during a subsequent presidential campaign.

— The events attract hordes of sitting elected officials, too. Of the more than 30 U.S. lawmakers who spoke to the group at its 2021 gathering were then-Senate Foreign Relations Chair Bob Menendez (D-N.J.), future House Speaker Kevin McCarthy and future House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries , according to a recap posted by the group.

— In the wake of this weekend’s military action, NCRI maintains that its requests of U.S. policymakers haven’t changed. “We’re not asking for boots on the ground. We’re not asking for appropriation of money. We’re not asking for arms, none of that,” Jafarzadeh told POLITICO.

— “Don’t give concessions to the Iranian regime, hold them accountable for their crimes and terrorism and recognize the right of the people of Iran to overthrow this regime,” he said. “Recognize the right of the resistance units, those forces on the ground who have been fighting the regime, recognize the right to confront the Revolutionary Guards, to fight them and to end the regime. That’s all that is really needed and asked for.”

GOT YOUR BACK: A pair of powerful First Amendment advocates are imploring a federal court to tread lightly in the foreign agent case against former CIA analyst and Korea policy expert Sue Mi Terry , warning that an overly broad reading of FARA “would sweep in a wide array of constitutionally protected speech and would likely violate the First Amendment.”

— Terry, who has worked for some of Washington’s most venerable foreign policy think tanks and was frequently quoted in the press — including POLITICO — as an expert on the Korean peninsula, was indicted last summer on charges of acting as an unregistered foreign agent of Seoul.

— A broad interpretation of FARA’s language could implicate “any number of innocuous actions” taken by someone in the U.S. who may have little or no actual relationship to a foreign individual or entity, reads an amicus brief filed Wednesday by Columbia University ’s Knight First Amendment Institute and the ACLU .

— Terry has pleaded not guilty and last week moved for the dismissal of her case. The strength of the case against her has been the subject of Beltway debate over whether Terry’s interactions with Korean intelligence officials — who allegedly gifted her designer goods, provided funding for programming at one of Terry’s think tanks and paid her $500 for an op-ed she wrote — amounted to an illicit foreign influence campaign or if they are fairly uncommon, if cringey, occurrences in the think tank world.

— In addition to the support this week from the Knight Institute and ACLU, Terry also found an ally in another FARA indictee — former Obama White House counsel Greg Craig , who was acquitted of FARA violations in 2019 and who in August called DOJ’s case against Terry “shockingly weak.”

— The amicus brief makes some of the same arguments as Craig. It laments that FARA “makes no distinction between an ‘agent’ who acts as a mouthpiece of a foreign adversary and one who works with” any organization that happens to be based outside the U.S.

— The filing goes on to highlight portions of Terry’s indictment that it says “illustrate some of the hallmarks of FARA’s speech-suppressive vulnerabilities,” including that she is being prosecuted “for engaging in what appears to be advocacy of her own views.”

— “Reading the statute broadly, an American freelance writer might be required to register under FARA simply for publishing a news article solicited by, say, The Economist (which is owned by a British company),” the filing argues.

— Even with FARA’s various exemptions, the brief says the statute’s extensive disclosure requirements and potential for criminal penalties would chill First Amendment-protected speech — including by media organizations, journalists and nonprofits — and would open FARA up to be further weaponized against political opponents, all without furthering any of the government’s legitimate interest in disclosure of foreign influence efforts.

body_text:
FARA FRIDAY: Advocacy groups representing journalists, civil rights groups, nonprofits, FARA practitioners and the business community alike roundly eviscerated the Justice Department’s first proposed changes to FARA in decades during the public comment period that ended earlier this week, taking aim at tweaks that they argued will only inject more uncertainty into the statute, which many commenters argued is already overly broad and ripe for abuse.

— The fate of the proposed changes was already unclear before new Attorney General Pam Bondi last month signaled the rollback of a nearly decadeold enforcement crackdown in the name of shifting the department’s resources and reducing weaponization — an apparent inconsistency that several comments seized upon.

— “The Department’s proposal would cast arguably the widest FARA registration net in the law’s history at a time when the Attorney General is ordering a prosecutorial focus on FARA’s core,” lawyers from Caplin & Drysdale wrote in their comment on the proposed regulations, arguing that one of DOJ’s key changes “would run counter to a basic intent of the Bondi Memorandum.”

— By far the biggest target of the nearly two dozen commenters were DOJ’s proposals to revamp the FARA carveout commonly referred to as the commercial exemption for activity in furtherance of bona fide trade or commerce that does not predominantly serve a foreign interest. The department proposed to drastically narrow that exemption and adopt a new “totality of circumstances” test to determine whether an agent’s activity would predominantly benefit a foreign interest or a domestic one.

— “Rather than providing the actual ‘test,’ however, the proposed language simply lists a set of non-exhaustive factors that may or may not be among those the Department would turn to,” the law firm Sandler Reiff Lamb Rosenstein & Birkenstock wrote in its comment .

— “If changed in this way the test would no longer operate as any workable test at all , but instead would become more of an invitation for the Department to apply whichever factors it wants, whenever it wants, thus raising — instead of removing — the specter of weaponization of the Act,” the firm said.

— The provision’s critics ranged from business groups including the Association for Accessible Medicines and the American Petroleum Institute to organizations representing journalists and nonprofits, who warned that rather than undertake the administrative burden of determining whether or not they are required to register under FARA, “potentially stifling legitimate ‘political activity,’ as defined in the statute,” API argued.

— Moreover, “in many situations, organizations do not have time or resources to request an advisory opinion. Waiting for an advisory opinion before taking an action can so delay the action or speech that its meaning is then lost — chilling First Amendment protected rights,” the International Center for Not-for-Profit Law warned .

— In the same vein, commenters railed against DOJ for declining as part of the rulemaking to formally define key terms in the statute — like what would make someone an “agent” of a foreign principal. The department argued in its rulemaking that it wanted to preserve flexibility in the statute, leaving the determination up to the highly fact-specific advisory opinion process.

— The admission that “potential registrants will frequently be unable to determine whether they need to register by simply reading FARA and its regulations, but instead must turn to the advisory system process,” only underscores the statute’s existing First Amendment concerns, the ICNL argued, conceding that addressing many of those issues would require congressional action.

— “However, instead of attempting to mitigate these constitutional concerns, the Department fails to even try to address them and many of its proposed regulations would instead exacerbate them,” the group argued.

— An advocacy group representing journalists went even further. “Were FARA enforced consistent with its expansive and ambiguous text, those actions would flatly violate the First Amendment,” the Reporters Committee for Freedom of the Press said in its comments .

— By handing more enforcement discretion to DOJ, it “would heighten the possibility that FARA could be applied in the future in an arbitrary and unconstitutional way, based on news coverage that the government perceives as critical or unfavorable,” RCFP wrote.

— Several commenters who expressed fears about FARA’s ambiguity being weaponized held up real-life examples to support their arguments. “In the 118th Congress a number of nonprofits were targeted by members of Congress for potential FARA investigations,” the ICNL wrote.

— The reporters’ committee noted that lawmakers have also issued demands for foreign-owned news organizations to register under FARA. “Textually, FARA could be applied to require registration not just by virtue of ownership structure but potentially based on relationships with foreign sources, journalists, and outlets,” the group added.

— AAM and the Pennsylvania-based biopharmaceutical company CSL raised concerns about what the FARA changes — if adopted as proposed — might mean for trade groups whose membership includes foreign-based companies. The comments came after FARA-related pressure from lawmakers last year that prompted the Biotechnology Innovation Organization to drop one of its China-based members.

— Another commenter had first-hand experience with running afoul of FARA. Pierre Girgis , a dual U.S.-Egyptian citizen who pleaded guilty in 2022 to a “failure to label” FARA violation, wrote in to opine about how FARA enforcement has tended to “come down hard on certain private individuals (often those tied to adversarial regimes or lacking political clout), while similar foreign influence activities by insiders or allies are frequently overlooked.”

body_text:
REVVING UP: Chinese electronics giant Xiaomi is bolstering its lobbying roster with a former adviser to President Donald Trump , who added the company to a Pentagon blacklist on his way out of office. Mercury Public Affairs’ Bryan Lanza began working last week for the smartphone maker to “provide strategic counsel and advocate on issues pertaining to possible sanctions,” according to a disclosure filed Friday.

— Amended versions of the disclosure filed over the weekend described Lanza’s work as providing “strategic guidance and counsel regarding commercial related interests and issues affecting the technology related industry.”

— “The issues identified in the original filing were not correct and within a few hours we amended the filing to more accurately reflect the issues that we expect to be working on,” a Mercury spokesperson said in a statement to PI.

— Xiaomi, one of the world’s biggest smartphone manufacturers, was part of a tranche of Chinese companies added in January 2021 to a Pentagon blacklist for companies with alleged ties to the Chinese military. The company’s inclusion would have blocked Americans from investing in Xiaomi, but the Biden administration reversed course months later and removed Xiaomi from the list after the company challenged its inclusion in court.

— In the years since, Xiaomi has joined other Chinese tech companies in jumping into the electric vehicle market — a decision Xiaomi’s chief executive said last year stemmed directly from the 2021 blacklisting . Xiaomi is now competing in the crowded Chinese EV market with Huawei , Elon Musk ’s Tesla and BYD as Trump embarks on a trade war against Beijing . (Chinese EVs are already subject to a 100 percent tariff in the U.S.)

— In addition to Mercury, Xiaomi also retains BGR Group , to which it paid $480,000 in 2024.

MORE NEW BUSINESS: Zoox , the driverless car division of e-commerce giant Amazon , has hired its first federal lobbyists. Finch Fulton of K&L Gates , who worked in Trump’s first Transportation Department, began monitoring autonomous vehicle technology policy for Zoox the day after Trump’s inauguration, according to a newly filed disclosure.

— The hire underscores optimism among AV companies run by Google , Uber and, of course, Musk — who had criticized the sluggish pace of green-lighting the industry and whose government cost-cutting initiative has slashed the workforce of the chief agency charged with regulating self-driving cars.

— And the Vogel Group has signed Chinese sporting goods retailer Li-Ning to lobby on tariffs and sanctions, according to a disclosure. John Hesse , Alex Vogel , Samir Kapadia and Ali Khimji will work on the account for the sports merchandiser, which has faced scrutiny from members of Congress and border officials alike over its supply chains and ties to forced labor.

— Meanwhile, the U.S. animal health arm of Boehringer Ingelheim has hired Capitol Counsel to lobby on FDA’s approval process for animal drugs. John Martin , a former FDA official during Trump’s first term, is working on the account for the drugmaker, which recently launched a new vaccine that it says offers protection from bird flu .

Wallwork is also a Greg Murphy , Tom Reed , Energy Department and Energy and Commerce alum.

— “They have collected large fees from clemency seekers who would not be eligible for second chances under apolitical criteria that are intended to guide a Justice Department system for recommending mercy for those who have served their time or demonstrated remorse and a lower likelihood of recidivism.”

— “Instead, clemency petitioners are mostly circumventing that system, tailoring their pitches to the president by emphasizing their loyalty to him and echoing his claims of political persecution,” with efforts underway on behalf of convicted Fugees rapper Pras Michel , the reality TV couple Todd and Julie Chrisley and more.

title: Ozempic maker goes on mini MAGA hiring spree
body_text:
NOVO ADDS MORE TRUMP-LINKED LOBBYISTS: Danish drugmaker Novo Nordisk, which manufactures the blockbuster weight-loss drugs Ozempic and Wegovy , added another new outside lobbying firm at the start of this year, including a longtime Hill budget wonk and a key health policy official from President Donald Trump ’s first term.

— The Nickles Group began lobbying for Novo Nordisk at the end of January on tax policy and issues related to prescription drugs, according to a newly filed disclosure.

— The team working on the account includes Greg D’Angelo , who served as the health care lead in the Office of Management and Budget during Trump’s first term. D’Angelo previously spent a decade working on health issues like Medicare and Medicaid for the Senate Budget Committee, helping draft several reconciliation bills during the first Trump administration before moving to K Street, where he was not shy about offering up procedural strategies for trying to strip out key drug provisions from the Inflation Reduction Act .

— Brett Baker , a former health adviser to four top GOP tax writers in Congress — including current Senate Finance Chair Mike Crapo (R-Idaho) — is also working on the account.

— Days after retaining the Nickles Group, Novo Nordisk also hired Checkmate Government Relations , the new D.C. outpost of a North Carolina-based lobbying firm whose staff has deep ties to Trump’s inner circle and a GOP first-term lawmaker, as PI reported last month .

— The hires come at a pivotal time for the drugmaker, which dropped a company record of nearly $5.3 million on lobbying in 2024. Novo took the Biden administration to court last year over its drugs’ inclusion in the Medicare price negotiation policy created by the IRA, a policy whose fate is now in the hands of the Trump administration and Republicans in Congress.

— At the same time, manufacturers of the costly weight-loss drugs have lobbied hard to expand Medicare coverage for their popular products — which have also sparked a fight between the FDA and drug compounders angling for a piece of the pie. And the pharmaceutical industry writ large is monitoring a number of different tax provisions as well as the president’s trade war.

— Nathan Trail is joining ITI to helm the new state advocacy operation from Supernal , an electric vertical take-off and landing division of Hyundai . He previously spent a decade with the Consumer Technology Association .

— Tech lobbyists have thus far had massive success in recent years in shaping laws on some of the industry’s most high-profile issues, and the focus on influencing state legislators is only expected to grow as narrowly divided chambers of Congress grapple with other issues like taxes, border security and energy for the foreseeable future.

— Earlier this month, the left-leaning tech lobby Chamber of Progress issued a memo laying out the top tech policy fights it will be keeping an eye on as they unfold in state capitals this year, including kids safety, delivery taxes, autonomous vehicles, ticketing reforms and fintech.

CONTINENTAL ADDS A PARTNER: Tim Costa is heading back downtown after serving for the past two years as chief of staff to Rep. Dan Meuser (R-Pa.), the chair of the House Financial Services subcommittee in charge of oversight and investigations. Costa is joining Continental Strategy , where he’ll be a partner. Before coming to the Hill, Costa spent a decade at the lobbying firm Buchanan Ingersoll & Rooney PC .

AD IT UP: DHS “ skipped a fully competitive bidding process to give two Republican-linked firms the first part of a $200 million television ad campaign that lauds President Donald Trump for his crackdown on illegal immigration,” The Associated Press’ Adriana Gomez Licon reports.

— “DHS told news outlets last month that it had undergone a ‘competitive procurement process’ for the campaign. But in a document posted Friday on a federal database, the department said Trump’s declaration of a national emergency at the U.S.-Mexico border constitutes ‘an unusual and compelling urgency,’ a circumstance that allows federal agencies to bypass the usual competitive process.”

— “One of the winning firms is People Who Think, LLC , which is owned by Jay Connaughton , a Louisiana-based political consultant who served as media adviser for Trump’s 2016 campaign. Connaughton appeared to have worked as recently as October 2023 with former Trump campaign manager Corey Lewandowski in the campaign of Jeff Landry , for governor of Louisiana. Lewandowski, a longtime Noem adviser going back to her tenure as South Dakota governor, mentioned him in a post on X as part of the team that helped elect Landry.”

— “The other firm selected for the contract was Safe America Media, LLC , which was incorporated in Delaware a few days before the solicitation with an address to a property owned by Republican consultant Mike McElwain . Safe America Media has already been awarded $16 million for the ad buy.”

PREIBUS’ NEXT ACT: Reince Priebus , who served briefly as Trump’s first White House chief of staff, is joining investment bank Centerview Partners as a senior adviser, per Semafor ’s Liz Hoffman , providing the Democratic-linked firm with more MAGA-friendly cachet as the corporate world jolts to the right.

— “He’ll advise companies trying to curry favor with — or simply make sense of — Trump’s Washington, where tariffs and politically tinged investigations have markets on edge and mergers on ice.”

— “His hiring is notable at Centerview, whose co-founder Blair Effron is a big player in Democratic politics and was among Kamala Harris ’ biggest backers last year. … Robert Rubin , Treasury secretary under President Bill Clinton , has worked at the firm since 2010. Even its resident Republican heavyweight, Richard Haass , has criticized Trump’s tariffs and foreign policy.”

— “Centerview’s business is advising CEOs, and CEOs want to know how to work with Trump — or at least stay out of his line of fire. Positioning a merger as pro-America or securing carve-outs from tariffs could be worth billions of dollars. Priebus can likely make that case.”

— “ Nada Wolff Culver , who served as the Bureau of Land Management’s principal deputy director during the Biden administration, and Natalie Landreth , former Interior deputy solicitor for land resources, launched Nashoba Consulting last month, according to their LinkedIn profiles.”

— “Culver in a LinkedIn post said the consulting shop would arm organizations aiming to protect public lands. ‘There will be many fronts in the upcoming battles to protect America’s public lands and today I am proud to announce another one,’ she wrote. ‘Our mission: to protect public lands from the coming onslaught.’”

— Culver added that the firm would aim to “bring information about the conservation, protection, acquisition, and management of public lands to Tribes, and to connect NGOs and Tribes with legal and policy expertise. Tribes and NGOs need to be ready to: defend the places and policies they value, seek short-term gains, and plan to engage with an administration that is supportive of Tribal and conservation priorities. Defend, organize and plan.”

title: Top Johnson aide returns to K Street
body_text:
FIRST IN PI: Dan Ziegler , a former top aide to House Speaker Mike Johnson , is returning to his former K Street home of Williams and Jensen . Ziegler, who served as executive director of the conservative Republican Study Committee , which Johnson chaired from 2019 to 2021, was previously a partner at Williams and Jensen before joining Johnson’s office as his policy director days after he was elected speaker in 2023. Ziegler left Johnson’s office at the beginning of this year.

— “The position that I was in uniquely positions me now to be able to help existing clients, and hopefully many new clients, be able to navigate this very complex legislative landscape” and its myriad moving pieces, Ziegler told PI.

title: Lobbyists lay out an ethics roadmap for using AI
body_text:
HOW TO LOBBY WITH AI: The National Institute for Lobbying & Ethics has unveiled its first set of recommendations for the use of artificial intelligence in lobbying campaigns. The guidelines urge lobbyists to disclose when they use AI and to be transparent with stakeholders about how AI is being used, and they recommend that lobbyists “implement measures to identify and mitigate biases in AI systems.”

— Lobbyists should use the technology to “enhance civic engagement” and participation in the democratic process, the recommendations say, while also “avoiding the dissemination of misleading or false information” with the help of AI.

— NILE also wants lobbyists to adopt several data privacy best practices as they incorporate AI into advocacy work, including obtaining informed consent for data collection that will be used in advocacy involving the use of AI, being transparent about data ownership and making sure data is secure.

— NILE first set to work last year to craft the new guidelines, which board Chair Paul Miller said draw on “extensive input from professionals across the industry.” But the organization stressed the ethics guardrails will continue to evolve along with advancements in AI and how it’s used to sway public opinion and shape policy.

— In addition to the recommendations laid out today, NILE said it’s working on several other related projects, including developing an AI ethics training program for members, standing up an internal watchdog committee and compliance mechanisms and crafting a standardized AI disclosure framework for the industry to adopt.

— The group is also planning to push for changes to the nation’s lobbying laws, calling for a “comprehensive rewrite” of the Lobbying Disclosure Act to modernize and update the statute to account for technological advances in the influence industry.

HOW TO LOBBY WITH AI: The National Institute for Lobbying & Ethics has unveiled its first set of recommendations for the use of artificial intelligence in lobbying campaigns. The guidelines urge lobbyists to disclose when they use AI and to be transparent with stakeholders about how AI is being used, and they recommend that lobbyists “implement measures to identify and mitigate biases in AI systems.”

— Lobbyists should use the technology to “enhance civic engagement” and participation in the democratic process, the recommendations say, while also “avoiding the dissemination of misleading or false information” with the help of AI.

— NILE also wants lobbyists to adopt several data privacy best practices as they incorporate AI into advocacy work, including obtaining informed consent for data collection that will be used in advocacy involving the use of AI, being transparent about data ownership and making sure data is secure.

— NILE first set to work last year to craft the new guidelines, which board Chair Paul Miller said draw on “extensive input from professionals across the industry.” But the organization stressed the ethics guardrails will continue to evolve along with advancements in AI and how it’s used to sway public opinion and shape policy.

— In addition to the recommendations laid out today, NILE said it’s working on several other related projects, including developing an AI ethics training program for members, standing up an internal watchdog committee and compliance mechanisms and crafting a standardized AI disclosure framework for the industry to adopt.

— The group is also planning to push for changes to the nation’s lobbying laws, calling for a “comprehensive rewrite” of the Lobbying Disclosure Act to modernize and update the statute to account for technological advances in the influence industry.

title: The lobbyist who rejected Harvard
body_text:
FIRST IN PI — MILLER DECLINED TO HELP HARVARD: Top GOP fundraiser Jeff Miller turned down an offer to represent Harvard University in February as the institution took on heavy fire from the Trump administration, two people familiar with the matter told your PI host and Daniel. Miller’s decision deprived the Ivy League school of a second lobbyist with strong connections to the White House ahead of its rapidly escalating standoff with President Donald Trump .

— A month earlier, in January, another Trump-connected firm, Ballard Partners , signed up Harvard for a retainer of $90,000 per quarter to provide “advocacy supporting education and educational research.” The firm’s founder, Brian Ballard , found himself in the crosshairs of Trump White House officials in recent weeks before scoring an Oval Office sitdown with Trump.

— Altogether, Harvard dropped $230,000 on federal lobbying during the first quarter of this year, up from $170,000 during the last three months of 2024 and $130,000 during the same time a year ago. The university also retains O’Neill, Athy & Casey . A spokesperson for Harvard didn’t respond to a request for comment.

— Ballard signed Harvard in early January, weeks before Trump’s new administration began its broader crackdown on college campuses. Ballard also represents the University of Michigan and Vanderbilt University .

— In this administration, lobbyists and lawyers need to pay attention to how potential or existing clients are viewed by the president. Trump wasn’t pleased, for example, when he learned that Quinn Emanuel lawyer Bill Burck was representing Harvard as a client at the same time he was working for the Trump Organization.

— In short order, Burck was fired by the Trump Organization . An attorney whom the Trump Org had hailed months earlier as “one of the nation’s finest and most respected lawyers” was dismissed by Trump in April as “not that good, anyway.”

— Ballard dropped POLITICO parent company Axel Springer earlier this month, but the firm still represents PBS , for which Trump has moved to revoke federal funds. And both Ballard and Miller represent Big Law firms that cut deals with the president earlier this year in order to avoid being targeted by executive orders. Miller also represents several other universities punished by Trump, including Cornell , Northwestern and Johns Hopkins .
