title: Brownstein launches a public affairs practice
body_text:
FIRST IN PI: Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck is forming a public affairs practice, opening up one more stream of revenue for the law firm and K Street’s top-earning lobbying shop. Brownstein has brought on Fora Partners co-founders Campbell Spencer and Max Hamel to lead the new practice, along with Sean Bartlett and Kristina Baum , who will be senior managers.

— Spencer and Hamel founded Fora in 2019. They’ve both worked at some of D.C.’s biggest public affairs shops. Spencer is an alum of the Obama administration, and Hamel previously worked for Republican former Virginia Gov. Jim Gilmore .

— Bartlett was most recently a deputy assistant secretary of State during the Biden administration and has served as a spokesperson for several top Democrats in Congress over the years. Baum joins from American Veterinary Medical Association , where she was director of strategic communications, and is an alum of the first Trump administration.

— A growing number of D.C. lobbying firms have added in-house strategic communications or public affairs offerings in recent years — though plenty have practices already — or else hired out for big jobs. Public affairs campaigns have become a more integral part of advocacy work with the rise of social media and hyperpartisanship.

— “We’re in this permanent political cycle, and that tends to reinforce the very reactive tendencies of either a closely divided Congress or state house or executive branch agencies,” Hamel told PI. “I think the concept is very straightforward: that firms that can wage a multi-dimensional effort that combines lobbying with public affairs and communications are going to have an advantage.”

— So in many ways, this was a long time coming for a firm that brought in more than $67 million in lobbying revenues last year. Nadeam Elshami , who co-chairs Brownstein’s lobbying practice, said in an interview that the firm had been debating the idea of adding a public affairs group on and off for at least as long as he’d been there. But those discussions got more serious over the past three years. “It took a while, but finding the right individuals, the right team, was paramount, and we did,” he said.

— “Brownstein’s clients have really been asking for this, as have ours,” Spencer told PI. “With the policy landscape being as fast-moving as it is, clients really want and are demanding strategic alignment across all of these advocacy verticals … and this partnership allows us to deliver that for them.”

— Bringing public affairs work in-house “completes the circle of giving our clients and prospective clients all the best ways to advance their priorities” within the Beltway and beyond, Elshami added.

AFP DEFENDS MEGABILL’S PRICE TAG: As select Republicans in Congress and a certain tech mogul duke it out with the White House and party leadership over the reconciliation bill, Americans for Prosperity is working to tamp down angst over the megabill’s effect on the national debt.

— “AFP fully supports efforts to root out more waste, fraud, and abuse now and in the future,” Emily Seidel , the Koch-funded conservative group’s president and CEO, said in a statement. But, she argued, sinking the reconciliation bill “because it doesn’t solve our debt crisis is reckless and wrong.”

— Seidel’s backing of the megabill isn’t new: AFP has pledged to spend $20 million getting Republicans’ extension of the 2017 tax cuts, which AFP also supported, over the finish line.

— But it’s still a striking stand by an organization that made a name for itself in part for its demands to shrink the budget deficit. And it comes one day after a Congressional Budget Office forecast that the House-passed package would increase the debt by $2.4 trillion over a decade .

— Seidel maintained that Republicans can and should get to tackling the deficit — after clearing the reconciliation bill. “We didn’t get here overnight, and Washington isn’t going to fix it with one bill,” she continued, adding that “even if this bill cuts enough spending to be fully offset, we’re still on a course for bankruptcy that requires comprehensive reforms to how Congress makes spending decisions.”

Happy Thursday and welcome to PI . What last-minute maneuvering are you doing over in the Senate? Which megabill lobbying battles are flying under the radar? You can add me on Signal , email me at [email protected] , and be sure to follow me on X : @caitlinoprysko .

WE GOOFED: Yesterday’s edition misstated which clients are joining Len Wolfson at his new firm. America’s Credit Unions and DeFi Education Fund are staying with Fed Hall Policy Advisors.

AUTOMAKER TROUBLES: The Alliance for Automotive Innovation has yet to present a unified public message on the Republicans’ megabill, as automakers have failed to reach a consensus on the legislation, our James Bikales writes. The rift comes as the Senate considers major rollbacks to electric vehicle and manufacturing tax credits.

— “The trade group had strongly defended the credits in Democrats’ climate law last year, and in recent months warned that rolling them back would threaten U.S. competitiveness and national security, given China’s heavy investment in EV manufacturing.”

— “But even as the Senate has moved quickly to take up the bill, the Alliance has yet to take a public stance because its members have failed to reach consensus on changes to a key tax credit claimed by automakers for producing EV batteries, according to the four people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive internal dynamics.”

ON THE AIRWAVES: Protect Our Jobs , a pro-clean-energy group, is running $1 million in TV and digital ads warning key Senate Republicans against following the House’s plan to in some cases sunset — and in other places eviscerate — the green tax credits created by the Biden-era climate law, our friends at Inside Congress report.

— “These politicians promised to bring down our monthly costs. But cutting America’s energy production will only make our costs go up,” the narrator says in the ad, which began running Monday on “Fox & Friends” and in the D.C. area, and will on Friday move into Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina and Utah.

— Sens. Jerry Moran of Kansas, John Curtis of Utah and Thom Tillis of North Carolina have all urged GOP leadership not to follow through with a full-scale repeal of the credits, warning it could harm investments back home. Tillis, who faces a potentially difficult reelection fight in his purple state, expressed some cautious optimism Wednesday that Senate Republicans want to find a “glide path” for businesses that already have projects in motion using the credits, but didn’t elaborate.

FLYING IN: The American Fleet Leadership Coalition , launched earlier this year to try and salvage the IRA’s tax credit for commercial electric vehicles, wrapped up a two-day fly-in today aimed at rallying support for the provision. The tax credit would wind down this year under the House-passed megabill.

— The coalition was slated to meet with members of the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee to make the case that incentivizing fleet upgrades will reduce overhead costs for businesses, nonprofits and municipalities, while boosting domestic manufacturing goals.

— And health executives across the industry convened in D.C. this week for the Healthcare Leadership Council ’s membership meeting, where they heard from officials including CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz and Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.).

— On the Hill, executives met with lawmakers from both parties, including Reps. Jake Auchincloss (D-Mass.), Buddy Carter (R-Ga.) and Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) to press for permanently extending enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits and telehealth permissions, among other things.

AI GOES TO WASHINGTON: Two privately held AI companies, OpenAI and Anthropic , are now ramping up their lobbying efforts and chasing contracts from the roughly $75 billion federal IT budget that largely focuses on AI, our Mohar Chatterjee writes. The two companies are increasing their Washington staff, and are among a handful of other AI companies expanding their lobbying efforts.

— Scale AI , a specialist contractor with the Pentagon and other agencies, has plans to expand its lobbying teams. And AI-focused chipmaker Nvidia hired its first in-house lobbyist in late March.

— “This lobbying push aims to capitalize on a wave of support from both the Trump administration and the Republican Congress, both of which have pumped up the AI industry as a linchpin of American competitiveness and a means for shrinking the federal workforce.”

DOG DAYS: Blue Dog Coalition , a caucus of the more moderate House members of the Democratic party, is launching a super PAC and nonprofit to take unlimited donations, Shane Goldmacher and Reid J. Epstein write for The New York Times .

— “The new nonprofit, which has not been previously reported, will be called the Blue Dog Action Fund, with Aisha Woodward , a former chief of staff to [Rep. Jared ] Golden , serving as executive director and overseeing a staff of five.”

— Blue Dog’s new fundraising efforts took place on the heels of WelcomeFest, a conference held Wednesday for center-left groups to discuss winning strategies for the Democratic Party.

HERE COMES HYDROGEN: “More than 200 organizations — including the regional hydrogen hub developers and major oil and gas trade groups — are pressing Republican senators to preserve the Inflation Reduction Act’s hydrogen production tax credit” in the reconciliation bill, per POLITICO ’s Kelsey Tamborrino .

— “In a letter to Senate leaders sent on Thursday, the organizations call for the hydrogen tax credit to remain in place for projects that commence construction by Dec. 31, 2029. That timeline would provide a runway for the industry to advance projects already in multiyear development cycles, they argue. ‘Anything less puts billions in committed investments — and tens of thousands of jobs — at risk,’ the groups wrote on Thursday.”

— The letter’s signatories include the Fuel Cell and Hydrogen Energy Association , American Petroleum Institute , National Association of Manufacturers , U.S. Chamber of Commerce and American Chemistry Council , Plug Power , Cummins and Toyota Motor North America .

FIRST IN PI: Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck is forming a public affairs practice, opening up one more stream of revenue for the law firm and K Street’s top-earning lobbying shop. Brownstein has brought on Fora Partners co-founders Campbell Spencer and Max Hamel to lead the new practice, along with Sean Bartlett and Kristina Baum, who will be senior managers.

— Spencer and Hamel founded Fora in 2019. They’ve both worked at some of D.C.’s biggest public affairs shops. Spencer is an alum of the Obama administration, and Hamel previously worked for Republican former Virginia Gov. Jim Gilmore.

— Bartlett was most recently a deputy assistant secretary of State during the Biden administration and has served as a spokesperson for several top Democrats in Congress over the years. Baum joins from American Veterinary Medical Association, where she was director of strategic communications, and is an alum of the first Trump administration.

— A growing number of D.C. lobbying firms have added in-house strategic communications or public affairs offerings in recent years — though plenty have practices already — or else hired out for big jobs. Public affairs campaigns have become a more integral part of advocacy work with the rise of social media and hyperpartisanship.

— “We’re in this permanent political cycle, and that tends to reinforce the very reactive tendencies of either a closely divided Congress or state house or executive branch agencies,” Hamel told PI. “I think the concept is very straightforward: that firms that can wage a multi-dimensional effort that combines lobbying with public affairs and communications are going to have an advantage.”

— So in many ways, this was a long time coming for a firm that brought in more than $67 million in lobbying revenues last year. Nadeam Elshami, who co-chairs Brownstein’s lobbying practice, said in an interview that the firm had been debating the idea of adding a public affairs group on and off for at least as long as he’d been there. But those discussions got more serious over the past three years. “It took a while, but finding the right individuals, the right team, was paramount, and we did,” he said.

— “Brownstein’s clients have really been asking for this, as have ours,” Spencer told PI. “With the policy landscape being as fast-moving as it is, clients really want and are demanding strategic alignment across all of these advocacy verticals … and this partnership allows us to deliver that for them.”

— Bringing public affairs work in-house “completes the circle of giving our clients and prospective clients all the best ways to advance their priorities” within the Beltway and beyond, Elshami added.

AFP DEFENDS MEGABILL’S PRICE TAG: As select Republicans in Congress and a certain tech mogul duke it out with the White House and party leadership over the reconciliation bill, Americans for Prosperity is working to tamp down angst over the megabill’s effect on the national debt.

— “AFP fully supports efforts to root out more waste, fraud, and abuse now and in the future,” Emily Seidel, the Koch-funded conservative group’s president and CEO, said in a statement. But, she argued, sinking the reconciliation bill “because it doesn’t solve our debt crisis is reckless and wrong.”

— Seidel’s backing of the megabill isn’t new: AFP has pledged to spend $20 million getting Republicans’ extension of the 2017 tax cuts, which AFP also supported, over the finish line.

— But it’s still a striking stand by an organization that made a name for itself in part for its demands to shrink the budget deficit. And it comes one day after a Congressional Budget Office forecast that the House-passed package would increase the debt by $2.4 trillion over a decade.

— Seidel maintained that Republicans can and should get to tackling the deficit — after clearing the reconciliation bill. “We didn’t get here overnight, and Washington isn’t going to fix it with one bill,” she continued, adding that “even if this bill cuts enough spending to be fully offset, we’re still on a course for bankruptcy that requires comprehensive reforms to how Congress makes spending decisions.”

Happy Thursday and welcome to PI. What last-minute maneuvering are you doing over in the Senate? Which megabill lobbying battles are flying under the radar? You can add me on Signal, email me at [email protected], and be sure to follow me on X: @caitlinoprysko.

WE GOOFED: Yesterday’s edition misstated which clients are joining Len Wolfson at his new firm. America’s Credit Unions and DeFi Education Fund are staying with Fed Hall Policy Advisors.

AUTOMAKER TROUBLES: The Alliance for Automotive Innovation has yet to present a unified public message on the Republicans’ megabill, as automakers have failed to reach a consensus on the legislation, our James Bikales writes. The rift comes as the Senate considers major rollbacks to electric vehicle and manufacturing tax credits.

— “The trade group had strongly defended the credits in Democrats’ climate law last year, and in recent months warned that rolling them back would threaten U.S. competitiveness and national security, given China’s heavy investment in EV manufacturing.”

— “But even as the Senate has moved quickly to take up the bill, the Alliance has yet to take a public stance because its members have failed to reach consensus on changes to a key tax credit claimed by automakers for producing EV batteries, according to the four people, who spoke on condition of anonymity to discuss sensitive internal dynamics.”

ON THE AIRWAVES: Protect Our Jobs, a pro-clean-energy group, is running $1 million in TV and digital ads warning key Senate Republicans against following the House’s plan to in some cases sunset — and in other places eviscerate — the green tax credits created by the Biden-era climate law, our friends at Inside Congress report.

— “These politicians promised to bring down our monthly costs. But cutting America’s energy production will only make our costs go up,” the narrator says in the ad, which began running Monday on “Fox & Friends” and in the D.C. area, and will on Friday move into Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina and Utah.

— Sens. Jerry Moran of Kansas, John Curtis of Utah and Thom Tillis of North Carolina have all urged GOP leadership not to follow through with a full-scale repeal of the credits, warning it could harm investments back home. Tillis, who faces a potentially difficult reelection fight in his purple state, expressed some cautious optimism Wednesday that Senate Republicans want to find a “glide path” for businesses that already have projects in motion using the credits, but didn’t elaborate.

FLYING IN: The American Fleet Leadership Coalition, launched earlier this year to try and salvage the IRA’s tax credit for commercial electric vehicles, wrapped up a two-day fly-in today aimed at rallying support for the provision. The tax credit would wind down this year under the House-passed megabill.

— The coalition was slated to meet with members of the tax-writing Senate Finance Committee to make the case that incentivizing fleet upgrades will reduce overhead costs for businesses, nonprofits and municipalities, while boosting domestic manufacturing goals.

— And health executives across the industry convened in D.C. this week for the Healthcare Leadership Council’s membership meeting, where they heard from officials including CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz and Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-Del.).

— On the Hill, executives met with lawmakers from both parties, including Reps. Jake Auchincloss (D-Mass.), Buddy Carter (R-Ga.) and Sen. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) to press for permanently extending enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits and telehealth permissions, among other things.

AI GOES TO WASHINGTON: Two privately held AI companies, OpenAI and Anthropic, are now ramping up their lobbying efforts and chasing contracts from the roughly $75 billion federal IT budget that largely focuses on AI, our Mohar Chatterjee writes. The two companies are increasing their Washington staff, and are among a handful of other AI companies expanding their lobbying efforts.

— Scale AI, a specialist contractor with the Pentagon and other agencies, has plans to expand its lobbying teams. And AI-focused chipmaker Nvidia hired its first in-house lobbyist in late March.

— “This lobbying push aims to capitalize on a wave of support from both the Trump administration and the Republican Congress, both of which have pumped up the AI industry as a linchpin of American competitiveness and a means for shrinking the federal workforce.”

DOG DAYS: Blue Dog Coalition, a caucus of the more moderate House members of the Democratic party, is launching a super PAC and nonprofit to take unlimited donations, Shane Goldmacher and Reid J. Epstein write for The New York Times.

— “The new nonprofit, which has not been previously reported, will be called the Blue Dog Action Fund, with Aisha Woodward, a former chief of staff to [Rep. Jared] Golden, serving as executive director and overseeing a staff of five.”

— Blue Dog’s new fundraising efforts took place on the heels of WelcomeFest, a conference held Wednesday for center-left groups to discuss winning strategies for the Democratic Party.

HERE COMES HYDROGEN: “More than 200 organizations — including the regional hydrogen hub developers and major oil and gas trade groups — are pressing Republican senators to preserve the Inflation Reduction Act’s hydrogen production tax credit” in the reconciliation bill, per POLITICO’s Kelsey Tamborrino.

— “In a letter to Senate leaders sent on Thursday, the organizations call for the hydrogen tax credit to remain in place for projects that commence construction by Dec. 31, 2029. That timeline would provide a runway for the industry to advance projects already in multiyear development cycles, they argue. ‘Anything less puts billions in committed investments — and tens of thousands of jobs — at risk,’ the groups wrote on Thursday.”

— The letter’s signatories include the Fuel Cell and Hydrogen Energy Association, American Petroleum Institute, National Association of Manufacturers, U.S. Chamber of Commerce and American Chemistry Council, Plug Power, Cummins and Toyota Motor North America.

title: The New York Times lobbies up
body_text:
FIRST IN PI — NYT HIRES BROWNSTEIN: The New York Times has registered to lobby for the first time in more than a decade. The news giant has retained K Street heavyweight Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck to represent it on a range of issues affecting the industry, from encroachments on press freedoms to the threats posed by artificial intelligence.

— The Times’ parent company first hired Brownstein last year, but the firm’s work didn’t trigger lobbying registration requirements until April, according to a spokesperson for the company and a draft disclosure filing shared with PI. More than half a dozen lobbyists are listed as working on the account for Brownstein: Republicans Marc Lampkin , Will Moschella and Greta Joynes and Democrats Al Mottur , Alice Lugo , Rob Robillard and John Menges .

— One issue drawing the paper off the lobbying sidelines is the increasing ubiquity of artificial intelligence and the thorny issues it poses for news organizations. The Times, for example, introduced a suite of AI tools for internal use earlier this year. And many news outlets ( including the Times , POLITICO and parent company Axel Springer ) have partnered with AI companies on licensing deals and consumer-facing products.

— But NYT is also one of several publishers facing off in court against ChatGPT creator OpenAI or other AI companies accused of copyright infringement for using outlets’ content to train its models without permission or compensation.

— In a congressional hearing on the issue last year, Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) warned that AI was “literally eating away at the lifeblood of our democracy” and contributing to an “existential crisis” among local publishers in particular. The last Congress also mulled legislation that would require online platforms like Google and Meta to negotiate with and pay news publishers in exchange for hosting their content.

— At the same time, Times publisher A.G. Sulzberger has been repeatedly sounding the alarm about threats to press freedom both around the world and from leaders in the U.S.

— In a speech last month that was republished as an essay in the Times, Sulzberger took note of President Donald Trump ’s escalating pressure campaign against news outlets already in his second term — from curtailing access to certain mainstream outlets in favor of friendlier partisan ones to suing, seeking to defund or opening federal probes of others and calling for the jailing of reporters.

— “It takes significant time, effort, and resources to produce The New York Times’s fact-based original journalism and other content. Because of that, we have for years taken steps to protect and defend our intellectual property rights and uphold its value,” a Times spokesperson told PI in a statement.

— “In line with these efforts, we have engaged a Washington, DC-based government affairs firm to ensure our rights and legal protections are clearly and accurately represented among policymakers and regulators focused on publishing, media, copyright law and press freedoms,” it added.

— The Times hasn’t lobbied at the federal level since 2014, when the company paid Keightley & Ashner $30,000 for three quarters of work related to a pension issue.

ALL ABOUT AVA: A coalition of budget airlines this week launched the Association of Value Airlines , a new industry group aimed at boosting low-budget carriers in policy debates often dominated by the trade association representing major carriers, Airlines for America . AVA’s founding members include Allegiant , Avelo , Frontier , Spirit and Sun Country .

— Chris Brown currently serves as the group’s interim executive director. He previously was vice president of legislative and regulatory affairs at larger industry trade association Airlines for America, and lobbied for low-fare airlines at the National Air Carrier Association .

— In an interview with PI, Brown said the goal of AVA is to amplify the priorities of budget airlines, as larger organizations encompassing a range of air carriers often lead to competing priorities. Those priorities, Brown said, include a focus on rising costs due to the pilot shortage and the implementation of simulator training programs within the current 1,500-hour training requirement for pilots.

— While the budget airlines business model thrived during the pandemic, they’re now at an inflection point, Brown said. Brown attributes these airlines’ success to ancillary fees, a model that other high-budget airlines have started to mirror. Southwest Airlines , for example, announced in March plans to do away with its free checked bag policy.

— “It’s a critical time for our carriers, because of where they are financially and wanting to take advantage of what should be a more favorable regulatory environment with the Trump administration,” Brown said.

PAUL WEISS LOSES ANOTHER BIG NAME: Another prominent lawyer has left Paul Weiss Rifkind Wharton & Garrison after the law firm struck a deal with the Trump administration to avoid being punished by an executive order.

— Damian Williams , the former U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, left the firm after just five months to join Jenner & Block as the co-chair of its litigation department and investigations, compliance and defense practice.

— Williams served as one of the nation’s top federal prosecutors during the Biden administration, securing several high-profile convictions including those of former crypto kingmaker Sam Bankman-Fried and former Sen. Bob Menendez (D-N.J.).

— Williams is the latest in a string of notable departures from Paul Weiss in the aftermath of its deal with the White House. Top Democratic attorney Karen Dunn and former top DOJ official Jeannie Rhee left the firm along with two other partners last month.

— But Williams’ landing spot is almost more notable: Jenner & Block became one of the first white shoe law firms targeted by Trump to take the president to court over his executive orders — and so far, they’ve been winning .

OFF TARGET: “A top Democratic organization strongly encouraged state campaigns to do much of their digital ad-buying business with a company that one of its members is set to soon join as CEO — a development that has puzzled and concerned some party insiders,” POLITICO ’s Holly Otterbein and Daniel report.

— “At a meeting in Little Rock, Arkansas last week, the Association of State Democratic Committees — an umbrella group for state parties — voted to recommend state races use one liberal firm, TargetSmart , for a major portion of digital ad buys, which could be worth millions.”

— “TargetSmart announced on May 7 that Liz Walters , outgoing chair of the Ohio Democratic Party, is taking over as CEO this summer. Walters, who made her departure public in a post on X, said she would leave the state party role by June 30. And until the week before the group’s meeting, she was part of the ASDC’s leadership team as treasurer.”

— Though Walters recused herself from the TargetSmart vote, the incident is prompting fears among the party of even the appearance of a conflict of interest as Democrats struggle to find their footing.

BLAST RADIUS: “The spectacular breakup between Elon Musk and President Donald Trump threatens to leave Tesla with few political friends ,” POLITICO ’s David Ferris reports. “Musk has spent the past few months alienating the electric automaker’s base of climate-minded car buyers by moonlighting as Trump’s government-slasher-in-chief. Now, the billionaire’s fixation on the GOP megabill has opened a dangerous rift with the president, who threatened Thursday to end all subsidies to Musk’s companies.”

— Musk’s competitors in the space industry, meanwhile, are already moving to take advantage of the split , according to our Sam Skove . The SpaceX founder has long been an avid proponent of next bringing humans to Mars, rather than the moon.

— But in some of the first significant pushback against Musk and SpaceX, “a number of major space companies … are launching an ad campaign going big on the moon, according to two industry officials granted anonymity to discuss the effort.”

— “A separate letter addressed to the Senate Commerce Committee, and obtained by POLITICO, backs investments in the moon, and is signed by a lengthy slate of prominent space companies — but not SpaceX.”

RELATED READ: “What do Musk and Tesla want from the Republican megabill?” by E&E News’ Kelsey Brugger .

SHE MEANS BUSINESS: Casey Means , Trump’s new nominee to be U.S. surgeon general, “ has repeatedly said the nation’s medical, health and food systems are corrupted by special interests and people out to make a profit at the expense of Americans’ health,” The Associated Press’ Michelle R. Smith and Ali Swenson write.

— But as Means “has criticized scientists, medical schools and regulators for taking money from the food and pharmaceutical industries, she has promoted dozens of health and wellness products — including specialty basil seed supplements, a blood testing service and a prepared meal delivery service — in ways that put money in her own pocket.”

— “In her newsletter, on her social media accounts, on her website, in her book and during podcast appearances, the entrepreneur and influencer has at times failed to disclose that she could profit or benefit in other ways from sales of products she recommends. In some cases, she promoted companies in which she was an investor or adviser without consistently disclosing the connection, the AP found.”

AI GROUP STAFFS UP: AI advocacy group Americans for Responsible Innovation is adding four new staffers to its policy team, Morning Tech reports. Brandie Nonnecke , previously an associate research professor at the UC Berkeley Goldman School of Public Policy, is now a senior policy director, while Rachel Hovde is joining as director of policy. She previously served as a senior advisor at the Bureau of Industry and Security.

— Sarah Kessel , who worked under former Senate Energy and Natural Resources Chair Sen. Joe Manchin (D-W.V.), is now ARI’s manager of government affairs, and Evan Sarnor has joined as a legislative analyst from Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld .

The New York Times lobbies up

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO 

06/06/2025 07:05 PM EDT

Presented by

With Katherine Long, Daniel Lippman

FIRST IN PI — NYT HIRES BROWNSTEIN: The New York Times has registered to lobby for the first time in more than a decade. The news giant has retained K Street heavyweight Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck to represent it on a range of issues affecting the industry, from encroachments on press freedoms to the threats posed by artificial intelligence.

— The Times’ parent company first hired Brownstein last year, but the firm’s work didn’t trigger lobbying registration requirements until April, according to a spokesperson for the company and a draft disclosure filing shared with PI. More than half a dozen lobbyists are listed as working on the account for Brownstein: Republicans Marc Lampkin, Will Moschella and Greta Joynes and Democrats Al Mottur, Alice Lugo, Rob Robillard and John Menges.

— One issue drawing the paper off the lobbying sidelines is the increasing ubiquity of artificial intelligence and the thorny issues it poses for news organizations. The Times, for example, introduced a suite of AI tools for internal use earlier this year. And many news outlets (including the Times, POLITICO and parent company Axel Springer) have partnered with AI companies on licensing deals and consumer-facing products.

— But NYT is also one of several publishers facing off in court against ChatGPT creator OpenAI or other AI companies accused of copyright infringement for using outlets’ content to train its models without permission or compensation.

— In a congressional hearing on the issue last year, Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) warned that AI was “literally eating away at the lifeblood of our democracy” and contributing to an “existential crisis” among local publishers in particular. The last Congress also mulled legislation that would require online platforms like Google and Meta to negotiate with and pay news publishers in exchange for hosting their content.

— At the same time, Times publisher A.G. Sulzberger has been repeatedly sounding the alarm about threats to press freedom both around the world and from leaders in the U.S.

— In a speech last month that was republished as an essay in the Times, Sulzberger took note of President Donald Trump’s escalating pressure campaign against news outlets already in his second term — from curtailing access to certain mainstream outlets in favor of friendlier partisan ones to suing, seeking to defund or opening federal probes of others and calling for the jailing of reporters.

— “It takes significant time, effort, and resources to produce The New York Times’s fact-based original journalism and other content. Because of that, we have for years taken steps to protect and defend our intellectual property rights and uphold its value,” a Times spokesperson told PI in a statement.

— “In line with these efforts, we have engaged a Washington, DC-based government affairs firm to ensure our rights and legal protections are clearly and accurately represented among policymakers and regulators focused on publishing, media, copyright law and press freedoms,” it added.

— The Times hasn’t lobbied at the federal level since 2014, when the company paid Keightley & Ashner $30,000 for three quarters of work related to a pension issue.

ALL ABOUT AVA: A coalition of budget airlines this week launched the Association of Value Airlines, a new industry group aimed at boosting low-budget carriers in policy debates often dominated by the trade association representing major carriers, Airlines for America. AVA’s founding members include Allegiant, Avelo, Frontier, Spirit and Sun Country.

— Chris Brown currently serves as the group’s interim executive director. He previously was vice president of legislative and regulatory affairs at larger industry trade association Airlines for America, and lobbied for low-fare airlines at the National Air Carrier Association.

— In an interview with PI, Brown said the goal of AVA is to amplify the priorities of budget airlines, as larger organizations encompassing a range of air carriers often lead to competing priorities. Those priorities, Brown said, include a focus on rising costs due to the pilot shortage and the implementation of simulator training programs within the current 1,500-hour training requirement for pilots.

— While the budget airlines business model thrived during the pandemic, they’re now at an inflection point, Brown said. Brown attributes these airlines’ success to ancillary fees, a model that other high-budget airlines have started to mirror. Southwest Airlines, for example, announced in March plans to do away with its free checked bag policy.

— “It’s a critical time for our carriers, because of where they are financially and wanting to take advantage of what should be a more favorable regulatory environment with the Trump administration,” Brown said.

PAUL WEISS LOSES ANOTHER BIG NAME: Another prominent lawyer has left Paul Weiss Rifkind Wharton & Garrison after the law firm struck a deal with the Trump administration to avoid being punished by an executive order.

— Damian Williams, the former U.S. attorney for the Southern District of New York, left the firm after just five months to join Jenner & Block as the co-chair of its litigation department and investigations, compliance and defense practice.

— Williams served as one of the nation’s top federal prosecutors during the Biden administration, securing several high-profile convictions including those of former crypto kingmaker Sam Bankman-Fried and former Sen. Bob Menendez (D-N.J.).

— Williams is the latest in a string of notable departures from Paul Weiss in the aftermath of its deal with the White House. Top Democratic attorney Karen Dunn and former top DOJ official Jeannie Rhee left the firm along with two other partners last month.

— But Williams’ landing spot is almost more notable: Jenner & Block became one of the first white shoe law firms targeted by Trump to take the president to court over his executive orders — and so far, they’ve been winning.

OFF TARGET: “A top Democratic organization strongly encouraged state campaigns to do much of their digital ad-buying business with a company that one of its members is set to soon join as CEO — a development that has puzzled and concerned some party insiders,” POLITICO’s Holly Otterbein and Daniel report.

— “At a meeting in Little Rock, Arkansas last week, the Association of State Democratic Committees — an umbrella group for state parties — voted to recommend state races use one liberal firm, TargetSmart, for a major portion of digital ad buys, which could be worth millions.”

— “TargetSmart announced on May 7 that Liz Walters, outgoing chair of the Ohio Democratic Party, is taking over as CEO this summer. Walters, who made her departure public in a post on X, said she would leave the state party role by June 30. And until the week before the group’s meeting, she was part of the ASDC’s leadership team as treasurer.”

— Though Walters recused herself from the TargetSmart vote, the incident is prompting fears among the party of even the appearance of a conflict of interest as Democrats struggle to find their footing.

BLAST RADIUS: “The spectacular breakup between Elon Musk and President Donald Trump threatens to leave Tesla with few political friends,” POLITICO’s David Ferris reports. “Musk has spent the past few months alienating the electric automaker’s base of climate-minded car buyers by moonlighting as Trump’s government-slasher-in-chief. Now, the billionaire’s fixation on the GOP megabill has opened a dangerous rift with the president, who threatened Thursday to end all subsidies to Musk’s companies.”

— Musk’s competitors in the space industry, meanwhile, are already moving to take advantage of the split, according to our Sam Skove. The SpaceX founder has long been an avid proponent of next bringing humans to Mars, rather than the moon.

— But in some of the first significant pushback against Musk and SpaceX, “a number of major space companies … are launching an ad campaign going big on the moon, according to two industry officials granted anonymity to discuss the effort.”

— “A separate letter addressed to the Senate Commerce Committee, and obtained by POLITICO, backs investments in the moon, and is signed by a lengthy slate of prominent space companies — but not SpaceX.”

RELATED READ: “What do Musk and Tesla want from the Republican megabill?” by E&E News’ Kelsey Brugger.

SHE MEANS BUSINESS: Casey Means, Trump’s new nominee to be U.S. surgeon general, “has repeatedly said the nation’s medical, health and food systems are corrupted by special interests and people out to make a profit at the expense of Americans’ health,” The Associated Press’ Michelle R. Smith and Ali Swenson write.

— But as Means “has criticized scientists, medical schools and regulators for taking money from the food and pharmaceutical industries, she has promoted dozens of health and wellness products — including specialty basil seed supplements, a blood testing service and a prepared meal delivery service — in ways that put money in her own pocket.”

— “In her newsletter, on her social media accounts, on her website, in her book and during podcast appearances, the entrepreneur and influencer has at times failed to disclose that she could profit or benefit in other ways from sales of products she recommends. In some cases, she promoted companies in which she was an investor or adviser without consistently disclosing the connection, the AP found.”

AI GROUP STAFFS UP: AI advocacy group Americans for Responsible Innovation is adding four new staffers to its policy team, Morning Tech reports. Brandie Nonnecke, previously an associate research professor at the UC Berkeley Goldman School of Public Policy, is now a senior policy director, while Rachel Hovde is joining as director of policy. She previously served as a senior advisor at the Bureau of Industry and Security.

— Sarah Kessel, who worked under former Senate Energy and Natural Resources Chair Sen. Joe Manchin (D-W.V.), is now ARI’s manager of government affairs, and Evan Sarnor has joined as a legislative analyst from Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld.

title: Rick Scott’s chief headed to Continental
body_text:
CONTINENTAL ADDS ANOTHER FLORIDA MAN: Continental Strategy is adding yet another tie to a powerful Floridian in Washington with the hire of Sen. Rick Scott ’s (R-Fla.) former top aide. Craig Carbone , who’s worked for Scott for a decade, most recently as chief of staff, is joining Continental’s D.C. office as a partner.

— Carbone joined Scott’s Florida gubernatorial office in 2015 as deputy chief of staff, and followed Scott up to D.C. in 2019 when he joined the Senate. He’ll join an already-deep bench of Floridians at Continental that includes founder Carlos Trujillo , a former state lawmaker who served in President Donald Trump ’s first administration, as well as the former chief of staff to now-Secretary of State Marco Rubio , a daughter of White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and a former staffer to Rep. Kat Cammack (R-Fla.).

KID ROCK-RELATED NEWS: Ticket resale giant StubHub has hired Continental for help facilitating meetings around Washington, after musician Kid Rock endorsed a key resale ticketing reform opposed by secondary marketplaces. The firm is the first outside lobbying hire by StubHub since 2020, when StubHub registered its first in-house lobbyists in D.C. and retained Franklin Square Group , according to PI’s analysis of disclosure filings.

— After ticketing reforms were dropped from a stopgap spending bill in December, the most recent activity at the federal level came in March, when Trump signed an executive order calling for tougher enforcement of existing laws related to ticket resellers and scalpers using online bots. The order also called for “price transparency” at every stage of the ticket-buying process.

— Kid Rock , a longtime Trump ally whose real name is Robert James Ritchie , accompanied Trump for the order’s signing. He argued that further down the line, he’d like to see reforms like caps on the cost of tickets on secondary markets. He added that the idea had the support of Michael Rapino , head of Ticketmaster parent company Live Nation . But ticket resellers like StubHub oppose such a move, which the company called “antiquated and ineffective” in a letter to Connecticut legislators in March opposing similar restrictions.

DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED —OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

MORE NEW BUSINESS: Smart ring makers Oura Ring have registered their first in-house lobbyist. Walter Kuhn , who previously worked for Shopify , Apple and Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.), joined the company last month and will work on a number of issues including regulations, tax benefits and insurance coverage for wearable health devices, intellectual property and defense acquisitions, according to a disclosure filing.

— Earlier this year, the Pentagon’s Defense Health Agency canceled a $96 million contract to purchase Oura’s biometric rings to track service members’ health and wellness after a rival wearables company and at least one Republican in Congress protested the sole-source contract. Oura Ring also has two outside firms on retainer: Defense lobbying firm J.A. Green and Company and Ballard Partners .

— Miller Strategies has registered to lobby for six new clients, including Koch Government Affairs , crypto firm Ava Labs and drone delivery company Zipline International . Miller Strategies, run by Trump fundraiser Jeff Miller , has signed more than 70 new clients since Trump’s election.

BRANCHING OUT: The Washington Post ’s Maura Judkis has unearthed more details about Executive Branch , the exclusive new Georgetown club launching this month from Donald Trump Jr. and investor Omeed Malik .

— For one, Judkis reports that the steep $500,000 fee to join covers “the highest tier of Executive Branch membership, which will include only some members, many of whom are out-of-towners,” with cheaper memberships available “that are in the low six figures, with annual dues in the four- or five-figures — still expensive, but aligned with other clubs of its caliber.”

— “Membership is capped around 200 people initially, and demand has far exceeded that number already. No reporters — not even MAGA-friendly ones — are allowed to join. And phones will be checked at the door.”

— And Malik is pushing back on accusations that the club — whose other co-founders or initial members include the sons of Trump’s Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff and White House AI czar David Sacks — amounts to a blatant pay to play scheme.

— “Members at Executive Branch are already plugged in — they don’t need to trek across town to Georgetown for access,” he told the Post in a statement. “This is not a space for fundraisers or lobbying. It’s a place for members to come and enjoy the best food and finest wine that DC has to offer in a private and relaxing environment.”

MEGABILL PUSHBACK: Executives from a number of large companies are heading to Washington this week to push back on an element of Trump’s “big, beautiful bill,” Gordon Smith , Tee Zhuo and Benjamin Wilhelm write for the Financial Times . Opponents of the bill argue that one component would raise taxes on foreign investments in the U.S., a move that could threaten millions of American jobs.

— “Critics say Section 899 of the bill could cause a drop in corporate investment and a retreat from US assets by international investors. The threat of higher taxes has unsettled the Global Business Alliance , which represents companies including Shell , Toyota and LVMH .”

— “The measure targets countries with what the US calls ‘unfair foreign taxes.’ These include most EU countries, the UK, Australia, Canada and others around the world. For foreign investors, Section 899 would increase taxes on dividends and interest on US stocks and some corporate bonds by 5 percentage points every year for four years. It would also impose taxes on the American portfolio holdings of sovereign wealth funds, which up to now have been exempt.”

TAX PLEA: A collection of top universities is proposing to spend 5 percent of their endowment’s value annually to avoid a component of Trump’s tax bill that would place a 21 percent annual tax on the wealthiest universities, Juliet Chung and Richard Rubin write for The Wall Street Journal .

— Supporters of the plan include Harvard , Yale , Princeton , Stanford , Johns Hopkins , Duke , Rice and the University of Chicago . The money would go toward things like student financial aid and teaching.

— “If enacted, the proposal from the group, called the Learn Alliance, would affect a larger group of several dozen schools whose endowments are subject to a tax on their investment incomes. Under the House bill, some schools would be subject to 14%, 7% or 1.4% tax rates depending on how many dollars their endowments manage per U.S. student. In place of the tiered system in the House bill, the schools propose a tax on investment income at 2.4% or 3.4%.”

CRYPTO OR NO CAREER: Crypto industry giants are sending a message to lawmakers: If you don’t support crypto, your career will end. But amid negotiations over the GENIUS Act, which would enact specific guardrails on crypto, some Democrats are concerned that the legislation omits a provision that would block the president and his family from profiting off cryptocurrency, Joey Cappelletti writes for The Associated Press .

— Lawmakers are keeping a closer eye on cryptocurrency following the industry’s influence on the 2024 elections and as Trump grows his personal crypto empire. Supporters of the GENIUS Act argue the legislation will help legitimize the industry.

— “The sticking point for many Democrats is that while the bill prohibits members of Congress and their families from profiting off stablecoins, it excludes the president from those restrictions.”

— Sixteen Senate Democrats joined Republicans in advancing the legislation, but pressure is mounting on other Democrats from industry leaders to support the legislation. Coinbase , the largest crypto trading company in the U.S., sent an email to Senators hours before a May 19 vote on the legislation. They warned that the vote would impact their “crypto-friendliness scores.”

— “Membership is capped around 200 people initially, and demand has far exceeded that number already. No reporters — not even MAGA-friendly ones — are allowed to join. And phones will be checked at the door.”

— And Malik is pushing back on accusations that the club — whose other co-founders or initial members include the sons of Trump’s Middle East envoy Steve Witkoff and White House AI czar David Sacks — amounts to a blatant pay to play scheme.

QATAR’S CAUSE TO CELEBRATE: President Donald Trump and his allies are enjoying a victory lap after yesterday’s announcement that a peace deal has been reached to end two years of conflict between Israel and Hamas. The ceasefire fulfills a central campaign promise for the president and goes a long way towards boosting his odds of winning a much-desired Nobel Peace Prize. Also celebrating the peace deal: the Qatar lobby, which has worked for years to change the narrative in Washington around the tiny Persian Gulf nation that played a major role in mediating peace talks.

— Among members of the Qatar lobby there is hope that the success of the ceasefire negotiations will establish Qatar’s reputation as a peacemaker in the region and quash accusations that Qatar is responsible for harboring terrorists and boosting anti-Israel sentiment within the United States.

— “I think it’s reasonable to assume that they put a certain amount of pressure on Hamas to accept the deal. That’s what a good negotiator has to do,” said former U.S. Rep. Jim Moran, who has lobbied for Qatar for nearly a decade. “I think the people who look at this objectively are going to give credit to Qatar.”

— A change in Washington’s perception of Qatar is precisely what its small army of lobbyists have been working on for the better part of the last decade. Qatar began heavily investing in lobbying during the first Trump administration when leaders realized their nation was lagging behind regional rivals like Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates in terms of Washington influence.

— Members of the Qatar lobby had already sought to present the country as a regional peacemaker, a role that will likely be highlighted even more should this peace deal hold. Brokering this deal “would solidify Qatar’s indispensable position as the world’s trusted mediator,” said Todd Webster of Cornerstone Government Affairs , a registered lobbyist for Qatar. “Time and again, the world has seen that when you want to make peace, you call Doha.”

— If Qatar is able to maintain the reputation of a peacemaker, that could open new doors for foreign investment in Qatar and Qatari investment in Western nations, said Ben Freeman , who studies Qatar’s influence for the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft .

— “Frankly, it gets a lot of folks to turn a blind eye to some of the human rights issues that surfaced after the World Cup,” Freeman said. “If you get this mediator image that really trumps some of these other concerns that countries might have.”

— So will all this make the job of the Qatar lobby in Washington easier? “I hope it does,” Moran said.

title: College commissioners push NIL bill
body_text:
D-I COMMISSIONERS MOVE TO TEE UP NIL BILL: The House may be at a standstill, but college athletic commissioners are working to position the federal name, image, likeness bill backed by the NCAA for quick floor action once the shutdown ends.

— In a letter to the bipartisan heads of the House Judiciary, Energy and Commerce and Education and Workforce committees this morning, the heads of all 31 NCAA Division-I conferences called for lawmakers to take up the SCORE Act, an NCAA-backed bill seeking to tame what the college sports world agrees is a Wild West of rules governing NIL compensation for athletes.

— The bill would give the NCAA crucial antitrust protections it has sought, insulating it from future lawsuits challenging its rulemaking authority. It would block colleges from designating student athletes as employees and codify a new revenue-sharing agreement struck by the NCAA and some college sports’ biggest conferences over the summer.

— The bill advanced out of the requisite House committees, mostly on party lines, in July. But it has been awaiting floor action amid concerns it may not have the votes. Wealthy athletic booster Cody Campbell , who was recently tapped by President Donald Trump to lead a commission focused on the future of college sports, has mounted an opposition campaign arguing that the SCORE Act hands the NCAA too much power, while not doing enough to help ensure the survival of so-called non-revenue and women’s sports.

— Senate Democrats introduced their own NIL proposal last month that does not include prohibitions on student athletes’ employment status — clarity the NCAA has demanded in any federal NIL bill.

— But the D-I commissioners sought to put many of those concerns to bed, framing today’s letter as a show of force — and agreement — across a broad swath of varying interests.

— “Collectively our conferences provide opportunities in higher education through sports to nearly 200,000 student-athletes,” the commissioners wrote. “Our campuses are urban, rural, historically Black, and land grant, and include United States service academies, small liberal arts colleges, large flagship state universities, and everything in between.”

— Yet “we believe we are on common ground not just among each other, but with members of both parties in Congress as well as the American public in our desire to have college sports return to a state of stability.”

— To hammer the point home, four of the top D-I conferences will air a new ad calling for passage of the SCORE Act during this weekend’s football games. The spot, which is supported by the Southeastern Conference , Big Ten , Atlantic Coast Conference and Big 12 , touts the conferences’ support of women’s and Olympic sports at the collegiate level. And it calls the SCORE Act a key way to “ensure the continued support” of those sports.

title: The ugly fight over ‘litigation finance’
body_text:
FIRST IN PI: In recent months a fight has kicked off in Washington over an effort to crack down on litigation finance — when hedge funds and other wealthy investors fund lawsuits against companies in an exchange for a share of the proceeds if they win, Daniel L. reports.

— It pits the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and insurance companies that want a crackdown on the practice against groups that say they represent consumers, including a Leonard Leo -linked outfit, that argue that it’s a critical tool to hold corporate America accountable for wrongdoing.

— The latest round of the feud has insurance giant Chubb tussling with the Leo-supported Consumers’ Research . The group launched a seven-figure ad campaign two weeks ago that went after Chubb and its CEO, Evan Greenberg . The ad accuses Greenberg of being “woke” and supporting DEI and other liberal ideas.

— Chubb responded that the group is coming after Greenberg because the insurance giant supports litigation finance reform legislation pending in Congress from Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.).

— “Chubb is not who this campaign is portraying us to be, and this campaign isn’t what it claims to be,” a Chubb spokesperson told PI in a statement. “Consumers’ Research doesn’t represent any consumers. It represents interests who are opposed to any regulation of the litigation finance racket that abuses our legal system.”

— Consumers’ Research has reportedly received millions of dollars through Leo-linked nonprofit Marble Freedom Trust . The Wall Street Journal reported in June that Leo’s network is tied to litigation-finance firm Vallecito Capital , which has indicated it will finance lawsuits against companies that have adopted progressive DEI and ESG initiatives.

— Consumers’ Research has attacked the legislation , which would attempt to rein in the industry by taxing its profits. It launched a microsite called “Woke Tillis” and put out an op-ed saying the bill “threatens to weaken the mechanisms we rely on to hold corporations accountable when they prioritize political and financial agendas over consumer interests.”

— Since 2013, Consumers’ Research has paid Leo’s public affairs firm, CRC Advisors , more than a million dollars, according to progressive government watchdog group Accountable.US . Consumers’ Research executive director Will Hild also has called Leo “a good friend and adviser to Consumers Research.”

— Greenberg has been vocal about his support for cracking down on litigation finance. In a July 2025 op-ed , he said that litigation finance is being abused by hedge funds and investors for financial gain.

— “Outside money has turned injury action into an investment scheme that treats individual misfortunes like penny stocks or subprime mortgage investments,” Greenberg wrote.

— In a statement to PI, Hild pushed back against Chubb’s criticism, saying “it is no surprise that a woke company like Chubb would be lobbying to remove tools like litigation finance from consumers’ arsenal.”

— “While there are areas, like mass tort, where litigation financing has been abused, and could be reformed, it has always been a critical tool for the conservative movement to advance the public good by taking on the liberal woke agenda,” Leo added in a statement.

CHERRY ON TOPPINGS: The American Investment Council has hired Chris Toppings , a key architect of the tax and financial services provisions of the GOP megabill, to co-lead the trade group’s government affairs shop.

— Toppings was most recently a senior policy adviser for Senate Majority Leader John Thune , for whom he worked on tax, trade and financial services issues. Before that, he was a longtime top aide to former Sen. Richard Burr (R-N.C.) and former Sen. Judd Gregg (R-N.H.)

— Toppings will split the duties of leading AIC’s lobbying shop with Lee Slater , who joined the private equity trade group at the beginning of the year after working at the White House under former President Joe Biden . FIRST IN PI: In recent months a fight has kicked off in Washington over an effort to crack down on litigation finance — when hedge funds and other wealthy investors fund lawsuits against companies in an exchange for a share of the proceeds if they win, Daniel L. reports.

— It pits the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and insurance companies that want a crackdown on the practice against groups that say they represent consumers, including a Leonard Leo-linked outfit, that argue that it’s a critical tool to hold corporate America accountable for wrongdoing.

— The latest round of the feud has insurance giant Chubb tussling with the Leo-supported Consumers’ Research. The group launched a seven-figure ad campaign two weeks ago that went after Chubb and its CEO, Evan Greenberg. The ad accuses Greenberg of being “woke” and supporting DEI and other liberal ideas.

— Chubb responded that the group is coming after Greenberg because the insurance giant supports litigation finance reform legislation pending in Congress from Sen. Thom Tillis (R-N.C.).

— “Chubb is not who this campaign is portraying us to be, and this campaign isn’t what it claims to be,” a Chubb spokesperson told PI in a statement. “Consumers’ Research doesn’t represent any consumers. It represents interests who are opposed to any regulation of the litigation finance racket that abuses our legal system.”

— Consumers’ Research has reportedly received millions of dollars through Leo-linked nonprofit Marble Freedom Trust. The Wall Street Journal reported in June that Leo’s network is tied to litigation-finance firm Vallecito Capital, which has indicated it will finance lawsuits against companies that have adopted progressive DEI and ESG initiatives.

— Consumers’ Research has attacked the legislation, which would attempt to rein in the industry by taxing its profits. It launched a microsite called “Woke Tillis” and put out an op-ed saying the bill “threatens to weaken the mechanisms we rely on to hold corporations accountable when they prioritize political and financial agendas over consumer interests.”

— Since 2013, Consumers’ Research has paid Leo’s public affairs firm, CRC Advisors, more than a million dollars, according to progressive government watchdog group Accountable.US. Consumers’ Research executive director Will Hild also has called Leo “a good friend and adviser to Consumers Research.”

— Greenberg has been vocal about his support for cracking down on litigation finance. In a July 2025 op-ed, he said that litigation finance is being abused by hedge funds and investors for financial gain.

— “Outside money has turned injury action into an investment scheme that treats individual misfortunes like penny stocks or subprime mortgage investments,” Greenberg wrote.

— In a statement to PI, Hild pushed back against Chubb’s criticism, saying “it is no surprise that a woke company like Chubb would be lobbying to remove tools like litigation finance from consumers’ arsenal.”

— “While there are areas, like mass tort, where litigation financing has been abused, and could be reformed, it has always been a critical tool for the conservative movement to advance the public good by taking on the liberal woke agenda,” Leo added in a statement.

title: Hollywood turns to K Street for help against AI threat
body_text:
— But the dizzying pace of new developments coming out of Washington right now, combined with the deeply personal stakes of issues like generative AI and the potential censorship of administration critics, are fueling a heightened interest in deploying influence peddlers to make their stand with the Trump administration and Congress.

— The latest sign of the seriousness came when famed talent agency Creative Artists Agency retained Washington lobbying shop Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck , as PI noted last week .

— In the two years since AI concerns propelled Hollywood actors and screenwriters to go on strike, unions representing directors, writers and crew members have also bolstered their lobbying footprints. So have top production studios and industry groups looking to ensure their perspectives are heard as Washington confronts thorny questions about how to balance the quest for AI dominance and the need for guardrails for safety and to protect intellectual property.

— There’s “no question that the risks and rewards created by AI are prompting more engagement in D.C. than I’ve seen in over a decade,” said Carl Thorsen , a co-founder of the lobbying firm Thorsen French Advocacy , which has represented the Directors Guild of America and the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees for a decade and a half.

— In addition to CAA, the issue has brought several other Hollywood newcomers to Washington over the past few years, including the National Association of Voice Actors and the Academy of Television Arts & Sciences .

— But AI anxieties aren’t the only Hollywood concern driving business on K Street. The industry, which took a major hit during the pandemic, is bleeding high-paying jobs as productions flee for cheaper locales overseas. President Donald Trump ’s jawboning of major media companies has been another pressure point for the industry.

— “In terms of what’s happening at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue and within some of the departments and agencies, I just don’t think there was a clear line of sight,” said one consultant for the industry who was granted anonymity to speak candidly about the dynamics at play.

— With their K Street hires, agents and other industry interests now have a team that “can help [them] navigate and walk both efficiently and effectively through these times, and be able to have those relationships to transact on.”

With Daniel Lippman

(ALARM) BELLS WILL BE RINGING: Hollywood’s relationship with Washington is at a crossroads, and its stars are turning to K Street A-listers for cover, your host reports. Entertainers are no strangers to lending their voices to advocacy fights in Washington. More often than not, those are ad hoc appearances, with studios, unions and industry organizations typically taking the lead.

— But the dizzying pace of new developments coming out of Washington right now, combined with the deeply personal stakes of issues like generative AI and the potential censorship of administration critics, are fueling a heightened interest in deploying influence peddlers to make their stand with the Trump administration and Congress.

— The latest sign of the seriousness came when famed talent agency Creative Artists Agency retained Washington lobbying shop Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck, as PI noted last week.

— In the two years since AI concerns propelled Hollywood actors and screenwriters to go on strike, unions representing directors, writers and crew members have also bolstered their lobbying footprints. So have top production studios and industry groups looking to ensure their perspectives are heard as Washington confronts thorny questions about how to balance the quest for AI dominance and the need for guardrails for safety and to protect intellectual property.

— There’s “no question that the risks and rewards created by AI are prompting more engagement in D.C. than I’ve seen in over a decade,” said Carl Thorsen, a co-founder of the lobbying firm Thorsen French Advocacy, which has represented the Directors Guild of America and the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees for a decade and a half.

— In addition to CAA, the issue has brought several other Hollywood newcomers to Washington over the past few years, including the National Association of Voice Actors and the Academy of Television Arts & Sciences.

— But AI anxieties aren’t the only Hollywood concern driving business on K Street. The industry, which took a major hit during the pandemic, is bleeding high-paying jobs as productions flee for cheaper locales overseas. President Donald Trump’s jawboning of major media companies has been another pressure point for the industry.

— “In terms of what’s happening at 1600 Pennsylvania Avenue and within some of the departments and agencies, I just don’t think there was a clear line of sight,” said one consultant for the industry who was granted anonymity to speak candidly about the dynamics at play.

— With their K Street hires, agents and other industry interests now have a team that “can help [them] navigate and walk both efficiently and effectively through these times, and be able to have those relationships to transact on.”

TESLA HIRES ANOTHER: Tesla isn’t done reshaping its lobbying roster following layoffs that hit the automaker’s public policy staff and an overhaul of its outside lobbying firms. Elon Musk’s EV giant hired Capitol Consulting Group’s Stephen Replogle in September to lobby on a range of issues, including transportation and mobility, solar energy and energy storage policy, according to a newly filed disclosure.

— That marks the second new lobbying hire for Tesla in as many months, with the EV company bringing on Continental Strategy at the beginning of October, as PI reported last week. Like with Continental, this latest hire appears aimed at bolstering Tesla’s standing on the right after Musk’s falling out with Trump this summer. Replogle is a former staffer for former Sen. Lamar Alexander (R-Tenn.), and Replogle previously worked for Cove Strategies, the consulting firm led by CPAC chief and Trump ally Matt Schlapp.

MORE NEW BUSINESS: Tesla isn’t the only automaker adding new lobbying help. The Alliance for Automotive Innovation — whose members include Hyundai, BMW, Suburau, Ford, Toyota and more — is one of four new clients signed by Ferox Strategies. Ferox’s Cristina Antelo, Mark Williams, Michael Taggart and Lauren Doepke will work on the account for the alliance, which previously added Rich Feuer Anderson this year, according to a disclosure filing.

— Ferox has also signed food service distribution giant Sysco Corporation, which has worked to help its clients manage tariff disruptions, as well as the National Electrical Manufacturers Association, where they’re working with NEMA’s Medical Imaging & Technology Alliance Positron Emission Tomography division on radiopharmaceutical issues related to medical imaging diagnostics and therapies.

PPHC EYES WALL STREET: “Investors looking to add a K Street lobbying stock to their portfolio might soon be able to invest in a company that owns several influence shops in Washington and state capitals,” Bloomberg’s Kate Ackley reports.

— “The Public Policy Holding Co., which owns the Alpine Group, Forbes Tate Partners, and Crossroads Strategies where ex-Sens. Trent Lott (R-Miss.) and John Breaux (D-La.) are on the roster, filed a registration statement with the Securities and Exchange Commission, paving a path for a public stock offering in the United States.”

— PPHC, which also owns the public affairs firm Seven Letter, went public on the London Stock Exchange in 2021. The holding company aims to list its common stock on Nasdaq under the same stock ticker, at which point it would be dual-listed on both Nasdaq and on the LSE’s Alternative Investment Market.

SPEAKING OF: PPHC is growing its footprint in Texas following the holdco’s acquisition this summer of the consulting firm founded by former state land commissioner George P. Bush and Alpine Group’s expansion to the Dallas-Fort Worth area. Forbes Tate Partners is following Alpine’s lead and opening its own office in the DFW metroplex, which is quickly becoming an economic and financial hub on top of Texas’ growing political influence within the U.S.

— To support Forbes Tate’s work in Texas, the firm is launching a new tool dubbed the Lone Star Index, which will aim to inform business leaders’ decisionmaking by analyzing policy, social and business dialogue happening across the state as well as how decisions made in Washington will impact the public policy landscape in Texas.

ANOTHER SPEED BUMP FOR CRYPTO: “A Senate GOP push to pass a sweeping crypto market structure bill that would establish a regulatory framework for digital assets is mired in controversy as Republicans and Democrats trade blame over stalled negotiations and struggle to agree on a path forward,” POLITICO’s Jasper Goodman reports.

— “Following a public spat between Senate negotiators last week, aides and lobbyists close to the process have become more pessimistic about the bill becoming law this year — a remarkable momentum shift after a blowout bipartisan House floor vote on market structure legislation breathed life into the effort in July.”

title: ADL switches Ballard from lobbying to advising
body_text:
BALLARD AND ADL ADJUST THEIR RELATIONSHIP: The Anti-Defamation League’s decision to hire Ballard Partners in the wake of last year’s general election raised eyebrows when it was originally disclosed. The Jewish advocacy group had long been antagonistic toward President Donald Trump , but hiring a Trump-connected lobbyist like Brian Ballard indicated a willingness on its part to reset the relationship and strike a friendlier tone with the new administration.

— So it was surprising to see a new disclosure filed today terminating that lobbying relationship less than a year after it started. But while Ballard’s lobbying work for the ADL is ending, a spokesperson for the organization tells PI it is not parting ways with Ballard entirely — rather, it is switching the firm’s role to an advisory capacity.

— The pivot comes after a few hard weeks for the ADL, which has faced an uphill battle to ingratiate itself in Trump’s Washington. The organization and its president, Jonathan Greenblatt , have struggled to overcome years of built-up resentment from some on the right who consider the group unfairly critical of Trump and his supporters.

— That job has gotten even harder in the wake of Charlie Kirk’s killing last month. In the days and weeks following Kirk’s death, far-right commentators on social media discovered that the ADL listed information about Kirk’s Turning Point USA on its website as part of the group’s Glossary of Extremism and Hate. “ADL sells hate,” Elon Musk wrote on X . “Disgraceful,” wrote Donald Trump Jr .

— Two weeks ago, FBI Director Kash Patel ended a partnership between the bureau and the ADL that provided training on hate crimes and antisemitism to all new agents. In a statement to Fox News , Patel referred to the ADL as “an extreme group functioning like a terrorist organization.”

— The ADL, which paid Ballard $130,000 total for its work since last December, is not dependent on outside help. The group is on track to spend more than $1 million on its in-house lobbying team this year and has had at least one outside firm, H&M Strategies , remaining on its payroll. Other than Ballard, the ADL had not hired a new outside firm since H&M Strategies in 2021.

PIRRO SIGNS NEW CLIENTS: Albert Pirro , ex-husband of U.S. Attorney for the District of Columbia Jeanine Pirro , one-time Trump real estate lawyer and recipient of one of the last pardons of Trump’s first term, has resumed signing lobbying clients, according to new disclosure reports.

— Pirro had lobbied for clients in New York and Washington throughout his career but had not registered a new client in Washington since 2021. Earlier this year, Pirro resumed representing the Greater New York Hospital Association , a longtime client. And this week, he filed disclosures for two new clients: Quantum Worldwide and Topspin Consumer Partners .

— According to the disclosures, Pirro started representing pharmaceutical ingredient producer Quantum in September. His work for private equity investors Topspin started in June and is focused on tariffs.

DINNER PARTY: President Donald Trump hosted a collection of wealthy donors and corporate executives at the White House Wednesday evening for a dinner celebrating their financial contributions toward the new White House ballroom.

— “So many of you have been really, really generous,” Trump said during his remarks, adding that some in attendance had promised up to $25 million donations for the project. Attendees included Trump donors such as Harold Hamm and Cameron and Tyler Winklevoss , according to a guest list reported by The New York Times’ Zolan Kanno-Youngs . Corporate representatives from Amazon , Apple , Booz Allen Hamilton , Comcast , Google , Lockheed Martin , Meta , Microsoft , Palantir , T-Mobile US , Union Pacific Railroad and more were also in attendance.

CHEMISTS AGAINST RAIL-MERGER: CEOs from the American Chemistry Council (ACC) member companies have sent a letter to President Trump detailing their opposition to the proposed merger between Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern railroads, arguing that combining the companies would make American manufacturing less competitive.

— Chemical manufacturers represented by the ACC depend on rail systems for the safe transportation of hazardous materials, a position that leaves them especially susceptible to consolidation in the market. “Past mergers have led to server service disruptions, rising rates, weakened supply chains and a less competitive U.S. industrial base,” the CEOs write. “We have no doubt that combining UP and NS into the nation’s largest railroad will make these problems worse.”

— The CEOs close by urging the president to allow the Surface Transportation Board, which reviews proposed railroad mergers, to do its job and evaluate the merger with a critical eye. In August, Trump fired one of the board’s Democratic appointees without explanation. The fired board member, Robert Primus , is challenging his dismissal.

CHAMBER SUES OVER H-1B VISAS: The U.S. Chamber of Commerce sued the Trump administration today over the imposition of a new $100,000 fee for H-1B visa applications, a rare contribution from the business lobby to the various legal challenges against administration policies.

— Last month’s announcement of the new fee prompted indignation from the business community, particularly among big tech companies who depend on H-1B visas for skilled foreign workers like software engineers. Today’s lawsuit accuses the Trump administration of overstepping its authority by setting a higher fee than the one approved by Congress.

— Former Rep. Chris Stewart (R-Utah) has been named chair of America First Policy Institute’s AI and emerging technology team. Also joining the newly formed team are Yusuf Mahmood as director, Dean Woodley Ball as senior fellow and Shea Throckmorton as campaign director.

— Former Rep. James Langevin (D-R.I.) has been named chair of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies’ Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation .

— Matt Corridoni is now communications director for Majority Democrats . He most recently served as vice president of communications for VoteVets and is a Harris alum.

— Sarah Corcoran has launched Corcoran Strategies Group , her own firm specializing in mental health, health and social services policy. She was most recently senior vice president and chief operating officer at Guide Consulting Services .

— Nicole Vele has joined GrayRobinson as a shareholder in the firm’s Washington office. She was most recently of counsel at Holland & Hart and previously served nearly 12 years as a judge advocate general in the U.S. Air Force.

— Trace Scruggs has joined The Herald Group as a vice president. He most recently served as senior director for public affairs at PLUS Communications .

— Maura Rezendes has joined Sidley Austin as a partner in the firm’s global arbitration, trade and advocacy practice. She was most recently a partner at A&O Shearman .

— Jake Edie has joined RenewComm as a managing partner. He was previously the vice president of marketing for Clean Energy Associates (now Intertek CEA ).

— The Steel Manufacturers Association has added Max Hyman as director of government affairs and Emily Bradshaw as senior manager of government affairs. Hyman was most recently director of transportation, infrastructure, and labor policy for the National Association of Manufacturers. Bradshaw was most recently a public affairs specialist in the office of the under secretary for international trade at the International Trade Administration .

— Marsha Anderson Bomar has been appointed president of the American Society of Civil Engineers . She most recently served as assistant general manager at the Metropolitan Atlanta Rapid Transit Authority .
