FIRST IN PI — CHARITY CASE: One of the largest charities in the country, United Way Worldwide (UWW) , has hired former Republican Sen. Richard Burr and the team at DLA Piper to lobby on its behalf as it attempts to make new inroads with Republican lawmakers.

title: Binance pardon lobby pays off
body_text:
TRUMP PARDONS BINANCE FOUNDER: President Donald Trump has pardoned Changpeng Zhao , founder of the cryptocurrency exchange Binance , POLITICO’s Declan Harty reported this afternoon, confirming a scoop first reported by The Wall Street Journal .

— The pardon comes after nearly a year of effort by Zhao and Binance to lobby Trump for clemency and marks a big win for Checkmate Government Relations and its founder Ches McDowell , who was hired by Binance in September. Binance paid the firm $450,000 in the third quarter for work on policy issues related to cryptocurrencies and “executive relief,” according to a disclosure report .

— Lobbying for Zhao in his personal capacity was BakerHostetler ’s Teresa Goody Guillén , a leading crypto lawyer who Trump once reportedly considered to lead the SEC. Zhao hired Goody Guillén in February to work exclusively on his pardon effort, according to disclosure reports, but she appears to have played a limited role in recent months, reporting no activity on Zhao’s behalf in the third quarter. In addition to her pardon work for Zhao, Goody Guillén is part of a BakerHostetler team lobbying on Binance’s behalf — a team that includes former U.S. Rep. Peter Roskam (R-Ill.) and former House Financial Services Committee chief counsel Kevin Edgar .

— Zhao served four months in prison last year after pleading guilty to charges that he intentionally ignored anti-money laundering laws and allowed Binance to be used by criminals looking to turn illicit crypto assets into clean cash. As part of the plea agreement, Zhao stepped down from his position as CEO of Binance and agreed to pay a $50 million fine. The company was separately fined $4 billion and has since been subject to compliance monitoring by the Justice and Treasury departments.

— Binance has an on and off history of lobbying in Washington. The company’s U.S. subsidiary, Binance.US , signed its first contracts with Ice Miller Strategies and Hogan Lovells in late 2021 and went on to spend more than $1 million on lobbying in 2022. In the first nine months of 2023, as Zhao and Binance negotiated their futures with federal prosecutors, the company spent nearly $1.2 million on lobbying.

— Following the guilty pleas, Binance’s lobbying spending plummeted to zero for the remainder of 2023. Neither Zhao nor the company reported spending a dime on lobbying in 2024. But Trump’s inauguration jolted the company’s lobbying effort back to life. So far in 2025, Binance has reported spending $860,000 on lobbyists, putting it on track to equal or beat its 2023 peak spend.

DURBIN-MARSHALL CREDIT CARD MANDATES WILL HARM MILITARY FAMILIES The Defense Credit Union Council is sounding the alarm on the Durbin–Marshall credit card mandates. This proposal would increase fraud risk, restrict access to credit, eliminate rewards, and hand a massive windfall to corporate mega-retailers at the expense of consumers, small businesses, and community financial institutions. DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED —OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

THE RACE TO WIN Q4 IS ON: While we’ve been having fun digging into Q3’s revenue numbers, some of the fastest growing firms in Washington have already started signing new business for Q4. Continental Strategy , which jumped from 15th place in Q2 to 9th in Q3’s rankings , has disclosed four new clients all signed after Oct. 1.

— The most recognizable name among the new clients is McCormick & Company . The spices and seasonings producer has enlisted Continental to lobby on trade and tariff issues, topics that will likely continue to drive business on K Street for the remainder of the year and beyond.

— The remaining new clients are: immunotherapy company ImmunityBio Inc. , online school provider Florida Virtual School and sustainable natural ingredients manufacturer Darling Ingredients .

KIRKLAND KEEPS PAYING: Earlier this year, when the president was striking fear into the hearts of Big Law firms everywhere with his executive orders targeting lawyers, three firms that ended up striking deals with the White House hired lobbyists with close ties to Trump. Only one of those firms, Kirkland & Ellis , is still paying, Abigail Adcox reports for the National Law Journal .

TRUMP PARDONS BINANCE FOUNDER: President Donald Trump has pardoned Changpeng Zhao, founder of the cryptocurrency exchange Binance, POLITICO’s Declan Harty reported this afternoon, confirming a scoop first reported by The Wall Street Journal.

— The pardon comes after nearly a year of effort by Zhao and Binance to lobby Trump for clemency and marks a big win for Checkmate Government Relations and its founder Ches McDowell, who was hired by Binance in September. Peter Roskam (R-Ill.) and former House Financial Services Committee chief counsel Kevin Edgar.

— Zhao served four months in prison last year after pleading guilty to charges that he intentionally ignored anti-money laundering laws and allowed Binance to be used by criminals looking to turn illicit crypto assets into clean cash. As part of the plea agreement, Zhao stepped down from his position as CEO of Binance and agreed to pay a $50 million fine. The company was separately fined $4 billion and has since been subject to compliance monitoring by the Justice and Treasury departments.

— Binance has an on and off history of lobbying in Washington. The company’s U.S. subsidiary, Binance.US, signed its first contracts with Ice Miller Strategies and Hogan Lovells in late 2021 and went on to spend more than $1 million on lobbying in 2022. FIRST IN PI — X JOINS COALITION FOR APP FAIRNESS: Congress has revived its push to wrest control of mobile app stores away from Apple and Google , and the effort is getting a big boost from X , the Elon Musk -owned social media giant. X is joining the Coalition for App Fairness , an advocacy group representing app developers including Spotify , Epic Games , Match Group and Proton .

— “We believe in a digital future where competition thrives, innovation is rewarded, and users have ultimate control,” X head of global government affairs Romina Khananisho said in a statement, calling the decision “a testament to our commitment to dismantling monopolistic practices and building a mobile ecosystem that truly serves its users and fosters growth for all.”

— This isn’t the first time Musk has weighed in on competition in the mobile app ecosystem. Even before he bought X’s predecessor, Twitter, in 2022, Musk complained online about fees for app developers and expressed support for Epic in its lawsuit against Apple .

— Shortly after acquiring Twitter, as the Open App Markets Act awaited floor action in Congress, Musk accused Apple of threatening to boot the social media site from its app store — though he later called it a misunderstanding .

— This summer, Musk renewed his criticisms, He questioned whether Apple was declining to feature his apps for political reasons or conspiring with rival artificial intelligence companies to prevent Musk’s AI firm from claiming the top spot in the app store. (X’s community notes debunked his latter claim.)

— The new addition to CAF comes as the Hill debate over regulating the mobile app ecosystem heats up. X’s endorsement of an effort to break up the Apple/Google app store duopoly could hold considerable weight with Musk-allied Republicans, particularly following the recent détente between Musk and President Donald Trump .

— The most notable proposal in the mix is the Open App Markets Act, the updated version of a bipartisan 2022 bill that died on the Senate floor. OAMA was reintroduced in June by Sens. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.), Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Mike Lee (R-Utah), Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) and Dick Durbin (D-Ill.).

— It aims to allow consumers “to download applications without having to use an official app store, such as Google Play; open the market to third-party app stores and alternative payment systems; prevent app stores from disadvantaging certain developers; and more,” per our friends at Morning Tech .

— But trade groups that count Apple and Google among their members have, predictably, hammered proposed app store legislation as an unnecessary — and potentially unconstitutional — government intervention that will threaten consumer privacy and security.

— “The Coalition for App Fairness is funded by a small group of powerful developers who simply don’t want to pay for the immense value they receive from Apple’s platforms and technologies,” an Apple spokesperson told PI, adding that “they represent only a very small portion of the broader developer community.”

Happy Tuesday and welcome to PI. Send K Street tips. Caitlin is on Signal at caitlinoprysko.17 and email her at coprysko@politico.com . Daniel is on Signal at danielbarnes.13 and email at dbarnes@politico.com . Also follow us on X: @caitlinoprysko and @dnlbrns .

THE BALL’S IN COURT: Congress has increasingly ceded its influence over major policy decisions to the executive branch, and the flood of legal challenges stemming from that activity has given the judiciary an outsize role in deciding federal policies crucial to K Street’s interests.

— “The Trump Administration is currently party to at least 500 lawsuits covering a range of issues,” DB3 , the lobbying firm formerly known as the Daschle Group, said in a recent presentation to clients titled “King of the Courts.”

— The litigation currently pending “concerns some of the most fundamental parts of our democracy, such as the limits to executive power, birthright citizenship, and the rules of Congressional redistricting,” the deck, which was shared with PI, notes.

— “The stakes are higher than with anything that will happen in Congress,” CEO Nathan Daschle told PI. So while the firm’s updates to clients usually center on upcoming elections, which shape the landscape for future policy fights, DB3’s latest presentation dives into six key cases before the courts, breaking down where things currently stand and how the cases could impact clients, ranging from immigration to tariffs.

UNTETHERED: “Stablecoin giant Tether is looking at spending money on US elections as it prepares to open a US entity and is considering options other than the political action committee that has won the support of big US crypto companies,” Bloomberg ’s Anna Irrera reports.

— “The chief executive officer of Tether, Paolo Ardoino , said in an interview with Bloomberg, that ‘everyone is upset with Fairshake ,’ the crypto PAC that rose to prominence during the 2024 election by spending $133 million on pro-crypto candidates,” in part because Ardoino said the PAC was “doing the bidding of one single company.”

— Though he declined to name the company, Fairshake was seeded by nearly $70 million in donations from Coinbase , which “is closely tied to USDC, a stablecoin that is the biggest competitor to Tether’s token.”

— Tether is currently headquartered in El Salvador, which disqualifies it from donating to U.S. campaigns. But Tether plans on setting up shop in the U.S. by the end of the year, in an office that will be led by former White House crypto czar Bo Hines .

DON’T CALL IT A COMEBACK: Less than five years after Trump pardoned him for financial fraud, lobbying violations and witness tampering, Paul Manafort , the president’s former campaign chair, has completed an “unlikely full-circle journey from high-flying global fixer to federal inmate and back,” Ken Vogel writes in a POLITICO Magazine excerpt of his new book, “Devils’ Advocates: The Hidden Story of Rudy Giuliani, Hunter Biden, and the Washington Insiders on the Payrolls of Corrupt Foreign Interests.”

— “In the weeks after Election Day, Manafort, sensing opportunity, began aggressively courting far-right populist interests around the world looking to align themselves with Trump,” Vogel reports.

— Manafort’s clients have included Sali Berisha , a former disgraced president and prime minister of Albania who tried and failed to make a political comeback in a parliamentary election this spring. Manafort has also “consulted with the party of Milorad Dodik , the pro-Russian authoritarian who has served as president of the self-governing Balkan territory of Republika Srpska,” on an upcoming election.

— Manafort has not registered as a foreign agent for any of his recent work. But the veteran fixer, who pleaded guilty to FARA violations stemming from work for a former Kremlin-aligned Ukrainian president, “says he is being careful to avoid anything that could even faintly resemble lobbying.”

— Manafort’s associates in these undertakings have included Trumpworld fixtures like 2024 campaign co-manager Chris LaCivita and longtime pollster Tony Fabrizio . And though “Manafort remains in Trump’s good graces, he is not nearly as close to the inner circle of foreign policy decision-making as he was under Reagan or Bush,” according to Vogel.

— Still, Manafort’s “formula of casting far-flung politicians as pro-Trump populists could be a blueprint for winning favor in Trump’s Washington in much the same way that opposing communism was during the Reagan and Bush administrations,” even if his record thus far has been mixed.

FIRST IN PI — X JOINS COALITION FOR APP FAIRNESS: Congress has revived its push to wrest control of mobile app stores away from Apple and Google, and the effort is getting a big boost from X, the Elon Musk-owned social media giant. X is joining the Coalition for App Fairness, an advocacy group representing app developers including Spotify, Epic Games, Match Group and Proton.

— “We believe in a digital future where competition thrives, innovation is rewarded, and users have ultimate control,” X head of global government affairs Romina Khananisho said in a statement, calling the decision “a testament to our commitment to dismantling monopolistic practices and building a mobile ecosystem that truly serves its users and fosters growth for all.”

— This isn’t the first time Musk has weighed in on competition in the mobile app ecosystem. Even before he bought X’s predecessor, Twitter, in 2022, Musk complained online about fees for app developers and expressed support for Epic in its lawsuit against Apple.

— Shortly after acquiring Twitter, as the Open App Markets Act awaited floor action in Congress, Musk accused Apple of threatening to boot the social media site from its app store — though he later called it a misunderstanding.

— This summer, Musk renewed his criticisms, He questioned whether Apple was declining to feature his apps for political reasons or conspiring with rival artificial intelligence companies to prevent Musk’s AI firm from claiming the top spot in the app store. (X’s community notes debunked his latter claim.)

— The new addition to CAF comes as the Hill debate over regulating the mobile app ecosystem heats up. X’s endorsement of an effort to break up the Apple/Google app store duopoly could hold considerable weight with Musk-allied Republicans, particularly following the recent détente between Musk and President Donald Trump.

— The most notable proposal in the mix is the Open App Markets Act, the updated version of a bipartisan 2022 bill that died on the Senate floor. OAMA was reintroduced in June by Sens. Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.), Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), Mike Lee (R-Utah), Amy Klobuchar (D-Minn.) and Dick Durbin (D-Ill.).

— It aims to allow consumers “to download applications without having to use an official app store, such as Google Play; open the market to third-party app stores and alternative payment systems; prevent app stores from disadvantaging certain developers; and more,” per our friends at Morning Tech.

— But trade groups that count Apple and Google among their members have, predictably, hammered proposed app store legislation as an unnecessary — and potentially unconstitutional — government intervention that will threaten consumer privacy and security.

— “The Coalition for App Fairness is funded by a small group of powerful developers who simply don’t want to pay for the immense value they receive from Apple’s platforms and technologies,” an Apple spokesperson told PI, adding that “they represent only a very small portion of the broader developer community.”

THE BALL’S IN COURT: Congress has increasingly ceded its influence over major policy decisions to the executive branch, and the flood of legal challenges stemming from that activity has given the judiciary an outsize role in deciding federal policies crucial to K Street’s interests.

— “The Trump Administration is currently party to at least 500 lawsuits covering a range of issues,” DB3, the lobbying firm formerly known as the Daschle Group, said in a recent presentation to clients titled “King of the Courts.”

— The litigation currently pending “concerns some of the most fundamental parts of our democracy, such as the limits to executive power, birthright citizenship, and the rules of Congressional redistricting,” the deck, which was shared with PI, notes.

— “The stakes are higher than with anything that will happen in Congress,” CEO Nathan Daschle told PI. So while the firm’s updates to clients usually center on upcoming elections, which shape the landscape for future policy fights, DB3’s latest presentation dives into six key cases before the courts, breaking down where things currently stand and how the cases could impact clients, ranging from immigration to tariffs.

UNTETHERED: “Stablecoin giant Tether is looking at spending money on US elections as it prepares to open a US entity and is considering options other than the political action committee that has won the support of big US crypto companies,” Bloomberg’s Anna Irrera reports.

— “The chief executive officer of Tether, Paolo Ardoino, said in an interview with Bloomberg, that ‘everyone is upset with Fairshake,’ the crypto PAC that rose to prominence during the 2024 election by spending $133 million on pro-crypto candidates,” in part because Ardoino said the PAC was “doing the bidding of one single company.”

— Though he declined to name the company, Fairshake was seeded by nearly $70 million in donations from Coinbase, which “is closely tied to USDC, a stablecoin that is the biggest competitor to Tether’s token.”

— Tether is currently headquartered in El Salvador, which disqualifies it from donating to U.S. campaigns. But Tether plans on setting up shop in the U.S. by the end of the year, in an office that will be led by former White House crypto czar Bo Hines.

DON’T CALL IT A COMEBACK: Less than five years after Trump pardoned him for financial fraud, lobbying violations and witness tampering, Paul Manafort, the president’s former campaign chair, has completed an “unlikely full-circle journey from high-flying global fixer to federal inmate and back,” Ken Vogel writes in a POLITICO Magazine excerpt of his new book, “Devils’ Advocates: The Hidden Story of Rudy Giuliani, Hunter Biden, and the Washington Insiders on the Payrolls of Corrupt Foreign Interests.”

— “In the weeks after Election Day, Manafort, sensing opportunity, began aggressively courting far-right populist interests around the world looking to align themselves with Trump,” Vogel reports.

— Manafort’s clients have included Sali Berisha, a former disgraced president and prime minister of Albania who tried and failed to make a political comeback in a parliamentary election this spring. Manafort has also “consulted with the party of Milorad Dodik, the pro-Russian authoritarian who has served as president of the self-governing Balkan territory of Republika Srpska,” on an upcoming election.

— Manafort has not registered as a foreign agent for any of his recent work. But the veteran fixer, who pleaded guilty to FARA violations stemming from work for a former Kremlin-aligned Ukrainian president, “says he is being careful to avoid anything that could even faintly resemble lobbying.”

— Manafort’s associates in these undertakings have included Trumpworld fixtures like 2024 campaign co-manager Chris LaCivita and longtime pollster Tony Fabrizio. FRESH WATER: Current Strategies , which launched at the end of September as the only public affairs firm in Washington focused exclusively on water infrastructure and policy, filed its first disclosure reports today, And it revealed a client list of state and local government coalitions, trade associations and one household name in water filtration.

— Water filter manufacturer Brita is Current’s first disclosed client. Firm founder and CEO Mae Stevens is joined on the account by Wendi Wilkes and Theodore Mondloch , both of whom followed Stevens from Banner Public Affairs to launch Current. All three previously represented Brita in their time at Banner, which first signed the water filter maker as a client in May 2024 and has reported being paid $100,000 per quarter since last Fall.

— In fact, all six of Current’s initial clients are registered as Banner clients and have not yet filed termination reports. Others in the initial class of clients include industry associations like the Water Quality Association and the Clean Water Construction Coalition , as well as the National Recreation and Park Association . Rounding out the list are two Washington-area clients: utility WSSC Water and the Metropolitan Washington Council of Governments .

IT’S 6 A.M. SOMEWHERE: The newest member of the Stagwell network is SixAM Strategies , a new bipartisan public affairs firm launched today aimed at using on-the-ground partners in all 50 states to produce hyperlocal communications campaigns for clients.

— Running the new operation will be longtime political strategists Maggie FitzGerald and Jessie Andrews Keady . FitzGerald, the GOP half of the firm, will serve as CEO. She most recently worked as an executive vice president at Targeted Victory , running the GOP firm’s hyperlocal practice.

— Keady comes to the new firm after a long career in Democratic politics, spending nearly 10 years in House staff positions before serving as chief of staff to New York Lt. Governor Antonio Delgado. She will serve as COO of the new firm.

— The firm plans to work with others in the Stagwell family, like SKDK and Targeted Victory, and plans to have a full-time staff of 10 employees by the start of next year, Eleanor Hawkins reports for Axios .

AHA CHIEF RETIRING: Rick Pollack is stepping down as president and CEO of the American Hospital Association after more than four decades with the powerful hospital lobby — including the past 10 years at its helm.

— Pollack first joined the AHA back in 1982, and he spent 24 years as the trade group’s executive vice president for advocacy and public policy before taking over as its leader in 2015. Since then, he’s seen the hospital industry through numerous crises, including the Covid-19 pandemic and GOP attempts to repeal and replace the Affordable Care Act.

— AHA, which represents more than 5,000 hospitals across the country, is regularly one of the top lobbying spenders in Washington. Last year, the trade group spent more than $24 million on federal lobbying, and AHA is set to exceed that this year following the industry’s fierce — but unsuccessful — campaign to fend off more than $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts enacted by Republicans as part of their reconciliation bill earlier this summer.

— The AHA has hired the executive search firm WittKieffer to find a new chief executive. Pollack will stay in his role through the transition.

PARAMOUNT WARNING SHOT: Lawmakers continued today to stake out their positions on the competing bids for Warner Bros. Discovery , with a pair of House Democrats warning that a Paramount Skydance triumph could pose “substantial national security consequences.”

— Several Middle East sovereign wealth funds backing Paramount’s bid agreed to give up voting rights in order to help a merger deal avoid scrutiny by the interagency Committee on Foreign Investment in the U.S. But in a letter to Warner Bros. board members and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent today, Reps. Sam Liccardo (D-Calif.) and Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) insisted that such a review take place. The headquarters of Paramount’s rival, Netflix , is located in Liccardo’s district.

— To help bankroll the hostile takeover bid launched by Paramount on Monday, the company said it had secured financing from sovereign wealth funds in Saudi Arabia, Qatar and the United Arab Emirates, along with Affinity Partners , the investment fund started by presidential son-in-law Jared Kushner that is also backed by Gulf money. Even without governance rights, investors could still gain access to sensitive user data, the lawmakers said.

— Liccardo and Pressley argued that forgoing a CFIUS review of any Paramount-WBD deal would represent “a serious lapse in fiduciary judgment” and could expose the company to regulatory or reputational risk. They warned that a future Congress (presumably one controlled by Democrats) could unwind key parts of the deal upon review.

— “The American public relies on Warner’s platforms for news, entertainment, and vital information,” they wrote. “Allowing foreign-backed investors to obtain influence over this ecosystem without the fullest possible scrutiny would be irresponsible and dangerous.”

— On the flip side, Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah), who chairs a key antitrust panel, told Semafor last night he has “grave doubts” about the ability of a Netflix-Warner Bros. deal to survive federal antitrust scrutiny.

TIM’S COOKING: Apple CEO Tim Cook huddled with lawmakers today “to lobby against pending children’s online safety legislation that would require app store operators to authenticate users’ ages, pressing instead for an alternate version that puts the burden of protecting kids on parents,” Bloomberg ’s Emily Birnbaum and Eric Wasson report.

— Cook’s closed-door appearance came ahead of a markup tomorrow morning where the House Energy and Commerce Committee will take up several bills to address kids’ online safety. Cook raised privacy concerns about language in the App Store Accountability Act that would require app stores to verify users’ ages. His trip to the Hill follows a letter from Apple’s global head of privacy last week making the same argument.

— “Republican Representative Gus Bilirakis of Florida, who chairs the panel’s technology subcommittee, said he met with Cook and doesn’t expect major changes to the bill. ‘It would be good if they would work with us, but we are going full speed ahead,’ said Bilirakis, who added the measure has support from both Republican and Democratic lawmakers.”

SPECIALTY CROPS’ BAILOUT PUSH: “Farmers who produce hundreds of varieties of fruits, vegetables, nuts and herbs are complaining that the Trump administration’s planned bailout package overlooks their needs — and they’re turning to GOP lawmakers for help,” POLITICO ’s Grace Yarrow reports.

— “Industry groups are asking Congress to appropriate additional money for specialty crop producers, who have borne the brunt of increased costs for labor, fertilizer, seeds and other needs and international market uncertainty as a result of President Donald Trump ’s trade wars.”

— “The appeal comes after officials announced Monday they will deliver $12 billion in farm aid to U.S. producers by the end of February, with $11 billion of that funding allocated for producers of major row crops like corn and soybeans. Just $1 billion will be reserved for aid for specialty crops, sugar and other commodities.

— “USDA also announced that applications for row crop producers would open in the coming weeks but offered no details for specialty crop producers.”

GONE WITH THE WIND: Trump “ has pushed America’s offshore wind industry to the breaking point ,” with the sector struggling “to react to a president who has said over and over that he opposes its very existence,” POLITICO ’s Benjamin Storrow , Kelsey Tamborrino and Jessie Blaeser write.

— “Since Trump returned to the White House, his regulators have moved to withdraw permits for six offshore wind projects along the East Coast and halted construction of two others. … He has also wiped out federal tax credits supporting wind and solar, while his agencies have opened reviews of the wind industry’s national security implications and alleged health hazards and erected barriers to turbine projects on both water and land.”

— “The uprooting of wind projects is especially striking at a time when political leaders from both parties are calling for a massive increase in electricity generation nationwide , citing rising consumer prices and the soaring power demands of data centers.”

— “And the ferocity of the president’s attacks stunned executives who had assumed they could work with him, even after a 2024 campaign in which Trump baselessly alleged that wind power causes cancer and has killed hundreds of whales.”

JOURNEY TO THE MANOSPHERE: The 2024 elections shined a spotlight on the widening political gap between men and women, vaulting terms like “manosphere” into the popular lexicon. And as Democrats have scrambled to find their way out of the political wilderness — in large part by trying to boost the party’s appeal to men — the progressive consultancy Precision Strategies is out with new research it hopes can help.

— In partnership with Tunnl , Precision has developed the “Manosphere Index” to provide campaigns and brands with insight into how to reach men by diving into what is shaping their worldview.

— Post-2024, “there was a lot of data and framing that very narrowly talked about this ‘masculinity crisis,’” said Krishana Davis, who leads Precision’s digital and multicultural engagement efforts. But much of that dialogue was “flattening the conversation, and basically looking at millions of men from a very monolithic view.” Or, she argued, it became “a shorthand of white men, when even white men are not a monolith.”

— Through thousands of interviews, Precision and Tunnl found that economic pressures, more than ideology, are shaping masculinity today. Religion is also playing a major role in men’s lives, especially among Gen Z, Davis said, with many finding a sense of community in faith in addition to platforms like YouTube and various podcasts rather than more traditional media institutions.

— “It’s not that advocacy organizations need to mimic influencers,” Davis said. “But they need to partner with them, work with them, and ensure that they’re also equipping them with these counter narratives, as it makes sense.”

FIRST IN PI – Bryan Lanza , who was a senior adviser on President Donald Trump ’s 2024 campaign, is now a consultant to the international division of Russia oil company Lukoil as it tries to find a buyer for its global assets after it was sanctioned last month, two people familiar with the matter told Daniel L.

Maloney joins the coalition from the American Gaming Association , where he’s served the past two years as senior vice president of strategic communications. Jeremy Kudron , SBA’s current president, will become chair of the alliance.

— Maloney also has experience from the league side of sports betting, having served as vice president of public affairs and strategic comms for the Washington Commanders prior to joining AGA.

— SBA will continue its push for the expansion of legal sports and online gambling under Maloney’s leadership, he told PI. Amid high-profile betting scandals just in the past few months , the industry’s job “is to continue to embrace” the increased scrutiny that has come with its growth, Maloney added..

— “The events of the last several weeks … have demonstrated that our companies, our legal operators, are actually on the front lines in identifying and reporting that activity so that investigation can ensue and bad actors can be brought to justice,” he argued. “And that continues to be a story that we absolutely need to tell.”

FanDuel and DraftKings — both SBA members — left the AGA last month amid the trade group’s campaign against online prediction markets ; Fanatics , another SBA member which launched its own sports prediction market last week, also quit AGA as a result. FIRST IN PI — CAPITOL HILL CELEBRATES JENNER & BLOCK: Congressional Republicans and Democrats came together last night for a bipartisan event celebrating the release of “ When Congress Comes Calling ,” a newly updated handbook on congressional investigations published by Jenner & Block and the Project on Government Oversight .

— Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) and Rep. Jim Jordan (R-Ohio), two of the president’s staunchest allies on Capitol Hill, were part of the crowd at the event, which celebrated the work of the government watchdog group and a law firm President Donald Trump previously accused of abusing its pro-bono practice to “engage in activities that undermine justice and the interests of the United States.”

— Jenner is one of four law firms that sued the Trump administration earlier this year in response to executive orders threatening their ability to do business. The order targeting Jenner accused the firm of engaging in “obvious partisan representations to achieve political ends.” It cited its previous hiring of former federal prosecutor Andrew Weissmann as justification for suspending security clearances held by firm lawyers, reviewing government contracts held by the firm and its clients and limiting the ability of its lawyers to enter government buildings and interact with government personnel.

— A federal judge ruled in May that the order was unconstitutional. The Justice Department is currently appealing that ruling.

— But you wouldn’t detect any of that from the tenor of last night’s event, which brought Johnson and Jordan together with Democrats like Sen. Cory Booker (D-N.J.) and Reps. Zoe Lofgren (D-Calif.), Ro Khanna (D-Calif.) and Mary Gay Scanlon (D-Pa.), per a tipster.

— In remarks, Jordan praised the work of lawyers on all sides of congressional investigations, including committee staff and the lawyers who represent witnesses. “You can’t get to the bottom of any of these investigations unless you have staff who are willing to do the work,” he said. “We got staff who are now on the other side [of the table], the counsel who make the process work, the folks at Jenner & Block, and all of you, all of these good folks. … When you bring in the witnesses, you can’t really make the whole process function unless those witnesses have good counsel like we have here.”

— The updated congressional investigations handbook is a 434-page compendium of the laws and processes that govern congressional investigations and is intended as an all-in-one guidebook for staff investigators and private lawyers. The handbook was last updated in 2017, leaving it in desperate need of an update to reflect case law around congressional inquiries developed during the first Trump administration and the Jan. 6 Committee investigation.

— “The work that you’re doing … is very important,” Lofgren, who served on the Jan. 6 Committee, said.

— “This edition of ‘When Congress Comes Calling’ will serve as a go-to guide for congressional investigators for years to come, and we’d like to thank the Project on Government Oversight for entrusting us with the responsibility of updating this seminal publication,” said Ashley Callen , co-chair of Jenner’s congressional investigations practice.

— Callen’s involvement in the project may help explain the bipartisan well wishes. Before joining Jenner in May, she served in the speaker’s office as general counsel, the capstone to more than two decades on the Hill working for Republican members and committees. Callen previously served as the Republican deputy staff director for the House Oversight Committee while Jordan was ranking member.

Lori Trahan (D-Mass.), said during yesterday’s subcommittee markup hearing.

title: Tim Scott’s chief heads to K Street
body_text:
HOLLAND & HART ADDS COGAR: The top aide to Senate Banking Chair Tim Scott (R-S.C.) is heading to K Street after nearly three decades on the Hill. Charles Cogar , who has worked for Scott since 2013 — most recently as chief of staff — has joined Holland & Hart as a senior director of federal affairs.

— Cogar’s hire is part of an expansion of the firm’s federal lobbying practice beyond energy, environmental and natural resources issues that have made up the bulk of its portfolio. That expansion is being led by Andrew Wheeler , who served as EPA administrator during President Donald Trump ’s first term.

— “We really see some synergies between what Chuck has focused on the last few years and what the firm is working on,” Wheeler said in an interview. He pointed to issues like banking and cryptocurrency as well as congressional oversight and implementation of this summer’s GOP megabill as areas where Cogar’s experience will be useful.

— Holland & Hart, which is based in the Mountain West, also does work on permitting reform, artificial intelligence and the energy needs of data centers. Those issues are poised to dominate policy debates across Washington in 2026. Wheeler does not lobby, but Cogar told PI he plans on registering to do so (though he is subject to a yearlong cooling-off period barring him from lobbying his former Senate colleagues).

— Wheeler’s hires over the past year and a half haven’t been limited to members of his own party. So far in 2025, the firm has hired former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola to help lead Alaska work, along with several former Democratic Hill aides.

But first it will have to overcome opposition from some House conservatives who say the bill to ease environmental reviews would undermine Trump’s assault on renewable energy, our friends at Morning Energy report .

— The leaders of several oil and gas trade groups are directly urging Trump to “prioritize” passage of the bipartisan SPEED Act this week in a move to counteract an effort from offshore wind foes who have tried to bait the president into opposing the bill.

— In a letter to Trump today , the heads of the National Ocean Industries Association , Energy Workforce & Technology Council , Independent Petroleum Association of America and Western Energy Alliance specifically called out the importance of the most controversial language in the bill that would limit presidential power to revoke permits for projects, a key priority across energy industries fearful of getting their approvals yanked depending on the party in power.

— A similar group of oil and gas leaders sent a letter to Speaker Mike Johnson on Friday that pushes back at House members who “have expressed concerns that the SPEED Act might give preference to other sectors at the expense of” the fossil fuel industry. “We do not share those concerns, and those sentiments do not reflect our position,” the industry leaders wrote.

— Earlier today, House Majority Whip Tom Emmer touted the support of more than 300 organizations for the SPEED Act, including the American Exploration & Production Council , American Gas Association , American Petroleum Institute , Edison Electric Institute , Data Center Coalition , Google , National Association of Manufacturers and National Stone, Sand & Gravel Association .

title: Tech revs up for the midterms
body_text:
SILICON VALLEY’S DATA CENTER PROBLEM: “Tech companies and lobbyists are investing millions of dollars to tackle a new political problem for the industry : Data centers, the lifeblood of the growing AI economy, are becoming toxic with voters,” POLITICO ’s Gabby Miller writes.

— “Alarmed by elections that candidates won by campaigning against new data centers, the industry is taking out ads and funding campaigns to flip the narrative and put data centers in a positive light — spinning them as job creators and economic drivers rather than resource-hungry land hogs.”

— “The new campaigns mark a sharp change for an industry that has long relied on tech’s image as an engine of growth and development,” and they “signal how concerned the tech sector is becoming about data centers in the 2026 midterm elections.”

Y COMBINATOR FORMS A PAC: Silicon Valley startup accelerator Y Combinator has taken another step to bolster Little Tech’s political maturation in Washington with the launch of its corporate PAC. The new PAC, which is also referred to in FEC filings as Little Tech PAC, comes as the startup community has sought to compete with more entrenched Big Tech interests to shape AI and competition policy in Washington.

— It also follows the launch of a network of super PACs focused specifically on AI policy. One group, Leading the Future , said it has already reached $100 million in commitments from the likes of venture capitalists Marc Andreessen and Ron Conway , OpenAI co-founder Greg Brockman and Palantir co-founder Joe Lonsdale . The super PAC will pour that money into midterm races to support candidates that align with the industry’s AI priorities and to defeat candidates who oppose tough AI regulations.

— Meta has also seeded multiple super PACs to help beat back AI regulations around the country, while former Reps. Chris Stewart (R-Utah) and Brad Carson (D-Okla.) are leading another set of super PACs to counter industry spending in the midterms.

— “Little tech needs a voice, and we’ll support candidates who get that and oppose those who don’t,” Luther Lowe , Y Combinator’s head of public policy, said of the decision to launch a PAC. In a statement, Lowe laid out some of the biggest policy concerns for Little Tech, including the lament that whether in consumer tech, defense or fintech, “incumbents have captured the rules to freeze out better products.”

— “How will consumers enjoy the fruits of AI — all these new apps and services — if they aren’t discoverable?” Lowe added. He also reiterated the tech industry’s preference for a federal AI framework over a patchwork of state laws as well as the need for immigration reforms to make it easier for “brilliant founders from outside the U.S. to obtain O-1 visas and create companies from scratch that go on to employ tens of thousands of Americans.”

— Unlike the industry super PACs — which can raise and spend unlimited funds as long as there is no coordination with candidates — Y Combinator’s corporate PAC will be restricted to donations from employees only. And though it can donate directly to candidates, those contributions are capped at $5,000.

title: Notre Dame adds K St. powerhouse
body_text:
LUCK OF THE IRISH: The University of Notre Dame has added another K Street heavyweight to its bench of outside lobbying firms. The prestigious Catholic university retained Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck at the beginning of November to provide “strategic counsel” and advocacy on education and tax policy issues affecting the school, according to a disclosure filing.

— Notre Dame will face a bigger tax bill beginning in 2027, thanks to the GOP megabill signed into law this summer that hiked taxes on wealthy colleges’ endowments. Instead of paying a 1.4 percent tax rate on its endowment, the university’s endowment tax rate will jump to 4 percent — bringing its tax bill to around $40-50 million from around $12 million in previous years, according to an August post from the school’s executive officers.

— The Notre Dame officers pledged to continue working with other religious universities to lobby for an exemption to the tax for such schools. An exception was included in the House’s version of the reconciliation bill but was dropped from the final version for procedural reasons.

— Among those working on the account for Brownstein are Marc Lampkin and Radha Mohan , both members of the firm’s higher education task force ; Bart Reising , a former top aide to House Majority Leader Steve Scalise ; Brian McGuire , a former Treasury and Mitch McConnell aide; and Harold Hancock , a former tax counsel for the House Ways and Means Committee.

— Notre Dame also retains BGR Group and Cornerstone Government Affairs , and it hired Lewis-Burke Associates in August.

— “ Future Forward USA Action , the so-called dark-money group of the main super PAC backing Joseph R. The nonprofit flipped around $252 million of that money to its affiliated super PAC, FF PAC .

— “Mr. Trump’s main nonprofit group, Securing American Greatness , collected about $275 million from donors in 2024, according to a separate filing obtained by The Times. Nearly $68 million of that headed to the nonprofit group’s affiliated super PACs.”

— “The filings show starkly how much the main Democratic super PAC leaned on its dark-money group, reflecting one way that the left has raced ahead of the right in campaign finance. Befitting the difference in scale between the two operations, the Democratic nonprofit group’s 2024 tax filing has twice as many pages as its Republican counterpart’s.”

— They also illustrate how 501(c)(4) nonprofits have continued to take on an outsize role in modern political campaigns. NICOTINE STARTUP HIRES CHECKMATE: A nicotine pouch startup aiming to compete with Zyn has hired Checkmate Government Relations as its first Washington lobbying firm, according to a newly filed disclosure report .

— Sesh+ , founded in 2020 and based in Austin, Texas, announced in September it had raised more than $40 million in funding as part of a push to take on Philip Morris’s Zyn, the dominant brand in the nicotine pouch market. In addition to support from venture capital firms such as 8VC , the company also boasts celebrity investors like Post Malone , Diplo , Zac Brown , Andrew Schulz and others.

— Checkmate began representing the company in Washington in mid-November, according to the disclosure report. Firm founder Ches McDowell is listed on the account along with Caitlin Koury , Muhammad Rahim and James Johnson . Chris LaCivita Jr. , the son of President Donald Trump’s 2024 co-campaign manager Chris LaCivita , rounds out the team that will be lobbying on “issues relating to the PMTA process.”

— Premarket tobacco product applications (PMTA) are submitted to the FDA as part of the approval process for any new tobacco product. Pouches produced by Sesh+ don’t contain tobacco, according to the company’s website, but are regulated as tobacco products under FDA guidelines.

— In September, Reuters reported that the FDA plans to fast-track review of nicotine pouches from four companies after receiving pressure from the White House. Sesh was not among the manufacturers receiving White House support, according to the report.

ICYMI: Earlier this week the Senate passed two bills aimed at increasing transparency around foreign influence efforts by closing loopholes in the Lobbying Disclosure Act and the Foreign Agent Registration Act.

— The bills would require lobbyists to indicate on disclosures if they are taking advantage of exemptions that allow them to represent foreign individuals without registering under FARA or if foreign governments have any interest, financial or otherwise, in their lobbying efforts. The measures were introduced by Sens. Chuck Grassley (R-Iowa) and Gary Peters (D-Mich.).

— House versions of the bills have languished in the Judiciary Committee since being introduced in March.

LUNAR LOBBYING : The United States is aiming to go back to the moon and commercial space companies are lobbying for NASA to use their rockets, POLITICO’S Audrey Decker reports in POLITICO Pro Space .

— A new proposal by the Commercial Space Federation , a trade group that represents companies like SpaceX and Blue Origin , urges the House to add language to a NASA reauthorization bill. It would allow the space agency to use commercial rockets for moon missions instead of the current Boeing system, which the agency plans to use for upcoming lunar flights.

— “Long-term, there’s consensus in the space industry that NASA needs cheaper commercial rockets to achieve a sustainable presence on the moon — since [the Boeing system] costs billions per launch. But there’s no clear agreement on when exactly that shift should happen,” Decker writes.

FULL STEAM AHEAD: Union Pacific Railroad Company ’s proposed acquisition of fellow rail-giant Norfolk Southern moved into its next phase today as the railroad filed an official merger application with the Surface Transportation Board, the government body that will have to approve the deal. — “Now, are we going to win some business from other railroads? Absolutely,” Vena said. “Customers have a choice.”

— But the Rail Customer Coalition , a collection of trade groups representing industries that depend on freight rail, said today’s application fails to show how the merger will improve service or enhance competition among railroads.

— “At a time when the top concern for Americans is the cost of living and inflation, policymakers must stand with consumers and reject any deal that fails to promote competition over monopolies and drives prices even higher,” Chris Jahn , president and CEO of the American Chemistry Council said in a statement. The ACC is a member of the Rail Customers Coalition along with the American Petroleum Institute , the Alliance for Automotive Innovation and more.

GAMIFYING LOBBYING: Toyota has an internal platform where employees can play games and earn rewards in exchange for listening to recordings of company lobbyists and contacting lawmakers to urge action on the automaker’s policy goals, Dharna Noor reports for The Guardian .

— The platform, called Toyota Policy Drivers, gives employees the ability to win points by playing retro-themed games and engaging with company messaging on issues like emissions regulations. Points can be exchanged for physical rewards like stickers, t-shirts and even trips. Calls to action on the platform encourage employees to contact their representatives to support Toyota’s policy positions.

— “On Monster Mansion, a game featuring cozy haunted house motifs, users can earn 100 points for listening to corporate recordings. In one, company lobbyists discuss how the company is affected by trade policy; in another, women Toyota dealers praise a Washington, D.C. company event with lawmakers. A third features Stephen Ciccone – the longtime vice-president of public affairs for Toyota in North America – criticizing environmental measures.”

BREAKING THE BANK: The American Bankers Association , along with bankers associations from all 50 states, D.C. and Puerto Rico, sent a letter to Congress yesterday urging lawmakers to take action on a loophole in the GENIUS Act. Closing the current loophole by clarifying that the prohibition extends to partners and affiliates would restore parity, protect consumers, and align practice with legislative intent,” the associations write.

— “The push to restrict stablecoin rewards beyond that agreed to in GENIUS is not a technical refinement or a consumer protection fix,” the crypto letter states. “It would prohibit the same types of incentive programs for stablecoin payments that banks have long offered on credit cards and other types of payment services.”

title: Higher ed gold rush on K Street continues
body_text:
A DIFFERENT KIND OF MARCH MADNESS: Lobbying firms have continued to hoover up new business from colleges and universities in the lead-up to this week’s escalation of President Donald Trump ‘s war with higher education . Newly filed disclosures show Purdue University hired Bose Public Affairs Group and Barnes & Thornburg at the beginning of March to lobby on issues including appropriations, science and technology and defense policy.

— The hires came days after Trump singled out one of the school’s research grants as an illustration of wasted federal resources and amid a broader onslaught targeting schools’ DEI practices and research funding.

— In a signal of the uphill battle universities like Purdue are facing as Trump doubles down on his collegiate pressure campaign, even would-be allies are warning that some concessions will be necessary. Mitch Daniels , the former Indiana governor who served as Purdue’s president up until a few years ago, bemoaned in a Washington Post op-ed this week the lack of “self-examination, repentance or acceptance of some need to mend ways” from university leaders around the country.

— In March, Cornell University hired Miller Strategies to work on oversight issues, according to a disclosure — though the hire didn’t keep the Trump administration from freezing more than $1 billion in federal funds for the Ivy earlier this week amid civil rights probes. And the regents of the University of California retained BGR Group to provide strategic counsel and advice on higher education and appropriations as several of the school system’s campuses face federal civil rights probes.

— Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck has registered to lobby for Teachers College , Columbia University ’s graduate school education program, on funding issues for higher education, per a disclosure filing. Despite Columbia’s acquiescence to a list of demands by the Trump administration last month, the administration froze another quarter billion dollars in federal research grants and other funding earlier in April.

— Other recently disclosed hires include Johns Hopkins University , which hired HB Strategies to lobby on issues related to federal funding, universities and endowment tax; Wabash College , a smaller school in Indiana that risks facing a major tax hike on its endowment and which also hired Barnes & Thornburg; Berea College , a private liberal arts school in Kentucky with an endowment of more than $1.5 billion, which retained Cogent Strategies (as a subcontractor of Penn Hill Group ); and Western Carolina University , which hired Thorn Run Partners to lobby on defense, energy and water appropriations.

— This is the first time Wabash and Western Carolina have hired federal lobbyists, according to disclosure filings, while Berea’s hires this year are the school’s first in more than two decades.

TGIF and welcome to PI . Send lobbying tips and rumors for me to chase down for the remainder of the Easter recess. You can add me on Signal , email me at [email protected] , and be sure to follow me on X : @caitlinoprysko .

MORE NEW BUSINESS: Here’s a few more interesting new lobbying registrations that have come in ahead of next week’s reporting deadline. Meta hired its first new lobbying firm in almost two years. The social media giant retained Mehlman Consulting this month to work on many of the usual issues, including data privacy, AI, kids online safety and online advertising.

— Insurance industry group AHIP brought on former Mitch McConnell aide Scott Raab of Raab Government Strategies , while the Federation of American Hospitals retained Cozen O’Connor Public Strategies , and tobacco giant Philip Morris International hired Checkmate Government Relations .

— BGR Group registered to lobby for shipping service Pirate Ship on postal issues and memory card maker Sandisk on trade and manufacturing policy affecting the tech industry, as well as for seasonings purveyor Spice World (via Vantage Knight ) on trade issues related to the garlic industry.

— Meanwhile the Flavor and Extract Manufacturers Association has tapped Keller and Heckman to lobby on policy and regulation of food additives, food safety and food labeling, according to a disclosure filing.

McGUIREWOODS LOBBYISTS HANG A SHINGLE: Rob Wasinger and Mike Andrews have left McGuireWoods to open their own lobbying shop, Ragnar Group . Wasinger spent close to 20 years on the Hill, including serving as chief of staff to former Sen. Sam Brownback (R-Kan.), before joining Trump’s 2016 campaign and transition as a Senate and gubernatorial liaison. He joined McGuireWoods in 2017.

— Andrews joined McGuireWoods in 2021 after serving as GOP staff director and chief counsel for the Senate Indian Affairs Committee. He previously worked in HUD’s Office of Native American Programs.

— Ragnar has already signed 29 clients, including Sinclair Broadcasting Network and taser manufacturer Axon Enterprise , and a number of tribal governments such as Cherokee Nation, the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, the Moapa Band of Paiutes and the Picayune Rancheria of the Chukchansi Indians.

CRAVING A CARVE-OUT : “Car companies, toy manufacturers, farmers, retail groups and others who face significant cost increases from President Donald Trump’s steep new tariffs on China are all ramping up their lobbying of the administration to press for carve-outs and assistance,” POLITICO ’s Daniel Desrochers reports.

— “But, with no formal process in place to submit their requests, and no direct line to the one decision-maker who matters, most businesses and industries are hitting a wall, so far. And those in the business world with connections to the White House figure it’s likely to stay that way until an industry can demonstrate to the president there’s a true crisis at hand.”

— “‘There’s only one person that can really authorize that exemption and that’s the president,’ said one business representative with close ties to the Trump administration, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. ‘So if you’re not a company that can whisper in the president’s ear or make the trip to Mar-a-Lago and do it persuasively, then you’re sort of frozen out of the process for now.’”

— “After insisting for weeks that there would be no special treatment in his trade war, Trump exempted a broad chunk of electronic products from the levies. But other industries so far haven’t had similar luck.”

IT’S NOT ALL BAD NEWS: The uncertainty of Trump’s trade war is looming large over many rural communities, but at least one sector of the ag world sees a potential opening in the disruption , POLITICO’s Jordan Wolman reports.

— “The biofuels industry and its supporters are stepping up advocacy at a time when the president’s tariffs are threatening farmers’ income from exports and his push to expand fossil fuel production shifts the energy landscape away from the Biden administration’s green agenda. They’re trying to sell climate-skeptical Trump officials on the idea that they can help increase domestic energy production while helping farmers weather the impact of retaliatory tariffs and funding cuts.”

AUTO TRADE GROUP ADDS 3: The Alliance for Automotive Innovation has added a bipartisan pair of former Hill staffers to its federal lobbying team as the auto industry stares down a raft of potentially drastic policy changes. Iain Hart and Gary Haglund have both joined the trade association as federal affairs directors.

— The coalition, which represents the country’s top automakers, as well as radio, battery and semiconductor manufacturers and other equipment suppliers, has also brought on Sandra Henriques as manager of growth operations.

— Haglund was most recently a policy adviser to Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), where his portfolio included Cassidy’s tax and trade work on the Senate Finance Committee. Haglund previously worked for another congressional Republican who’s playing a starring role in this year’s tax debate — now-House Ways and Means Chair Jason Smith (R-Mo.) — and for conservative advocacy group Americans for Prosperity .

— Hart comes to the group after more than a decade on the Hill, including most recently serving as deputy chief of staff and legislative director for Rep. John Garamendi (D-Calif.). Henriques joins from the Republican firm Targeted Victory , where she was a client strategy manager.

WHAT’S KEEPING NONPROFITS UP AT NIGHT: “The close-knit world of liberal donors and the nonprofit groups they support has spent the last week in a state of fear and anxiety, worried that any day now, President Trump could go after their assets or their tax-exempt status ,” The New York Times’ Teddy Schleifer and Lisa Friedman write.

— That panic “all seemed purely speculative” until yesterday, when Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that “he was potentially seeking to pull Harvard’s tax-exempt status , in an apparent act of retaliation for the university’s refusal to bow to a long list of demands. And he said there ‘could be’ others, suggesting that the Internal Revenue Service could also take action against organizations that support immigrants or the environment” — though the legality of such a move is dubious.

— Trump also singled out the watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington , and environmental groups and the progressive online donation platform ActBlue have already been under scrutiny by Republican policymakers.

— “Many groups that are taking steps to avoid being targeted are doing so quietly, concerned about provoking the administration,” but others are putting up a more public fight. “Last week, three prominent liberal philanthropic foundations announced what they called the ‘Unite in Advance’ solidarity campaign,” urging their peers in an open letter to take proactive action, getting “legal teams on speed dial, crisis plans dusted off, reserves lined up — and most importantly, a plan to speak up loudly and together.”

ANNALS OF FUNDRAISING : “Expiration of the GOP’s 2017 tax law is speeding campaign contributions from big business and other interests seeking to woo lawmakers in charge of the renewal,” Bloomberg ’s Zach Cohen and Chris Cioffi report. “House and Senate Republican tax writers saw a more than 60% fundraising first quarter bump compared with the same period two years ago. It comes as lawmakers work on a multitrillion-dollar bill to extend individual and business tax cuts that expire at year’s end if Congress doesn’t act.”

In a fragmented global landscape, understanding how policy and politics intersect across borders is critical. Forecast synthesizes POLITICO’s global reporting to connect key developments and global convenings, giving readers a clearer view of what’s ahead. Subscribe Now .

A DIFFERENT KIND OF MARCH MADNESS: Lobbying firms have continued to hoover up new business from colleges and universities in the lead-up to this week’s escalation of President Donald Trump‘s war with higher education. Newly filed disclosures show Purdue University hired Bose Public Affairs Group and Barnes & Thornburg at the beginning of March to lobby on issues including appropriations, science and technology and defense policy.

— The hires came days after Trump singled out one of the school’s research grants as an illustration of wasted federal resources and amid a broader onslaught targeting schools’ DEI practices and research funding.

— In a signal of the uphill battle universities like Purdue are facing as Trump doubles down on his collegiate pressure campaign, even would-be allies are warning that some concessions will be necessary. Mitch Daniels, the former Indiana governor who served as Purdue’s president up until a few years ago, bemoaned in a Washington Post op-ed this week the lack of “self-examination, repentance or acceptance of some need to mend ways” from university leaders around the country.

— In March, Cornell University hired Miller Strategies to work on oversight issues, according to a disclosure — though the hire didn’t keep the Trump administration from freezing more than $1 billion in federal funds for the Ivy earlier this week amid civil rights probes. And the regents of the University of California retained BGR Group to provide strategic counsel and advice on higher education and appropriations as several of the school system’s campuses face federal civil rights probes.

— Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck has registered to lobby for Teachers College, Columbia University’s graduate school education program, on funding issues for higher education, per a disclosure filing. Despite Columbia’s acquiescence to a list of demands by the Trump administration last month, the administration froze another quarter billion dollars in federal research grants and other funding earlier in April.

— Other recently disclosed hires include Johns Hopkins University, which hired HB Strategies to lobby on issues related to federal funding, universities and endowment tax; Wabash College, a smaller school in Indiana that risks facing a major tax hike on its endowment and which also hired Barnes & Thornburg; Berea College, a private liberal arts school in Kentucky with an endowment of more than $1.5 billion, which retained Cogent Strategies (as a subcontractor of Penn Hill Group); and Western Carolina University, which hired Thorn Run Partners to lobby on defense, energy and water appropriations.

— This is the first time Wabash and Western Carolina have hired federal lobbyists, according to disclosure filings, while Berea’s hires this year are the school’s first in more than two decades.

TGIF and welcome to PI. Send lobbying tips and rumors for me to chase down for the remainder of the Easter recess. You can add me on Signal, email me at [email protected], and be sure to follow me on X: @caitlinoprysko.

MORE NEW BUSINESS: Here’s a few more interesting new lobbying registrations that have come in ahead of next week’s reporting deadline. Meta hired its first new lobbying firm in almost two years. The social media giant retained Mehlman Consulting this month to work on many of the usual issues, including data privacy, AI, kids online safety and online advertising.

— Insurance industry group AHIP brought on former Mitch McConnell aide Scott Raab of Raab Government Strategies, while the Federation of American Hospitals retained Cozen O’Connor Public Strategies, and tobacco giant Philip Morris International hired Checkmate Government Relations.

— BGR Group registered to lobby for shipping service Pirate Ship on postal issues and memory card maker Sandisk on trade and manufacturing policy affecting the tech industry, as well as for seasonings purveyor Spice World (via Vantage Knight) on trade issues related to the garlic industry.

— Meanwhile the Flavor and Extract Manufacturers Association has tapped Keller and Heckman to lobby on policy and regulation of food additives, food safety and food labeling, according to a disclosure filing.

McGUIREWOODS LOBBYISTS HANG A SHINGLE: Rob Wasinger and Mike Andrews have left McGuireWoods to open their own lobbying shop, Ragnar Group. Wasinger spent close to 20 years on the Hill, including serving as chief of staff to former Sen. Sam Brownback (R-Kan.), before joining Trump’s 2016 campaign and transition as a Senate and gubernatorial liaison. He joined McGuireWoods in 2017.

— Andrews joined McGuireWoods in 2021 after serving as GOP staff director and chief counsel for the Senate Indian Affairs Committee. He previously worked in HUD’s Office of Native American Programs.

— Ragnar has already signed 29 clients, including Sinclair Broadcasting Network and taser manufacturer Axon Enterprise, and a number of tribal governments such as Cherokee Nation, the Ute Mountain Ute Tribe, the Moapa Band of Paiutes and the Picayune Rancheria of the Chukchansi Indians.

CRAVING A CARVE-OUT: “Car companies, toy manufacturers, farmers, retail groups and others who face significant cost increases from President Donald Trump’s steep new tariffs on China are all ramping up their lobbying of the administration to press for carve-outs and assistance,” POLITICO’s Daniel Desrochers reports.

— “But, with no formal process in place to submit their requests, and no direct line to the one decision-maker who matters, most businesses and industries are hitting a wall, so far. And those in the business world with connections to the White House figure it’s likely to stay that way until an industry can demonstrate to the president there’s a true crisis at hand.”

— “‘There’s only one person that can really authorize that exemption and that’s the president,’ said one business representative with close ties to the Trump administration, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly. ‘So if you’re not a company that can whisper in the president’s ear or make the trip to Mar-a-Lago and do it persuasively, then you’re sort of frozen out of the process for now.’”

— “After insisting for weeks that there would be no special treatment in his trade war, Trump exempted a broad chunk of electronic products from the levies. But other industries so far haven’t had similar luck.”

IT’S NOT ALL BAD NEWS: The uncertainty of Trump’s trade war is looming large over many rural communities, but at least one sector of the ag world sees a potential opening in the disruption, POLITICO’s Jordan Wolman reports.

— “The biofuels industry and its supporters are stepping up advocacy at a time when the president’s tariffs are threatening farmers’ income from exports and his push to expand fossil fuel production shifts the energy landscape away from the Biden administration’s green agenda. They’re trying to sell climate-skeptical Trump officials on the idea that they can help increase domestic energy production while helping farmers weather the impact of retaliatory tariffs and funding cuts.”

AUTO TRADE GROUP ADDS 3: The Alliance for Automotive Innovation has added a bipartisan pair of former Hill staffers to its federal lobbying team as the auto industry stares down a raft of potentially drastic policy changes. Iain Hart and Gary Haglund have both joined the trade association as federal affairs directors.

— The coalition, which represents the country’s top automakers, as well as radio, battery and semiconductor manufacturers and other equipment suppliers, has also brought on Sandra Henriques as manager of growth operations.

— Haglund was most recently a policy adviser to Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-La.), where his portfolio included Cassidy’s tax and trade work on the Senate Finance Committee. Haglund previously worked for another congressional Republican who’s playing a starring role in this year’s tax debate — now-House Ways and Means Chair Jason Smith (R-Mo.) — and for conservative advocacy group Americans for Prosperity.

— Hart comes to the group after more than a decade on the Hill, including most recently serving as deputy chief of staff and legislative director for Rep. John Garamendi (D-Calif.). Henriques joins from the Republican firm Targeted Victory, where she was a client strategy manager.

WHAT’S KEEPING NONPROFITS UP AT NIGHT: “The close-knit world of liberal donors and the nonprofit groups they support has spent the last week in a state of fear and anxiety, worried that any day now, President Trump could go after their assets or their tax-exempt status,” The New York Times’ Teddy Schleifer and Lisa Friedman write.

— That panic “all seemed purely speculative” until yesterday, when Trump told reporters in the Oval Office that “he was potentially seeking to pull Harvard’s tax-exempt status, in an apparent act of retaliation for the university’s refusal to bow to a long list of demands. And he said there ‘could be’ others, suggesting that the Internal Revenue Service could also take action against organizations that support immigrants or the environment” — though the legality of such a move is dubious.

— Trump also singled out the watchdog group Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, and environmental groups and the progressive online donation platform ActBlue have already been under scrutiny by Republican policymakers.

— “Many groups that are taking steps to avoid being targeted are doing so quietly, concerned about provoking the administration,” but others are putting up a more public fight. “Last week, three prominent liberal philanthropic foundations announced what they called the ‘Unite in Advance’ solidarity campaign,” urging their peers in an open letter to take proactive action, getting “legal teams on speed dial, crisis plans dusted off, reserves lined up — and most importantly, a plan to speak up loudly and together.”

ANNALS OF FUNDRAISING: “Expiration of the GOP’s 2017 tax law is speeding campaign contributions from big business and other interests seeking to woo lawmakers in charge of the renewal,” Bloomberg’s Zach Cohen and Chris Cioffi report. “House and Senate Republican tax writers saw a more than 60% fundraising first quarter bump compared with the same period two years ago. It comes as lawmakers work on a multitrillion-dollar bill to extend individual and business tax cuts that expire at year’s end if Congress doesn’t act.”

title: Ballard’s big Q1 haul
body_text:
RAKING IT IN: Numbers are still rolling in ahead of tonight’s filing deadline for first quarter lobbying reports, but there’s one eye-popping number that demonstrates where the power lies on K Street in Donald Trump ’s Washington before more broadly diving into the revenue rankings tomorrow.

— Ballard Partners will report $14 million in lobbying revenues for the first three months of 2025 — a huge surge in business that’s more than double the $6.2 million Ballard brought in last quarter and triple the $4.2 million the firm reported during the first quarter of 2024.

— Many of the largest firms on K Street have yet to report their first quarter revenues ahead of Monday’s midnight deadline, but Ballard’s haul will likely place it close to the top. The beginning of any new administration tends to be lucrative for the lobbying industry — and business was already booming before Trump swept into office again — but Trump’s second term has been especially marked by upheaval and retribution on top of the already massive stakes for clients with Congress looking to move a tax bill this year.

— To put Ballard’s haul in context, Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck topped the revenue rankings with $16.9 million in revenue in the fourth quarter of 2024, according to a PI analysis, while the runner-up, Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld , reported $14.6 million that quarter. Brownstein’s revenue dipped slightly in the first quarter of 2025, to $16.8 million, while Akin’s jumped up to $16.4 million, according to figures shared by the firms.

— Ballard, which has disclosed more than 130 new clients since the election, isn’t the only firm with ties to the administration to be inundated with business since November. Miller Strategies , Mercury Public Affairs , Michael Best Strategies and Continental Strategies have also signed dozens of new clients over the past six months, and PI will be tracking their Q1 numbers as well.

WHO FUNDED TRUMP’S INAUGURATION?: Speaking of massive sums of money, Trump’s inaugural committee reported last night that it raked in more $239 million — shattering Trump’s previous record-breaking haul of $107 million in 2017.

— The inaugural committee raised money from more than 800 individual donors, companies and PACs — many of whom were happy to publicize their donations. Close to 150 donors cut checks for at least $1 million, but the fund’s top donors overall were the poultry company Pilgrim’s Pride , which gave $5 million; crypto firm Ripple Labs , which gave $4.9 million; and Warren Stephens , the investment banker who gave $4 million the same day he was announced as Trump’s nominee for ambassador to the U.K.

— Almost a dozen donors to the inauguration have been nominated or confirmed to posts in the administration, including Stephens. They include Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent (who donated $250,000) and Education Secretary Linda McMahon (who gave $1 million). Dan Newlin , Trump’s pick for ambassador to Colombia, Ken Howery , Trump’s pick for ambassador to Denmark, and Tilman Fertitta , Trump’s pick for ambassador to Italy, all gave $1 million as well. Melinda Hildebrand , Trump’s nominee for ambassador to Costa Rica, gave $500,000 (as did her husband).

— Of course, virtually every inaugural donor has business of some sort before the new administration. But a new analysis from watchdog group Public Citizen found that the inaugural fund took in $50 million from 58 companies who were facing federal investigations , enforcement actions or lawsuits when Trump entered office. Cases against 11 of those corporations have since been dismissed or paused , the watchdog found, including cases involving Bank of America , Pfizer , GEO Group , Capital One , Ericsson and Ripple Labs.
