MALONEY JUMPS TO EEI: The Edison Electric Institute has tapped Drew Maloney as its president and CEO. Maloney has spent the past six years as head of the private equity industry’s main trade group in Washington, the American Investment Council . Before that he served as assistant secretary for legislative affairs at Treasury during the first Trump administration, and as vice president of global government affairs and public policy at Hess .

— Maloney joins EEI at a crucial moment for the power companies it represents, but also following internal turmoil at the trade group. The association’s former previous leader, former Trump Energy Secretary Dan Brouillette , left EEI in October amid flagging confidence from utility executives in Brouillette’s ability to steer the group. He had only been in the role for 10 months.

TECH OF THE TOWN: This morning’s White House Easter egg roll served as “yet another effort by Big Tech companies to make nice with the Trump administration,” Business Insider ’s Lauren Edmonds reports in a rundown of which companies took Trump up on his pitch for corporate sponsorships of the annual event.

— “ Meta will provide an ‘AI-Powered Experience and Photo Opportunity,’ while Amazon will provide a reading nook and a ‘Family Photo Opportunity Celebrating Reading.’ YouTube , owned by Google , arranged the Bunny Hop Stage. The New York Stock Exchange also agreed to partner and provide a ‘Ringing of the Bell Photo Opportunity,’” according to a program released by the White House on Friday.

— Meta, Amazon and Google, of course, all were among the donors to Trump’s inaugural committee who ponied up $1 million. “Whatever for?” you might ask. “This week marks a moment of truth for Washington’s push to rein in Big Tech — a yearslong and often fruitless battle to curb the power of the world’s richest companies,” POLITICO ’s Brendan Bordelon and Gabby Miller report.

— “After years of empty threats from Congress, two major antitrust cases have landed two companies in court at once. Google has now lost twice to the Department of Justice and faces a remedy trial Monday that could see the company broken up to fix its illegal monopoly in online search. Just down the hallway, Meta will kick off its second week in court defending itself against a breakup threat from the Federal Trade Commission.”

— “[I]f the government gets its way, the trials raise the real possibility of a reshaped Silicon Valley. But Big Tech breakups are by no means assured,” they write, and Trump “is the biggest wildcard.”

— On the other hand, POLITICO’s Ruth Reader reports that Meta is making headway elsewhere in Washington . CEO Mark Zuckerberg “is flooding Washington with ads aimed at convincing lawmakers to require his rivals’ app stores to verify shoppers’ ages and require parental consent for kids to download social media apps,” Ruth writes — a move that would shift the onus to Apple and Google — after successfully derailing a bipartisan kids online safety bill last year that would have targeted Meta-owned Facebook and Instagram .

FIRST IN PI — NARRATIVE ADDS BOEHM: Cassie Boehm has left Adfero , where she was a vice president, to join Narrative Strategies as a managing director. Boehm joined Adfero in 2019 as a media specialist, and worked her way up to become the leader of the firm’s public affairs practice. Before Adfero, Boehm was an advocacy communications manager at the Wine & Spirits Wholesalers of America and worked on the Hill as a spokesperson.

— In addition to adding Boehm, Narrative has promoted Connor James to strategic communications associate and Mariska Bogaard to operations associate.

GOT ME CURSING THE DAYLIGHT (SAVING TIME): Trump’s recent ambivalence on daylight saving time has kicked off a lobbying frenzy , POLITICO’s Ben Leonard reports. “After calling on Congress to ‘eliminate Daylight Saving Time’ back in December, Trump then called it a ‘50/50 issue’ in March before suggesting last week that lawmakers should make daylight saving time permanent. That would mean more daylight in the evening hours and most Americans would no longer have to change their clocks twice a year.”

— “Those latest comments … set off a flurry of activity among a small but highly engaged cadre of lobbyists and advocates for industries that would benefit from permanent daylight saving time — and those that want to stick with standard time. It’s an issue that has pitted the golf industry and retail interests against sleep doctors and Christian radio broadcasters, as well as people pursuing passion projects on both sides.”

— “These advocates are now planning new outreach to the Trump administration — including Elon Musk ’s Department of Government Efficiency and Robert F. Kennedy Jr. ’s Department of Health and Human Services — as well as to members of Congress who came close but fell short in advancing legislation to make daylight saving time permanent in 2022. Activity is picking up around the issue among conservative influencers, too.”

NOT THAT AARP: The leading advocacy group for older Americans is moving to shut down a flood of questions it got over the weekend after a flurry of litigation related to Trump’s effort to deport another wave of Venezuelan men under the Alien Enemies Act, Josh writes in.

— The Supreme Court’s order early Saturday blocking those deportations was issued under the caption A.A.R.P. v. Trump , based on the initials for one of the Venezuelans facing expulsion. That caused some distress to the elder-advocacy organization AARP , formerly known as the American Association of Retired Persons, whose lawyers filed a motion Saturday asking the lower court where the case originated to change its title.

— “AARP is concerned that the nomenclature adopted by the caption of this case will create substantial confusion among journalists and the public. Indeed, in the 72 hours since the litigation was filed, it has already resulted in numerous misplaced inquiries to AARP,” the group’s lawyers wrote. The American Civil Liberties Union , which represents the potential deportees, and the Justice Department, which represents the Trump administration, do not object to renaming the case, the filing said.

Ballard’s big Q1 haul

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO 

04/21/2025 06:07 PM EDT

Presented by

With Daniel Lippman, Josh Gerstein

RAKING IT IN: Numbers are still rolling in ahead of tonight’s filing deadline for first quarter lobbying reports, but there’s one eye-popping number that demonstrates where the power lies on K Street in Donald Trump’s Washington before more broadly diving into the revenue rankings tomorrow.

— Ballard Partners will report $14 million in lobbying revenues for the first three months of 2025 — a huge surge in business that’s more than double the $6.2 million Ballard brought in last quarter and triple the $4.2 million the firm reported during the first quarter of 2024.

— Many of the largest firms on K Street have yet to report their first quarter revenues ahead of Monday’s midnight deadline, but Ballard’s haul will likely place it close to the top. The beginning of any new administration tends to be lucrative for the lobbying industry — and business was already booming before Trump swept into office again — but Trump’s second term has been especially marked by upheaval and retribution on top of the already massive stakes for clients with Congress looking to move a tax bill this year.

— To put Ballard’s haul in context, Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck topped the revenue rankings with $16.9 million in revenue in the fourth quarter of 2024, according to a PI analysis, while the runner-up, Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld, reported $14.6 million that quarter. Brownstein’s revenue dipped slightly in the first quarter of 2025, to $16.8 million, while Akin’s jumped up to $16.4 million, according to figures shared by the firms.

— Ballard, which has disclosed more than 130 new clients since the election, isn’t the only firm with ties to the administration to be inundated with business since November. Miller Strategies, Mercury Public Affairs, Michael Best Strategies and Continental Strategies have also signed dozens of new clients over the past six months, and PI will be tracking their Q1 numbers as well.

WHO FUNDED TRUMP’S INAUGURATION?: Speaking of massive sums of money, Trump’s inaugural committee reported last night that it raked in more $239 million — shattering Trump’s previous record-breaking haul of $107 million in 2017.

— The inaugural committee raised money from more than 800 individual donors, companies and PACs — many of whom were happy to publicize their donations. Close to 150 donors cut checks for at least $1 million, but the fund’s top donors overall were the poultry company Pilgrim’s Pride, which gave $5 million; crypto firm Ripple Labs, which gave $4.9 million; and Warren Stephens, the investment banker who gave $4 million the same day he was announced as Trump’s nominee for ambassador to the U.K.

— Almost a dozen donors to the inauguration have been nominated or confirmed to posts in the administration, including Stephens. They include Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent (who donated $250,000) and Education Secretary Linda McMahon (who gave $1 million). Dan Newlin, Trump’s pick for ambassador to Colombia, Ken Howery, Trump’s pick for ambassador to Denmark, and Tilman Fertitta, Trump’s pick for ambassador to Italy, all gave $1 million as well. Melinda Hildebrand, Trump’s nominee for ambassador to Costa Rica, gave $500,000 (as did her husband).

— Of course, virtually every inaugural donor has business of some sort before the new administration. But a new analysis from watchdog group Public Citizen found that the inaugural fund took in $50 million from 58 companies who were facing federal investigations, enforcement actions or lawsuits when Trump entered office. Cases against 11 of those corporations have since been dismissed or paused , the watchdog found, including cases involving Bank of America, Pfizer, GEO Group, Capital One, Ericsson and Ripple Labs.

The New York Stock Exchange also agreed to partner and provide a ‘Ringing of the Bell Photo Opportunity,’” according to a program released by the White House on Friday.

— “After years of empty threats from Congress, two major antitrust cases have landed two companies in court at once. Google has now lost twice to the Department of Justice and faces a remedy trial Monday that could see the company broken up to fix its illegal monopoly in online search. Just down the hallway, Meta will kick off its second week in court defending itself against a breakup threat from the Federal Trade Commission.”

— “[I]f the government gets its way, the trials raise the real possibility of a reshaped Silicon Valley. But Big Tech breakups are by no means assured,” they write, and Trump “is the biggest wildcard.”

— On the other hand, POLITICO’s Ruth Reader reports that Meta is making headway elsewhere in Washington. CEO Mark Zuckerberg “is flooding Washington with ads aimed at convincing lawmakers to require his rivals’ app stores to verify shoppers’ ages and require parental consent for kids to download social media apps,” Ruth writes — a move that would shift the onus to Apple and Google — after successfully derailing a bipartisan kids online safety bill last year that would have targeted Meta-owned Facebook and Instagram.

FIRST IN PI — NARRATIVE ADDS BOEHM: Cassie Boehm has left Adfero, where she was a vice president, to join Narrative Strategies as a managing director. Boehm joined Adfero in 2019 as a media specialist, and worked her way up to become the leader of the firm’s public affairs practice. Before Adfero, Boehm was an advocacy communications manager at the Wine & Spirits Wholesalers of America and worked on the Hill as a spokesperson.

— In addition to adding Boehm, Narrative has promoted Connor James to strategic communications associate and Mariska Bogaard to operations associate.

GOT ME CURSING THE DAYLIGHT (SAVING TIME): Trump’s recent ambivalence on daylight saving time has kicked off a lobbying frenzy, POLITICO’s Ben Leonard reports. “After calling on Congress to ‘eliminate Daylight Saving Time’ back in December, Trump then called it a ‘50/50 issue’ in March before suggesting last week that lawmakers should make daylight saving time permanent. That would mean more daylight in the evening hours and most Americans would no longer have to change their clocks twice a year.”

— “Those latest comments … set off a flurry of activity among a small but highly engaged cadre of lobbyists and advocates for industries that would benefit from permanent daylight saving time — and those that want to stick with standard time. It’s an issue that has pitted the golf industry and retail interests against sleep doctors and Christian radio broadcasters, as well as people pursuing passion projects on both sides.”

— “These advocates are now planning new outreach to the Trump administration — including Elon Musk’s Department of Government Efficiency and Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s Department of Health and Human Services — as well as to members of Congress who came close but fell short in advancing legislation to make daylight saving time permanent in 2022. Activity is picking up around the issue among conservative influencers, too.”

NOT THAT AARP: The leading advocacy group for older Americans is moving to shut down a flood of questions it got over the weekend after a flurry of litigation related to Trump’s effort to deport another wave of Venezuelan men under the Alien Enemies Act, Josh writes in.

— The Supreme Court’s order early Saturday blocking those deportations was issued under the caption A.A.R.P. v. Trump, based on the initials for one of the Venezuelans facing expulsion. That caused some distress to the elder-advocacy organization AARP, formerly known as the American Association of Retired Persons, whose lawyers filed a motion Saturday asking the lower court where the case originated to change its title.

— “AARP is concerned that the nomenclature adopted by the caption of this case will create substantial confusion among journalists and the public. Indeed, in the 72 hours since the litigation was filed, it has already resulted in numerous misplaced inquiries to AARP,” the group’s lawyers wrote. The American Civil Liberties Union, which represents the potential deportees, and the Justice Department, which represents the Trump administration, do not object to renaming the case, the filing said.

WHAT THE NUMBERS MEAN: Donald Trump ’s return to Washington lit a new fire under an already-hot lobbying market, but no firms experienced a bigger boon in the first quarter than those with close ties to the president, according to a PI analysis of disclosure filings.

— Lobbying revenues were up nearly across the board during the first three months of this year for many of K Street’s top shops, as Trump steamed into office and immediately began pumping out executive orders, targeting perceived enemies and moving to upend global trade and geopolitical alignments before sometimes retreating abruptly.

— The huge payday for K Street also comes as congressional Republicans roll back key Biden-era regulations, dig in on regulating the cryptocurrency and AI industries,attempt to extend Trump’s prized 2017 tax break and enact the president’s domestic agenda. And that’s not even to mention the upheaval and confusion triggered by Elon Musk ’s haphazard slashing of federal programs and the federal workforce.

— Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld , whose $16.4 million in lobbying revenues were second only to Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck ’s $16.8 million, saw its strongest quarter ever, according to Brian Pomper , the co-head of Akin’s lobbying practice. Akin’s lobbying revenues were up more than 12 percent compared to the fourth quarter of 2024 and almost 19 percent compared to the same period a year ago. Their new lobbying registrations last quarter were about triple the average number of new registrations per quarter in 2024.

— But the biggest story is the handful of firms that are cashing in on their ties to the president and his inner circle. Among these Trump-connected firms, Continental Strategy saw the biggest boost to business, relative to previous quarters. Continental hauled in more than $3.6 million in lobbying revenues in Q1. That’s up almost tenfold from last quarter, when the firm disclosed earning $373,000. During the same period in 2024, Continental reported just $128,000 in lobbying revenues.

— As PI reported yesterday , Ballard Partners saw its lobbying revenues skyrocket to $14 million in Q1, compared to $4.3 million a year ago. The increase was enough to vault Ballard from 16th in PI’s revenue rankings for all of 2024 to fourth in the revenue rankings for Q1.

— Also popping into the top 20 this year are Miller Strategies and Mercury Public Affairs , which employs former Trump adviser Bryan Lanza and previously employed White House chief of staff Susie Wiles . Miller pulled in $7.2 million in lobbying fees last quarter — an 80 percent increase compared to the fourth quarter and a 152 percent increase compared to the first quarter of 2024. And Mercury saw its lobbying revenues more than double, to $5.2 million, since the end of 2024.

— Lobbying revenues at Michael Best Strategies increased by almost 70 percent quarter-over-quarter, to $2.1 million, while several other firms with contingents of well-connected GOP lobbyists saw boosts as well. The all-Republican firm CGCN Group reported $3.8 million in lobbying income last quarter, up 47 percent from Q4. S-3 Group saw its lobbying revenues increase by 45 percent, to $5.6 million. Squire Patton Boggs , Vogel Group and BGR Group reported increases of nearly a quarter compared to the final three months of 2024.

— “Competition breeds competition,” said Nadeam Elshami , the co-head of Brownstein’s lobbying practice, when asked about the flood of new business into Trump-linked firms. “We welcome that,” Elshami added, noting that his firm also has robust legal and international offerings.

— The longtime head of another top-20 lobbying practice mused today that “the industry has developed a new type of firm” that is eating into “the ‘normal’ transition” that follows turnover in Washington — an apparent reference to the scale of the surge in business for those hyper-connected Trump firms.

GM, DRUGMAKERS NOTCH LOBBYING RECORDS: Several of the top spenders on federal lobbying reported record outlays during the first quarter. That includes General Motors , which disclosed $9.9 million in lobbying expenditures as the Trump administration went back and forth on various iterations of tariffs affecting the auto industry. That’s almost double GM’s next-highest quarterly lobbying expenditures from Q1 of 2023.

— The drug lobbying powerhouse PhRMA also broke its own quarterly record, dropping $12.9 million on lobbying at the start of the year as drugmakers pushed for PBM reforms and changes to the Inflation Reduction Act’s drug price negotiation process, and faced attacks by new HHS Secretary and vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The drugmakers Novartis and Amgen disclosed record lobbying outlays last quarter, as did the top trade group representing insurers, AHIP .

— But the main industry group representing pharmacy benefit managers, the Pharmaceutical Care Management Association , reduced its lobbying expenditures by 18 percent last quarter, to $4.1 million.

WHERE EVERYTHING’S BIGGER: Alpine Group is opening up a new office in the Dallas-Fort Worth area as an increasing number of major companies flock to set up shop in the Lone Star State.

— “Dallas-Fort Worth is absolutely leading the conversation right now,” said Keenan Austin Reed , the firm’s chief executive, pointing to the metroplex’s growing financial hub, or “Y’all Street.”

— “We feel that this is exactly where the market is headed,” she said in an interview, adding that the firm sees it as increasingly important to have an “actual foothold” in the area. “One thing I’ve seen on the ground is that Texas respects authenticity and they respect you playing on their turf,” she told PI ahead of a launch party today that featured remarks from local GOP Rep. Beth Van Duyne .

— Alpine Group’s Barry Brown , a Dallas native and former chief of staff to a pair of former Republican lawmakers who represented the region, Kay Granger and Michael Burgess , will help lead the new office. “38 states are smaller than the North Texas region,” Brown told PI.

— The firm already represents several major companies and institutions that call Dallas-Fort Worth home, including AWS , BNSF Railway , Atmos Energy , CAE , Eaton , Lyft , Match Group , NEC , North Texas Commission , Siemens , Texas Woman’s University , Vistra , Innovative Signal Analysis , Southland Holdings , NextDecade and Primoris .

WHAT THE NUMBERS MEAN: Donald Trump’s return to Washington lit a new fire under an already-hot lobbying market, but no firms experienced a bigger boon in the first quarter than those with close ties to the president, according to a PI analysis of disclosure filings.

— Lobbying revenues were up nearly across the board during the first three months of this year for many of K Street’s top shops, as Trump steamed into office and immediately began pumping out executive orders, targeting perceived enemies and moving to upend global trade and geopolitical alignments before sometimes retreating abruptly.

— The huge payday for K Street also comes as congressional Republicans roll back key Biden-era regulations, dig in on regulating the cryptocurrency and AI industries,attempt to extend Trump’s prized 2017 tax break and enact the president’s domestic agenda. And that’s not even to mention the upheaval and confusion triggered by Elon Musk’s haphazard slashing of federal programs and the federal workforce.

— Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld, whose $16.4 million in lobbying revenues were second only to Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck’s $16.8 million, saw its strongest quarter ever, according to Brian Pomper, the co-head of Akin’s lobbying practice. Akin’s lobbying revenues were up more than 12 percent compared to the fourth quarter of 2024 and almost 19 percent compared to the same period a year ago. Their new lobbying registrations last quarter were about triple the average number of new registrations per quarter in 2024.

— But the biggest story is the handful of firms that are cashing in on their ties to the president and his inner circle. Among these Trump-connected firms, Continental Strategy saw the biggest boost to business, relative to previous quarters. Continental hauled in more than $3.6 million in lobbying revenues in Q1. That’s up almost tenfold from last quarter, when the firm disclosed earning $373,000. During the same period in 2024, Continental reported just $128,000 in lobbying revenues.

— As PI reported yesterday, Ballard Partners saw its lobbying revenues skyrocket to $14 million in Q1, compared to $4.3 million a year ago. The increase was enough to vault Ballard from 16th in PI’s revenue rankings for all of 2024 to fourth in the revenue rankings for Q1.

— Also popping into the top 20 this year are Miller Strategies and Mercury Public Affairs, which employs former Trump adviser Bryan Lanza and previously employed White House chief of staff Susie Wiles. Miller pulled in $7.2 million in lobbying fees last quarter — an 80 percent increase compared to the fourth quarter and a 152 percent increase compared to the first quarter of 2024. And Mercury saw its lobbying revenues more than double, to $5.2 million, since the end of 2024.

— Lobbying revenues at Michael Best Strategies increased by almost 70 percent quarter-over-quarter, to $2.1 million, while several other firms with contingents of well-connected GOP lobbyists saw boosts as well. The all-Republican firm CGCN Group reported $3.8 million in lobbying income last quarter, up 47 percent from Q4. S-3 Group saw its lobbying revenues increase by 45 percent, to $5.6 million. Squire Patton Boggs, Vogel Group and BGR Group reported increases of nearly a quarter compared to the final three months of 2024.

— “Competition breeds competition,” said Nadeam Elshami, the co-head of Brownstein’s lobbying practice, when asked about the flood of new business into Trump-linked firms. “We welcome that,” Elshami added, noting that his firm also has robust legal and international offerings.

— The longtime head of another top-20 lobbying practice mused today that “the industry has developed a new type of firm” that is eating into “the ‘normal’ transition” that follows turnover in Washington — an apparent reference to the scale of the surge in business for those hyper-connected Trump firms.

GM, DRUGMAKERS NOTCH LOBBYING RECORDS: Several of the top spenders on federal lobbying reported record outlays during the first quarter. That includes General Motors, which disclosed $9.9 million in lobbying expenditures as the Trump administration went back and forth on various iterations of tariffs affecting the auto industry. That’s almost double GM’s next-highest quarterly lobbying expenditures from Q1 of 2023.

— The drug lobbying powerhouse PhRMA also broke its own quarterly record, dropping $12.9 million on lobbying at the start of the year as drugmakers pushed for PBM reforms and changes to the Inflation Reduction Act’s drug price negotiation process, and faced attacks by new HHS Secretary and vaccine skeptic Robert F. Kennedy Jr. The drugmakers Novartis and Amgen disclosed record lobbying outlays last quarter, as did the top trade group representing insurers, AHIP.

— But the main industry group representing pharmacy benefit managers, the Pharmaceutical Care Management Association, reduced its lobbying expenditures by 18 percent last quarter, to $4.1 million.

WHERE EVERYTHING’S BIGGER: Alpine Group is opening up a new office in the Dallas-Fort Worth area as an increasing number of major companies flock to set up shop in the Lone Star State.

— “Dallas-Fort Worth is absolutely leading the conversation right now,” said Keenan Austin Reed, the firm’s chief executive, pointing to the metroplex’s growing financial hub, or “Y’all Street.”

— “We feel that this is exactly where the market is headed,” she said in an interview, adding that the firm sees it as increasingly important to have an “actual foothold” in the area. “One thing I’ve seen on the ground is that Texas respects authenticity and they respect you playing on their turf,” she told PI ahead of a launch party today that featured remarks from local GOP Rep. Beth Van Duyne.

— Alpine Group’s Barry Brown, a Dallas native and former chief of staff to a pair of former Republican lawmakers who represented the region, Kay Granger and Michael Burgess, will help lead the new office. “38 states are smaller than the North Texas region,” Brown told PI.

— The firm already represents several major companies and institutions that call Dallas-Fort Worth home, including AWS, BNSF Railway, Atmos Energy, CAE, Eaton, Lyft, Match Group, NEC, North Texas Commission, Siemens, Texas Woman’s University, Vistra, Innovative Signal Analysis, Southland Holdings, NextDecade and Primoris.

MENENDEZ’S WIFE CONVICTED: “A Manhattan jury on Monday found former Sen. Bob Menendez’s wife guilty on 15 public corruption charges” stemming from the accusations that Nadine Menendez was “being her husband’s partner in crime and acting as go-between as the couple sold his power in exchange for cash, gold and a Mercedes convertible,” POLITICO’s Ry Rivard reports.

— “Bob Menendez was found guilty last year on 16 counts of corruption. He is scheduled to go to federal prison for an 11-year sentence beginning in June. Following the verdict, she echoed her husband’s criticism that the case was political.”

— But the couple’s trials “may be the end of an era for the Manhattan U.S. attorney’s office, formally known as the Southern District of New York. The latest major public corruption case brought by the office — charges against New York City Mayor Eric Adams — just went down in flames after an order from Trump’s Department of Justice to drop the charges.”

title: Automakers want the iPhone treatment on tariffs
body_text:
BANDING TOGETHER: Half a dozen of the top industry groups representing car manufacturers and dealers have joined forces in an effort to wave the Trump administration off of new tariffs for the industry set to go into effect next weekend.

— The new 25 percent duties on imported auto parts “will scramble the global automotive supply chain and set off a domino effect that will lead to higher auto prices for consumers, lower sales at dealerships and will make servicing and repairing vehicles both more expensive and less predictable,” six heads of the major auto trade groups wrote in a letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent , Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer this week.

— The letter was signed by the Alliance for Automotive Innovation , American Automotive Policy Council , American International Automobile Dealers Association , Autos Drive America , MEMA and National Automobile Dealers Association.

— The groups — which wrote that their member companies collectively “support 10 million American jobs in all 50 states, underpin the industrial base and pump $1.2 trillion into the economy every year” — sought to highlight the “exceedingly fragile” auto supply chain that reconfigured itself most recently under the trade pact with Mexico and Canada that President Donald Trump negotiated during his first term in office. The industry can’t do so again overnight, the trade group chiefs argued.

— The auto groups pointed to Trump’s recent move to grant tariff carveouts for consumer electronics and semiconductors. Doing the same for the auto tariffs, they wrote, “would be a positive development and welcome relief.”

— “Most auto suppliers are not capitalized for an abrupt tariff induced disruption,” and “many are already in distress and will face production stoppages, layoffs and bankruptcy,” the letter continues.

ANDRES HEADS TO THE CHAMBER: The U.S. Chamber of Commerce is bringing aboard Doug Andres , who left the Hill in December after a decade-and-a-half serving as a spokesperson to some of the top Republican leaders.

— Andres most recently spent six years as a national press secretary and senior adviser to former Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell following a stint at FDA during the first Trump administration.

— Before that, he was a top spokesperson for Paul Ryan , beginning when the Wisconsin Republican was chair of the House Ways and Means Committee and stretching into Ryan’s time as speaker of the House.

— Andres will be vice president of political communications at the Chamber, and his hire comes at a critical stretch for the business community, which is working to navigate the Trump administration’s trade policies while shepherding through a reconciliation bill to extend the 2017 tax law — legislation spearheaded by Andres’ former bosses.

Overhear any juicy conversations in line for the bar? Spot any odd bedfellows catching up at the check-in table? SPEAKING OF THOSE TARIFF EXEMPTIONS: Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) wants to hear more from Apple CEO Tim Cook about his conversations with the White House ahead of Trump’s move to exempt electronics — like Apple’s iPhones — from the administration’s China tariffs, per Bloomberg ’s Mark Gurman .

— “The circumstances surrounding Apple’s exemptions raise fresh concerns about influence-peddling by huge well-connected corporations, and their ability to gain special favors from President Trump,” Warren wrote in a letter to Cook today.

— The tariffs Trump rolled out last month “would have either dramatically cut into Apple’s profit margins on iPhones, which are primarily built in China, or significantly raised prices. But a couple of weeks later, the administration announced carve outs on several types of electronics that benefited the iPhone maker,” Bloomberg notes.

— Citing news reports about Cook’s behind-the-scenes maneuvering and his seven-figure donation to Trump’s inaugural committee, Warren pressed the Apple chief to outline the nature of his discussions with the Trump administration, when those discussions took place and when the company learned about Trump’s carveouts.

— “At best, your work to eliminate the tariffs on Apple products, and President Trump’s subsequent decision to exempt certain Apple products, creates the appearance of impropriety,” Warren wrote. “However, recent reporting also raises serious questions about the extent to which it is possible for massive corporate special interests to use their money and influence to secure tariff exemptions that are unavailable to Main Street small businesses.”

BACK IN THE FOLD: AstraZeneca has rejoined the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America , less than two years after leaving the top drug lobbying group.

— “We are committed to working with PhRMA and policymakers to ensure the U.S. remains the global leader in biomedical innovation and that medicines are affordable for everyone who needs them,” AstraZeneca CEO Pascal Soriot said in a statement Tuesday that bore no mention about the drugmaker’s departure from the trade group in 2023.

— AstraZeneca was one of a handful of pharmaceutical companies to ditch industry groups like PhRMA following the passage of the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022. For the first time, the law allowed Medicare to negotiate the cost of certain medications, dealing the industry a major blow after an aggressive lobbying campaign to block the drug pricing provisions.

— With Republicans in power in Washington, drugmakers see an opening to make tweaks to the program and crack down on pharmacy benefit managers. But the industry also faces the prospect of tariffs as well as new regulators, like HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. , who have blasted drug companies.

— And POLITICO’s Danny Nguyen reports that while drug companies might be sweating those new policy challenges, the industry’s lobbyists “are doing just fine. Some of the biggest biotech and pharmaceutical companies have ramped up their lobbying since Trump took office ,” according to an analysis of first quarter lobbying reports.

— Companies who reported lobbying increases of double-digit percentages included Eli Lilly , Pfizer , Bristol Myers Squibb , AbbVie and Merck .

MORE INCOMING FOR SILICON VALLEY: “Social media giant Meta said that fines handed down by the European Commission Wednesday for violation of its Digital Markets Act are ‘a multi-billion-dollar tariff’ on Meta and an attempt to ‘handicap’ successful American firms,” POLITICO ’s Francesca Micheletti writes.

— “The Commission slapped tech giants Apple and Meta with penalties for breaching the EU’s new digital rulebook. Apple faces a €500 million fine for breaking the regulation’s rules for app stores, while Meta drew a penalty of €200 million for its ‘pay or consent’ advertising model.”

— “‘The European Commission is attempting to handicap successful American businesses while allowing Chinese and European companies to operate under different standards,’ Meta’s Chief Global Affairs Officer, Joel Kaplan , said in a statement shared shortly after the Commission’s announcement.”

— Kaplan’s assertion echoed recent comments from FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson , who described the European rules as “a tax on American firms.” And his rhetoric is also sure to pique the interest of a certain U.S. president intensely focused on trade reciprocity right now.

— “‘This isn’t just about a fine; the Commission forcing us to change our business model effectively imposes a multi-billion-dollar tariff on Meta while requiring us to offer an inferior service,’ Kaplan said.” Apple also blasted the fine as well, and vowed, like Meta, to appeal the ruling.

GUESS WHO’S BACK: Peter Thiel “sat on the sidelines during the 2024 election, saying he would not fund candidates after a busy 2022 cycle,” when he “donated heavily to two of his former colleagues: now-Vice President J.D. Vance in the Ohio Senate race and AZ SEN nominee Blake Masters .”

— But Thiel is “ opening up his checkbook again as Republicans look to defend their narrow congressional majorities against what could be difficult political headwinds next year. Already he’s contributing more than $1.3 million in the first three months of the off-year,” National Journal ’s James Downs reports.

— This cycle, “Thiel has focused on House Republicans, the center of the political fight for 2026. Thiel has shelled out more than $850,000 to Speaker Mike Johnson ’s joint fundraising committee, a mechanism that helps candidates line their coffers as the speaker fundraises. He’s also given more than $300,000 to the NRCC ,” and maxed out to several House GOP frontliners, as well as future nominee funds and a pair of state GOP committees.

SPOTTED at the French Embassy on Tuesday for a private showing of Delta Air Lines ’ documentary, “Why We Dream,” per a tipster: French Ambassador Laurent Bili , French defense Attaché Maj. Gen. Bertrand Jardin , Delta’s Tim Mapes , Bob Somers and Drake Springer , Clear ’s Brian Worth , Common Securitization Solutions ’ Lea Laman , Amazon ’s Mattie Duppler and Meredith Danluck and Casey Engelhardt and Matthew Shattuck of the Pulse Films team that partnered with Delta on the project.

— Bijan Mehryar is now vice president of congressional relations at the American Bankers Association . He most recently was global public policy lead at Block .

— Matthew Miller is returning to Vianovo as a partner, part of a new geopolitical risk practice. He previously was State Department spokesperson in the Biden administration.

— Matt Bower has joined Icebreaker Strategies as a senior vice president. Bower was previously a professional staff member on the House Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense.

— Mayer Brown has added Thea Kendler as a partner and co-head of the export controls and sanctions practice and Aiysha Hussain as a partner. Kendler previously was assistant secretary for export administration at the Commerce Department’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and Hussain was her senior policy adviser.

— Robert Schwartz is joining Morgan Lewis as a partner in its investment management practice. He previously was general counsel at the CFTC.

— WestExec Advisors has added Susannah Marshall and Sara Shah as senior associates. Marshall previously was senior policy adviser to the Commerce secretary, and Shah previously was deputy chief of staff of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security.

— Gaby Marks is now government relations comms manager at Bentley Systems . She previously was deputy communications director for Sen. John Barrasso (R-Wyo.).

— Muqaddesa Yourish is now a senior adviser at DGA-Albright Stonebridge Group . She most recently was a visiting professor at the Elliott School of International Affairs at George Washington University .

— Rachel Rossi has been named the new president of Alliance for Justice . She most recently was director of the Office for Access to Justice in the Biden Justice Department.

— Mark Mellman will leave his role as president of Democratic Majority for Israel , which he co-founded, per Jewish Insider .

— Ryan Nelson will be senior executive adviser to the CEO at Sanford Health , per The Dakota Scout ’s Jonathan Ellis . He previously was chief of staff to Sen. John Thune (R-S.D.).

Automakers want the iPhone treatment on tariffs

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO 

04/23/2025 07:59 PM EDT

Presented by

With help from Daniel Lippman

BANDING TOGETHER: Half a dozen of the top industry groups representing car manufacturers and dealers have joined forces in an effort to wave the Trump administration off of new tariffs for the industry set to go into effect next weekend.

— The new 25 percent duties on imported auto parts “will scramble the global automotive supply chain and set off a domino effect that will lead to higher auto prices for consumers, lower sales at dealerships and will make servicing and repairing vehicles both more expensive and less predictable,” six heads of the major auto trade groups wrote in a letter to Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer this week.

— The letter was signed by the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, American Automotive Policy Council, American International Automobile Dealers Association, Autos Drive America, MEMA and National Automobile Dealers Association.

— The groups — which wrote that their member companies collectively “support 10 million American jobs in all 50 states, underpin the industrial base and pump $1.2 trillion into the economy every year” — sought to highlight the “exceedingly fragile” auto supply chain that reconfigured itself most recently under the trade pact with Mexico and Canada that President Donald Trump negotiated during his first term in office. The industry can’t do so again overnight, the trade group chiefs argued.

— The auto groups pointed to Trump’s recent move to grant tariff carveouts for consumer electronics and semiconductors. Doing the same for the auto tariffs, they wrote, “would be a positive development and welcome relief.”

— “Most auto suppliers are not capitalized for an abrupt tariff induced disruption,” and “many are already in distress and will face production stoppages, layoffs and bankruptcy,” the letter continues.

ANDRES HEADS TO THE CHAMBER: The U.S. Chamber of Commerce is bringing aboard Doug Andres, who left the Hill in December after a decade-and-a-half serving as a spokesperson to some of the top Republican leaders.

— Andres most recently spent six years as a national press secretary and senior adviser to former Senate Minority Leader Mitch McConnell following a stint at FDA during the first Trump administration.

— Before that, he was a top spokesperson for Paul Ryan, beginning when the Wisconsin Republican was chair of the House Ways and Means Committee and stretching into Ryan’s time as speaker of the House.

— Andres will be vice president of political communications at the Chamber, and his hire comes at a critical stretch for the business community, which is working to navigate the Trump administration’s trade policies while shepherding through a reconciliation bill to extend the 2017 tax law — legislation spearheaded by Andres’ former bosses.

Happy Wednesday and welcome to PI, where we want to hear all your gossip from the White House Correspondents Dinner parties kicking off over the next few days. Overhear any juicy conversations in line for the bar? Spot any odd bedfellows catching up at the check-in table? SPEAKING OF THOSE TARIFF EXEMPTIONS: Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) wants to hear more from Apple CEO Tim Cook about his conversations with the White House ahead of Trump’s move to exempt electronics — like Apple’s iPhones — from the administration’s China tariffs, per Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman.

— “The circumstances surrounding Apple’s exemptions raise fresh concerns about influence-peddling by huge well-connected corporations, and their ability to gain special favors from President Trump,” Warren wrote in a letter to Cook today.

— The tariffs Trump rolled out last month “would have either dramatically cut into Apple’s profit margins on iPhones, which are primarily built in China, or significantly raised prices. But a couple of weeks later, the administration announced carve outs on several types of electronics that benefited the iPhone maker,” Bloomberg notes.

— Citing news reports about Cook’s behind-the-scenes maneuvering and his seven-figure donation to Trump’s inaugural committee, Warren pressed the Apple chief to outline the nature of his discussions with the Trump administration, when those discussions took place and when the company learned about Trump’s carveouts.

— “At best, your work to eliminate the tariffs on Apple products, and President Trump’s subsequent decision to exempt certain Apple products, creates the appearance of impropriety,” Warren wrote. “However, recent reporting also raises serious questions about the extent to which it is possible for massive corporate special interests to use their money and influence to secure tariff exemptions that are unavailable to Main Street small businesses.”

BACK IN THE FOLD: AstraZeneca has rejoined the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America, less than two years after leaving the top drug lobbying group.

— “We are committed to working with PhRMA and policymakers to ensure the U.S. remains the global leader in biomedical innovation and that medicines are affordable for everyone who needs them,” AstraZeneca CEO Pascal Soriot said in a statement Tuesday that bore no mention about the drugmaker’s departure from the trade group in 2023.

— AstraZeneca was one of a handful of pharmaceutical companies to ditch industry groups like PhRMA following the passage of the Inflation Reduction Act in 2022. For the first time, the law allowed Medicare to negotiate the cost of certain medications, dealing the industry a major blow after an aggressive lobbying campaign to block the drug pricing provisions.

— With Republicans in power in Washington, drugmakers see an opening to make tweaks to the program and crack down on pharmacy benefit managers. But the industry also faces the prospect of tariffs as well as new regulators, like HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who have blasted drug companies.

— And POLITICO’s Danny Nguyen reports that while drug companies might be sweating those new policy challenges, the industry’s lobbyists “are doing just fine. Some of the biggest biotech and pharmaceutical companies have ramped up their lobbying since Trump took office,” according to an analysis of first quarter lobbying reports.

— Companies who reported lobbying increases of double-digit percentages included Eli Lilly, Pfizer, Bristol Myers Squibb, AbbVie and Merck.

MORE INCOMING FOR SILICON VALLEY: “Social media giant Meta said that fines handed down by the European Commission Wednesday for violation of its Digital Markets Act are ‘a multi-billion-dollar tariff’ on Meta and an attempt to ‘handicap’ successful American firms,” POLITICO’s Francesca Micheletti writes.

— “The Commission slapped tech giants Apple and Meta with penalties for breaching the EU’s new digital rulebook. Apple faces a €500 million fine for breaking the regulation’s rules for app stores, while Meta drew a penalty of €200 million for its ‘pay or consent’ advertising model.”

— “‘The European Commission is attempting to handicap successful American businesses while allowing Chinese and European companies to operate under different standards,’ Meta’s Chief Global Affairs Officer, Joel Kaplan, said in a statement shared shortly after the Commission’s announcement.”

— Kaplan’s assertion echoed recent comments from FTC Chair Andrew Ferguson, who described the European rules as “a tax on American firms.” And his rhetoric is also sure to pique the interest of a certain U.S. president intensely focused on trade reciprocity right now.

— “‘This isn’t just about a fine; the Commission forcing us to change our business model effectively imposes a multi-billion-dollar tariff on Meta while requiring us to offer an inferior service,’ Kaplan said.” Apple also blasted the fine as well, and vowed, like Meta, to appeal the ruling.

GUESS WHO’S BACK: Peter Thiel “sat on the sidelines during the 2024 election, saying he would not fund candidates after a busy 2022 cycle,” when he “donated heavily to two of his former colleagues: now-Vice President J.D. Vance in the Ohio Senate race and AZ SEN nominee Blake Masters.”

— But Thiel is “opening up his checkbook again as Republicans look to defend their narrow congressional majorities against what could be difficult political headwinds next year. Already he’s contributing more than $1.3 million in the first three months of the off-year,” National Journal’s James Downs reports.

— This cycle, “Thiel has focused on House Republicans, the center of the political fight for 2026. Thiel has shelled out more than $850,000 to Speaker Mike Johnson’s joint fundraising committee, a mechanism that helps candidates line their coffers as the speaker fundraises. He’s also given more than $300,000 to the NRCC,” and maxed out to several House GOP frontliners, as well as future nominee funds and a pair of state GOP committees.

SPOTTED at the French Embassy on Tuesday for a private showing of Delta Air Lines’ documentary, “Why We Dream,” per a tipster: French Ambassador Laurent Bili, French defense Attaché Maj. Gen. Bertrand Jardin, Delta’s Tim Mapes, Bob Somers and Drake Springer, Clear’s Brian Worth, Common Securitization Solutions’ Lea Laman, Amazon’s Mattie Duppler and Meredith Danluck and Casey Engelhardt and Matthew Shattuck of the Pulse Films team that partnered with Delta on the project.

title: SoFi lobbies up amid Trump student loan overhaul
body_text:
LOBBYING UP: Private student loan lender SoFi Technologies has signed up its first in-house lobbyist.

— Matt Cameron , a Remitly , Amazon , Notarize and CFPB veteran who joined the fintech firm in February as director of policy and government affairs, registered to lobby beginning today on “general issues in financial services, technology, and banking, including digital assets, cryptocurrency, and student lending,” according to a disclosure filing.

— SoFi has lobbied the federal government through outside firms since 2013, according to disclosure filings. The company most recently retained financial services-focused firm Mindset Advocacy beginning in 2023. That contract ended last April, but SoFi has had one other outside firm on retainer: Rich Feuer Anderson .

— The registration of SoFi’s first in-house lobbyist comes as the Trump administration moves to upend federal student loan programs as part of a push to shutter the Education Department, with President Donald Trump teasing a plan last month to shift the federal student loan portfolio to the Small Business Administration. At the same time, Trump has moved to roll back financial regulations and neuter the CFPB, which had begun to crack down on fintechs under former President Joe Biden .

— POLITICO ’s Jasper Goodman reported on Wednesday that Republicans on the House Financial Services Committee are eying the consumer finance watchdog as the cornerstone of their budget cuts to offset the cost of the GOP’s reconciliation package.

MORE NEW BUSINESS: The Autonomous Vehicle Industry Association has hired Navigators Global to lobby on AV technology and policy issues, as the industry grows bullish on the prospect for easing the regulatory path for self-driving cars, thanks in part to the influence of AV proponent Elon Musk . Earlier today, the Transportation Department unveiled a new framework aimed at streamlining some of the industry’s hurdles.

— Meanwhile the U.K.’s McLaren Automotive , which is facing a 25 percent tariff from the Trump administration, has hired Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck to lobby on manufacturing issues and reciprocal tariffs, according to a disclosure filing. It’s the first time the luxury automaker has hired lobbyists in Washington.

— The Schizophrenia Policy Action Network has also hired its first lobbyists. The advocacy group retained the health care lobbying firm Horizon Government Affairs to push for CDC funding for patient education and outreach and for a report on the “total cost of schizophrenia.”

— The firm will also advocate for increased access to treatment and for the EPIC Act, which takes aim at what drugmakers have dubbed the “pill penalty” — language in the Inflation Reduction Act’s drug-pricing provisions that gives small-molecule drugs like pills a shorter exemption from price negotiation than biologics like vaccines. Pharmaceutical companies and some patient advocate groups argue that the provision, which Trump recently signaled support for eliminating, threatens the development of innovative drugs that could treat conditions like schizophrenia.

Happy Thursday and welcome to PI. Another reminder that PI wants to hear all your gossip from the White House Correspondents Dinner parties over the next few days. Drop me a line with any juicy tips — I’ll keep you anonymous! You can add me on Signal , email me at [email protected] , and be sure to follow me on X : @caitlinoprysko .

ACTBLUES: Trump has “ directed the Justice Department to investigate ActBlue , the fund-raising platform that powers virtually every Democratic candidate and cause,” The New York Times ’ Maggie Haberman , Reid Epstein and Ken Vogel write, in the latest shot across the bow of Democratic political organs. POLITICO ’s Megan Messerly and Calder McHugh first broke the news of Trump’s imminent plans earlier today.

— “Trump called for an investigation by Attorney General Pam Bondi into ActBlue, which is used across the Democratic Party’s ecosystem to collect donations online. The inquiry is ostensibly meant to look into possible illegal donations made by people in someone else’s name, known as straw donations, as well as hard-dollar contributions from foreign donors. Mr. Trump asked for a report on the results of Ms. Bondi’s investigation within 180 days.”

— “Mr. Trump’s action represents a threat to one of the key financial cogs of the left, potentially hindering Democrats’ ability to compete in elections. It is likely to please elements of his base, for whom ActBlue has become a top target. Congressional Republicans have separately been investigating what they claim are the platform’s insufficient security provisions.”

WITHER, PHARMA: “Big Pharma isn’t sure how to handle Donald Trump’s Republican Party . Trump is pledging to impose tariffs on drug imports, while Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has vilified the drug industry’s profits and questioned the safety of its products,” POLITICO ’s Lauren Gardner and David Lim report.

— “Long a lobbying powerhouse in Washington, pharma’s struggling to settle on a strategy for defending itself, according to six industry lobbyists and three company officials who spoke to POLITICO. … ‘It’s just paralyzing. You don’t know what’s going to happen next,’ said one of the lobbyists.”

— “The industry’s plight marks a remarkable turn, given how close it once was with Republicans, and shows how Trump has upended alliances that were once a bedrock of the GOP. Executives and lobbyists for the industry told POLITICO that full-throated opposition to Trump is unlikely to sway him and would imperil the policy victories the companies hope are still attainable and for which they need congressional support, including the restoration of a tax break worth billions.”

MAKING RUBBER HIT ROAD: “Getting the Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights to investigate a complaint has never been a speedy process. Under President Donald Trump’s second administration, however, right-leaning nonprofits targeting transgender athletes are finding their complaints jumping to the front of the line,” according to NOTUS ’ Violet Jira .

— “Steadily, the Department of Education has been churning out investigation after investigation on instances of alleged noncompliance with Trump’s directives on Title IX. A number of these investigations originate from complaints made by conservative nonprofits like the Defense of Freedom Institute and America First Legal , which was founded by White House political adviser Stephen Miller .”

— “Many of these groups have been working for years in pursuit of the same policy changes regarding transgender students that Trump made law on Day 1 . Some have ongoing lawsuits against Biden-era policies. Today, they have a Department of Education that is in lockstep with them on policy [that is] willing to investigate the issues they highlight.”

DAYLIGHT SAVING FOES EYE MAHA: With Trump signaling a shift in his position on the fate of Daylight Saving Time , one advocacy group in favor of eliminating the time change is hoping to find new allies among supporters of Kennedy’s “Make America Healthy Again” movement, per Fortune ’s Greg McKenna .

— “Trump’s reversal was a disappointing development for Jay Pea , the founder and president of Save Standard Time, a volunteer-run nonprofit that works with sleep medicine groups to lobby in Congress and state legislatures.”

— “‘We need to try to get him to see that golf will still happen with standard time,’ Pea said in an interview with Fortune. ‘And if we want to make Americans healthy again, we need standard time.’ Pea said his organization’s messaging has picked up steam” within the MAHA movement. “‘We just haven’t gotten through yet to the people at the top of the MAHA [movement],’ Pea said. ‘I’m hopeful to turn their heads soon.’”

— “Pea and other standard time advocates say it’s better for peoples’ circadian rhythms, or ‘biological clocks,’ and, therefore, public health and safety, as well as productivity. … Nonetheless, efforts in Congress to stop the changing of clocks have so far exclusively called for a switch to daylight saving time, based, in part, on the premise Americans would prefer an extra hour in the evening to spend time outdoors, shop, or otherwise enjoy the sunshine.”

LOBBYING UP: Private student loan lender SoFi Technologies has signed up its first in-house lobbyist.


— Matt Cameron, a Remitly, Amazon, Notarize and CFPB veteran who joined the fintech firm in February as director of policy and government affairs, registered to lobby beginning today on “general issues in financial services, technology, and banking, including digital assets, cryptocurrency, and student lending,” according to a disclosure filing.

— SoFi has lobbied the federal government through outside firms since 2013, according to disclosure filings. The company most recently retained financial services-focused firm Mindset Advocacy beginning in 2023. That contract ended last April, but SoFi has had one other outside firm on retainer: Rich Feuer Anderson.

— The registration of SoFi’s first in-house lobbyist comes as the Trump administration moves to upend federal student loan programs as part of a push to shutter the Education Department, with President Donald Trump teasing a plan last month to shift the federal student loan portfolio to the Small Business Administration. At the same time, Trump has moved to roll back financial regulations and neuter the CFPB, which had begun to crack down on fintechs under former President Joe Biden.

— POLITICO’s Jasper Goodman reported on Wednesday that Republicans on the House Financial Services Committee are eying the consumer finance watchdog as the cornerstone of their budget cuts to offset the cost of the GOP’s reconciliation package.


MORE NEW BUSINESS: The Autonomous Vehicle Industry Association has hired Navigators Global to lobby on AV technology and policy issues, as the industry grows bullish on the prospect for easing the regulatory path for self-driving cars, thanks in part to the influence of AV proponent Elon Musk. Earlier today, the Transportation Department unveiled a new framework aimed at streamlining some of the industry’s hurdles.

— Meanwhile the U.K.’s McLaren Automotive, which is facing a 25 percent tariff from the Trump administration, has hired Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck to lobby on manufacturing issues and reciprocal tariffs, according to a disclosure filing. It’s the first time the luxury automaker has hired lobbyists in Washington.

— The Schizophrenia Policy Action Network has also hired its first lobbyists. The advocacy group retained the health care lobbying firm Horizon Government Affairs to push for CDC funding for patient education and outreach and for a report on the “total cost of schizophrenia.”

— The firm will also advocate for increased access to treatment and for the EPIC Act, which takes aim at what drugmakers have dubbed the “pill penalty” — language in the Inflation Reduction Act’s drug-pricing provisions that gives small-molecule drugs like pills a shorter exemption from price negotiation than biologics like vaccines. Pharmaceutical companies and some patient advocate groups argue that the provision, which Trump recently signaled support for eliminating, threatens the development of innovative drugs that could treat conditions like schizophrenia.

Happy Thursday and welcome to PI. Another reminder that PI wants to hear all your gossip from the White House Correspondents Dinner parties over the next few days. Drop me a line with any juicy tips — I’ll keep you anonymous! You can add me on Signal, email me at [email protected], and be sure to follow me on X: @caitlinoprysko.

ACTBLUES: Trump has “directed the Justice Department to investigate ActBlue, the fund-raising platform that powers virtually every Democratic candidate and cause,” The New York Times’ Maggie Haberman, Reid Epstein and Ken Vogel write, in the latest shot across the bow of Democratic political organs. POLITICO’s Megan Messerly and Calder McHugh first broke the news of Trump’s imminent plans earlier today.

— “Trump called for an investigation by Attorney General Pam Bondi into ActBlue, which is used across the Democratic Party’s ecosystem to collect donations online. The inquiry is ostensibly meant to look into possible illegal donations made by people in someone else’s name, known as straw donations, as well as hard-dollar contributions from foreign donors. Mr. Trump asked for a report on the results of Ms. Bondi’s investigation within 180 days.”

— “Mr. Trump’s action represents a threat to one of the key financial cogs of the left, potentially hindering Democrats’ ability to compete in elections. It is likely to please elements of his base, for whom ActBlue has become a top target. Congressional Republicans have separately been investigating what they claim are the platform’s insufficient security provisions.”

WITHER, PHARMA: “Big Pharma isn’t sure how to handle Donald Trump’s Republican Party. Trump is pledging to impose tariffs on drug imports, while Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has vilified the drug industry’s profits and questioned the safety of its products,” POLITICO’s Lauren Gardner and David Lim report.

— “Long a lobbying powerhouse in Washington, pharma’s struggling to settle on a strategy for defending itself, according to six industry lobbyists and three company officials who spoke to POLITICO. … ‘It’s just paralyzing. You don’t know what’s going to happen next,’ said one of the lobbyists.”

— “The industry’s plight marks a remarkable turn, given how close it once was with Republicans, and shows how Trump has upended alliances that were once a bedrock of the GOP. Executives and lobbyists for the industry told POLITICO that full-throated opposition to Trump is unlikely to sway him and would imperil the policy victories the companies hope are still attainable and for which they need congressional support, including the restoration of a tax break worth billions.”

MAKING RUBBER HIT ROAD: “Getting the Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights to investigate a complaint has never been a speedy process. Under President Donald Trump’s second administration, however, right-leaning nonprofits targeting transgender athletes are finding their complaints jumping to the front of the line,” according to NOTUS’ Violet Jira.

— “Steadily, the Department of Education has been churning out investigation after investigation on instances of alleged noncompliance with Trump’s directives on Title IX. A number of these investigations originate from complaints made by conservative nonprofits like the Defense of Freedom Institute and America First Legal, which was founded by White House political adviser Stephen Miller.”

— “Many of these groups have been working for years in pursuit of the same policy changes regarding transgender students that Trump made law on Day 1. Some have ongoing lawsuits against Biden-era policies. Today, they have a Department of Education that is in lockstep with them on policy [that is] willing to investigate the issues they highlight.”

DAYLIGHT SAVING FOES EYE MAHA: With Trump signaling a shift in his position on the fate of Daylight Saving Time, one advocacy group in favor of eliminating the time change is hoping to find new allies among supporters of Kennedy’s “Make America Healthy Again” movement, per Fortune’s Greg McKenna.

— “Trump’s reversal was a disappointing development for Jay Pea, the founder and president of Save Standard Time, a volunteer-run nonprofit that works with sleep medicine groups to lobby in Congress and state legislatures.”

— “‘We need to try to get him to see that golf will still happen with standard time,’ Pea said in an interview with Fortune. ‘And if we want to make Americans healthy again, we need standard time.’ Pea said his organization’s messaging has picked up steam” within the MAHA movement. “‘We just haven’t gotten through yet to the people at the top of the MAHA [movement],’ Pea said. ‘I’m hopeful to turn their heads soon.’”

— “Pea and other standard time advocates say it’s better for peoples’ circadian rhythms, or ‘biological clocks,’ and, therefore, public health and safety, as well as productivity. … Nonetheless, efforts in Congress to stop the changing of clocks have so far exclusively called for a switch to daylight saving time, based, in part, on the premise Americans would prefer an extra hour in the evening to spend time outdoors, shop, or otherwise enjoy the sunshine.”

title: Steelmaker enlists GOP lobbyists for rail dispute
body_text:
STEEL GIANT LOBBIES UP FOR AFRICAN RAIL FIGHT: Luxembourg-based steelmaker ArcelorMittal is bringing on lobbying firepower with ties to Secretary of State Marco Rubio and a top Senate Republican as the steel conglomerate seeks to defend its control over a key Liberian railway corridor .

A message from the Defense Credit Union Council:

DURBIN-MARSHALL CREDIT CARD MANDATES WILL HARM MILITARY FAMILIES The Defense Credit Union Council is sounding the alarm on the Durbin–Marshall credit card mandates. This proposal would increase fraud risk, restrict access to credit, eliminate rewards, and hand a massive windfall to corporate mega-retailers at the expense of consumers, small businesses, and community financial institutions. DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED —OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

— ArcelorMittal has retained Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner ’s Dave Russell , a former chief of staff to former Sen. Ted Stevens (R-Alaska). BCLP in turn has enlisted a team at Navigators Global to help work on the account that includes Cesar Conda — Rubio’s first Senate chief of staff — and Andy Keiser — a deputy national security adviser on President Donald Trump ’s 2016 transition. Hollier & Associates’ Will Hollier , a former chief of staff to Sen. Mike Crapo (R-Idaho), will also pitch in as a subcontractor on the account.

— The dispute revolves around a 2005 mineral development agreement between ArcelorMittal and the Liberian government that gave the company operational control over the strategic Yekepa-Buchanan railway corridor in exchange for its rehabilitation. Ivanhoe Atlantic , formerly known as HPX, has been lobbying officials in both the U.S. and Liberia for access to the railway in order to transport iron ore from a mine just over the border in Guinea to a key Liberian port.

— ArcelorMittal’s new lobbyists plan on framing the feud in terms of Chinese geopolitical influence in Africa by highlighting Ivanhoe Atlantic’s ties to China — which ArcelorMittal accused last year of pumping out cheap steel — as they press the Trump administration and members of Congress to intervene with the Liberian government on the steelmaker’s behalf. Hong Kong-based Century Vision Holdings holds a 21 percent stake in the company, according to a 2023 lobbying disclosure that was referenced in a new filing last week.

— Ivanhoe Atlantic/HPX retains Brownstein Hyatt Farber & Schreck and Yorktown Solutions , while ArcelorMittal also retains Kelley Drye & Warren and KRL International .

PEDAL TO THE METAL: Automakers and auto industry groups have continued bringing on new lobbying help as the sector faces numerous potential policy threats and planning begins for a surface transportation reauthorization bill slated for 2026.

— Electric truck and SUV manufacturer Rivian recently hired a bipartisan pair of lobbyists to help protect tax incentives to boost domestic EV sales and production, according to disclosure filings. In March, Rivian retained former Trump campaign adviser David Urban and earlier this month hired Pioneer Public Affairs’ Charlie Ellsworth , a former aide to Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer .

— Meanwhile, Sweden’s Volvo Trucks and German auto giant Volkswagen retained Capitol67 Strategies and TSG Advocates D.C. , respectively, to work on transportation issues including tariffs and tax credits for “alternative energy automobiles.” As PI reported on Thursday, the U.K.’s McLaren Automotive also brought on lobbying help in recent weeks to work on tariff issues.

— Drive Action Fund , an advocacy group pushing for the Transportation Department to “implement a crash test dummy that accurately represents female physiology, including differences in muscle mass, bone density, and body shape,” has registered its first lobbyist to advocate for a bill from Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.) that directs officials to do just that.

TGIF and welcome to PI. Another reminder that PI wants to hear all your intel from the White House Correspondents’ Dinner parties this weekend. Drop me a line with any juicy tips — I’ll keep you anonymous! You can add me on Signal , email me at [email protected] , and be sure to follow me on X : @caitlinoprysko .

A message from the Defense Credit Union Council:

HEADING BACK TO K STREET: Joe Kasper is departing the Pentagon after all , and plans on heading back to the influence industry following several tumultuous months as a top aide to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth , Daniel and Jack Detsch report.

— Kasper “ was originally expected to transition to another role within the Defense Department” before the decision to leave his post was made, but he told Daniel and Jack that he’ll “continue to support and advise the Pentagon … as a special government employee. This will limit him to performing temporary jobs for just 130 days a year.”

— “A former longtime chief of staff to indicted Rep. Duncan Hunter , Kasper was a leading figure in the firings of senior adviser Dan Caldwell , Hegseth deputy chief of staff Darin Selnick and Colin Carroll , the chief of staff to Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg. The trio were ousted last week in a leak investigation.”

— After leaving the Hill, Kasper worked in the first Trump administration before joining Ervin Graves Strategy Group , the lobbying firm led by former Rep. Tom Graves (R-Ga.). Kasper reported lobbying the Pentagon, among other federal entities, on behalf of almost a dozen clients at the end of 2024, disclosures show.

INSIDE THE GLP-1 LOBBYING FRENZY: “Pharma companies are mobilizing to ensure the craze for highly effective anti-obesity drugs keeps spreading,” Lauren Gardner and Daniel report. “The Trump administration is under heavy pressure to decide how widely available the medications should be and whether Medicare should cover them. So far, it has sided against the makers of the weight-loss medications, but the issue is far from settled.”

— “The political battle over the anti-obesity drugs is reaching a crescendo in Washington after a yearslong supply shortage sparked by historic demand. From 2022 to 2024, cheaper copycat versions filled the void. But now that supplies have recovered, brand-name companies are pressing federal officials to clamp down on those less expensive versions, known as compounded drugs.”

— “Separately, the drug industry is lobbying to repeal a 20-year-old law prohibiting Medicare from covering weight-loss drugs. Trump administration officials have cited cost concerns in opposing such a move so far. But proponents say billions in upfront expenses would be more than offset over time as fewer Americans face chronic conditions exacerbated by obesity.”

— “In the first quarter of 2025, Ozempic and Wegovy ’s maker, Novo Nordisk , spent more than $3 million on lobbying. So did Eli Lilly , which makes the weight-loss drug Zepbound and Mounjaro , a similar drug tailored to diabetes patients. Together, the two companies hired more than 10 lobbying firms, including top Washington shops Avoq , Holland & Knight and Williams and Jensen , according to a POLITICO review of lobbying records.”

— “ Hims , the prominent telehealth company that sells a copycat drug, also hired lobbyists, and competitor Ivim Health has tapped Sean Spicer , the former Trump administration press secretary, to serve as a Washington spokesperson. Both sell weight-loss drugs.”

— “And when the president met with the CEOs of Eli Lilly, its rival Pfizer and PhRMA , the brand-name drug lobby, in the Oval Office in the early weeks of his new term, obesity drugs came up during the conversation, according to a lobbyist familiar with the meeting.”

MUSK READ: “ Elon Musk joined President Donald Trump’s interview with Air Force secretary nominee Troy Meink , according to Meink’s own disclosure to Congress — a highly unusual move that raises serious conflict of interest concerns about the space mogul’s role in the selection process,” per POLITICO ’s Joe Gould and Sam Skove .

— “The disclosure is significant because Musk has billions of dollars in national security and defense contracts at stake as CEO of SpaceX . … But his involvement in a personnel decision for a top Air Force post marks a new level of political reach for the billionaire entrepreneur — and a potential breach of ethical norms that discourage contractors from influencing leadership decisions in agencies that oversee their contracts.”

— “Meink wrote that Musk ‘was one of many people present’ during the December interview but ‘the president was the only one who asked me questions.’ He did not seek Musk’s support, he wrote, and Musk made no requests of him in return. ‘I have no relationship with SpaceX or Mr. Musk outside of a professional relationship in the execution of my current duties,’ Meink said.”

TRANSPARENCY FOR THEE, BUT NOT FOR ME: Trump “signed two executive actions this week professing to bring more transparency to how foreign money infiltrates American institutions — one on money to universities, another on elections. But it remains unclear whether he’ll extend the transparency effort to his own vehicle to accept foreign donations: his presidential library fund,” NOTUS’ Claire Heddles reports.

— “Donating to presidential libraries is one of the few options foreign individuals or companies have to donate directly to presidents since federal election law bars foreign citizens from contributing to elections or to inaugural committees. Trump’s inaugural committee refunded a few hundred thousand dollars to two companies and an individual with foreign addresses, according to campaign finance filings released this past Sunday.”

— “Trump’s executive actions on foreign money this week don’t change any existing rules — both simply advise agency heads to enforce laws that already exist. … There is another Trump transition fund that could theoretically accept foreign money: his tax-exempt organization, Trump Vance Transition Inc. Susie Wiles , now Trump’s chief of staff, vowed last fall the fund would not do so. She also stated donors would be made public, which still hasn’t happened .”

— “That leaves the presidential library fund, created in December , and whose donors are not required to be made public. The largest known donation is from an ABC News settlement with Trump promising $15 million to the new organization.”

— “Last Congress, a bipartisan pair of Florida congressmen filed a bill to make presidential library donors public — including foreign donors. Members have filed similar bills for years, but they’ve never advanced.”

A message from the Defense Credit Union Council:

CONGRESS MUST REJECT DURBIN–MARSHALL

The Defense Credit Union Council is sounding the alarm on the Durbin–Marshall credit card mandates. This proposal would increase fraud risk, eliminate rewards programs, restrict access to credit, and hand a massive windfall to mega-retailers at the expense of consumers, small businesses, and community financial institutions. “This repeats the same mistakes consumers already paid for,” warns DCUC President & CEO Anthony Hernandez. A one-size-fits-all rewrite of the payments system would weaken fraud protections and hit servicemembers, veterans, and working families hardest. DCUC STRONGLY OPPOSES THIS BILL AND URGES ACTION TO SAFEGUARD THOSE WHO SERVE!

Jobs report

— Marylee Jenkins and Susan Natland are joining the Council for Innovation Promotion ’s advisory board.

— Aaron Levy is now the vice president of government relations at the International Code Council . He was most recently division chief for outreach and external affairs at NIST’s Manufacturing Extension Partnership and is a FEMA alum.

— Issue One has promoted Alix Fraser to vice president of advocacy and Nicole Lagace to vice president of communications. Fraser previously led Issue One’s technology reform portfolio and Lagace was previously communications director.

— Chip Smith has joined the board of directors at Avoq . He’s a founder and former CEO of the Glover Park Group (now known as FGS Global ) and was most recently executive vice president of global public affairs and policy at 21st Century Fox Group .

— Martin Fiore is being promoted to vice chair of tax for the Americas at EY . Fiore was previously deputy vice chair of tax at the firm.

— Elaine Dalpiaz is now vice president for government affairs and policy at the National Alliance for Caregiving . She previously was vice president for health systems policy and strategic partnerships at First Focus on Children and is an AARP and Hill alum.

Duncan Hunter, Kasper was a leading figure in the firings of senior adviser Dan Caldwell, Hegseth deputy chief of staff Darin Selnick and Colin Carroll, the chief of staff to Deputy Defense Secretary Stephen Feinberg.
