This proposal would increase fraud risk, restrict access to credit, eliminate rewards, and hand a massive windfall to corporate mega-retailers at the expense of consumers, small businesses, and community financial institutions. DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED —OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

FIRST IN PI — WHO’S COMING TO DINNER: The NRCC is hosting its winter meeting at the Ritz-Carlton Hotel in Key Biscayne, Florida, today through Sunday, Daniel reports. Dozens of House Republicans are attending, including Speaker Mike Johnson , Whip Tom Emmer (R-Minn.) and NRCC Chair Richard Hudson (R-N.C.).

— Of course, dozens of lobbyists are attending as well, according to a list of expected attendees obtained by PI. They include BlackRock ’s Benjamin Cantrell , Hogan Lovells’ Aaron Cutler , Juul Labs’ Bruce Gates , J.A. Green ’s Jeff Green , BGR Group ’s Dan Greenwood , Williams & Jensen ’s Susan Hirschmann , NextEra Energy ’s Phil Musser , Oracle ’s Josh Pitcock , American Petroleum Institute ’s Mike Sommers , Akin Gump Strauss Hauer & Feld ’s Geoff Verhoff and former Reps. Kevin Yoder (R-Kan.), now with Venture Government Strategies , and Mike Ferguson (R-N.J.), now with AT&T.

GREENS GO RED: “A conservation group founded by young conservatives has pulled out all the stops in the hopes of being a player with Republicans in Washington,” per POLITICO’s E&E News’ Tim Cama . But “whether that push from the American Conservation Coalition bears fruit remains a big question.”

— “Over the past several years, the group has made inroads with key officials who went on to join President Donald Trump ’s Cabinet. It co-hosted a glitzy influencer party the night before Trump’s inauguration alongside TikTok , the social media app. And its co-founder helped spark the idea for a first-of-its kind House GOP caucus dedicated to climate.”

— “After laying that groundwork, ACC is now trying to influence Republicans in power as the party seeks to overhaul federal permitting standards and forest management laws. It’s also hoping to push Trump’s ‘energy dominance’ agenda with an environmental lens, among other initiatives.”

AND THEY WERE ROOMMATES: “In 2021, Steve Berger , an evangelical pastor who has attacked the separation of church and state as ‘a delusional lie’ and called multinational institutions ‘demonic,’ set off on an ambitious project. His stated goal: minister to members of Congress so that what ‘they learn is then translated into policy.’ His base of operations would be a six-bedroom, $3.7 million townhouse blocks from the U.S. Capitol,” ProPublica ’s Joshua Kaplan , Justin Elliott and Alex Mierjeski write.

— “Recently, the pastor scored a remarkable coup for a political influence project that has until now managed to avoid public scrutiny. … House Speaker Mike Johnson has been staying at the home since around the beginning of this year, according to interviews and videos obtained by ProPublica.” Doing so would not be against ethics rules as long as Johnson is paying a fair market rate for rent, which could be as much as $7,000 in the neighborhood.

— The townhouse is owned by GOP donor and car dealer Lee Beaman , “who has joined Berger in advocating for and against multiple bills before Congress,” including “a bill that would make it easier to fire federal employees and a regulation that would reduce fuel efficiency standards for the automotive industry.”

— And Johnson isn’t the only influential Republican in the Bergers’ circle — former Rep. Dan Bishop (R-N.C.), who’s been nominated for a key post in the White House budget office, “seems to have also lived in the home last year while he was still a congressman,” according to ProPublica.

INAUGURAL LEADER HEADS TO FGS: FGS Global has snapped up Richard Walters , a longtime Republican operative who served as the executive director of Trump’s second inaugural committee. He’ll be a partner in the firm’s government affairs practice.

— Walters served as the longest running RNC chief of staff before stepping down in 2022, but he stayed on with the committee to help lead planning for last year’s Republican National Convention in Milwaukee and served as a senior adviser and chief of staff to former Chair Ronna McDaniel .

JASSY: TRUMP ADMIN. ‘CARES’ WHAT BUSINESS THINKS: Amazon chief executive Andy Jassy had kind words for the second Trump administration on its receptiveness to hearing out the business community in an interview with Bloomberg TV ’s Caroline Hyde on Thursday.

— “I would say that some administrations are more receptive to it than others, but this administration cares about what business thinks,” Jassy said, adding that the e-commerce giant has sought to build a “productive relationship” with every White House. “I’ve always been surprised that it isn’t obvious that the best economic results for a country are going to be when the public and the private sector collaborate,” he argued, telling Bloomberg he’s been “encouraged” by the Trump administration’s early posture toward industry.

— “When healthcare access declines, productivity suffers, absenteeism rises, and businesses bear the cost of lost workdays,” the officials continued. “That burden does not disappear — it shifts to emergency rooms, state budgets, and small businesses that rely on a stable workforce.”

— Hospital associations, grassroots organizations and other advocates are springing into action to block any potential cuts as part of congressional Republicans’ bid to offset new spending on tax, immigration and energy policy.

— The backlash has already prompted handwringing within the party and put GOP leaders on the defensive, denying their proposals will result in a direct hit to people’s Medicaid benefits — though it’s unclear how lawmakers will manage to scrounge up enough savings by just targeting waste and fraud.

title: Ballard plants a flag in Canada as tariff threat looms
body_text:
BALLARD LANDS IN THE GREAT WHITE NORTH: Ballard Partners announced yet another addition to its roster of global partnerships. The firm today said it’s teaming up with Quebec-based communications and public affairs firm TACT , offering Ballard a foothold in Canada just as trade tensions ratchet up with President Donald Trump ’s expected imposition of 25 percent tariffs on Canadian imports at midnight tonight.

— It’s the latest expansion of the Ballard Global Alliance, which launched last year and includes strategic partnerships with consultancies across the globe, including in Japan, South Korea, Latin America, the U.K. and Italy.

— “Understanding the evolving U.S. political landscape is essential for businesses operating in Canada,” TACT co-founder Daniel Matte said in a statement, adding that the partnership “will give our clients unparalleled access to Ballard Partners’ expertise.”

— Ballard is just the latest firm moving to establish ties across the border amid Trump’s tariff threats and broader needling of the top U.S. ally. Several weeks before Trump took office, Capitol Counsel announced its own cross-border partnership with the Canadian firm Rubicon Strategy Inc. , which the firms pledged would provide “a seamless solution to clients seeking to influence policy and manage cross-border trade issues.”

PELTOLA LANDS ON K STREET: Mary Peltola , the Alaska Democrat who unexpectedly flipped the state’s lone congressional seat in 2022 but lost reelection last year, has joined the law and lobbying firm Holland & Hart as senior director of Alaska affairs. Anton McParland , who was Peltola’s chief of staff, is also joining the firm as senior director of federal affairs.

— Peltola is the latest big get for Holland & Hart, which last year hired President Donald Trump ’s former EPA Administrator Andrew Wheeler to lead its lobbying practice and expand its presence in the nation’s capital. The firm also counts former Trump acting EPA Deputy Administrator Doug Benevento among its ranks.

— During Peltola’s only term in Congress, she routinely bucked her party on energy and natural resources issues and sought to carve out a centrist lane in the Democratic caucus. Nearly all of Holland & Hart’s federal lobbying clients work in the energy and mining space, disclosures show, including Rio Tinto Services , Global Mining Holding Company , Hudbay Minerals , Monarch Investments , Cenovus Energy and Diamondback Energy .

ISRAEL HIRES SKDK, TARGETED VICTORY: The Democratic powerhouse firm SKDK on Friday registered under FARA for the Israeli government for work on Israeli hostages in Gaza, Daniel reports.

— The filing said that SKDK was consulting with the Israeli foreign ministry on media relations and that a written contract and terms were still being finalized. The work focused on the tragedy of the Bibas family as the bodies of Shiri , Ariel and Kfir Bibas were coming home from Gaza, according to a person familiar with the matter.

— The work is being performed by a team from SKDK, Sloane & Company and a subsidiary of Targeted Victory , which registered as a foreign agent today. This is the first time that SKDK has worked for the government of Israel, but the firm has worked for numerous pro-Israel causes before, including helping American families with loved ones being held hostage.

ADDRESSING THE ADDRESS: As President Donald Trump puts the finishing touches on his big speech to a joint session of Congress tonight, trade associations are laying out some of the priorities they want him to cover. The Independent Petroleum Association of America will be searching for any breadcrumbs on the president’s tariff plans after he allowed steep levies on goods from Canada and Mexico go into effect overnight.

— The fossil fuel group’s President and CEO Jeff Eshelman had rave reviews for energy policy so far under Trump and the GOP-controlled Congress, but in a statement warned that steel and aluminum tariffs “could undermine the successes of the Administration’s goal of American Energy Dominance” by raising the cost of constructing new wells and pipelines.

— Meanwhile the U.S. Chamber of Commerce will be looking for Trump to reaffirm his commitment to pushing for his 2017 tax cuts to be made permanent as part of lawmakers’ ongoing reconciliation push. The Chamber is out with new polling today — from the president’s own pollster John McLaughlin , no less — aimed at shoring up the GOP’s resolve.

— Their survey found that when told about the 2017 tax law “reducing and simplifying the federal tax burden on families and businesses, stimulating economic growth, creating jobs, and enhancing the global competitiveness of American companies,” voters supported permanently extending them by a margin of 64 percent to 20 percent.

— Meanwhile, the polling found that nearly two-thirds of voters would be more likely to support a candidate who voted to permanently extend the tax cuts. ( Toplines can be found here .)

— In the meantime, the Chamber also brought members of its small business council to meet with lawmakers on the Hill today to share personal stories of how the tax cuts impacted their businesses and employees.

Happy Tuesday and welcome to PI . What did you think of Trump’s big speech? Where did it hit? Where did it miss? No reaction is too minor — we’ll keep you anonymous! Email me at: [email protected] And be sure to follow me on X : @caitlinoprysko .

A message from the Defense Credit Union Council:

DURBIN-MARSHALL CREDIT CARD MANDATES WILL HARM MILITARY FAMILIES The Defense Credit Union Council is sounding the alarm on the Durbin–Marshall credit card mandates. This proposal would increase fraud risk, restrict access to credit, eliminate rewards, and hand a massive windfall to corporate mega-retailers at the expense of consumers, small businesses, and community financial institutions. DCUC STANDS FIRMLY OPPOSED —OUR MILITARY AND THEIR FAMILIES DESERVE BETTER!

DASCHLE GROUP TEAMS UP WITH RFK JR. ALUM: The Daschle Group , the lobbying firm started by former Senate majority leader and one-time HHS nominee Tom Daschle , has struck up a partnership with former Robert F. Kennedy Jr. adviser Carlos Sierra to help the health care industry navigate Kennedy’s tenure atop the nation’s health care agencies.

— Sierra, the head of Renegade Public Affairs , previously worked for the late Sen. John McCain (R-Ariz.) and led former Louisiana Gov. Buddy Roemer ’s 2012 independent presidential campaign. This past cycle, he was a ballot access consultant and campaign director for the southwest U.S. for Kennedy’s independent presidential campaign.

— In an interview, Sierra said the idea behind the partnership is “to take on clients that we can basically help navigate the whole MAHA-MAGA” alliance, which formed during last year’s campaign when Kennedy and his base of vaccine, health and food industry skeptics — the “Make America Healthy Again” coalition — joined forces with Trump’s supporters.

— “Not many people know RFK Jr., not many people have been in his world, and so there are a lot of questions about him,” said Daschle Group President Nathan Daschle , who has known Sierra for about a decade and a half. “We have existing clients who want to learn more about what RFK Jr. is thinking,” and are scrambling to figure out which of Kennedy’s campaign trail crusades “will manifest into his term as secretary and what won’t.”

— “I realized that if we added what my firm brings to the table along with what he brings to the table, then it’s a pretty compelling offering in D.C.,” Daschle added. For his part, that’s the “decades of experience in health care policy” his firm offers. Sierra, meanwhile, “brings an incredible set of relationships and expertise and insight into RFK Jr.’s world, as well as a number of the people who are starting to get hired over there at HHS,” Daschle said.

— Sierra told PI he isn’t ruling out lending his help to clients that Kennedy has long railed against, like drugmakers. “Just understand, like, the way it was before … isn’t going to happen with Bobby there,” he said, when asked about some of the main things that needed to be conveyed to the health industry about what to expect from Kennedy’s HHS.

— “I’d rather be a coalition and bridge builder than kind of just go to war with everyone,” he added later. “You’re probably not going to get everything you want, but, you know, let’s try to build at least the relationship because … during the campaign, it was very adversarial.” Now, drug companies “have to accept that Kennedy is in there” and need “to find a way to work together,” Sierra said.

— Mental health issues is one area where both men identified an opportunity for the partnership to broker a compromise between Kennedy and the health industry — in particular on reforms like loosening restrictions for cannabis or psychedelics like psilocybin, on which the Daschle Group does a fair bit of work.

FLORIDA’S HOTTEST CLUB IS: “Guests are paying millions of dollars to dine and meet with President Donald Trump at special events held at his Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida,” per Wired ’s Leah Feiger , Louise Matsakis and Jake Lahut .

— “Business leaders can secure a one-on-one meeting with the president at Mar-a-Lago for $5,000,000, according to sources with direct knowledge of the meetings. At a so-called Candlelight Dinner held as recently as this past Saturday, prospective Mar-a-Lago guests were asked to spend $1,000,000 to reserve a seat, according to an invitation obtained by WIRED.”

— “‘You are invited to a candlelight dinner featuring special guest President Donald J. Trump,’ the invitation reads, under a ‘ MAGA INC. ’ header. MAGA Inc, or Make America Great Again Inc, is a super PAC that supported Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign.”

— “‘It’s everyone else who missed the boat,’ a Trumpworld source with knowledge of the meetings says, referring to latecomers to the Trump agenda. The source pointed specifically to the tech sector, where executives have scrambled to show fealty to the new administration. … The $5 million one-on-one meetings have become a ‘hot ticket’ in the business community, says a source familiar with them.”

— While “it’s unclear where the money is going and what it will be used for … one source with direct knowledge of the dinners said ‘it’s all going to’” Trump’s forthcoming presidential library.

— Trump hosted similarly billed dinners in the lead-up to his second inauguration and appeared at fundraisers during his first term, when he had announced he was running for reelection. While second-term presidents like Trump have “have held fundraisers for their parties, the nature, timing, location, and price tag of Trump’s dinner all raise flags for experts.”

INSURANCE LOBBYIST JUMPS TO SALT POINT: Veronica Jackson has left Humana , where she served as director of federal affairs, to join Salt Point Strategies as a senior vice president. Prior to joining Humana, Jackson led outreach to the Senate and the Biden administration on behalf of Blue Cross Blue Shield , and was director of strategic planning at HHS during the Obama administration.

— She’s the latest health care hire for Salt Point, which was founded by former Trump NTIA Administrator David Redl and earlier this year acquired the health lobbying firm alb solutions .

FLY-IN SZN: The Association of Dental Support Organizations will kick off its fly-in tomorrow. Members are slated to meet with more than two dozen House and Senate offices to discuss retaining oral care benefits for children on Medicaid and CHIP and emphasize the connection between oral health and overall health.

— A national coalition of cleantech startups and incubators, led by the Los Angeles Cleantech Incubator and the National Coalition of Clean Energy Incubators , are already in the midst of a three-day fly-in during which participants are pushing for policies and funding to bolster the development, commercialization and adoption of innovative energy technologies. They have meetings on the books with nearly 30 different offices, including member-level meetings with Sens. Ed Markey (D-Mass.) and Dick Durbin (D-Ill.).

— Also on the Hill this week is the Society of Thoracic Surgeons , which flew in 50 cardiothoracic surgeons to meet with more than 100 congressional offices today. The surgeons planned to discuss reversing the physician pay cuts under Medicare, funding for mobile lung cancer screening units and the restoration of funding for NIH indirect research costs.

— Dozens of executives from top chipmakers descended today as part of a fly-in organized by the Semiconductor Industry Association . The industry has about 75 meetings on the books with lawmakers or their staff to touch on a wide range of issues, including chip manufacturing incentives, tax policy, energy and environmental regulations, workforce development, export controls and competitiveness with China, to name a few.

DEPT. OF BLURRED LINES: “Earlier this year, the Air Force revealed that the general who oversaw its lobbying before Congress had inappropriate romantic relationships with five women, including three who worked on Capitol Hill,” ProPublica ’s Robert Faturechi reports.

— “The Air Force inspector general’s report redacted the names of the women who worked on the Hill. But one of the women whose relationship with [Maj. Gen. Christopher Finerty ] was scrutinized by the inspector general was Sen. Joni Ernst , according to two sources with knowledge of the investigation.”

— “The Iowa Republican and combat veteran is one of the most influential voices on the Hill about the military, and she sits on the Senate’s Armed Services Committee, which oversees the Pentagon and plays a crucial role in setting its annual budget.”

— “Three other sources told ProPublica that around 2019 Ernst had a previous romantic relationship with a legislative affairs official for a different branch of the military, the Navy. Ernst and the officials were not married at the time and Senate rules do not bar lawmakers from entering into romantic relationships with lobbyists or other legislative advocates. But ethics experts say such relationships can create a conflict of interest, and other lawmakers have been criticized for such behavior in the past.”

— “A spokesperson for Ernst would not address whether the senator had any relationships with military legislative liaisons but said the lawmaker maintained her independence: ‘The fake news media is clearly too busy gossiping to report the real news that Senator Ernst is focused on cutting waste at the Pentagon. Her votes and work in the Senate are guided by the voices of Iowans who elected her and her constitutional duty alone. Any insinuation otherwise by tabloid “journalism” is a slanderous lie — full stop.’ Finerty’s lawyer also declined to say whether the general had a romantic relationship with Ernst while he was advocating for the Air Force in Congress.”

title: K Street scours for silver lining amid Trump’s trade chaos
body_text:
CHAOS RULES THE DAY: Wednesday’s remarkable reversal by President Donald Trump in his trade war set off another yet another scramble on K Street to digest the 90-day pause on Trump’s so-called reciprocal tariffs and chart the best path forward for clients over the next three months.

— “Folks just have to accept there’s going to be more baseline uncertainty, more frequent changes, and a real need to be nimble and in front of everybody,” Mehlman Consulting ’s Bruce Mehlman told PI.

— “The sum total of the day is that the frenetic, chaotic, herky jerk policy on tariffs continues,” another Republican downtown conceded this week after Trump’s announcement. “We’ve had more — often, it looks like whimsical — activity in this world than I’ve ever seen on any subject at any level of government in my time in town.”

— “‘Roller coaster’ is not a strong enough analogy to describe where we currently are,” said one executive at a trade association, who like others was granted anonymity to speak candidly,

— While the pause — which the administration has said will allow it to negotiate new trade deals with dozens of countries — is welcome, “uncertainty, unfortunately, still hangs over the industry like a wet blanket,” the industry lobbyist added. “What’s the old saying? When life gives you lemons, make lemonade. I think in this case, we’d rather just keep the lemons, because I don’t see any cause for optimism.”

— “We are operating under the assumption that rather than this being a 90-day pause, it’s really a day-to-day pause, because we know that the administration could reverse course and come out tomorrow with a new announcement that contradicts the previous one,” they continued.

— That doesn’t mean K Street isn’t seizing on the opportunities it can, working to make sure clients are well-positioned to capitalize on Trump’s negotiations with other countries.

— “There’s a lot of trade irritants that have been in place for many, many years, and this 90-day pause provides a door to go in and negotiate those away,” said Everett Eissenstat , a White House trade adviser in Trump’s first term who’s now at Squire Patton Boggs . “If there’s a market access barrier, this is the time to go after it.”

— That provides an opening for the agriculture industry, for example, along with tech companies bristling about foreign digital service taxes. But Trump’s escalating trade war with China means that the stakes are still extraordinarily high.

— “I don’t think anything can quite make up for the loss of the Chinese market, but there definitely is interest in doing whatever possible to secure … greater market access” to countries negotiating deals with the Trump administration, said one trade lobbyist.

— Sean Kennedy , the executive vice president of public affairs at the National Restaurant Association , told PI that many restaurants depend on China for importing kitchen equipment and furniture that undergoes heavy use for 12 to 14 hours each day.

— And for the first time this week, Trump himself cracked open the door to doling out exemptions . But some industry groups are looking for a bit more formality for that process than the president’s stated criteria Wednesday of going off “instinct.”

— “If you’re talking about exempting entire sectors of the economy or exclusions — even if they’re temporary exclusions from the tariffs, there needs to be a process for that,” said Ed Brzytwa , the vice president of international trade at the Consumer Technology Association .

— The whiplash of the last few weeks has also dredged up new issues for K Street that will need to be addressed. For farmers facing market access barriers who are now getting locked out of China, for instance, “regaining that market share, once it’s lost, can be very hard,” said the trade lobbyist.

— The lobbyist also pointed to world leaders around the world who are rethinking their alliances with the U.S. as a result of the tariff drama. Losing the U.S. as a reliable trading partner “is the more lasting effect of the uncertainty,” they argued.

— With tariffs in place, “you can at least figure out how to live under those conditions and build your business,” the trade association executive said. “The uncertainty means that everything grinds to a halt. So from our perspective, yes, the uncertainty is far worse, and we plan to be very vocal about that.”

Happy Friday and welcome to PI . What’s going on out there? Add me on Signal , email me at [email protected] , and be sure to follow me on X : @caitlinoprysko .

HUNGRY FOR MORE: Such is the scale of upheaval and the pace of new developments, officials with trade associations representing a broad range of industries told PI this week that the level of engagement they’re seeing from members and the demand for information right now is at or above what they experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic.

— “We are spending almost as much time educating our members on what’s happening in Washington [as] we are educating Washington on what’s happening in restaurants,” Kennedy said.

— “There’s a hunger for information, and it’s not being satisfied,” said Brzytwa. “Maybe that’s intentional, we don’t know, but it’s the responsibility of the government to give stakeholders the information to help them comply, and we’re not getting that.”

— But that doesn’t mean the influence industry isn’t gobbling up every crumb of potential insight into the administration after the last 48 hours.

— For example, Trump’s decision to back down “gives restaurant owners more comfort that there will not be a global trade war with our partners,” according to Kennedy. The GOP lobbyist called it an encouraging sign that, “even in this administration, at some point, cooler heads, adults in the room can prevail.”

— And Eissenstat said at least affected industries have more time to digest the rules in case they do end up being reimposed in 90 days. “Having this time to understand the regime is actually, I think, going to be very helpful for a lot of companies,” he argued.

FIRST IN PI — DEI DIES AT MICHAEL BEST: Michael Best & Friedrich LLP, the law firm that former Trump White House chief of staff Reince Priebus helps lead, has quietly done away with its DEI committee, Daniel reports.

— As Trump attempts to root out DEI initiatives across American institutions, Michael Best recently scrubbed all references to DEI from its website and has instead created an “Access and Engagement Committee.”

— Priebus, who remains close to Trump, is president and chief strategist of the Michael Best law firm but spends most of his time with Michael Best Strategies LLC , a separate-but-connected government relations firm in Washington.

— The firm also deleted its old DEI webpage, which highlighted the firm’s work to develop “programs and policies to foster an inclusive environment, put our commitment to DEI into action, and make sure that each member of our team has the support and resources to achieve their Best,” according to an archived version of the site .

— The site had previously touted the firm’s support for different employee groups like “Women’s Initiative,” “Best Pride,” “Minority Network” and “Michael Best Parents & Caregivers.” It also showcased the firm’s “Diversity, Equity & Inclusion Scholarship” and a “Diversity Scholarship” for a patent engineering internship and scholarship program.

— Asked for comment on the change, David Krutz, firm managing partner of Michael Best, said the firm has made “internal updates responsive to evolving market and industry dynamics.”

— “However, we always have been and continue to be in full compliance with President Trump’s executive orders and are proud to be among one of the most successful full-service business law firms that have balanced all of the different views that are reflected in our changing world,” he said in a statement to PI. “Consistent with our 175+ year mission, we believe in fairness and merit-based hiring to ensure our clients receive effective counsel and service from our market-leading team.”

— But the website for the new Access and Engagement Committee still has some nods to diversity. It notes the firm’s membership with the Utah Center for Legal Inclusion, the Leadership Council on Legal Diversity, the Chicago Committee (a group focused on minority attorneys) and the Wisconsin LGBT Chamber of Commerce .

FARA FRIDAY: Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) is pressing the Justice Department to ditch its plans to let up on FARA prosecutions and other efforts to curtail illicit foreign influence campaigns, and to support legislation giving DOJ additional resources to uncover foreign influence campaigns.

— “I am deeply concerned that your recent decisions suggest a conscious effort to turn a blind eye to — if not welcome — foreign influence,” Blumenthal wrote in a letter to Attorney General Pam Bondi . And far from diverting DOJ resources away from “more pressing priorities” and carrying the taint of alleged weaponization, he argued, “our current efforts at combating foreign influence are insufficient.”

— The senator pointed to an analysis this week from Responsible Statecraft that found that disclosure filings of informational materials required by FARA declined following Bondi’s February directive to limit criminal FARA prosecutions, and to his own efforts to investigate a Saudi sovereign wealth fund’s commercial investments in the U.S.

— Blumenthal pointed to the Public Investment Fund ’s efforts to stymie that probe, in part by taking its own consultants to court to prevent them from complying with Blumenthal’s subpoenas. The senator asked Bondi to support his bill that would more explicitly subject sovereign wealth funds like PIF and provide DOJ with additional civil investigative authorities.

— “The PIF’s efforts prove an essential point — many foreign actors do not want the United States government to have a full understanding of their U.S. investments. It is important that we learn what they’re hiding and why,” he argued. “I urge you to not only support this legislation, but to also use the tools you already have and to reconsider your recent decisions in order to achieve our shared goal of keeping our country safe.”

FLY-IN SZN: Members of the GPS Innovation Alliance , including representatives from John Deere , Trimble , Garmin , Trustpoint , Apple and Lockheed Martin , were on the Hill this week for a fly-in focused on investing in building and launching new GPS satellites to modernize the country’s GPS constellations. Attendees had meetings on the books with more than a dozen congressional offices, the NTIA and the FCC.

SPOTTED on the GrayRobinson rooftop last night for a toast to recess in honor of the Congressional Tax and Trade Staff Association , hosted by the Associated Equipment Distributors , the National Stone, Sand and Gravel Association , the National Association of Truck Stop Operators , Manufactured Housing Institute and the National Asphalt Pavement Association , per a tipster: Connor Rabb of Rep. Brendan Boyle ’s (D-Pa.) office and Elle Collins of Rep. Jason Smith ’s (R-Mo.) — Kierra Newton has joined Nareit as director of REITPAC and political outreach. She previously was PAC and mid-Atlantic finance director at the DCCC .

— Krister Holladay is now vice president of government relations for SSA Marine . Holladay was most recently vice president of U.S. government relations for America President Lines and is a Kay Granger , Saxby Chambliss and Newt Gingrich alum.

CHAOS RULES THE DAY: Wednesday’s remarkable reversal by President Donald Trump in his trade war set off another yet another scramble on K Street to digest the 90-day pause on Trump’s so-called reciprocal tariffs and chart the best path forward for clients over the next three months.

— “Folks just have to accept there’s going to be more baseline uncertainty, more frequent changes, and a real need to be nimble and in front of everybody,” Mehlman Consulting’s Bruce Mehlman told PI.

— “The sum total of the day is that the frenetic, chaotic, herky jerk policy on tariffs continues,” another Republican downtown conceded this week after Trump’s announcement. “We’ve had more — often, it looks like whimsical — activity in this world than I’ve ever seen on any subject at any level of government in my time in town.”

— “‘Roller coaster’ is not a strong enough analogy to describe where we currently are,” said one executive at a trade association, who like others was granted anonymity to speak candidly,

— While the pause — which the administration has said will allow it to negotiate new trade deals with dozens of countries — is welcome, “uncertainty, unfortunately, still hangs over the industry like a wet blanket,” the industry lobbyist added. “What’s the old saying? When life gives you lemons, make lemonade. I think in this case, we’d rather just keep the lemons, because I don’t see any cause for optimism.”

— “We are operating under the assumption that rather than this being a 90-day pause, it’s really a day-to-day pause, because we know that the administration could reverse course and come out tomorrow with a new announcement that contradicts the previous one,” they continued.

— That doesn’t mean K Street isn’t seizing on the opportunities it can, working to make sure clients are well-positioned to capitalize on Trump’s negotiations with other countries.

— “There’s a lot of trade irritants that have been in place for many, many years, and this 90-day pause provides a door to go in and negotiate those away,” said Everett Eissenstat, a White House trade adviser in Trump’s first term who’s now at Squire Patton Boggs. “If there’s a market access barrier, this is the time to go after it.”

— That provides an opening for the agriculture industry, for example, along with tech companies bristling about foreign digital service taxes. But Trump’s escalating trade war with China means that the stakes are still extraordinarily high.

— “I don’t think anything can quite make up for the loss of the Chinese market, but there definitely is interest in doing whatever possible to secure … greater market access” to countries negotiating deals with the Trump administration, said one trade lobbyist.

— Sean Kennedy, the executive vice president of public affairs at the National Restaurant Association, told PI that many restaurants depend on China for importing kitchen equipment and furniture that undergoes heavy use for 12 to 14 hours each day.

— And for the first time this week, Trump himself cracked open the door to doling out exemptions. But some industry groups are looking for a bit more formality for that process than the president’s stated criteria Wednesday of going off “instinct.”

— “If you’re talking about exempting entire sectors of the economy or exclusions — even if they’re temporary exclusions from the tariffs, there needs to be a process for that,” said Ed Brzytwa, the vice president of international trade at the Consumer Technology Association.

— The whiplash of the last few weeks has also dredged up new issues for K Street that will need to be addressed. For farmers facing market access barriers who are now getting locked out of China, for instance, “regaining that market share, once it’s lost, can be very hard,” said the trade lobbyist.

— The lobbyist also pointed to world leaders around the world who are rethinking their alliances with the U.S. as a result of the tariff drama. Losing the U.S. as a reliable trading partner“is the more lasting effect of the uncertainty,” they argued.

— With tariffs in place, “you can at least figure out how to live under those conditions and build your business,” the trade association executive said. “The uncertainty means that everything grinds to a halt. So from our perspective, yes, the uncertainty is far worse, and we plan to be very vocal about that.”

Happy Friday and welcome to PI. What’s going on out there? Add me on Signal, email me at [email protected], and be sure to follow me on X: @caitlinoprysko.

HUNGRY FOR MORE: Such is the scale of upheaval and the pace of new developments, officials with trade associations representing a broad range of industries told PI this week that the level of engagement they’re seeing from members and the demand for information right now is at or above what they experienced during the Covid-19 pandemic.

— “We are spending almost as much time educating our members on what’s happening in Washington [as] we are educating Washington on what’s happening in restaurants,” Kennedy said.

— “There’s a hunger for information, and it’s not being satisfied,” said Brzytwa. “Maybe that’s intentional, we don’t know, but it’s the responsibility of the government to give stakeholders the information to help them comply, and we’re not getting that.”

— But that doesn’t mean the influence industry isn’t gobbling up every crumb of potential insight into the administration after the last 48 hours.

— For example, Trump’s decision to back down “gives restaurant owners more comfort that there will not be a global trade war with our partners,” according to Kennedy. The GOP lobbyist called it an encouraging sign that, “even in this administration, at some point, cooler heads, adults in the room can prevail.”

— And Eissenstat said at least affected industries have more time to digest the rules in case they do end up being reimposed in 90 days. “Having this time to understand the regime is actually, I think, going to be very helpful for a lot of companies,” he argued.

FIRST IN PI — DEI DIES AT MICHAEL BEST: Michael Best & Friedrich LLP, the law firm that former Trump White House chief of staff Reince Priebus helps lead, has quietly done away with its DEI committee, Daniel reports.

— As Trump attempts to root out DEI initiatives across American institutions, Michael Best recently scrubbed all references to DEI from its website and has instead created an “Access and Engagement Committee.”

— Priebus, who remains close to Trump, is president and chief strategist of the Michael Best law firm but spends most of his time with Michael Best Strategies LLC, a separate-but-connected government relations firm in Washington.

— The firm also deleted its old DEI webpage, which highlighted the firm’s work to develop “programs and policies to foster an inclusive environment, put our commitment to DEI into action, and make sure that each member of our team has the support and resources to achieve their Best,” according to an archived version of the site.

— The site had previously touted the firm’s support for different employee groups like “Women’s Initiative,” “Best Pride,” “Minority Network” and “Michael Best Parents & Caregivers.” It also showcased the firm’s “Diversity, Equity & Inclusion Scholarship” and a “Diversity Scholarship” for a patent engineering internship and scholarship program.

— Asked for comment on the change, David Krutz, firm managing partner of Michael Best, said the firm has made “internal updates responsive to evolving market and industry dynamics.”

— “However, we always have been and continue to be in full compliance with President Trump’s executive orders and are proud to be among one of the most successful full-service business law firms that have balanced all of the different views that are reflected in our changing world,” he said in a statement to PI. “Consistent with our 175+ year mission, we believe in fairness and merit-based hiring to ensure our clients receive effective counsel and service from our market-leading team.”

— But the website for the new Access and Engagement Committee still has some nods to diversity. It notes the firm’s membership with the Utah Center for Legal Inclusion, the Leadership Council on Legal Diversity, the Chicago Committee (a group focused on minority attorneys) and the Wisconsin LGBT Chamber of Commerce.

FARA FRIDAY: Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) is pressing the Justice Department to ditch its plans to let up on FARA prosecutions and other efforts to curtail illicit foreign influence campaigns, and to support legislation giving DOJ additional resources to uncover foreign influence campaigns.

— “I am deeply concerned that your recent decisions suggest a conscious effort to turn a blind eye to — if not welcome — foreign influence,” Blumenthal wrote in a letter to Attorney General Pam Bondi. And far from diverting DOJ resources away from “more pressing priorities” and carrying the taint of alleged weaponization, he argued, “our current efforts at combating foreign influence are insufficient.”

— The senator pointed to an analysis this week from Responsible Statecraft that found that disclosure filings of informational materials required by FARA declined following Bondi’s February directive to limit criminal FARA prosecutions, and to his own efforts to investigate a Saudi sovereign wealth fund’s commercial investments in the U.S.

— Blumenthal pointed to the Public Investment Fund’s efforts to stymie that probe, in part by taking its own consultants to court to prevent them from complying with Blumenthal’s subpoenas. The senator asked Bondi to support his bill that would more explicitly subject sovereign wealth funds like PIF and provide DOJ with additional civil investigative authorities.

— “The PIF’s efforts prove an essential point — many foreign actors do not want the United States government to have a full understanding of their U.S. investments. It is important that we learn what they’re hiding and why,” he argued. “I urge you to not only support this legislation, but to also use the tools you already have and to reconsider your recent decisions in order to achieve our shared goal of keeping our country safe.”

FLY-IN SZN: Members of the GPS Innovation Alliance, including representatives from John Deere, Trimble, Garmin, Trustpoint, Apple and Lockheed Martin, were on the Hill this week for a fly-in focused on investing in building and launching new GPS satellites to modernize the country’s GPS constellations. Attendees had meetings on the books with more than a dozen congressional offices, the NTIA and the FCC.

title: More institutions under fire add Trump-tied firms
body_text:
BIG LAW LOBBIES UP: Three of the Big Law firms that recently brokered deals with the White House to avoid retaliation for a litany of perceived slights to President Donald Trump or his allies did so after enlisting the help of lobbyists close to the president, according to disclosures filed over the weekend.

— Kirkland & Ellis and Simpson Thacher & Bartlett — two of the five firms Trump announced last week had agreed to provide at least $100 million in pro bono legal work for causes supported by Trump — retained Ballard Partners last month to provide “advice related to employment practices,” the disclosure filings show.

— Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom , meanwhile, retained Miller Strategies’ Jeff Miller , a top Trump fundraiser, and Stefan Passantino , who served as deputy White House counsel during Trump’s first term, according to a filing. Days after Miller began lobbying for Skadden in March, it became the first to preemptively strike a deal with Trump to dodge an executive order like a handful of its white-shoe peers.

— Davis Polk & Wardwell , which has scrubbed references on two of its attorneys’ bio pages to their work on special counsel Robert Mueller ’s Russia probe, also retained Miller Strategies at the end of March, according to a disclosure filing. The firm has yet to become a target of Trump’s executive orders, nor has any preemptive deal to avoid such a move been announced.

— Miller Strategies also signed another major institution the Trump administration has sought to bend to its will: Northwestern University , for which Trump moved last week to freeze $790 million in federal funds pending the outcome of civil rights investigations into alleged antisemitism and racial discrimination. Miller and James Min , a longtime top aide to former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy , began working for the university last month on issues related to oversight of higher education, according to a disclosure filing.

— Northwestern is one of nearly a dozen colleges that has disclosed new lobbying hires in April alone amid a crackdown from the Trump administration over their handling of protests on campuses, diversity practices and transgender issues, among other things.

Happy Monday and welcome to PI . What’s going on out there? Add me on Signal , email me at [email protected] , and be sure to follow me on X : @caitlinoprysko .

POLITICO Forecast

In a fragmented global landscape, understanding how policy and politics intersect across borders is critical. Forecast synthesizes POLITICO’s global reporting to connect key developments and global convenings, giving readers a clearer view of what’s ahead. Subscribe Now .

TRUMP’S LAW FIRM FIXER: In total, some of the nation’s top law firms have agreed to provide around $1 billion in free legal services to Trump-friendly causes in order to avoid the president’s ire. To broker those deals, Trump has turned to Boris Epshteyn , a personal lawyer who does not work in the government, The Wall Street Journal ’s Josh Dawsey and C. Ryan Barber report.

— “Epshteyn, who has been indicted in Arizona on charges related to Trump’s 2020 election loss, has emerged as the face of the Trump administration’s campaign against large law firms that it views as hostile to the president and his causes, according to lawyers at seven of the firms and White House officials.”

— “In a series of meetings and phone calls, Epshteyn has extracted large commitments of pro bono work for Trump-supported causes and changes to the law firms’ hiring practices to Trump’s preferences, the lawyers and officials said.”

— He “has never tried a criminal or civil case and carries a white business card that reads, ‘Boris Epshteyn, Esq.’ that lists his Gmail email account and a cellphone number. He calls a steakhouse in Washington where he hosts meetings every week his unofficial office. … Epshteyn earned Trump’s trust by overseeing his legal team after Trump left office and is regularly at the White House, administration officials said.”

— “Some of the law firms privately worried about negotiating with a lawyer who wasn’t employed by the government and didn’t have a government email address, some of the lawyers said. But they decided talking with Epshteyn was their best path to avoid a government investigation or executive order, the people said, after determining he had serious sway with Trump.”

CIGNA LOBBYIST MOVES TO GOODRX: Prescription-drug discount provider GoodRx has hired Gary Kline as senior vice president and head of the platform’s D.C. office. Kline has spent the past five years as a senior principal at Cigna Group , and worked for seven years before that as an in-house lobbyist for pharmacy benefit manager Express Scripts prior to its acquisition by Cigna.

INSIDE META’S ANTITRUST TRIAL: “ Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg became the first witness to testify Monday at the Federal Trade Commission’s landmark antitrust trial that seeks to break up his company,” POLITICO ’s Brendan Bordelon reports from the courtroom.

— The trial that kicked off today is the culmination of a six-year process that began during Trump’s first term, and could result in the FTC seeking to unwind the $1.4 trillion company’s acquisitions of Instagram and WhatsApp more than a decade ago — the biggest forced disentangling in generations.

— “Meta’s opening argument suggests the company will focus overwhelmingly on combating the FTC’s definition of the ‘personal social networking’ market,” with its lawyers today arguing that the “government’s definition of the market — a key step in establishing if there is a monopoly — excludes rivals like TikTok , YouTube and iMessage.”

— “While Meta’s social media products are free to use — making it impossible to prove that its alleged monopoly harmed consumers through higher prices, the typical route in antitrust cases — [lead attorney Daniel ] Matheson said the FTC will show that the Instagram and WhatsApp acquisitions still harmed consumers.”

WILL HE OR WON’T HE: “A string of mixed signals from the Trump administration over the weekend regarding tariffs on smartphones, laptops and other electronics fueled fresh uncertainty over U.S. trade policy , setting up another chaotic week on Wall Street and in Washington,” per WSJ’s Amrith Ramkumar and John McCormick .

— “Tech investors briefly rejoiced when a notice from U.S. Customs and Border Protection posted late Friday said computers, tablets, Apple watches, computer monitors, semiconductor equipment and other electronics were exempt from many tariffs on Chinese products and a 10% tariff on all U.S. imports.”

— Trump and other administration officials over the weekend pushed back on characterizing the exclusions as just that and said that some of those products will face their own tariffs in due course. POLITICO ’s Ari Hawkins reported that the administration plans to announce a national security probe that could lead to tariffs on semiconductors specifically, while Trump said in a social media post that the probe could be expanded to include the broader electronics supply chain.

— “Look, I’m a very flexible person. I don’t change my mind, but I’m flexible, and you have to be,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office today, adding that he had “helped” Apple CEO Tim Cook recently, without providing more details. “I don’t want to hurt anybody,” Trump said.

— At least one industry group found a silver lining amid the whiplash. “The Trump Administration’s decision to exclude certain consumer tech products from tariffs is long-overdue recognition that these duties hurt U.S. consumers and the economy — something CTA has warned for over a year,” Consumer Technology Association chief executive Gary Shapiro said in a statement.

— But “the tech exclusion is not a permanent solution,” Shapiro warned. He also highlighted the administration’s shift in its legal basis for future tech tariffs — from invoking Trump’s emergency powers to relying on a national security probe — a move he said reveals the White House’s “desire for a more durable justification. But claiming that downstream consumer tech products qualify as ‘semiconductors’ is a stretch.”

CHECKING THE ROI: “At the end of a three-hour hearing last month, Senator Ruben Gallego , Democrat of Arizona, sided with a group of Republicans in a hotly contested debate. He voted to advance the GENIUS Act, a bill backed by the cryptocurrency industry. … The vote, 18 to 6, was only preliminary, advancing a bill that will require approval from the full Senate. But in the crypto world, it was celebrated as a moment of vindication ,” The New York Times ’ David Yaffe-Bellany writes.

— “Gallego is part of an increasingly influential cohort in Congress: beneficiaries of the crypto industry’s largess. During a tight Senate race last year, he was aided by $10 million from super PACs financed by three large crypto companies, including the Coinbase digital currency exchange. The money funded ads that promoted Mr. Gallego’s military service and support for border enforcement.”

— “Now he and dozens of other lawmakers supported by the super PACs are taking steps in Congress to advance crypto priorities, handing a series of long-awaited victories to an industry with an extensive history of fraud and volatility.”

More institutions under fire add Trump-tied firms

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO 

04/14/2025 07:28 PM EDT

Presented by

With help from Daniel Lippman

BIG LAW LOBBIES UP: Three of the Big Law firms that recently brokered deals with the White House to avoid retaliation for a litany of perceived slights to President Donald Trump or his allies did so after enlisting the help of lobbyists close to the president, according to disclosures filed over the weekend.

— Kirkland & Ellis and Simpson Thacher & Bartlett — two of the five firms Trump announced last week had agreed to provide at least $100 million in pro bono legal work for causes supported by Trump — retained Ballard Partners last month to provide “advice related to employment practices,” the disclosure filings show.

— Skadden, Arps, Slate, Meagher & Flom, meanwhile, retained Miller Strategies’ Jeff Miller, a top Trump fundraiser, and Stefan Passantino, who served as deputy White House counsel during Trump’s first term, according to a filing. Days after Miller began lobbying for Skadden in March, it became the first to preemptively strike a deal with Trump to dodge an executive order like a handful of its white-shoe peers.

— Davis Polk & Wardwell, which has scrubbed references on two of its attorneys’ bio pages to their work on special counsel Robert Mueller’s Russia probe, also retained Miller Strategies at the end of March, according to a disclosure filing. The firm has yet to become a target of Trump’s executive orders, nor has any preemptive deal to avoid such a move been announced.

— Miller Strategies also signed another major institution the Trump administration has sought to bend to its will: Northwestern University, for which Trump moved last week to freeze $790 million in federal funds pending the outcome of civil rights investigations into alleged antisemitism and racial discrimination. Miller and James Min, a longtime top aide to former House Speaker Kevin McCarthy, began working for the university last month on issues related to oversight of higher education, according to a disclosure filing.

— Northwestern is one of nearly a dozen colleges that has disclosed new lobbying hires in April alone amid a crackdown from the Trump administration over their handling of protests on campuses, diversity practices and transgender issues, among other things.

TRUMP’S LAW FIRM FIXER: In total, some of the nation’s top law firms have agreed to provide around $1 billion in free legal services to Trump-friendly causes in order to avoid the president’s ire. To broker those deals, Trump has turned to Boris Epshteyn, a personal lawyer who does not work in the government, The Wall Street Journal’s Josh Dawsey and C. Ryan Barber report.

— “Epshteyn, who has been indicted in Arizona on charges related to Trump’s 2020 election loss, has emerged as the face of the Trump administration’s campaign against large law firms that it views as hostile to the president and his causes, according to lawyers at seven of the firms and White House officials.”

— “In a series of meetings and phone calls, Epshteyn has extracted large commitments of pro bono work for Trump-supported causes and changes to the law firms’ hiring practices to Trump’s preferences, the lawyers and officials said.”

— He “has never tried a criminal or civil case and carries a white business card that reads, ‘Boris Epshteyn, Esq.’ that lists his Gmail email account and a cellphone number. He calls a steakhouse in Washington where he hosts meetings every week his unofficial office. … Epshteyn earned Trump’s trust by overseeing his legal team after Trump left office and is regularly at the White House, administration officials said.”

— “Some of the law firms privately worried about negotiating with a lawyer who wasn’t employed by the government and didn’t have a government email address, some of the lawyers said. But they decided talking with Epshteyn was their best path to avoid a government investigation or executive order, the people said, after determining he had serious sway with Trump.”

CIGNA LOBBYIST MOVES TO GOODRX: Prescription-drug discount provider GoodRx has hired Gary Kline as senior vice president and head of the platform’s D.C. office. Kline has spent the past five years as a senior principal at Cigna Group, and worked for seven years before that as an in-house lobbyist for pharmacy benefit manager Express Scripts prior to its acquisition by Cigna.

INSIDE META’S ANTITRUST TRIAL: “Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg became the first witness to testify Monday at the Federal Trade Commission’s landmark antitrust trial that seeks to break up his company,” POLITICO’s Brendan Bordelon reports from the courtroom.

— The trial that kicked off today is the culmination of a six-year process that began during Trump’s first term, and could result in the FTC seeking to unwind the $1.4 trillion company’s acquisitions of Instagram and WhatsApp more than a decade ago — the biggest forced disentangling in generations.

— “Meta’s opening argument suggests the company will focus overwhelmingly on combating the FTC’s definition of the ‘personal social networking’ market,” with its lawyers today arguing that the “government’s definition of the market — a key step in establishing if there is a monopoly — excludes rivals like TikTok, YouTube and iMessage.”

— “While Meta’s social media products are free to use — making it impossible to prove that its alleged monopoly harmed consumers through higher prices, the typical route in antitrust cases — [lead attorney Daniel] Matheson said the FTC will show that the Instagram and WhatsApp acquisitions still harmed consumers.”

WILL HE OR WON’T HE: “A string of mixed signals from the Trump administration over the weekend regarding tariffs on smartphones, laptops and other electronics fueled fresh uncertainty over U.S. trade policy, setting up another chaotic week on Wall Street and in Washington,” per WSJ’s Amrith Ramkumar and John McCormick.

— “Tech investors briefly rejoiced when a notice from U.S. Customs and Border Protection posted late Friday said computers, tablets, Apple watches, computer monitors, semiconductor equipment and other electronics were exempt from many tariffs on Chinese products and a 10% tariff on all U.S. imports.”

— Trump and other administration officials over the weekend pushed back on characterizing the exclusions as just that and said that some of those products will face their own tariffs in due course. POLITICO’s Ari Hawkins reported that the administration plans to announce a national security probe that could lead to tariffs on semiconductors specifically, while Trump said in a social media post that the probe could be expanded to include the broader electronics supply chain.

— “Look, I’m a very flexible person. I don’t change my mind, but I’m flexible, and you have to be,” Trump told reporters in the Oval Office today, adding that he had “helped” Apple CEO Tim Cook recently, without providing more details. “I don’t want to hurt anybody,” Trump said.

— At least one industry group found a silver lining amid the whiplash. “The Trump Administration’s decision to exclude certain consumer tech products from tariffs is long-overdue recognition that these duties hurt U.S. consumers and the economy — something CTA has warned for over a year,” Consumer Technology Association chief executive Gary Shapiro said in a statement.

— But “the tech exclusion is not a permanent solution,” Shapiro warned. He also highlighted the administration’s shift in its legal basis for future tech tariffs — from invoking Trump’s emergency powers to relying on a national security probe — a move he said reveals the White House’s “desire for a more durable justification. But claiming that downstream consumer tech products qualify as ‘semiconductors’ is a stretch.”

CHECKING THE ROI: “At the end of a three-hour hearing last month, Senator Ruben Gallego, Democrat of Arizona, sided with a group of Republicans in a hotly contested debate. He voted to advance the GENIUS Act, a bill backed by the cryptocurrency industry. … The vote, 18 to 6, was only preliminary, advancing a bill that will require approval from the full Senate. But in the crypto world, it was celebrated as a moment of vindication,” The New York Times’ David Yaffe-Bellany writes.

— “Gallego is part of an increasingly influential cohort in Congress: beneficiaries of the crypto industry’s largess. During a tight Senate race last year, he was aided by $10 million from super PACs financed by three large crypto companies, including the Coinbase digital currency exchange. The money funded ads that promoted Mr. Gallego’s military service and support for border enforcement.”

— “Now he and dozens of other lawmakers supported by the super PACs are taking steps in Congress to advance crypto priorities, handing a series of long-awaited victories to an industry with an extensive history of fraud and volatility.”

title: How K Street is schooling universities on Trump
body_text:
GETTING SCHOOLED: President Donald Trump swept into power earlier this year and almost immediately began using his bully pulpit — and the federal government’s leverage, in the form of massive amounts of funding for contracts and grants — to embark on an unprecedented pressure campaign seeking to bend some of the country’s oldest and most revered universities to his will.

— Universities have historically operated at somewhat of a remove from the wheeling and dealing of Washington, but the scale and speed of the upheaval — and lack of transparency into the administration’s next targets — has caught the world of higher education off guard. K Street is cashing in on the panic as schools scramble for well-connected fixers who can offer guidance on how they might stave off some of the deepest cuts.

— In response to the demand from schools, Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck has launched a higher education task force to advise universities on how to navigate the whims of the Trump administration. The firm’s clients include Yale University , DePaul University , Davidson College , the Baylor College of Medicine , Colorado State University and Washington University in St. Louis , among others.

— Your host spoke to the three leaders of the task force — Republican strategist Marc Lampkin , education and tax policy expert Radha Mohan and Evan Corcoran , who served as Trump’s personal attorney — to hear how they’re helping bridge the divide between the cosseted world of higher education and the rough and tumble realm of politics, the biggest threats facing higher education right now and how universities can hope to navigate the competing pressures in Washington and on their campuses. You can read the full Q&A here , but we’ve picked out a few highlights.

— “All of these universities, they don’t intuitively get Washington,” said Lampkin. “And so what we do is we help them understand how to navigate it, with a unique understanding about the issues that they deal with on campus. … You’ve got the pressures from all of these parties around you, all the while you’re now being drawn into Washington and have to face things that, for some universities, could mean the difference between succeeding and failing.”

— “The Trump administration got started pretty quickly” on this issue, Mohan said of what universities are looking for out of their engagement with K Street. “And then on top of that, with the Republican majority in Congress, you also have the opportunity to legislate on this. … They’re looking for a firm with the political connections that can actually reach into the administration and have an in with Congress.”

— More than emerging differences in how universities and the new GOP-controlled Congress come down on various policy fights, “the process is very different, and it’s different in a way that makes knowing the key decision makers extremely important,” Corcoran said. “The personalities that are involved in these key decisions that affect institutions. You’ve got to know them, and you’ve got to understand how they think, how they make decisions, what’s important to them, what they’re trying to achieve.”

FERGUSON ON THE MOVE: As Trump crusades against the follies of globalized trade, one foreign automaker has defied the odds and managed to find itself in the president’s good graces.

— But Hyundai isn’t letting its foot off the gas as the company seeks to navigate Trump’s trade war, despite being hailed as a tariff success story by Trump. Korea’s largest automaker has hired former Rep. Drew Ferguson (R-Ga.), who served as a member of House GOP leadership, to lead the company’s D.C. office starting next month as it seeks to expand its manufacturing footprint in the U.S.

— Ferguson left office this year after eight years in Congress, including the past four years as GOP chief deputy whip, and had originally joined the lobbying firm Alston & Bird in January before being pulled away to join Hyundai, which he described in an interview with PI as “a once in a lifetime opportunity.”

— His new role with Hyundai represents a full-circle moment, Ferguson said, noting that he was serving as mayor of West Point, Georgia, when Hyundai-owned Kia opened its first assembly plant there in 2009. “To me, this is a bit of a legacy track … to go in and work with a company that we helped birth in Georgia, and so I’m really excited about it,” he said. Ferguson is still barred from lobbying his former colleagues on the Hill but said he’s prepared to lobby the Trump administration as needed.

— Hyundai’s leaders were at the White House last month , where Trump touted a pledge by the automaker to invest $21 billion in the U.S. over the next four years across a range of industries, including building a new steel plant in Louisiana.

— But Hyundai has also heavily invested in electric vehicles. Days after the White House photo op, Hyundai opened a new assembly plant in Georgia that was, initially, slated to produce only EVs — just as Trump and Ferguson’s former Republican colleagues have pledged to repeal a slew of EV manufacturing incentives from the Inflation Reduction Act that Hyundai had taken advantage of.

— Between Trump’s tariffs, which Ferguson said are “front and center” for Hyundai, and Republicans’ tax plans, “there are many challenges on the horizon, and I think my experience from my time in D.C., as a member of Congress and a member of the Ways and Means Committee, will serve me well in helping them to navigate this new environment,” he noted. Hyundai is also concerned about workforce development issues, and is angling for a piece of the market for new technologies like robotics, robotaxis and electric vertical takeoff-and-landing vehicles.

BET ON IT: “Gambling firms have fanned out across the U.S. , lobbying an array of state capitals against consumer protections that experts say could help reduce addiction-related harms,” according to The Guardian ’s Anna Betts .

— “A new report by the Campaign for Accountability , shared with the Guardian, lists a string of proposed regulations — from restrictions on advertising and promotions to deposit limits — against which firms pushed back.”

— “It follows a surge in online gambling since a 2018 ruling by the U.S. supreme court that set the stage for the vast expansion of legalized sports betting, now available in 39 states and Washington D.C. Americans placed around $150bn in wagers last year.”

— “The Campaign for Accountability, an advocacy organization, has documented the gambling industry’s lobbying efforts at the state level over recent years against a number of proposed regulations that problem gambling advocates say are aimed at protecting consumers from gambling-related harms. Some of the efforts have been successful.”

THE MAN BEHIND THE CURTAIN: Monday’s White House meeting between Trump and El Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele “isn’t just another international handshake — it’s the capstone of a multi-million-dollar foreign lobbying blitz aimed at building deep ties with Trumpworld and reshaping U.S. policy toward El Salvador. This meeting was years in the making—and it didn’t come cheap,” Anna Massoglia reports in Influence Brief .

How K Street is schooling universities on Trump

By CAITLIN OPRYSKO 

04/15/2025 06:11 PM EDT

Presented by

With help from Daniel Lippman

GETTING SCHOOLED: President Donald Trump swept into power earlier this year and almost immediately began using his bully pulpit — and the federal government’s leverage, in the form of massive amounts of funding for contracts and grants — to embark on an unprecedented pressure campaign seeking to bend some of the country’s oldest and most revered universities to his will.

— Universities have historically operated at somewhat of a remove from the wheeling and dealing of Washington, but the scale and speed of the upheaval — and lack of transparency into the administration’s next targets — has caught the world of higher education off guard. K Street is cashing in on the panic as schools scramble for well-connected fixers who can offer guidance on how they might stave off some of the deepest cuts.

— In response to the demand from schools, Brownstein Hyatt Farber Schreck has launched a higher education task force to advise universities on how to navigate the whims of the Trump administration. The firm’s clients include Yale University, DePaul University, Davidson College, the Baylor College of Medicine, Colorado State University and Washington University in St. Louis, among others.

— Your host spoke to the three leaders of the task force — Republican strategist Marc Lampkin, education and tax policy expert Radha Mohan and Evan Corcoran, who served as Trump’s personal attorney — to hear how they’re helping bridge the divide between the cosseted world of higher education and the rough and tumble realm of politics, the biggest threats facing higher education right now and how universities can hope to navigate the competing pressures in Washington and on their campuses. You can read the full Q&A here, but we’ve picked out a few highlights.

— “All of these universities, they don’t intuitively get Washington,” said Lampkin. “And so what we do is we help them understand how to navigate it, with a unique understanding about the issues that they deal with on campus. … You’ve got the pressures from all of these parties around you, all the while you’re now being drawn into Washington and have to face things that, for some universities, could mean the difference between succeeding and failing.”

— “The Trump administration got started pretty quickly” on this issue, Mohan said of what universities are looking for out of their engagement with K Street. “And then on top of that, with the Republican majority in Congress, you also have the opportunity to legislate on this. … They’re looking for a firm with the political connections that can actually reach into the administration and have an in with Congress.”

— More than emerging differences in how universities and the new GOP-controlled Congress come down on various policy fights, “the process is very different, and it’s different in a way that makes knowing the key decision makers extremely important,” Corcoran said. “The personalities that are involved in these key decisions that affect institutions. You’ve got to know them, and you’ve got to understand how they think, how they make decisions, what’s important to them, what they’re trying to achieve.”

Happy Tuesday and welcome to PI. What are you up to this recess? Add me on Signal, email me at [email protected], and be sure to follow me on X: @caitlinoprysko.

POLITICO Forecast

In a fragmented global landscape, understanding how policy and politics intersect across borders is critical. Forecast synthesizes POLITICO’s global reporting to connect key developments and global convenings, giving readers a clearer view of what’s ahead. Subscribe Now.

FERGUSON ON THE MOVE: As Trump crusades against the follies of globalized trade, one foreign automaker has defied the odds and managed to find itself in the president’s good graces.

— But Hyundai isn’t letting its foot off the gas as the company seeks to navigate Trump’s trade war, despite being hailed as a tariff success story by Trump. Korea’s largest automaker has hired former Rep. Drew Ferguson (R-Ga.), who served as a member of House GOP leadership, to lead the company’s D.C. office starting next month as it seeks to expand its manufacturing footprint in the U.S.

— Ferguson left office this year after eight years in Congress, including the past four years as GOP chief deputy whip, and had originally joined the lobbying firm Alston & Bird in January before being pulled away to join Hyundai, which he described in an interview with PI as “a once in a lifetime opportunity.”

— His new role with Hyundai represents a full-circle moment, Ferguson said, noting that he was serving as mayor of West Point, Georgia, when Hyundai-owned Kia opened its first assembly plant there in 2009. “To me, this is a bit of a legacy track … to go in and work with a company that we helped birth in Georgia, and so I’m really excited about it,” he said. Ferguson is still barred from lobbying his former colleagues on the Hill but said he’s prepared to lobby the Trump administration as needed.

— Hyundai’s leaders were at the White House last month, where Trump touted a pledge by the automaker to invest $21 billion in the U.S. over the next four years across a range of industries, including building a new steel plant in Louisiana.

— But Hyundai has also heavily invested in electric vehicles. Days after the White House photo op, Hyundai opened a new assembly plant in Georgia that was, initially, slated to produce only EVs — just as Trump and Ferguson’s former Republican colleagues have pledged to repeal a slew of EV manufacturing incentives from the Inflation Reduction Act that Hyundai had taken advantage of.

— Between Trump’s tariffs, which Ferguson said are “front and center” for Hyundai, and Republicans’ tax plans, “there are many challenges on the horizon, and I think my experience from my time in D.C., as a member of Congress and a member of the Ways and Means Committee, will serve me well in helping them to navigate this new environment,” he noted. Hyundai is also concerned about workforce development issues, and is angling for a piece of the market for new technologies like robotics, robotaxis and electric vertical takeoff-and-landing vehicles.

BET ON IT: “Gambling firms have fanned out across the U.S., lobbying an array of state capitals against consumer protections that experts say could help reduce addiction-related harms,” according to The Guardian’s Anna Betts.

— “A new report by the Campaign for Accountability, shared with the Guardian, lists a string of proposed regulations — from restrictions on advertising and promotions to deposit limits — against which firms pushed back.”

— “It follows a surge in online gambling since a 2018 ruling by the U.S. supreme court that set the stage for the vast expansion of legalized sports betting, now available in 39 states and Washington D.C. Americans placed around $150bn in wagers last year.”

— “The Campaign for Accountability, an advocacy organization, has documented the gambling industry’s lobbying efforts at the state level over recent years against a number of proposed regulations that problem gambling advocates say are aimed at protecting consumers from gambling-related harms. Some of the efforts have been successful.”

THE MAN BEHIND THE CURTAIN: Monday’s White House meeting between Trump and El Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele “isn’t just another international handshake — it’s the capstone of a multi-million-dollar foreign lobbying blitz aimed at building deep ties with Trumpworld and reshaping U.S. policy toward El Salvador. This meeting was years in the making—and it didn’t come cheap,” Anna Massoglia reports in Influence Brief.

— “So how did the self-described ‘world’s coolest dictator’ win over so many in the MAGA movement and Trump’s inner circle? … Damian Mathías Merlo Denebardi, a Bukele advisor who was a key architect of El Salvador’s strategy to attract the Make America Great Again movement in the United States, registered with the U.S. Justice Department as foreign agent of El Salvador’s government in January 2022.”

— “Since the start of 2022, the Office of the President of El Salvador paid Merlo’s firm about $1.5 million for lobbying and influence operations targeting the U.S., an analysis of Foreign Agents Registration Act filings shows.”

title: The Chamber, gemstone dealers and Quince add trade lobbying help
body_text:
NEW BUSINESS: The U.S. Chamber of Commerce has hired a new outside firm. The business group this month retained HB Strategies to lobby on tax, trade and manufacturing issues, according to a disclosure filing. Stacy McBride and Richard Eddings — both former top aides to ex-Sen. Roy Blunt (R-Mo.) — and former House clerk Joe Novotny are working on the account.

— HB Strategies is just the second outside firm on retainer for the Chamber, with Fulcrum Public Affairs as the other. The Chamber, of course, spends tens of millions of dollars each year on its own lobbying efforts, and its various offshoots and affiliate groups also employ their own outside firms.

— Meanwhile, the American Gem Trade Association , which represents gemstone importers and dealers, has brought on lobbying help as it pushes for loose-colored gemstones and finished jewelry to be exempted from President Donald Trump ’s so-called reciprocal tariffs. The trade group hired Tim Hecht and Franklin Phifer Jr. of Hecht Latham Spencer & Associates earlier this month.
